events.title: Americans' trust in the food safety net is spoiling
events.summary: Data: Gallup; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Americans' confidence in the safety of food on grocery store shelves — and in the federal government's ability to regulate it — has plummeted to new lows according to a new Gallup poll. The big picture: Simultaneous illness outbreaks put federal regulators under a microscope earlier this year, as layoffs across the nation's health apparatus were already causing food safety angst. By the numbers: Less than half of U.S. adults have a great deal (11%) or a fair amount (36%) of confidence in the federal government to ensure food safety, according to the poll, which was conducted last month. On the flip side, a majority have not much or no confidence in the government's ability to police their food — a first in Gallup's trend, which has been intermittent for two decades. Zoom out: Meanwhile, Americans' confidence in the food sold at grocery stores has mirrored that drop, falling to a record low of 65% saying they are somewhat or very confident. That share has plunged from the 81% recorded in 2019. Zoom in: That growing food safety suspicion is driven by Democrats and independents, while Republicans have actually become more confident in grocery store food. The partisan chasm over the federal government's ability to ensure food safety has flipped — and widened — under the second Trump administration. In 2024, half of Republicans had a great deal or fair amount of confidence in the government to ensure food safety, while nearly three-quarters of Democrats agreed. By 2025, Democrats' confidence fell to 48%, and to 30% in 2026. Republicans, meanwhile, found new faith, with their confidence climbing from 62% in 2025 to 70% to 2026. Catch up quick: This year's polling occurred during and after the federal government declared the end of an outbreak of Cyclospora, a parasite that caused stomach illnesses, two deaths and saw more than 500 hospitalizations across 21 states. Federal health officials eventually traced the rapidly spreading surge to iceberg lettuce from supplier Taylor Farms . But the food woes didn't stop there: This summer saw a flurry of overlapping recalls and FDA investigations, while health experts warned administration cuts had weakened the public health infrastructure responsible for detecting outbreaks. Meanwhile, significant shares of Americans report concerns or strain about affording those groceries. The food-at-home CPI, for grocery store or supermarket food purchases, was up 2.2% between August 2025 and 2026. Friction point: That collides with an administration that's pushed whole foods as part of its "Make America Healthy Again" campaign under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. But Gallup's polling indicates Republicans have digested that food safety message far better than Democrats and independents. Go deeper: America's next grocery shock is brewing

events.title: Embedding the human factor into AI agent adoption
events.summary: When implementing any kind of technology, the difference between offering employees training and supporting them in adoption is all too frequently misunderstood. But the difference is a significant one. Training is usually a time-limited, structured educational initiative to help people build technical competence and learn how a system works. Adoption, on the other hand, is a continuous, long-term process by which employees use technology to change how they work in order to deliver more value. Nowhere is this distinction more vital than in the emerging world of agentic AI. To date, many organizations have been experimenting with the technology to automate discrete tasks, particularly in areas such as software engineering, customer support, and operations. Over the next two years though, Gartner expects deployment to jump from the current 17 percent of businesses to more like 60 percent. Their key aims in going down this route include automating complex multistep workflows, boosting operational efficiency, and maximizing productivity. But despite the perceived value of agentic AI here, many organizations are currently struggling to create such value in real terms. This includes generating a return on investment. Identifying the value gap In fact, according to WalkMe's 'The State of Digital Adoption 2026' report, a huge 40 percent of all expenditure on digital transformation underperforms expectations, mainly due to user adoption challenges. As the study, which is based on input from 3,750 respondents worldwide, says: "The technology does what it's supposed to do. The adoption execution around it doesn't." As such, it found the average employee loses a full working day each week (7.9 hours) to "friction". For example, they spend 1.34 hours per week re-entering the same information across multiple applications. Another hour disappears on finding workarounds when tools are unable to communicate effectively. A further 3.69 hours vanish due to a lack of guidance on how to use such tools. This includes 1.03 hours being spent trying to understand unclear instructions. A final 1.88 hours each week are spent on reworking AI prompts and waiting for faulty tools to be fixed. Ofir Hatsor is WalkMe's Senior Vice President of Sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa. He believes that a good chunk of this friction is due to the complex and highly regulated environment in which enterprises function. This means many of them struggle to change how they operate day-to-day - even though it is only in doing so that they can create true value for the business. "There's currently a very big gap between perceived value and existing value, or the actual value that will follow," he points out. "I think over time this gap will be mitigated, but it's not going to be tomorrow - more like the next three, five, or seven years, and in some companies, it'll never close." The difficulties in affecting change As to why affecting meaningful operational change is often so difficult to achieve, especially when moving to an agentic AI environment, Hatsor points to several reasons. The first is a "visibility gap". As WalkMe's study indicates, most executives believe their organizations use an average of 35 applications when the actual number is 661 - a visibility gap of 1,789 percent. For AI-powered tools in particular, leaders estimate teams use 21 when the real count is 80. The point here, as the report says, is that: "You can't optimize workflows you can't see, govern AI tools you don't know exist, or measure productivity when your instrumentation covers a fraction of where work actually happens." A key part of the problem is shadow AI. For instance, 45 percent of workers admitted to using unapproved AI tools in the previous 30 days as authorized systems failed to fit current workflows. Unfortunately, 36 percent of them also used confidential company data in the process. A big challenge, Hatsor explains, is the ease with which employees can get hold of AI development tools today. "So, they create their own little vibe-coding applications and share them between themselves," he says. "But if I'm the chief information officer or chief security officer, my visibility into that landscape is limited at best." This is made even harder when employees aren’t honest with their employers or themselves about AI use. WalkMe’s most recent AI Pulse Survey showed 32.5 percent of workers have passed AI work off as their own, and 28.3 percent have pretended to know AI in a meeting. An improvement over 2025, but still some way to go. Unsurprisingly, this lack of official approval or control is creating big risks for companies, not least in terms of data privacy and governance. The upshot is that many organizations are slowing their rate of agentic AI adoption until they are in a position to see, mitigate and reduce such risks. Traversing murky waters A second challenge many organizations face, meanwhile, is the actual cost of implementing agentic AI versus its real-world benefits. A key issue here is the underlying assumptions that many proposed financial gains are based on. These include boosting productivity and cutting headcount when the real benefits may actually be found in enhancing work quality and augmenting human activity. A third consideration is AI tokens. The problem here is that many organizations do not know either the number of tokens they are consuming or what they cost, which "can become very expensive". "So, there are many murky waters, which make it very difficult to get a real hard return on investment at this point because of all the moving parts and uncertainties," Hatsor says. The situation is made even more tricky by the sheer amount and speed of change that AI is generating. This is especially true among employees who usually have less access to new tools than their leaders and tend to be slower technology adopters anyway. Many are also fearful about a future that feels uncertain. Unsurprisingly then, according to the WalkMe report, there is a huge chasm between leaders who believe employees have been given access to adequate tooling (88 percent) compared with employees who take the same view (21 percent). This situation is inevitably hitting adoption. As Hatsor points out: "We're not giving our workforce the tools, or the confidence to use the tools, but there's also a lack of understanding of the difference between training and adoption. We can train someone to use a tool, but unless we help them adopt it and make it their own, they won't use it effectively." The power of Digital Adoption Platforms This is where systems, such as WalkMe's Digital Adoption Platform (DAP), come in. DAP offers in-app guidance - in a similar fashion to GPS systems - to navigate employees through a specific workflow. It offers information in a range of formats based on individual preferences, such as walk-through demonstrations, long-form text, or video. events.title: Russia's internet giant Yandex halts operations at major data center after drone attack
events.summary: Russia's Yandex paused operations at one of its key data centers after a drone strike. The attack caused a fire to break out but the company said its core services were unaffected. Ukraine has ramped up attacks on Russia's infrastructure in the latest phase of the war. Russian internet giant Yandex suspended operations at one of its key data centers on Thursday after a drone strike as Ukraine continues to target the country's infrastructure. The attack caused a fire at the company's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan, in western Russia, and affected part of its infrastructure, Yandex said in a statement to CNBC. The data center has stopped operating entirely, and some Yandex services may be unavailable to users, it added. "There are no casualties, and emergency services are on site dealing with the aftermath," Yandex said. Moscow-headquartered Yandex, known as the Google of Russia, provides the country's most widely used search engine. It also developed the region's leading generative AI model, YandexGPT. events.title: Singapore’s EDBI, Roblox CEO back Universal Quantum start-up in US$100 million Series A round
events.summary: Universal Quantum is among a wave of start-ups and corporate labs striving to create new machines capable of solving problems classical computers cannot, potentially leading to breakthroughs in fields like medicine and finance. Universal Quantum raised US$100 million in a Series A round led by DCVC and Firgun Ventures, with Singapore’s EDBI and Roblox CEO David Baszucki among the investors. The British start-up will use the money to expand research hubs in Germany and Singapore, as it works towards a useful quantum computer within the next decade. Quantum computing is drawing major state and private backing, but the technology is still mainly for research and remains hard to build, with no clear timeline. A British start-up seeking to build a working quantum computer has raised US$100 million (S$128.1 million) from a range of investors, including a Singapore government fund and Roblox chief executive officer David Baszucki. Universal Quantum will use the Series A financing to expand research hubs in Germany and Singapore, it said in a statement on Oct 8 . Investment firm DCVC and Firgun Ventures co-led the round, with participation from Singapore’s Economic Development Board Investments (EDBI), Baszucki and others. The investor base is “meant to be as global and sovereign as possible, aligning where we’d like to be more active”, Universal Quantum CEO Sebastian Weidt said. He declined to share the company’s valuation. Several quantum firms have gone public recently as the technology moves closer to useful applications. Major banks have hired experts in the technology, and governments are investing in the sector that has the potential to break existing encryption standards that protect data online. Still, quantum machines currently are mainly used for research. In May, the US agreed to invest US$2 billion into companies developing quantum computers and chips. Earlier in 2026 , the UK government pledged to spend £1 billion (S$1.7 billion) on the tech over the next four years. Universal Quantum has won contracts to develop computers for the German government. Weidt, who co-founded the start-up from research at England’s University of Sussex, said the company did not get UK public support in the latest funding round. He said Universal Quantum’s current commercial strategy operates like a consultant, where his engineers help public agencies and businesses prepare to run software on the start-up’s computers once they are functional. He declined to share revenue figures. Universal Quantum is backing a trapped-ion system, which uses suspended charged atoms and lasers to perform quantum calculations. Some of its competitors, including Google and Microsoft, are building larger machines that use processors made from superconducting materials. Weidt said his approach offers the best way to create a dependable working computer with minimal errors. He expects to build a useful working quantum computer within the next decade, although he declined to give a precise date. “It’s hard to build these machines,” he said. “No one can map this out.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: Southampton manager Eckert can stay on despite role in ‘spygate’ scandal
events.summary: Tonda Eckert let off with fine and reprimand but avoids ban and will continue in his role with the club. Southampton boss Tonda Eckert has escaped major punishment for his role in the so-called “spygate” scandal after the English Football Association (FA) announced a suspended ban . Eckert was fined 28,000 British pounds ($37,000) and given a reprimand but avoided a lengthy ban in the announcement on Wednesday, and he is free to continue in his role at the English Championship club. The Saints were kicked out of last season’s Championship playoff final and were docked four points in the current campaign after admitting to three breaches of English Football League (EFL) regulations following being caught snooping on semifinal opponents Middlesbrough and two other teams. An EFL independent disciplinary commission ruled in May that Eckert had “specifically authorised” the spying, throwing his future at the English second-tier club into doubt. The 33-year-old accepted full responsibility and was charged by the FA with misconduct. The German coach attended an FA hearing at the start of the current international break. The outcome means he can continue in his role against rivals Portsmouth on Sunday. “Tonda Eckert subsequently admitted the charges, and an independent regulatory commission imposed a six-week suspension from all football and football-related activity, which is suspended until the end of the 2027-28 season, a £28,000 fine and a reprimand following a hearing,” the FA said in a statement on Wednesday. “The suspended sanction will come into effect in the event he is found to have committed a breach of rules or regulations by requesting, authorising, taking, or using information from any observation of the training of another club, in whatever guise that observation may take.” Southampton said in a statement that this brings a “regrettable period of our history to a conclusion”. The club, which sits 13th in the Championship, said that “measures have been put in place to ensure that such errors in judgement never happen again at our club”. Southampton owner Dragan Solak said, “I’m pleased that the independent panel has come to a decision and that we have an outcome. “We have already suffered enough, and we appreciate the panel’s recognition of that. “We are confident the manager has learned from this matter, and a suspended sentence allows him to continue in his role.” Eckert was appointed permanent Southampton boss in December 2025, leading the club to fourth spot in the Championship table after a poor start to the season.

events.title: A partial building collapse in Istanbul traps at least 7 people, including a child
events.summary: A seven-story building in Istanbul has partially collapsed, trapping at least seven people, including a 6-year-old ISTANBUL -- A seven-story building in Istanbul partially collapsed on Thursday, trapping at least seven people inside, including a 6-year-old, officials said. The reason for the collapse was not immediately known and an investigation was underway. Rescue teams were working to reach those trapped even as there were warnings of a further collapse of the building. The building’s three lower floors, including a ground-floor shop, caved in before dawn in the district of Maltepe, on the Asian side of Istanbul, a city that is bisected by the Bosporus Strait. Residents from the upper floors were safely evacuated while rescue teams pulled five more people from the rubble and were continuing with efforts to reach the seven others, said Davut Gul, the governor of Istanbul. events.title: Wizz Air cancels winter season flights to Abu Dhabi and Dubai
events.summary: Wizz Air has postponed the planned restart of its Abu Dhabi and Dubai routes, cancelling all flights to and from both destinations for the winter season. The airline had planned to operate UAE flights from October 25 to March 27. The low-cost airline said last month that it was resuming flights to Abu Dhabi and Dubai, alongside routes to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia and Amman in Jordan. The airline had said this week it would delay the launch of some routes to Abu Dhabi until January, following security updates from Europe's aviation regulator. "Regional airspace restrictions extended on September 30 require significantly longer routings to these destinations, increasing flight times and costs and making both A321neo and A321XLR operations commercially unviable under current conditions," the airline said in a statement to The National . It also confirmed that flights to and from Amman are affected by the EU Aviation Safety Agency's latest conflict zone information bulletin, which recommends that airlines do not operate within Jordanian airspace. "We regret the disruption to travel plans and will continue to monitor developments, reassessing operations as safety guidance and operating conditions evolve," Wizz Air said. International airlines have been forced to adjust schedules for Middle East flights in the aftermath of the US-Iran war as airspace restrictions persist. Wizz Air suspended its European-operated services to the Middle East in late February due to the regional conflict. The UAE services were part of a wider restoration of 12 routes and 49 weekly flights to the Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Jordan over the winter, providing 470,000 seats across services to nine European cities. The airline was set to resume operations after its low-cost subsidiary, Wizz Air Abu Dhabi, ceased operations in September 2025.

events.title: The Indian billionaire investing in Trump's refinery project is also buying more Venezuelan crude
events.summary: Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries has emerged as the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude outside the U.S. In September, India imported 257,000 barrels per day of Venezuelan crude, of which 76% went to Reliance Industries, Kpler data showed. In March, Trump had announced that the U.S. would build its first refinery in 50 years with investment from India's Reliance Industries Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries , which is investing in a historic U.S. oil refinery project proposed by President Donald Trump, has now emerged as the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude outside the U.S. Trump has been pushing India to buy more Venezuelan oil , but while state-owned oil companies are making opportunistic purchases, Reliance has been the primary buyer, according to Kpler data shared with CNBC. It shows that outside the U.S., India is the biggest destination for these supplies, with Reliance purchasing the bulk of that crude. "Reliance's Jamnagar complex has been the main destination for Venezuelan crude in India, and we expect it to remain the primary buyer," Sumit Ritolia, lead research analyst at Kpler, told CNBC. In September, India imported 257,000 barrels per day of Venezuelan crude, of which 76% went to Reliance Industries, data showed. The Jamnagar refinery is the world's " largest and most complex single-site refinery" with crude processing capacity of 1.4 million barrels per day, according to Reliance. Venezuelan heavy and extra-heavy grades of crude are relatively difficult barrels to process and are not universally suitable across India's refining system, Ritola said, adding that the Jamnagar complex is particularly well configured for these barrels. In March, Trump had announced that the U.S. will build its first refinery in 50 years with investment from India's Reliance Industries. The president had thanked Reliance for this "tremendous investment." While Reliance has not confirmed the size of investment, Trump in a Truth Social post had said that "THIS IS A HISTORIC $300 BILLION DOLLAR DEAL — THE BIGGEST IN U.S. HISTORY." Reliance is the most valued company in India, with a market capitalization of more than $169 billion. Reliance's Venezuelan purchases come at a time when India's procurement of Russian oil has drawn the ire of the U.S., where lawmakers have given Trump the power to impose up to 100% tariffs on countries buying energy from Moscow. Despite mounting pressure to buy more energy from the U.S. and cut its dependence on Russian oil, the Indian government has insisted that its decisions are driven by the need to ensure energy security for its people. While oil supplies in September from Russia to India have "moderated" from exceptionally high levels in June and July, that is largely driven by the stronger competition between Beijing and New Delhi and not the threat of tariffs, Ritolia said. India is the largest destination for Russian crude, securing a supply of 1.82 million barrels per day in September versus China's 1.49 mbd, according to Kpler data, much more than Venezuelan purchases. For October, 350,000 barrels per day of crude supplies from Venezuela are bound for India, though some of these could land in November because of the long voyage time, Ritolia said.

events.title: True Fitness, True Yoga’s liquidators received claims from over 3,000 creditors
events.summary: The move comes after special resolutions were passed at extraordinary general meetings for both companies on Oct 7. True Yoga and True Fitness liquidators have received claims from around 3,300 creditors after the firms entered creditors’ voluntary liquidation. Creditors can continue to submit or revise their claims through the appointed liquidator RSM Singapore claims portal. The True Singapore group shut all seven outlets here overnight on Sept 10, with many staff and members arriving at gym premises the next day only to find doors locked. SINGAPORE - The liquidators for True Yoga and True Fitness have received claims from around 3,300 creditors, following the decision to place the fitness chains into creditors’ voluntary liquidation. The move comes after special resolutions were passed at extraordinary general meetings for both companies on Oct 7, according to a media statement by appointed liquidators RSM Singapore on Oct 8. During meetings held on Oct 7, creditors confirmed the appointment of the liquidators and voted to establish a Committee of Inspection (COI) comprising up to five members to represent stakeholder interests. The liquidators will now focus on the “orderly administration of the companies’ affairs” and the recovery of assets. They will also consult with the COI and other key stakeholders throughout the winding-up process. Creditors, including affected members, vendors and employees, can continue to submit or revise their claims through the RSM creditors’ claims portal . They can also contact the liquidators’ office via the emails below: True Fitness Members: RF-TFitnessMembers@rsmsingapore.sg True Yoga Members: RF-TYogaMembers@rsmsingapore.sg True Fitness Vendors & Other Creditors: RF-TFitness@rsmsingapore.sg True Yoga Employees, Vendors & Other Creditors: RF-TYoga@rsmsingapore True Yoga and True Fitness come under the True Singapore Group, which also operated fitness and yoga centres TFX and Yoga Edition here. The group abruptly shuttered all its seven outlets overnight on Sept 10, notifying employees via an email sent just an hour before the shutdown took effect. Many staff and members arrived at gym premises the following morning only to find doors locked and repossession notices posted across entrances. On Sept 11, Consumers Association of Singapore said it received hundreds of complaints from members, with losses exceeding $609,000 in unused memberships, packages and services. The True Singapore Group has been under mounting financial strain, recording substantial losses and net liabilities, even as it continued to generate notable revenue, said its Hong Kong-listed parent company Kontafarma China Holdings. As at end-August, it owed Kontafarma HK$309.7 million (S$50.6 million). Alyssa Woo is a business correspondent at The Straits Times. events.title: Cristiano Ronaldo pays tribute to Lionel Messi after Argentina farewell
events.summary: ‘I have the utmost respect for what you’ve accomplished with Argentina,’ Ronaldo writes in response to Messi’s post. Cristiano Ronaldo has hailed his longtime adversary Lionel Messi in a tribute to the Argentinian icon, who bid a grand farewell to international football. The Portuguese forward wrote the message in response to Messi’s social media post on Wednesday, a day after Argentina’s friendly match against Benin in Buenos Aires, where the local idol and global icon bid an emotional goodbye. list 1 of 4 ‘He is our idol:’ Why Lionel Messi means so much to fans in India list 2 of 4 Harmanpreet Kaur: The captain who changed how India’s women played cricket list 3 of 4 The return of Palestinian football: ‘We are a people who must live’ list 4 of 4 Migrants ‘are not to blame’: How the Ceuta crisis engulfed Spanish football “Leo, ‌‌after so many years of defending your country, you’ve made history that will last forever,” Ronaldo said in his reply to Messi’s Instagram post in which the Argentinian poured out his emotions after hanging up his boots for his country. “I have the utmost respect for what you’ve accomplished with Argentina,” Ronaldo added, ending the message with: “A hug”. The careers of Messi and Ronaldo followed a similar trajectory and crossed paths for many years in club and international football. It resulted in a hotly contested rivalry, mostly between the two players’ supporters over the past two decades. The pair dominated the sport for more than 15 years, winning the prestigious Ballon d’Or award 13 times between them. Their rivalry grew over the nine years in which they faced off against each other in Spain, with Messi starring for Barcelona and Ronaldo for Real Madrid. Messi, 39, announced his retirement from international football after leading his country to the World Cup final in July in the United States, where the 2022 champions were runners-up behind Spain. “Yesterday was my last game, and I already miss wearing the blue and white. I know I’m making the right decision,” Messi said in a lengthy message a day after his final match in the famous number 10 blue and white shirt. “It’s been an incredible journey, full of ‌‌joy and also some sadness, but I know for sure that every step I took was worth it.” “I don’t want to forget Diego [Maradona], who put our country where it deserved to be and who, as I always say, I know helped us both by being here with us and also from heaven, with every step we took,” he said. “Thank you to the clubs where I played, for always ⁠⁠respecting my feelings and allowing me to dedicate myself to ⁠⁠my country whenever it was time to put on the national team jersey.” Messi scored Argentina’s final goal in a 3-0 win and provided assists for the other two as the Albiceleste played in front of 85,000 fans at the Monumental Stadium. Messi captained Argentina to the 2022 World Cup title and Copa America triumphs in 2021 and 2024, while also helping them win ⁠⁠the 2022 Finalissima. “I am grateful. I love you all very much; I’m going to miss you, and I will always thank ⁠⁠you for having been by our side, by my ⁠⁠side,” the Inter Miami playmaker added. Messi and Ronaldo have vied for recognition as the greatest player of their generation throughout their illustrious careers. The 41-year-old Portuguese forward was among the hundreds of thousands who responded to Messi’s post. Messi’s final game came the same day Ronaldo apologised for his controversial departure from the Portuguese national team’s camp after a fallout with coach Jorge Jesus. It remains unclear whether Ronaldo will play for his country again, despite his apology for walking out, which leaves the door open to a return. Messi and Ronaldo last met on the pitch in an exhibition match in Saudi Arabia in January 2023 , when they took fans back in time to the heyday of their storied rivalry, as both forwards got on the scoresheet. Ronaldo, who plays for Saudi Pro League champions Al Nassr, was part of a Riyadh Season Team that took on Messi’s then-club Paris Saint-Germain (PSG).

events.title: Mine backed by US, Australia and Gina Rinehart moves towards construction
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Ground broken for Arafura Rare Earths mine in remote Central Australia Members of the NT government and Arafura Rare Earths staff break ground at the Nolans mine in Central Australia. ( ABC News: Elsie Lange ) A year after a multi-billion dollar critical minerals deal was signed between the US and Australian governments, one of its key projects has taken a significant step forward. A ground breaking ceremony was held today at Arafura Rare Earth's Nolans Project, north of Alice Springs, with a promise that the mine and a processing plant will be built over the next three years. The mine is set to have a life span of nearly 40 years, and officials say they hope it can create an economic windfall for Australia and the NT. A $1.8 billion rare earths mine with the backing of the US and Australian governments, and Australia's richest woman Gina Rinehart, has hit a major milestone in Central Australia. After two decades in development, ground has finally been broken at Arafura Rare Earths' Nolans mining project about 135 kilometres north of Alice Springs. Company officials and politicians have pledged the Nolans mine will help upset China's dominance of the global rare earths market, create billions of dollars and bring hundreds of jobs to the Northern Territory. Lia Finocchiaro, centre, says the project will change the critical minerals landscape. ( ABC News: Elsie Lange ) NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said the mining project was significant not just for the Territory and Australia, "but for our global allies and partners". "This is about the Northern Territory stepping up and showcasing its capability to the world and playing its role in this nation's sovereignty," she said at the Arafura site today. How critical minerals power our daily lives from the moment we wake up Come inside, look around the house, and see how each room relies on the elements. Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King also attended the ceremony and described the Arafura mine as a "nation-building project". "It's of vital importance to the Northern Territory, it's of vital importance to the country and it's of global significance as well," she said. The Arafura project is focused on producing the rare earths neodymium and praseodymiu m, which are used by global magnet manufacturers and a part of the supply chain for electric vehicles, wind turbines and defence capabilities. Mine set for life span of 'more than half century' According to Arafura Rare Earths, it has supply agreements in place with South Korean auto company Hyundai, Kia, Siemens Gamesa Renewable Energy and GE. Chief executive and managing director Darryl Cuzzubbo said in a statement that the next three years would see the construction of the mine and processing plant at the site. "Over the next three years, hundreds of people will build a mine and a processing plant here, in one of the most remote parts of the country," he said. Darryl Cuzzubbo says the Nolans mine will globally significant. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) "It will be built in the same way we've built our partnerships with traditional owners, lenders, customers and other stakeholders — with integrity and respect at the core. "Nolans will be here for more than half a century. The Arafura project reached a final investment decision earlier this year , after receiving significant financial backing from Australia and its allies. Arafura Rare Earths' flagship Nolans project was green-lit in May this year. ( Supplied: Arafura Rare Earths ) Ms King said the federal government had supported the Arafura rare earths mine "to the tune of $1.2 billion". The mine was among the projects cited in a critical minerals deal signed between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and US President Donald Trump in Washington DC last year . The deal, which also included projects in Victoria, Queensland and New South Wales, was reported to be worth up to $US8.5 billion. US Consul General Colin Crosby was in attendance for today's event and said he would brief the Trump administration about the project's latest milestone. "I will certainly do that as soon as I leave here, as a representative of the administration," he said. "We are following up on the commitment that the prime minister and the president made on the critical minerals framework last October, so it's great to have that come to life here." Ms Hancock's company Hancock Prospecting also owns a significant stake in the company.

events.title: Finding Critical Defects Before They Become Costly Failures: Process Control For Hybrid Bonding And Advanced Packaging
events.summary: In advanced packaging, value accumulates layer by layer, component by component, and process step by process step. By the time chiplets, high-bandwidth memory stacks, or hybrid-bonded devices reach assembly, manufacturers have invested substantial material and processing resources in those devices. An undetected defect at this stage can place the larger assembly at risk. Compounding this challenge, shrinking package features are bringing advanced packaging requirements closer to the tolerances historically associated with front-end fabrication. Going forward, manufacturers will face increasing pressure to detect smaller defects and characterize increasingly complex structures. However, the challenge extends beyond smaller surface defects. Advanced packaging processes can present surface, sidewall and subsurface inspection challenges, including particles, cracks, embedded defects, microbump irregularities and bonding voids. They also require precise measurements of bump height and surface profile. As defect types and process control requirements become more diverse, manufacturers need the flexibility to apply complementary inspection and metrology techniques within a unified workflow. Manufacturers consequently need process control strategies that can address the specific risk at each layer. High-sensitivity 2D inspection can identify surface particles and pattern-related anomalies, while high-speed infrared sub-surface inspection can reveal voids and embedded defects that otherwise remain hidden. 3D metrology can measure critical microbump height and surface profiles, helping manufacturers characterize advanced packaging structures more completely. The objective is to give process engineers the information they need at the point where a manufacturing decision must be made. Sensitivity, however, cannot come at the expense of productivity. As features shrink, inspection must detect smaller and subtler defects while maintaining the throughput required for high-volume manufacturing. If an inspection throughput is too low, it can become a bottleneck in an already capital-intensive production flow. Advanced optical architectures, multiple illumination angles, and purpose-built imaging techniques can help improve the visibility of difficult defects. Multi-angle illumination can improve the visibility of sidewall and low-contrast defects that may be difficult to detect with conventional brightfield or darkfield inspection. But greater visibility is only part of the challenge. Fig. 1: Manufacturers must align inspection and metrology capabilities with the specific risks and decision points associated with that layer. Each layer presents distinct process control requirements. Manufacturers must align inspection and metrology capabilities with the specific risks and decision points associated with that layer (Figure 1). The chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) step used to prepare surfaces for hybrid bonding illustrates this challenge. Because the prepared surfaces must meet stringent requirements, even a small imperfection can become yield limiting. As bond pitches shrink, manufacturers need greater inspection sensitivity and tighter process control at this critical stage. Greater sensitivity creates another challenge: determining which defects require action. Since advanced packaging combines varied materials, structures and surface conditions, increasing the number and diversity of detected events, engineers can spend valuable time reviewing nuisance or low-priority detections without effective classification. More detections do not automatically lead to better decisions. Manufacturers need more than a defect map. Effective classification helps separate likely yield-relevant defects from nuisance defects and turns inspection results into actionable process information. Earlier, more confident decisions Advanced packaging manufacturers must protect growing device value while detecting smaller defects and distinguishing among a wider range of defect types. Ultimately, a production-worthy process control strategy should help manufacturers answer five questions: Should this device continue to the next process step? Is the process beginning to drift? Which defects are most likely to affect yield? Can those defects be found without slowing production? Can the inspection strategy adapt as structures and requirements change? Today’s manufacturers need a flexible, integrated platform that brings together complementary inspection and metrology capabilities to answer these questions across the process flow. Bringing these capabilities together on a single platform gives manufacturers the flexibility to address varied process requirements within a unified workflow while improving cost of ownership and making more efficient use of valuable fab floor space. By finding relevant defects, prioritizing their potential impact, and delivering actionable information before compromised devices move downstream, manufacturers can make earlier disposition decisions, respond more effectively to process variation, and better protect yield. In our next blog in this series, we will examine how manufacturers can extend this integrated approach into front-end process control, connecting information from the wafer surface, edge, and backside to support better manufacturing decisions. We hope you will join us. events.title: Demonstrating Plasma As A Viable Alternative To KOH For LCP Metallization Applications
events.summary: This blog examines the use of plasma technology as an alternative surface treatment method for liquid crystal polymer (LCP) materials. The study demonstrates how optimized plasma processing can achieve effective surface roughening and activation, providing a viable alternative to conventional KOH treatment while delivering the coverage and adhesion required for subsequent electroless copper plating. The challenge LCP is a high-performance engineering plastic widely used in the electronics, automotive, medical, and communications industries because of its excellent mechanical properties, thermal stability, and electrical insulation characteristics. However, untreated LCP surfaces are extremely smooth, exhibit low surface energy, and have poor wettability. As a result, direct electroless copper plating typically cannot achieve the adhesion and coverage required for manufacturing processes. Traditionally, KOH treatment has been the only widely accepted industrial solution for processing LCP materials. However, KOH is a strong alkaline chemical that requires special safety precautions and dedicated process infrastructure. Many PCB manufacturers do not have KOH desmear capability and are reluctant to add a chemical process to their production facilities. The objective of this project was to determine whether plasma processing could provide a practical alternative to KOH by addressing several key challenges: Demonstrate surface roughening performance comparable to KOH treatment. Achieve both surface roughening and activation of the LCP material. Effectively process thicker LCP boards, which are more difficult to treat than conventional PCB materials. Application development process Nordson’s applications team evaluated plasma processing using the Nordson MARCH MaxVIA system, a high-performance platform engineered for high-volume PCB plasma treatment. Featuring an advanced power-power electrode configuration, the system delivers outstanding etchback and desmear uniformity while ensuring excellent process consistency. Together with sophisticated vacuum and gas-flow control and enhanced temperature management, the MaxVIA system enables reliable, repeatable plasma processing for demanding manufacturing applications. Initial process development The team used a three-step plasma process: Material Warm-Up. Hole Wall Roughening. Surface Activation. Initial evaluation confirmed that both etch rate and process uniformity met specification requirements while leaving no detectable LCP residue on copper surfaces. Cross-sectional analysis and SEM inspection verified successful roughening throughout the treated structures, as shown in Figures 1 and 2. Surface activation evaluation Experiments compared process results with and without the H₂/N₂ activation step, as shown in Figures 3 and 4. The results demonstrated that the activation step was necessary to achieve good plating coverage, indicating that roughening alone was insufficient for optimal performance. Process optimization Additional experiments evaluated the effect of treatment duration on process efficiency. Comparative testing at 20, 30, and 60 minutes demonstrated that the treatment time could be reduced to 30 minutes while maintaining acceptable results, as shown in Figures 5-7. The optimized process enabled effective treatment of LCP material while reducing overall processing time and maintaining the required surface characteristics for subsequent metallization. The conclusion The optimized plasma process successfully demonstrated that plasma treatment can serve as a practical alternative to KOH processing for LCP materials. The plasma treatment effectively roughened and activated the material surface, producing the surface characteristics required for reliable metallization, as shown in Figures 8–12. Surface analysis showed significant texturing after plasma treatment compared with untreated LCP. Results following activation demonstrated good plating coverage and adhesion. Solder float testing further confirmed process effectiveness on both four-core and eight-core structures. Key results Plasma proved to be a suitable alternative to KOH treatment for LCP materials. Plasma treatment successfully roughened and activated the LCP surface. Activated samples demonstrated good copper coverage and adhesion performance. Process optimization reduced treatment time to 30 minutes while maintaining successful results The post Demonstrating Plasma As A Viable Alternative To KOH For LCP Metallization Applications appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.title: Closing The Visibility Gap
events.summary: Key Takeaways: No single test, inspection, model, or monitoring technique provides a complete view of an advanced device. Each has physical, spatial, temporal, or contextual blind spots. Important failure evidence often already exists, but it may be scattered across inspection images, test data, manufacturing history, simulation, or field measurements that were never connected. Better coverage increasingly depends on correlation between those views, so one measurement can narrow the uncertainty left by another rather than trying to make every tool see everything. Advanced chips now come with an extraordinary amount of evidence about them. They’re modeled before they exist, measured during fabrication, inspected during assembly, electrically tested at the wafer and package levels, characterized under thermal and power loads, and increasingly monitored from inside the silicon after deployment. In some ways, engineers can see more of a device than ever before. The problem is that each of those views is partial. A measurement can be accurate in every respect and still be pointed at the wrong part of the system. “For X-ray and test technologies, we focus on the interconnect between the chips, and chips and the outside world,” said Yipeng Zhou, product line manager for Test Products at Nordson Test & Inspection . “Voids, cracks in the solder, and head-in-pillow are a few predominant defect types that pass electrical test due to the presence of physical contact. But these defects usually lead to premature failure. It’s like putting a screw in without tightening it.” This gets at the broader visibility issue. The electrical test isn’t necessarily wrong. There’s a conductive path, and under the conditions of that test, the device may work exactly as expected. The harder question is whether the physical structure carrying that current is sound enough to keep doing so over the long term, and that’s where the visibility gap increasingly lives. Every tool has a blind spot As interconnects shrink, it becomes harder to catch defects before they escape. A defect that once occupied enough area to stand out might now be buried among dense stacks of bumps, wires, vias, and surrounding materials. Even when the right inspection technology exists, there’s usually a tradeoff between what engineers would like to see and what they can practically examine in production. “For testing, there is a gap in pull testing for copper pillars and RDL integrity measurement due to the high precision requirement for the system,” said Zhou. “For X-ray, there are still gaps in inspecting overlays of wires and solder bumps from stacked dies and extremely small features in TSVs. In addition, repeatable and quantifiable measurement is a challenge for X-ray. Users also have to make choices between power, throughput, and resolution.” Some of those limitations are simply physical. Higher resolution takes more time, greater penetration requires more power, and higher throughput means less attention for any one structure. The problem quickly becomes more complicated than finding a bad feature, because engineers first have to figure out what’s worth looking at most closely. “It’s really not practical to just do a brute-force high-resolution X-ray scan, because high resolution means small pixels, means it’s slow, means you’ve got gigabytes worth of data, or terabytes worth of data in some cases,” said Thomas Rodgers, senior director of market strategy and head of business sector electronics at ZEISS Microscopy. “You need to have some heuristics to first know where you’re going to look.” Failure analysis becomes less about finding one perfect tool and more about progressively narrowing uncertainty. Electrical test identifies the neighborhood, and acoustic or optical inspection might narrow it further. X-ray can look inside buried structures without immediately destroying the sample, and electron microscopy, which usually requires cross-sectioning, can then resolve the physical mechanism once engineers know where it makes sense to focus. The same logic applies at the wafer level. A broad inspection may not tell engineers exactly what’s gone wrong, but it can show that one area, wafer, or lot looks different enough to justify a closer look. Wafer-scale macro inspection plays that screening role alongside the higher-resolution tools. “If you’re struggling with a problem that comes with a new substrate or a more advanced node, you may need X-ray, IR, or another technique to get at that specific defect,” said Mike LaTorraca, vice president of marketing at Microtronic . “But a tool like ours can still act as a sanity check on everything. It’s your eye in the sky. It sees everything from a higher level, but you don’t stop there. It coexists with these other micro tools.” The more useful question in production isn’t which tool can see the smallest feature. It’s whether each view reduces enough uncertainty for engineers to know what to look at next. The missing information may already exist Not every blind spot comes from something engineers failed to measure. Sometimes the evidence is already there, buried in a data stream that didn’t look important until something else happened later. “Test escapes aren’t always caused because we have missing measurements,” said Eli Roth, smart manufacturing product manager at Teradyne . “The signal may already be somewhere in the wafer data.” The signal might also be sitting in equipment telemetry, manufacturing history, final-test results, or field data. The harder part is that those records often live in different tools, different engineering groups, or completely different points in the device’s life. A number captured early in the flow has no way to announce that it’ll become important six process steps later, which is why retained history can matter so much. A wafer that eventually breaks during a thermal process, for example, may have looked perfectly fine earlier in the flow. But if engineers have kept the inspection images, they can work backward and sometimes find that the final crack began as a much smaller deformation at the wafer edge. “One of the keys is just having the historical images,” said Errol Akomer, applications director at Microtronic. “You may get breakage at a thermal process close to the end of line, and you can trace back with the images and look at that point of origin.” Once the failure is known, an earlier feature that seemed inconsequential can become the most useful clue in the record. Negative evidence helps, too, and working backward through the images can be just as revealing as watching a defect develop forward. “It’s so helpful to know where it’s not, because if you start going backward, you can blow up a certain area and keep looking at it,” said Reiner Fenske, president at Microtronic. “At some point, that little line or mark goes away. If it’s there in one image and not the previous one, then you know the problem had to start somewhere in between.”

events.title: From Silicon To Systems: Redefining Competitive Advantage, Part 3
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports The next generation of industry leaders may look very different from the last. For most of the semiconductor industry’s history, value was captured in fairly predictable places. Smaller transistors, better processing nodes, and higher-performance chips. But the industry is going into a new era. Today, some of the most important breakthroughs are happening outside the transistor itself: in advanced packaging, in AI infrastructure, in system integration, in software, data, and platform ecosystems. And perhaps most importantly, value is beginning to shift from individual components towards the ability to integrate increasingly complex technology into scalable systems. Because in the age of AI, performance is no longer determined by a single chip itself. It is shaped by how efficiently the entire system can move data, manage energy, coordinate compute, and operate across interconnected systems. Which means the next generation of industry leaders may look very different from the last. The winners may not simply be those with the best technology, but those who can combine technology, platforms, partnerships, and strategic positioning into coherent systems of value creation. Advantest’s Dong Ong sits down with Salah Nasri, CEO & co-founder of ISIG (International Semiconductor Industry Group), to discuss where the semiconductor industry is going and what competitive advantage might look like in the next decade. events.title: Shift Left Complicates Fab Data Management
events.summary: Key Takeaways: “Shift left” improves yield by moving detection earlier. Fabs are using real-time equipment sensor data and AI/ML to identify process excursions inside the process module and improve advanced process control. Higher sampling rates, hundreds of sensor parameters, and sub-second analysis are increasing the volume, velocity, and variety of manufacturing data. Data context and connectivity remain important. However, module-level optimization affects both. Semiconductor fabs are leveraging AI/ML models and raw equipment data to speed up yield learning, but the volume of data they are collecting — in some cases, hundreds of petabytes a year — is forcing some tough decisions about optimization versus context. The amount of data they are wrestling with has exploded due to increased sampling from inspection and metrology tools, which is used to detect yield issues. This includes data that is streaming from equipment sensors, which is a relatively new contributor to the data volume. AI/ML inference models use this sensor data for in-situ analysis, which enables more responsive advanced process control (APC) and quicker identification of changes that could adversely impact downstream yield. “Over the last five years, the equipment data segment has grown exponentially,” said Ashish Gupta, senior data engineering manager for automation at Intel Foundry . “This explosion is primarily the result of fabs engaging in shift-left efforts into in-situ, real-time process control.” Others agree that the increased use of equipment data has become a source of exponential data growth. “Equipment data has expanded along three dimensions,” said Jae Yong Park, vice president of enterprise software business at Onto Innovation . “Suppliers have added hundreds of parameters over the past few years, sampling rates have increased from about once per second to every tens of milliseconds, and engineers are increasingly working with raw trace data instead of summary data. Together, these changes have dramatically increased the volume of streaming data.” More equipment data increases the data volume, velocity, and variety. Real-time usage of data within a process module now requires sub-second processing. Hundreds of equipment sensors have increased data variety by at least 10× from a decade ago. “There’s been a firehose of data that’s been coming out of pretty much everywhere,” said Kartik Venkataraman, senior director of product management at Synopsys . “Even what fabs have, in terms of access to data from all their equipment suppliers, is a small fraction of the total generated by that equipment. That’s partly because OEMs want to keep some of that information to themselves. That’s their IP. A lot of times, though, it’s because the fab literally cannot handle it. If you take something like an RF plasma source in an etch chamber or a CVD chamber, that’s operating at a megahertz level. But if it’s pulsing — and pulsing is such a critical parameter — it’s operating at kilohertz. Every pulse has a waveform, which has a shape to it. It has a certain transient response and a certain droop. It has characteristics and features in there, some of which may be actionable and tell you something about your process, but you can’t possibly monitor every pulse. You’re talking about megabytes per second of data.” For advanced device nodes, the growth in real-time/in-situ data analytics improves yield learning and advanced process control. Typically, engineers wait days, weeks, or months for a yield excursion signal from subsequent screening steps, such as electrical test. With AI/ML models, fabs can often shift identification and decisions to within the process module itself. Decisions can adjust process module settings or abort a process mid-operation. This shift requires continuous monitoring of high-resolution data on a grand scale. Fabs shift more left Semiconductor test has been shifting more test content left in the flow for decades. The goal was to increase yield at final or system-level test by adding test content to wafer-level test. More recently, due to the proliferation of chiplets, an additional test step has been added for singulated die. Earlier screening increases confidence that known good die (KGD) are being shipped. This, in turn, increases the final product’s yield and quality. Similarly, wafer fabs are shifting equipment data left in the flow, using process module data to detect yield excursions and to improve advanced process control algorithms. By relying on equipment sensor data and purpose-built virtual metrology models, process modules can quickly self-identify adverse, yield-impacting shifts within the tool. As a result, process engineers don’t need to wait for downstream screening to flag yield issues. AI/ML inference model results can identify causes of yield issues in near real-time. “Shifting left occurs within each macro phase (Design => Fab => Sort => Advanced Packaging => Final Test),” said Intel Foundry’s Gupta. “But moving detection upstream inside the fab module, inside the design cycle, or inside the test cell is where the data engineering challenge intensifies. Instead of waiting for summary bin results or post-step inspections, in-phase shift left requires continuous, high-resolution surveillance, in-situ/in-chamber analytics, anomaly detection, virtual metrology, adaptive test, etc. These activities contribute to a 4Vs (volume, velocity, variety, veracity) data tsunami.” Fundamentally, the shift to monitoring within a process module adds three steps. AI/ML inference models access real-time equipment sensor data. These models can flag questionable wafer processing that requires either an adjustment of equipment parameters or an abort command. For the latter, a root-cause analysis will indicate subsequent corrective actions, such as maintenance. The explosive growth of heterogeneous integration, from 2.5D interposers and CoWoS to hybrid bonding and 3D stacking, is redefining what it means to “ramp a process.” Advanced packaging technologies exhibit yield sensitivities and defect mechanisms fundamentally different from front-end logic or standard packaging technology, yet the industry has lacked purpose-built metrology, characterization, and analytics frameworks to address these new challenges at scale. events.title: The FAaST Track: Enabling Advanced Packaging Through Electrical Process Control
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports The next frontier in process control isn’t just visual—it’s electrical. The semiconductor industry is entering an era where packaging innovation is as important as transistor scaling. Artificial intelligence, high-performance computing systems, advanced smartphones, automotive electronics, and next-generation networking platforms increasingly depend on advanced packaging technologies to deliver the bandwidth, power efficiency, and functionality these applications demand, often in increasingly smaller footprints. While much of the advanced packaging process control discussion focuses on defect detection, some challenges take of the form of subtle electrical conditions that can impact downstream yield, device reliability, and manufacturing consistency. These electrical effects are often invisible to traditional inspection and metrology methods, yet they can negatively affect downstream process performance, device reliability, and overall yield. Residual charge control has emerged as a particularly important requirement for advanced packaging. As manufacturers adopt new package architectures, they are also introducing a growing number of hygroscopic films and materials which are often combined with insulating layers and substrates. These materials require tighter environmental control, and in drier environments, residual and static charge can become a significant process concern. Plasma-based processing, deposition, cleaning, surface preparation, and bonding steps can further generate localized charge buildup across wafers and panels. events.title: CPO Testing Faces A Moving Target Problem
events.summary: Key Takeaways: The industry is busy developing different connector designs and laser sources, while massive data centers with the first levels of CPO are being built. In the absence of design-for-test, companies have to test each individual waveguide, resonator or photodiode, which is inefficient and does not scale. Optical components are much more sensitive to slight offset than electronic components, making issues like thermal and warpage particularly troublesome. Experts At The Table : The steep data center build-out contains an increasing amount of near-packaged optics (NPO) and co-packaged optics (CPO), putting pressure on test manufacturers to produce high-volume manufacturing tooling. Semiconductor Engineering sat down with Matt Griffin, senior product manager for optoelectronics test at Teradyne ; Ira Leventhal, vice president of research and venture at Advantest America ; Dave Armstrong, fellow at ISE Labs, a subsidiary of ASE Group ; and Kazuo Yamaguchi, silicon photonics researcher and engineer at Keysight Technologies . Fig. 1: (L-R): Teradyne’s Griffin; Keysight’s Yamaguchi; ISE Labs’ Armstrong; Advantest’s Leventhal. SE: Some people liken the testing of optical devices to testing electronic devices several decades ago. What are the most significant challenges associated with testing photonic devices? Griffin : There are two key changes we’re making to the test cells to support co-packaged optics. One is the optical instrumentation itself at the wafer, optical engine, or package level. The second is the automation. So how do I optically interface with the device under test (DUT)? That could be a fiber alignment at wafer, a connector alignment, or receptacle alignment at the package or optical engine level. This is what needs to change to enable high volume. Some of the photonics engineers will say, ‘Well, what’s the big deal? I’ve been testing optical transceivers for 20 years. I’ve been designing optical transceivers for 20 years.’ The difference is the scale of going to high-volume manufacturing, where you’re deploying many testers on a test floor. You want to support high-volume software, data analysis, and test programming capabilities, so it’s not as simple as bringing rack-and-stack instrumentation onto a test cell or designing your own custom optical alignment system like you would in your characterization lab. That is really where the challenges lie. Leventhal : It really comes down to maturity level, and if we wind the clock back 40 years, with each generation of electronics, there’s some new capability being added. In the beginning of my career, ATE was strictly digital test. But we kept getting greater levels of integration, bringing together digital, analog, mixed-signal, RF, and now millimeter wave, in a single package. Photonics is yet another progression of new technology. There’s a less mature ecosystem for the optical part of the test content, and that needs to mature to enable us to truly bring up this technology at scale. For example, customers are still trying to determine which connection technologies they’re going to use and what laser sources they’re going to use. A lot is still evolving. I don’t see this as a fundamentally different challenge, but the signal is optical and not electronic, so electrical engineers are looking at things like polarization extinction ratio, for example, so it takes that next level of learning to evolve this to HVM. Armstrong : Ira hit on an important point. A lot of what we’re doing harkens back to the old days of digital logic before we had scan test. At that time, a lot of people were trying to take rack-and-stack or bench equipment and use it for production test, which tended to be clunky, cumbersome, and slow. Then we got design for testability (DFT) integrated into the logic. We haven’t done DFT for optical. People are trying to deploy some PRBS (pseudo-random binary sequence) type approaches, which have existed in logic devices for a while, but in large part we don’t have DFT, so we have to test each waveguide component, ring, modulator, etc., one at a time, and it is slow and laborious. There’s a lot of different perspectives on what needs to be tested and how to test it, and I’d say one of the biggest challenges is, as Matt alluded, we don’t have a hybrid engineer. We’ve got two different camps of people who have a hard time learning each other’s core capability, so we have to get people on the same page, educated similarly both for electrical and optical, with similar standards in place. Yamaguchi : Optical alignment must be extremely precise and can slow down testing. For this reason, using an optical probe card would be ideal but is difficult — not only because of the non-contact mechanical implementation, but also because optical calibration is needed to make reliable and traceable measurements. The multi-channel optical connectivity with the FAU has design variation from unit-to-unit and channel-to-channel, resulting in channel-performance uncertainty. For example, a measurement on channel 1 of a waveguide is different from the same measurement on channel 2. A slight offset due to pitch and x,y mismatch causes an optical alignment offset, which is more impactful than a similar offset at electrical probe. SE: How does the addition of photonics change test flows? Armstrong : We all share a very similar view of insertions. Insertion one is for PIC (photonics IC) testing. Insertion two is wafer-level optical engine testing. Insertion three is die-level optical engine. Insertion four is module test, and insertion five is system-level test. You can add insertion 1.5, wafer-level burn-in, a stability bake of your optical components, and it’s a must for lasers to get rid of infant mortality. PIC testing is certainly done broadly today, although some people who have the most experience in the market say it may not need to be done in the future. Optical engine testing is a must, and that’s where most of the effort is. So insertions two, three, and four feel like a must for the hyperscalers, which feels like a follow-on effort to what hyperscalers have been doing for years with a large ATE high-power test of the heterogeneous integration. Griffin : I’ve been working in this space for about ten years, and almost every insertion has felt like the most important one at some point, depending on which customer or which part of the market you’re talking to. Our goal is to provide test solutions across all insertions and give our customers the flexibility to shift coverage as they gain more insight into the volume manufacturing flow and where they need to optimize. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters UK funds flying broadband stations with power beamed from below 21 days ago Anthropic proposes plumbing spec to link AI agents to lab kit and robots August 28, 2026 Cyborg cockroaches may soon deliver life-saving drugs to disaster victims August 27, 2026 Hugging Face offers $399 robot duck to help you quack the AI code August 27, 2026 Gates warns society faces an AI-pocalypse unless we get more socialist August 26, 2026 The ALBATROSS, a sailboat drone prototype developed by researchers at Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD), lacks the aerial grace of its avian namesake. It doesn't so much fly as plummet – an unsettling start to a sea launch, more so because it's designed to spin like a maple leaf seed as it descends. The sailboat drone's rotation slows its fall and minimizes its impact with the water. This eliminates the engineering challenge of implementing hardware for two modes of mobility. There's no need for landing gear, actuators, or sensors to manage both flying and floating. Watch and download graphics and videos of ALBATROSS here. Developed by SUTD researchers Shane Kyi Hla Win, Danial Sufiyan, Brian Leonard Suhadi, Luke Soe Thura, Xinyu Cai, Wei Jun Ang, and Shaohui Foong, the ALBATROSS represents an achievement in both acronym construction and engineering. The Airborne Lander with Buoyant AuToROtating Sailing Sensor is described in a Science paper as a hybrid robotic system that combines a bio-inspired design for controlled aerial descent with autonomous sailing. Beyond the bio-inspired operation of the rigid wingsails for creating aerodynamic lift during descent and propulsion on the water, the ALBATROSS further cribs from nature's bag of tricks with a rudder that acts like a caudal fin – it moves side to side like a tailfin to generate thrust. And it does so with just three actuators and three primary sensors. Practically, the boat drone, which weights 1.107 kg, was built to fill the gap between expendable aircraft-deployed ocean instruments and floating robots deployed from ships or shore. Its light weight and adaptability make it well suited for rapid aerial deployment followed by energy-efficient persistence on the water, as might be required to monitor an oil spill or time-sensitive weather events. It is intended to be an alternative to large automated sailboats like Saildrone and Sailbuoy that may require ground- or ship-based management. And it has far greater deployment range than hybrid aquatic micro aerial vehicles: more than 100 km, compared to about 7 km for SailMAV , or so its makers claim. "Building on prior work on guided autorotation, ALBATROSS is designed to be released from an aircraft or UAV, passively enter autorotation for a controlled, low-impact water landing, self-right without actuation, and seamlessly transition into a wind-powered sailboat," the researchers explain. "Unlike many hybrid aerial-marine systems, ALBATROSS eliminates the need for aerial propulsion, complex mechanical reconfiguration, or active stabilization during the air-water transition and can sail back to shore at the end of a mission." The prototype takes flight amid a market doing the same. Last year, PwC's Strategy& consultancy issued a report [PDF] that forecasts a sea drone market worth €18.9 billion (~$21.2 billion) by 2030, based on a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15.5 percent. By the end of the decade, most of that (84 percent) is expected to be for civilian uses like scientific research, commercial, recreational, and engineering applications, and search and rescue operations.

events.title: AI startup Manus raises $500 million in first funding round since Meta breakup
events.summary: Manus has raised more than $500 million in its first funding round since U.S.-based Meta Platforms was forced to reverse its acquisition. Bloomberg reported last month that Manus was set to double its valuation in this financing round to $4 billion, what would make it the country's most valuable AI agent maker. The raise suggests investors aren't deterred by Beijing's unprecedented order to block Meta's short-lived $2 billion acquisition. AI agent startup Manus has raised more than $500 million in its first funding round since Meta was forced to abandon its acquisition of the company. Butterfly Effect, Manus' parent company, said Thursday that the round was led by private equity firm Boyu Capital and venture investor IDG Capital, with follow-on investment from existing shareholders Tencent , HSG and ZhenFund. The company did not disclose its post-funding valuation. Bloomberg reported last month that Manus was set to double its valuation to $4 billion in this financing round, making it the country's most valuable AI agent maker. The raise suggests investors aren't deterred by Beijing's unprecedented order to block Meta's short-lived $2 billion acquisition. Meta was working to integrate Manus' team and technology into its system when authorities blocked the deal. It also shows that appetite for AI-agent startups has held up, even as the underlying foundation models improve quickly and price competition intensifies. "The fundraising shows that the short-term fallout of the Meta case has been contained and investors are willing to back Manus as an independent company," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group, also noting the renewed confidence in the commercial potential of AI agents. Manus could ultimately aim for a public listing but the more imminent task would be revamping its business and ownership structure to prove profitability and align with Beijing's regulatory requirement, analysts say. "The immediate task for Manus now is proving scale, profitability and regulatory alignment," said Han Lin, China country director at The Asia Group. Earlier this month, Manus said it had resumed independent operations after its split from Meta and that its founding team would continue to push forward generative AI agents for users globally. Once seen as a blueprint for Chinese startups seeking global reach, Manus has become a cautionary tale for companies squeezed between regulators in Beijing and Washington. The company launched in early 2025 in China, then moved its staff to Singapore after winning backing from U.S. venture firm Benchmark. Meta announced the acquisition in December. Chinese regulators later blocked it. The National Development and Reform Commission said it had decided to "prohibit foreign investment in the Manus project." By then, Meta had begun integrating Manus' team and technology into its own. Since the split, the AI startup has unveiled Manus 2.0, built on a new in-house execution system called Cascade. It also launched Cue , a standalone personal-agent app in which each agent has its own email address, phone number, and mobile wallet. Meta has pressed ahead with its own personal AI agent, launching its Muse agent in early September , modeled on the open-source AI agent OpenClaw. The "close integration" with Manus "does not disappear when the transaction is reversed," said Matthias Hendrichs, a Singapore-based adviser to global AI firms. "You can separate companies, but you cannot make engineers forget what they learned."
