events.title: Yemen’s government needs tribes to defeat the Houthis. Will they join?
events.summary: Yemen’s tribes could prove crucial to government’s fight against the Houthis, but many may wait for evidence of sustained military gains before choosing sides. Sanaa, Yemen – The Yemeni government’s new military offensive against the Houthis is testing more than the balance of forces in the country – it is also testing whether the government can persuade powerful tribes in Houthi-controlled areas that the balance of power is beginning to shift. For years, many of the tribes hostile or wary of the Iran-backed Houthis have stopped short of openly confronting the movement, deterred by their military strength and by previous failed uprisings. Those same tribes are now looking to the internationally recognised government’s newly-activated frontlines – on the Red Sea coast, Marib and al-Jawf primarily – to see if the limited advances made since the Dawn of Yemen military operation launch this week can turn into sustained gains . list 1 of 3 Three killed, 36 injured in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, Riyadh says list 2 of 3 More than 200,000 displaced as fighting escalates in Yemen, UN says list 3 of 3 Yemen’s Houthis attack Aden airport; Saudi forces down missile near Riyadh The offensive by the Saudi Arabia-backed government forces follows major Houthi gains in September, when the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) swept across the country’s Red Sea coast. The Houthis captured vital trade corridors, including the port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important shipping routes. While airstrikes have inflicted losses on Houthi forces over the past few days, pushing towards Houthi strongholds where the group has been entrenched since the war started in 2014, including Sanaa, Saada, and Amran, remains a formidable challenge. With the government declaring an all-out war on the Houthis, pledging to recapture Sanaa, tribal distrust of the government may diminish, prompting tribes to shift positions at the right time, experts say. The role of the tribes could therefore prove critical to the government’s ability to advance deeper into Houthi-controlled territories. On Monday, Marib governorate – the government’s stronghold in the north – saw a large tribal rally attended by tribal sheikhs and local anti-Houthi fighters from tribes such as the Jadan from Marib, Nihm from Sanaa and other allied tribes. The rally announced a general mobilisation to support the armed forces in the battle to “restore the state and topple the Houthi coup”. “If this tribal support translates into actual mobilisation and sustained participation in the battle, tribes will help government troops advance toward Houthi-controlled areas and the Houthi heartland, including Sanaa,” said Adel Dashela, a researcher at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies. Over the past decade of war in Yemen, tribes have repeatedly mobilised against the Houthis at a local level, but deep divisions and a lack of sustained outside backing have prevented the emergence of a unified tribal front. Nevertheless, tribes can potentially be a key source of manpower and influence for the government. “Tribal fighters remain indispensable to any future campaign against the Houthis. But to be effective, their military engagement must occur through formalised state and coalition command structures, rather than as an independent vanguard,” Dashela said. Tribes in Yemen do not want to risk confronting Houthi forces without support, and they “wait for the right time” to act, Abdulsalam Mohammed, chairman of the Yemeni Abaad Studies and Research Center, said. “The tribes seek a powerful state, and once they find the state reliable, they can side with it,” Mohammed said. He added that tribes do not want to repeat mistakes made by tribes that had rebelled against the Houthis, and then not received enough support from the government. “Those tribes revolted against the Houthis, and they were crushed amid the absence of the government’s effective role,” Mohammed said. In January 2019, fighting broke out between the Houthis and the Hajoor tribe in northwest Yemen’s Hajjah, lasting several weeks. The Houthis eventually captured the Hajoor areas in March of the same year. At the time, Saudi Arabia dropped food, medical supplies and weapons to besieged Hajoor fighters, but this did not prevent the tribe’s defeat by the Houthis. Mohammed said that even in areas where the Houthis have local support, some tribes could gradually shift their allegiance towards the government, if they saw it as serving their interest. “Not all tribes fighting for the Houthis are staunch supporters. Their motivations range from pragmatism to ideological loyalty and material necessity,” Mohammed said. Over the past decade, the Houthis have weakened traditional tribal power structures in areas under their control, co-opting some leaders and replacing others with loyalists.

events.summary: Patekar won three National Film Awards and received the Padma Shri, one of the country’s highest civilian honours. Nana Patekar, an acclaimed Indian actor and filmmaker known for his ⁠fiery performances ⁠in Bollywood films and theatre, has died aged 75. Patekar died of a suspected cardiac arrest, the Press Trust of India news agency reported on Thursday, citing a doctor at the hospital where he was pronounced dead. list 1 of 3 Iconic Bollywood romance marks 30 years of nonstop run at Mumbai theatre list 2 of 3 Bollywood ‘He-Man’ Dharmendra Deol dies at 89 list 3 of 3 Why a Bollywood spy film sparked a political storm in India and Pakistan Born in 1951 in India’s western state of Maharashtra, Patekar built a career spanning nearly five decades in Hindi and Marathi language cinema. He was known for intense performances and roles that often portrayed complex or unconventional characters. Patekar made his film debut in the 1978 Hindi film Gaman, and later earned acclaim for Parinda and Krantiveer. He gained wider international recognition with filmmaker Mira Nair’s Oscar-nominated Salaam Bombay! He won three National Film Awards, India’s highest film honours, and received the Padma Shri, one of the country’s highest civilian honours. Prime Minister Narendra Modi mourned Patekar’s death, praising his “intensity, individuality and unmistakable presence” as an actor. “He brought remarkable versatility and creativity to every role and gave us characters that will be remembered for generations,” Modi wrote on X. He played a variety of roles, sharing screen space with actors such as Amitabh Bachchan and Shah Rukh Khan ⁠and excelling in both serious and comic roles. “He was one of those rare actors who never needed to do too much to make you sit up and watch. ‌That voice, that intensity, that honesty in every performance… he was completely his own,” said actor Akshay Kumar, who starred with ‌Patekar ‌in several movies. Patekar is survived by his wife, from whom he was separated, and a son.

events.title: DBS, OCBC and UOB shares extend losses
events.summary: All three lenders were down more than 4% by midday on Oct 8. - DBS, OCBC and UOB shares fell again on Oct 8, after earlier losses, as investors took profits and worried about earnings and global bond market volatility. - Citi downgraded OCBC to “sell” on Oct 7, citing softer third-quarter 2026 earnings expectations and doubts about Singapore-dollar rates and wealth income. - Analysts said near-term volatility may continue, but strong capital and dividends limit downside; a recovery needs resilient NIM, stable fees and controlled credit costs. SINGAPORE – Shares of Singapore’s three local banks extended their losses on Oct 8 following declines the day before. At the midday trading break, OCBC shares were down 4.29% to $29, with over 14.9 million shares changing hands. DBS shares fell 4.48% to $74.02, with more than 9.6 million shares traded, while UOB declined 4.92% to $40.35, with 4.14 million shares changing hands. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said the continued weakness in Singapore bank shares appears to reflect profit-taking, concerns over earnings expectations and broader volatility in global bond markets. Citi on Oct 7 cited softer-than-expected third-quarter 2026 earnings expectations for OCBC and downgraded the stock to “sell”. The downgrade also raised questions about whether market expectations for Singapore-dollar interest rates are too optimistic, and whether the banks can sustain their strong wealth-related income from the first half of the year. Higher global bond yields are also adding pressure, as they could weigh on credit demand, bond portfolios and investor appetite for dividend stocks. Still, the recent declines are not expected to be the start of a prolonged downturn across the banking sector, given the lenders’ strong capital positions and dividend support. “In the near term, further volatility is possible as investors reassess earnings expectations and valuations,” said Chanana. “A more sustained recovery would likely depend on third-quarter earnings showing that net interest margins (NIM) remain resilient and recurring fee income can offset any normalisation in wealth-related revenue.” NIM is the core profitability metric for banks. It measures how much money a bank makes on its loans and investments compared with the interest it pays on deposits and borrowings. James Ooi, market strategist at Tiger Brokers, said higher Singapore-dollar interest rates may not necessarily benefit banks, as rising funding costs could offset the higher returns earned on loans and other assets. “For banks, what matters is not just where rates are going, but whether asset yields can keep pace with rising funding costs to defend net interest margins,” he said. Ooi added that the upcoming earnings season in about a month should provide a clearer picture of whether these concerns are reflected in the banks’ financial results. Eugene Koh, sales trader at CMC Markets Singapore, said DBS has the strongest profitability among the three banks, but its premium valuation means that earnings meeting expectations may not be enough to support its share price. Investors will be watching whether OCBC’s strong fee, trading and insurance income in the first half of the year can be sustained, while UOB faces the risk of higher credit costs eating into revenue growth despite its less demanding valuation. Koh expects trading to remain volatile ahead of the banks’ results in November, although their strong profitability and capital buffers suggest that a “balance-sheet crisis” is unlikely. “A sustained recovery needs resilient underlying earnings, controlled credit costs and reassurance that capital-return commitments hold. Better sentiment alone will not be enough,” he said. They were among 11 stocks selected for the board lot size reduction and saw immediate trades in the smaller trade quantities on Oct 5, according to SGX. From Oct 5, for stocks priced between $10 and $100 a share, the minimum trading quantity was cut from 100 units to 10. Timothy Goh is a business correspondent at The Straits Times. He covers commodities and currencies, with occasional forays into listed companies.

events.title: How October 7 redrew the map of the Middle East
events.summary: Three years of war have upended alliances, weakened US influence and reshaped the region’s power balance. In the past three years, following the October 7 attacks and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the wider region has been marked by conflict, economic turmoil, and a shattering of the balance of power. The network of alliances maintained by Iran, long central to its regional power, has been hit hard and severely weakened. Yemen’s Houthi rebels remain one notable exception. list 1 of 4 Trump launches midterms campaign blitz amid record low approval ratings list 2 of 4 New aircraft carrier, 10,000 US troops: Is the Iran war about to escalate? list 3 of 4 Trump vs Europe as US presses for release of emergency diesel stocks list 4 of 4 G7 nations to release oil and diesel stocks, will it bring down the prices? Israel has made gains. Many of the leaders of the Lebanese group Hezbollah and the Palestinian group Hamas have been killed, while Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was also assassinated in February. Israel occupies most of Gaza, where it has also killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and reduced much of the enclave to rubble. Its military aggression has come at a cost, isolating it from its traditional allies and making it globally unpopular, including in the United States. The potential for more normalisation deals with Arab countries seems unlikely, at least in the short term. Instead, Israel continues to launch attacks across the region, crossing previously held red lines – such as the 2025 attack on Doha, Qatar – and making many governments around the world view it as the primary source of unrest in the Middle East. “Before October 7, the US’s entire policy in the Middle East rested on normalising Israel’s presence in the region through its so-called Abraham Accords,” HA Hellyer of the Royal United Services Institute said, referring to the normalisation deals with several Arab states, including the United Arab Emirates. “Israel’s response to the October 7 attack ended that.” Instead, rather than a stable Middle East with Israel at its centre, the US entered into a war with Iran this year, and has since looked on as Tehran targeted US allies across the Gulf, shattering the perceived security of the US security umbrella. Drones and missiles hit Qatar’s Ras Laffan gas hub and started fires near Dubai airport and at Fujairah’s oil zone. In September, the Houthis surged down Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking the port of Mocha and nearby islands. Their gains tightened their grip on the Bab al-Mandeb strait, threatening a key route for global trade and energy supplies that had become even more important amid disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. “There’s been a loss of faith in the US as a singularly sufficient security guarantor,” Hellyer continued. “This is why you’re seeing many in the region talk to other external actors, in addition to continuing, and in some cases deepening their US ties, as well as initiatives such as the Mecca security pact as states in the region look elsewhere for ways to safeguard their security,” he said, referring to the defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, signed in August, agreeing that an attack on one was to be regarded as an attack on all. Alongside the loss of confidence in the US as a security guarantor has come a dramatic reordering of alliances and rivalries. Much of Iran’s network – most notably Hezbollah, whose reputation had long served as a deterrent against Israeli attack – appeared to buckle under Israeli pressure. That, in turn, emboldened an Israeli military push that saw troops invade Lebanon in October 2024 and again in March 2026 , and seize Syrian territory during the brief power vacuum that followed Bashar al-Assad’s ouster in 2024 . “The Middle East has always been multi-aligned. However, now it’s even more so,” Sanam Vakil, the director of the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House, said of the increased leverage given to external actors, such as Turkiye in Syria and China’s involvement in negotiations over the end to war on Iran, as Beijing finds its own energy supplies under threat. “It’s ironic, since October 7, it’s Israel that has emerged as the revisionist power and Iran almost as the status quo power,” she said of the apparent reversal in status of the two belligerents, with Tehran seemingly more focused on regaining the ground it has lost in the last three years rather than advancing beyond them. However, none of this was to overstate Israeli influence, or liken it to a regional superpower, Vakil cautioned. “Israel may currently be the preponderant military power in the Middle East, but real power is typically classed as being able to project stability, which Israel hasn’t shown itself able or willing to do,” she said. While Israel and the US hoped February’s attacks would swiftly topple Iran’s government, they have instead opened a new front.

events.title: What did Palestinians take when they fled after October 7?
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Gaza Strip - When Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began after October 7, 2023, hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were forced to leave their homes, many under forced displacement orders to move south. By September 27, 2026, at least 74,018 Palestinians had been killed and 175,079 injured in Gaza since the start of the war, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health. Some fled with nothing, leaving behind homes, belongings and memories. Others managed to grab just what they could not bear to leave behind: A book, a musical instrument, a toy, a pet or a keepsake. We asked people in Gaza what they took with them when they fled their homes after October 7 - and what stays with them after repeated displacements during the war. When Omar Abdel Hakim Hamad, 30, received a displacement order in Beit Hanoon, north of Gaza, at about midnight, he decided to stay a little longer despite the heavy bombardment. He wanted to collect what he could from his home, fearing he might never return. The first thing he thought of saving was his personal library of about 500 books. He managed to take about 200, prioritising old and rare books that he felt could not be replaced. Since leaving Beit Hanoon on October 30, 2023, Omar has been displaced 13 times, moving first to Gaza City and later south to the Maghazi refugee camp, where he remains displaced. For Omar, the books were more than possessions. “They are part of who I am,” he says, describing how his love of reading began at 15. Among the books he carried with him is a 1933 edition of Kalila wa Dimna. During the famine-like conditions that plagued Gaza for large parts of the war, he even considered exchanging his entire library for one or two kilogrammes of flour, but says he is grateful that he managed to keep most of it. Today, his Phoenix Library (at the centre of Gaza city) contains about 7,000 books, including about 3,000 rescued from libraries destroyed during the war and another 4,000 that were bought. When Shahd Abu Khosa, 30, left her home in Gaza’s al-Jalaa neighbourhood on October 16, 2023, she took her two dogs, Lily and Bobby, with her. Her displacement took her from al-Shifa Hospital to Tal al-Hawa south of Gaza City, then to a house and finally to a school shelter. The journey was difficult for both dogs, especially Lily, who was frightened by the sound of bombardment and would hide whenever shelling began. Bobby died of starvation after food became unavailable. “I never thought of leaving Lily behind,” Shahd says, describing her as part of the family. During the famine, Lily survived by eating what the family ate, including lentils and bread, while Shahd continued to share what little food they had with her. Shahd says she had once been afraid of dogs, but that changed after her sister brought Lily and Bobby from Egypt. Lily became especially close to her, spending much of her time with Shahd and sharing her food. She describes Lily as loyal and gentle, saying the dog would sense when Shahd was in danger and try to protect her. Shahd hopes all pets in Gaza can find a safe place where they have food, water and somewhere to sleep, “away from fear and harm, and without being thrown out”. As Yaseen al-Qubt, 16, left his home in Beit Lahiya on October 12, 2023, he took his oud with him. His family moved to az-Zawaida in central Gaza, while their home was later bombed and the instrument was left beneath the rubble. Yaseen had owned the oud since January 2023 and had learned to play with the help of a neighbour who was an oud player. He later managed to recover his oud from under the ruins. He picked it up again and continued playing. For Yaseen, playing is also a way to comfort children in the displacement camp. When the sound of Israeli drones frightens them, he plays the oud to give them a few moments of calm. He dreams of leaving Gaza to continue studying music, playing on large stages and eventually owning a professional oud that will help him develop his skills. For now, he says, he remains attached to the instrument because “we still have something beautiful to offer.” When Huda Helassa, 20, left her home in Tal al-Hawa, southern Gaza city, in the first hours of the war, she took a signed T-shirt from the Access Microscholarship Program, a United States-funded programme that provides English-language and cultural education to young people. Her classmates had signed the shirt on September 15, 2023, during their final class, two years before she graduated on September 27. “When we left our home on the first day of the war, the T-shirt was one of the first things that came to my mind,” Huda says. She put it in her bag almost instinctively, wanting to hold on to something from a part of her life that had ended just days earlier.

events.title: EU sends envoy to Beijing as rising exports from China raise economic anxiety
events.summary: The European Union is bracing for a confrontation with China as a trade deficit exceeding $1 billion a day heightens anxiety over potential job losses and pushes the bloc’s political leaders to take a more aggressive approach toward its second-largest ... BRUSSELS -- The European Union is bracing for a confrontation with China as a trade deficit exceeding $1 billion a day heightens anxiety over potential job losses and pushes the bloc’s political leaders to take a more aggressive approach toward its second-largest trading partner. The European Commission’s top trade envoy, Maroš Šefčovič, will be in Beijing Thursday for a two-day meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. The goal is narrowing the EU’s 360 billion euro ($410 billion) trade deficit with China. Earlier this year, he gave Beijing a deadline of October to provide meaningful results in doing so. Politicians and economists across the 27-nation bloc consider China’s massive subsidies and exports a major threat to core industrial sectors from steel foundries to car factories. China diverted many of its exports to the EU and other markets after the U.S. raised tariffs . In a debate Tuesday in European Parliament in Strasbourg, lawmakers overwhelmingly expressed anxiety alongside defiance over trade with China. On Wednesday, they voted 454 to 86 on a resolution to toughen up on China that centered on a call for “economic reciprocity and a proportionate EU response if China does not open its markets.” Ahead of the vote, Hilde Vautmans, the Belgian lawmaker who led the resolution, said that “Europe has economic power, it’s time we used it.” Despite the seeming European unity this week, it remains unclear what the EU can or is willing to do. It has already rolled out trade measures against Chinese steel imports and e-commerce small parcels . France’s High Commission for Strategy and Planning in February called for swift action, like 30% tariffs on many of China’s exports, and a devaluation of the euro against the Chinese currency. Sales of German autos are plummeting in China , but China is also poised to gobble up market share in Europe by undercutting European automakers on price thanks to heavy state subsidies. There have already been mass layoffs at major manufacturers like Volkswagen. A letter by France and Germany, a copy of which was seen by The Associated Press, called for a sweeping rethink of the EU’s China policy. Among other actions, it proposed making it easier for the European Commission to use the bloc’s so-called “trade bazooka,” the Anti-Coercion Instrument . This is a never-used-before raft of measures for blocking or restricting trade and investment from countries found to be putting undue pressure on EU member nations or corporations. Yet not all EU nations agree on such tough measures. Spain, the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy, has been less adversarial toward China in recent years. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited Beijing four times in three years. The European Policy Centre in Brussels said in June that European battery producers, solar panels, steel, electric vehicles, chemicals and machinery are already hemorrhaging jobs and capacity and called for a trade investigative body modelled on Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the phenomenon another “ China shock ” for Europe, similar to what happened in the U.S. in the early 2000s when hundreds of thousands of factory jobs in the American heartland were wiped out. The EU’s ailing economy requires both a domestic overhaul and a more aggressive foreign trade policy, especially with China, said Tim Rühlig, a China analyst at the European Union Institute for Security Studies, the bloc’s internal think tank. Rühlig also said that European businesses and political leadership bear some blame. “It’s clear that just protecting yourself from China is not the future,” Rühlig said. “But to have a chance of making yourself ready for future technologies and to remain competitive in the coming 15-20 years, you have to protect yourself.” It is impossible to disengage completely with China as the EU did with Russia following its invasion of Ukraine, Rühlig said, but there is robust momentum now to reset trade relations with Beijing. “Where do we make ourselves independent or at least more diverse? And where do we still work with the Chinese?” Rühlig asked. events.title: A tech crowd was polled on buying Anthropic shares at a $3 trillion valuation. Only 3 hands went up.
events.summary: Anthropic's IPO will be a test of whether the hype train can withstand the scrutiny of the public markets. Business Insider An audience at SF Tech Week was asked if they would buy Anthropic shares at a $3 trillion valuation. Only three hands went up. The room's response reflects the broader uncertainty in this IPO market. In San Francisco, the signs that Tech Week had arrived were hard to miss. Planes towed banners advertising startups above the city. Inflatable company mascots greeted commuters outside transit stations. And hundreds of people lined up outside Anthropic's Claude Founder House for the chance to get inside. But a few blocks away, the mood was more measured. On Wednesday night, a crowd gathered in the Dogpatch for the Tech Insider: Growth Mode event, sponsored by Fidelity. Minutes after interviewing Anthropic investor Matt Murphy onstage, Business Insider chief correspondent Ben Bergman put a question to the room: When Anthropic goes public, would you buy shares at a $3 trillion valuation? Three hands went up. How about $1.5 trillion? A few more hands rose. It was a surprisingly muted response for the company that has become one of the clearest symbols of the artificial-intelligence gold rush . Its long-awaited public offering is expected to test how much of that hype can survive the scrutiny of the public markets. Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy backed Anthropic when it was worth $4.1 billion. The company is now aiming to go public at a $2 trillion valuation. Business Insider The IPO market is having a strange year. By dollars raised, it has been one of the biggest on record, propelled by SpaceX's blockbuster debut. The prospect of Anthropic following before year-end could push that figure into the stratosphere. But the headline numbers obscure a far thinner market underneath. There have been relatively few offerings, and some of the most closely watched candidates have stumbled. Just last week, smart-ring maker Oura pulled its planned IPO at the eleventh hour, pointing to choppy market conditions. For Heidi Mayon, a partner at the law firm Simpson Thacher, who worked on Oura's planned offering, the delay reflected a wait-and-see attitude she's seeing across the market. She told the room that companies have been reluctant to go public before Anthropic and OpenAI do. "There's sort of an overarching feeling that there isn't enough public investor capital available until those deals get done," Mayon said. SpaceX showed that may not be true, she added, but few companies want to compete with the model providers for investor attention. The bigger challenge, she said, is that artificial intelligence has pushed valuations sky-high in the private markets. Rather than squeeze every possible dollar out of an offering, Mayon said, some companies may be better off pricing their shares more conservatively. That could leave room for a first-day "pop" and the momentum that comes with it. Journalist Adam Rogers interviews Lenka Haase (center) and Jill Hallquist from Fidelity onstage at the Tech Insider: Growth Mode event in San Francisco. Business Insider Jack Cassel, Nasdaq's senior vice president and head of new listings, had a different message for the room: There is still plenty of capital to take companies public, but the bar has changed. After years of growth at all costs, investors are now looking for "growth with cash efficiencies and discipline," Cassel told the room. They are asking tougher questions about the business models, a company's product plans, and what comes after the stock launch. That scrutiny may keep consumer and software companies on the sidelines until one or both of the frontier labs go public, he said. Other corners of the market are still moving. Biotech has produced 22 IPOs this year, he noted, with more expected before the end of the year. When Anthropic finally goes public, it will be the biggest test yet of whether the artificial-intelligence hype train has the financial horsepower to back it up. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Big tech has piled in with plenty of asks, but faces a fight as eight applicants want .api and seven seek .agi You could own AI.slop, if applicant for new global top-level domains get their way August 27, 2026 ICANN again intervenes to defend AFRINIC May 27, 2026 ICANN opens applications for new generic top-level domains for the first time since 2012 May 1, 2026 Friendster rises from the grave to make social media great again April 27, 2026 United Nations agrees to persist with multi-stakeholder internet governance December 18, 2025 ICANN has revealed the applicants for new generic top-level domains (GTLDs). As The Register reported in August , this is just the second time ICANN has accepted applications for GTLDs, strings like “.com” or “.net”. For years, only ICANN could create and operate GTLDs. The governance body changed that policy and in 2012 allowed over 1,200 new GTLDs. The organization decided to repeat the process this year and on Wednesday announced it received 1,615 applications. A process is now under way to confirm those applications are viable. ICANN has made information about all of the applications available in a searchable form here along with a downloadable list that The Register has pored over to bring you news of the following applications. OpenAI wants 15 GTLDs, among them .chatgpt and .agi – the latter likely the acronym for artificial general intelligence. Six other entities also want that string. The AI upstart also wants .mcp, which probably refers to the open source Model Context Protocol. Google bid for this GTLD, too, as have three other entities. The Big G, through its subsidiary Charleston Road Registry, is in an eight-way tussle to score .api. It has applied for over 30 new names, most pertaining to its products. Anthropic wants only its own name and .claude. Microsoft is another that hopes for just a pair of names: .copilot and .msft. Meta will have to fight another contender to control .superintelligence, but is the only entity trying to claim .wearables. 13 entities hope to claim .agent, with Meta and Google among the contenders. Salesforce wants its own name, plus .force, .slack, and .tableau. An outfit named Fomalhaut Exploration wants .intel. That could be Chipzilla acting through a third party, or the beginning of a legal tussle. Three contenders want to be the home of .drone, while nine are fighting over .brand. Ten applicants want to build their own .hub, while two hope to take GTLDs to .mars. Seven operators hope to run .official, the kind of domain that brands buy defensively so they end up with [companyname].official before someone cynical nabs the name. North America was home to most applicants – 864 – followed by 506 Europeans, 218 from Asia Pacific, 16 from Africa, and just 11 from Latin America and the Caribbean. When multiple parties apply for the same GTLD, ICANN first applies a “community priority evaluation” process that tries to find the most appropriate home for a string. If that fails, rights to the GTLD go to auction. All applications must be decided by November 17, aka String Confirmation Day, after which successful applicants can start the work to establish a registry for their new GTLDs. events.title: Young bankers to manage AI agents from start, Goldman exec says
events.summary: Goldman Sachs Group’s Kevin Sneader said they are focused on how roles would be reshaped. Goldman Sachs’ Kevin Sneader said new bankers will manage AI agents from day one, which could change the usual career ladder and reduce the role of middle managers. Panel speakers said AI will do more routine work, so banks may need fewer entry-level staff and more workers who can supervise AI systems. Singapore’s regulator is training staff and graduates for this shift, while Sneader said AI also makes it easier for young people to start new businesses. SINGAPORE – The newest hires in finance will not have to wait years to become managers. They will be overseeing artificial intelligence agents from the time they join, raising the question of what happens to the current middle managers, according to Goldman Sachs Group’s Kevin Sneader. “When our young folks now start work, they’re managing agents,” Sneader, who leads the Wall Street bank’s business in Asia-Pacific outside Japan, said on Oct 8 at the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore. “They have to make the most of this virtual army that they’ve now got.” Previous generations often spent years in the job before they got to manage anyone, and re-deploying these managers will be the “generational challenge for many, many segments”, he added. His comments suggest AI could upend the traditional banking career path, where junior staff spend years on analysis and preparatory work before moving up to manage others. Rather than fretting about mass job losses due to the technology, Sneader and others speaking on a panel about AI and finance were focused on how roles would be reshaped. “That management task no longer sits with the middle manager; it sits with the front line,” Sneader said. “We don’t quite know what’s going to happen to that group.” Sandra Peterson, an operating partner at investment firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice, said the traditional career ladder may not survive. “It used to be that professional service firms were pyramids,” she said. “You’d show up, and you know, you march your way through, and if you survived, you got to the next level, the next level, the next level.” She said that with AI doing much of the grunt work, it is not clear firms would need as many entry-level positions. Singapore’s financial regulator sees the same shifts happening. Operations staff will need to become managers and supervisors of AI agents, Chia Der Jiun, managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said at the same panel. Banks will also need fewer fresh graduates for analysis and preparatory work, he said. The city-state has been preparing for these changes through training bank staff in AI skills as well as working with the universities to ensure its graduates are ready for the new world, Chia said. For young people however, Sneader said the upside goes beyond angling for a finance job. “There’s never been a better time to be an entrepreneur to create something,” he said, noting that fewer resources are needed to start a business nowadays. “That’s quite an exciting part of the future when we’re all spending too much time, perhaps worrying about the old world.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: US colleges could face a $70,000 fee for international students to work after graduation
events.summary: The DHS has proposed a new rule that might require US colleges to pay a fee for their international students' OPT work authorization. Bloomberg/Getty Images US universities might need to pay $70,000 or more to secure employment for their international graduates. The DHS has proposed new, restrictive rules for the Optional Training Period tied to the F-1 student visa. This is the latest in a slew of policy proposals aimed at slimming down the US's foreign workforce. US colleges might soon have to fork out cash to help their international graduates land jobs in the US. The Department of Homeland Security announced a proposed rule on Wednesday that would require schools to pay fees before recommending F-1 students for Optional Practical Training. OPT is a temporary work authorization for jobs linked to a student's field of study. It generally allows eligible international graduates to work in the US for up to a year; those with eligible STEM degrees can seek a 24-month extension. If it goes through, the proposal would require US schools to pay $70,000 for a student's initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for any extension. "Optional Practical Training was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labor, or a prize for those who game the system," a DHS spokesperson said in the release. "DHS is upskilling OPT to require foreign students to justify their worth to employers." An ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement to Business Insider that the DHS has encountered more employers, schools, and students "engaged in schemes to exploit current regulations for fraudulent purposes." The agency is seeking public comment on the proposal until November 9 before imposing any changes. If implemented, the collected fees would be deposited in the US Treasury, DHS said in the release. This proposal is the latest move by the Trump Administration to clamp down on foreign talent and protect American workers. Over the past year, several policy changes  have targeted workers on H-1B  visas, a non-immigrant work visa for skilled foreign workers. Last September, President Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring US companies to pay $100,000 for each new H-1B application. This order was struck down by a federal judge in June. A few months later, in August, the DHS issued a new proposal for a $103,265 fee for new H-1B petitions. This has not yet gone into effect. International students have already been caught up in the administration's visa policy changes. In July, the DHS announced a new rule that prevents students on the F-1 visa from staying in the US for more than 4 years, regardless of the length of the visa holder's course. This rule, too, was temporarily blocked in September by a federal judge. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Why single Ebola death in Kenya has prompted fears of wider African spread
events.summary: According to the WHO, the Kenyan patient first got sick in the DRC, where they had been living, and was treated there. Kenya reported its first death from a deadly strain of Ebola virus which had spread widely, starting in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) earlier this year. The Bundibugyo (BDBV) strain of Ebola was first detected in Uganda in 2007, according to the WHO. The ongoing outbreak in the DRC has killed at least 4,148 people out of 8,300 reported cases. It also spread across the border to Uganda, which had about 20 cases before being declared Ebola-free in July. list 1 of 4 DR Congo’s Ebola outbreak spreads to two new health zones, WHO says list 2 of 4 Funeral held for DR Congo politician killed after defending Ebola response list 3 of 4 Ebola cases surpass 8,000 as DRC struggles to control outbreak list 4 of 4 EU unlocks humanitarian aid for crises worldwide However, the person who died in Kenya from the disease had travelled from the DRC to Uganda over land before taking a flight to Nairobi, raising questions about Uganda’s status as “Ebola-free”, concerns about the rigidity of Kenya’s screening processes for people coming into the country and fears that Ebola may have spread further than previously thought. On Tuesday, the World Health Organization said the Kenyan government is now enhancing its disease surveillance with more targeted screening at high-risk points of entry. But Wolfgang Preiser, a professor and head of medical virology at Stellenbosch University in South Africa, explained that while efforts are being made to bring the outbreak under control, it has grown so much that “sheer numbers and the speed of spread are overwhelming for many systems. “I am not surprised that cases have reached other provinces in DRC and neighbouring countries. I expect that this will continue to happen until such time that the trajectory has been reversed and case numbers are in decline,” he told Al Jazeera. It is a serious, potentially deadly viral infection which can be caught when a person comes into contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person or wild animal, including fluid lingering on surfaces. People have also been known to contract the disease through eating contaminated meat. There have been many outbreaks in Central, West and East Africa. A West African outbreak from 2014 to 2016 killed at least 11,300 people of a reported 28,600 cases and accelerated the push to develop a vaccine. That was a different strain of the Ebola virus, known as Zaire, for which there is now a vaccine. The strain behind the latest outbreak is Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), which is believed to have been caused by a new transmission from animals to humans, before then spreading between humans, rather than by variants linked to earlier outbreaks. There is no vaccine for Bundibugyo. Symptoms can appear between two and 21 days after infection and can start suddenly with flu-like symptoms, including a high temperature, fatigue, and a headache. It can lead to internal and external bleeding, impaired liver and kidney function and organ failure. How did this case of Ebola reach Kenya? Kenyan Health Minister Aden Duale told reporters that the Kenyan patient, who has not been named, first became sick one month ago in the DRC, where they had been living for several years, and was treated there. On October 2, the patient travelled by road to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, via Beni, then flew to Nairobi, arriving the next day. After he arrived at the airport in Kenya, a relative and a friend took him to a hospital, where he was quickly isolated, and tests showed he had the virus, Duale said. Despite receiving care, the patient died from the virus on Monday and was buried on Tuesday in line with the country’s Ebola protocol. So far, health authorities in Kenya have identified 28 potential contacts, including family members and health workers who cared for the infected patient. Authorities are also separately tracking 23 passengers and four crew members from his flight, “with arrangements under way for appropriate follow-up and quarantine of people assessed to be at risk”, the WHO reported. Jean Bisimwa Nachega, a professor in infectious diseases at Stellenbosch University, emphasised that the virus does not “re spect national borders”. “Population mobility, displacement, cross-border trade, and fragile healthcare systems make containment particularly challenging. In eastern DRC, ongoing insecurity further complicates surveillance, contact tracing, and access to affected communities,” he told Al Jazeera. “Regional cooperation is therefore essential.” How did a sick patient get past screening in Uganda and Kenya? Passengers travelling to, from or through Uganda and Kenya must pass multiple airport temperature checks and complete at least two digital forms intended to flag any potential exposure to the virus in the DRC. Somehow, the infected person in this case was missed by these checks.

events.title: America shut out Chinese EVs. Britain welcomed them — and now faces a difficult choice
events.summary: Britain faces a finely balanced choice over whether to follow the EU in imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs, as it seeks closer post-Brexit ties while risking retaliation from Beijing. Chinese automakers are rapidly gaining ground in Britain. Analysts warn EV tariffs alone may not curb China’s advance, with hybrid sales also surging and Chinese brands benefiting from advantages in cost, supply chains and product development. The U.K. broke with the U.S. by opening its doors to China's electric vehicle juggernaut . Chinese EVs face only a 10% standard import duty in Britain, one of the largest major overseas markets without additional China-specific tariffs. Japan and Norway also lack them. It's in contrast to the U.S., where a 100% tariff effectively shut Chinese EVs out. The European Union , the U.K.'s biggest trading partner, has manufacturer-specific duties on Chinese EVs of up to 35.3%, in addition to a standard 10% import duty on all foreign cars. Now, the U.K. faces a difficult choice, as EU proposals may force it to impose tariffs to match the bloc's. At the weekend, The Sunday Times reported that U.K. Business Minister Jonathan Reynolds is considering matching the EU's levy on Chinese EVs to avoid the pain of so-called " Made in Europe " proposals, which could hurt domestic companies selling into the EU. A U.K. government spokesperson reiterated to CNBC that it had not imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs but added: "We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector's and UK's national interests." The Made in Europe legislation, part of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act , is designed to protect the bloc's industries from unfair international competition by prioritizing European-made goods. An EU official told the Financial Times in September that London would need to raise tariffs on Chinese EVs and align more closely with EU trade policy to avoid "Made in Europe" barriers. The decision is finely balanced, given Prime Minister Andy Burnham's desire to reset relations with the EU , which the U.K. formally left in 2020, and the likelihood of China responding with retaliatory measures. A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said it had expressed "serious concern" to Britain about the reports about potential tariffs. "China is firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products," a spokesperson said Tuesday. "We will continue to follow developments and respond accordingly," they said. Chinese automakers rapidly made inroads in the U.K. Chinese car brands have swiftly captured market share in the U.K. Analysis by JATO Dynamics found that registrations of Chinese automakers, or original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), across both battery-electric and hybrid powertrains, rose to 519,424 between the start of January and the end of August, lifting their total market share to 28.1%. That's up sharply from 12.9% in the same period in 2025. Hybrids accounted for the larger increase, adding 62,655 registrations versus 32,565 for battery-electric vehicles. "That matters for policy," Paul Hilton, head of retail at JATO Dynamics, told CNBC by email. "Tariffs aimed only at Chinese-built battery EVs could slow one part of the expansion, but would not address hybrid growth, vehicles made outside China or the underlying advantages in cost, product cadence and supply chains," Hilton said. "A durable UK response should pair any evidence-based trade remedy with incentives for local production, competitive energy and battery costs, charging infrastructure, skills and alignment with European market-access rules." The bestselling car in the U.K. last month was not a Tesla or a Ford — but the Jaecoo 7 from China. The mid-size SUV, nicknamed the “Temu Range Rover,” starts at about £29,000 ($38,350) in the U.K., compared with roughly £45,500 for a Land Rover Discovery Sport. The Jaecoo 7's nationwide sales climbed to 10,814 in September, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, outpacing the Tesla Model 3, Ford Puma and Kia Sportage. Rico Luman, senior sector economist for transport and logistics at ING, said the growing policy gap between Britain and the EU is leaving the U.K. with limited options, besides tariffs, if it wants to maintain a level playing field with the bloc. Speaking to CNBC by email, Luman said exclusion from the Made in Europe initiative could have “significant consequences” for existing businesses, making closer alignment with EU trade policy increasingly difficult to avoid. "It's generally quite remarkable that batteries from China are exempted from EU tariffs," Luman said. "At the same time this is logical as production in Europe isn't up to speed and Europe lacks the rare earth minerals and refinery capacity behind it," he added.

events.title: Elon Musk blames Indian 'oligarchs' for stalling Starlink launch
events.summary: The Indian telecom and internet service market is dominated by Mukesh Ambani's Jio and Sunil Mittal's Airtel, with both companies together holding over 80% market share. Musk said Starlink would enable high-speed, affordable internet connectivity in India for "those who cannot afford current prices." The Indian government said suggestions that its regulatory framework is unfair or discriminatory is "baseless and misconceived." SpaceX founder Elon Musk has accused vested interests of blocking the launch of his company's satellite internet service, Starlink, to protect their hold over consumers, calling it "a crime against the people of India" The country's telecom and internet service market is dominated by Reliance Chairman Mukesh Ambani's Jio and Sunil Mittal's Airtel , with both companies together holding over 80% market share . "We are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people," Musk said Wednesday stateside in a post on X, without naming his rivals. "You can guess who they are," he said. On Thursday, the Indian government said suggestions that its regulatory framework was unfair or discriminatory were " baseless and misconceived ." Licenses have been granted to three global satellite communication services providers, the government said, without naming the companies, adding that every licensee was "required to demonstrate compliance with security conditions." Starlink received the government license last year. In a second post, Musk said Starlink in India would "enable high-speed, affordable internet connectivity for those who cannot afford current prices." At present, Reliance Industries-owned Jio is the country's largest telecom operator and has been widely credited for slashing high-speed mobile data costs in the country since the company's launch a decade ago. In June, Jio Platforms announced plans to roll out low-orbit satellite communications in the country. Akash Ambani, the son of Mukesh, told shareholders that the company is partnering with leading global constellation providers to lease satellite capacity as it looks for a quick rollout of satellite connectivity. SpaceX last year had announced deals with Jio and India's second-largest telecom service provider, Bharti Airtel , to roll out Starlink internet services across India. There seems to have been little progress on that front, with Starlink yet to launch its service in the country. CNBC has reached out to Airtel and Reliance Industries for comments. There are 11,000 Starlink satellites currently in orbit that provide service to people in over 170 countries, Lauren Dreyer, SpaceX's Vice President of Starlink business operations, said while speaking at India Mobile Congress on Wednesday. Starlink works with government and private companies to close the digital divide by providing internet access to people in remote places, she said, adding that it has been "working for years" in India to do the same, and mentioned the company's memorandum of understanding with Airtel and Reliance Jio. Elon Musk's satellite internet services company is also facing pushback from regulators in India over security concerns, which the company has denied. In June, Bloomberg reported that regulators in New Delhi had frozen approvals for Starlink over fears that its terminals could be used despite the service not being licensed. The Indian government is concerned about a foreign player operating in a sensitive technology like satellite communications, and there are questions around how Starlink's terminals will be "geofenced" and whether the data will be localized, said Neil Shah, a partner at Counterpoint Research. Starlink is likely to get approval to launch around the time when Indian companies also develop their own satellite internet services, Shah said. If Starlink is launched without creating a "level playing field," it will dominate satellite communications services in India, he added.

events.title: Biggest coal-producing state fears impact of High Court emissions decision
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Queensland mining sector worried by implications of High Court emissions ruling The Queensland government says the state is the biggest producer of coal. ( Supplied ) The High Court on Wednesday ruled planning authorities in New South Wales needed to consider overseas emissions when approving a mine expansion. It's sparked concerns from the mining sector in Queensland – the country's largest coal-producing state. The industry says it's working through how the decision will impact the state, while the government says the laws are already strong and will strengthen them if needed. A High Court ruling that planning authorities needed to take overseas emissions into account when approving projects could spook investors, the industry fears. Yesterday, the High Court ruled in favour of a New South Wales community group which had been fighting the expansion of a coal mine in the Hunter Valley region. The court ruled the state's planning body had failed to consider the emissions of coal burnt overseas when approving the project. The High Court yesterday ruled in favour of a community group which fought to block an expansion of a coal mine in New South Wales. ( Supplied: Zoe Lonergan ) Speaking to the ABC, federal industry minister Tim Ayres was quick to downplay broader impacts, saying it was "squarely a NSW decision", which would be worked through by the state government. He stressed there would not be implications for either jobs or investment in the sector. "It is a High Court decision, but it's absolutely confined to the provisions of the New South Wales Act and the way … the planning authority did their work," he told the ABC. Resources minister Madeline King agreed it was a "pretty technical ruling" which she believed would not impact other states unless their planning legislation contained similar provisions. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli says the state is "open for business" when it comes to investment in mining. ( ABC News: Brendan Mounter ) Premier says Queensland laws 'bulletproof' In Queensland, Australia's largest coal producing state, Premier David Crisafulli sought to allay industry fears, saying the state's "already bulletproof" laws would be amended if needed in response to the ruling. "We have the best laws in the country, and we have the highest environmental standards and we are the most pro-mining government in the nation," he said. The state's peak industry association for the resources sector feels the ruling could have further-reaching impacts. Overseas emissions, known as 'scope three' emissions, are already considered by regulators, according to the Environmental Protection Act. National Coordinator at Lock the Gate Alliance Ellen Roberts welcomed the New South Wales ruling. She said it was important for decision makers to take these emissions into account because they impacted not only people overseas but people in Australia. But Queensland Resources Council chief executive Janette Hewson said she was concerned by any changes to the interpretation of laws and regulation because it increased risk in the sector. Janette Hewson is the chief executive of the Queensland Resources Council. ( ABC News: Erin Byrnes ) "We are very concerned that our international partners, whether they're investors or customers, will look at what's been happening in Australia," she said. Those concerns were echoed by the Minerals Council of Australia — the group going as far as to say the ruling would send "shudder's down everyone's spine" in the industry. Qld parliament to debate mining law changes Proposed laws in Queensland would restrict who can object to a mine. Its chief executive Tanya Constable described herself as "very concerned", and although she conceded the decision affected New South Wales, said it would set a "bad precedent" in other jurisdictions. The MCA's concerned the decision would spook investors, leading them to fund overseas projects rather than in Australia. Queensland senator Matt Canavan was even more scathing, imploring "all governments" to overturn the High Court's decision by passing laws through state or federal parliaments. He said it was "ridiculous" to have a situation where the viability of Australian mining projects, as well as jobs, were threatened because of emissions created overseas. Professor John Rolfe said it could be hypocritical for Australian mining projects to have to take overseas emissions into account.

events.title: Skims cofounder Emma Grede says leaders can be empathetic without treating employees like family
events.summary: Skims cofounder Emma Grede says tough decisions and empathy can go hand in hand. The Hapa Blonde/GC Images Emma Grede said leaders need to balance empathy with what's best for business. The SKIMS cofounder said being a boss doesn't mean treating everyone like family. However, she believes employees shouldn't be blindsided by tough conversations about their performance. Skims cofounder Emma Grede said good leaders won't let their employees get blindsided at work. During an appearance on the "Boardroom" podcast hosted by Rich Kleiman, the entrepreneur discussed how she approaches difficult decisions as a leader. To Grede, effective leadership is about balancing empathy with what the business needs. "You can, at once, be an extremely empathetic leader and have the needs of your team and your people at the absolute forefront of what you're doing," Grede told Kleiman. "And yet, what you must have is an enterprise mentality to do what is right for the business." At the end of the day, a company also needs to be financially healthy before it can properly support its people, Grede said. As founder and CEO, she said her first responsibility is to make decisions that serve the business, even when that means acknowledging that some employees may no longer be the right fit as it grows. "As the leader, you have to make difficult decisions," she said. "It is not my job to be your friend. It is not my job to treat everybody as though this were a family. But that doesn't mean that you miss empathy or that you treat people badly." Grede recalled a lesson from Mellody Hobson, the former chair of the Starbucks board, who taught her that being honest does not require being harsh or brutal. As the cofounder of several consumer brands , including denimwear brand Good American and sports fashion brand Off Season, Grede said she works in an environment where "radical honesty" is required. That means employees are rarely caught off guard by feedback about their performance, Grede said — and because those conversations happen regularly, "nobody's surprised." "It is not the job of me or any other woman in a position of leadership to have to kind of cottonball everybody along the way," she said. "We run a business just like anybody else, and that is with an enterprise mentality to do the best things that are right for the company," Grede added. Beyond her approach to leadership, Grede has also been candid about the demanding work ethic and level of commitment she believes are necessary to build a successful career and business. In May 2025, Grede said she sees it as a red flag when job candidates talk about work-life balance . "Work-life balance is your problem. It isn't your employer's responsibility," she said. In April, she took a firm stance against remote work, calling it "career suicide " and saying that being around colleagues can be especially valuable early in a career. Grede's approach to work and motherhood also sparked discussion earlier this year when she described herself as a " max three-hour mum " on weekends in an April interview with The Wall Street Journal. events.title: Protesters in Colombia rally against ties with Israel
events.summary: Hundreds took to the streets of Bogota to protest the ongoing genocide in Gaza. Protesters have rallied in Colombia’s capital opposing the new far-right government’s policy towards Israel. Hundreds took to the streets of Bogota on Wednesday to protest against the ongoing genocide in Gaza and the Colombian government’s decision to restore diplomatic and economic relations with Israel. list 1 of 3 Drone attacks by Colombian armed groups more than double in early 2026 list 2 of 3 Colombia eases gun restrictions despite fears of more violence list 3 of 3 Colombia extradites leader of armed group to US in shift towards Washington The protesters, who began their rally in front of the Israeli embassy in Bogota, criticised President Abelardo de la Espriella’s decision to open a new Colombian embassy in Jerusalem. The rally marked three years since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, which were followed by Israel launching a genocidal war on Gaza. “When diplomatic relations with Israel were broken off, the message was that we would not be a nation complicit in their atrocities,” Nicolas Isaza, who took part in the protest, told Al Jazeera. “Today our government is no longer drawing a line against the atrocities being committed in Palestine,” he added. De la Espriella, who was sworn in as president in August, promised close relations with the US and Israel during his election campaign as a way to combat armed groups in his country. Colombia’s government has since restored relations with Israel after former President Gustavo Petro, who criticised Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, severed diplomatic relations and halted Israeli arms imports. The Colombian government also recognised Israel’s claim of sovereignty over the occupied Syrian Golan Heights, just days after the new president took power.

UK Foreign ⁠Minister ⁠Ed Miliband says consulate building in occupied East Jerusalem will not be closing as Israeli deadline expires. British Foreign ⁠Secretary ⁠Ed Miliband says the United Kingdom’s consulate in occupied ⁠East Jerusalem will continue operations on a smaller scale and be known as a “UK mission” after Israel ordered it to close in a diplomatic row. Israel had ordered the consulate to be shut down by Thursday over the UK’s plans to impose sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which are illegal under international law. list 1 of 3 Palestine weekly: Olive harvest opens under assault list 2 of 3 ‘Not the act of a friend’: Israel’s deadline to close UK consulate nears list 3 of 3 How genocide in Gaza pulled Britons into the Palestine movement Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said on Thursday that Israel has authorised the UK to continue to operate from the building in a limited scope with seven diplomats. He said 20 diplomats, including the British consul general, were ending their assignments and would leave Israel. Earlier, journalists from the Reuters news agency saw ‌workers remove a plaque reading “British Consulate General” from the building on Thursday as well as another sign for its consular section. The UK flag was still flying over the building. Miliband said his country does not accept that Israel has the legal right to close the consulate. The consulate is in a part of Jerusalem that Israel captured in a ‌1967 war and has occupied ever since. Miliband said in a statement that after discussions with Israel, “our Consulate General building will not be closing, and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from today.” Miliband said the mission “will continue to deliver vital services and our work with the Palestinian people”. Thursday marks 30 days since Israel ordered the closure of the consulate. The move was in response to the UK’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, including a ban on importing goods produced there. “We have established a clear principle – no action can be taken against Israel without Israel taking appropriate retaliatory measures,” Saar wrote in a post on X. Israel has been adamant the consulate will close even as the UK has sought to keep it open, including sending the country’s top national security adviser to Israel last week for talks. The UK’s presence in the city dates back almost 200 years, long before the state of Israel was established in 1948. The closure order does not affect the UK’s embassy in Tel Aviv, which handles diplomatic relations with Israel’s government. The consulate in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East Jerusalem handles the UK’s relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem, ‌the occupied West ⁠Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians. Despite the current strains, the ⁠UK and Israel are close economic, security and intelligence partners.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts St Andrew's Hospital has notified government authorities of a data breach with an undisclosed number of individuals affected. St Andrew's Hospital has reported a data breach "affecting a group of individuals". It says the individuals affected and federal privacy and cyber security agencies have been notified. SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said he is expecting to be briefed on the breach later on Thursday. An Adelaide private hospital has notified individuals and cyber security authorities of a data breach of personal information. In a limited statement, St Andrew's Hospital on Thursday morning confirmed it had been investigating a breach of personal information affecting "a group of individuals". The precise number of people impacted, and the circumstances around the breach, are currently unknown. St Andrew's Hospital did not confirm the numbers or nature of the breach in response to questions from the ABC, however its chief information officer Nathan Crettenden said an internal investigation "identified that a subset of data from our servers was downloaded". "As soon as the incident was identified, our team took our systems offline as a precaution, worked to secure our environment and strengthen our security protocols, and engaged specialist forensic experts to conduct an investigation," said Mr Crettenden. "We are taking all reasonable steps to limit the impact of the incident and improve our security posture in response to the incident." Agencies, affected individuals notified In the statement, the hospital's CEO Angela McCabe said an "investigation into the nature and extent of the incident has now progressed to the point where we can communicate directly with affected individuals, in line with our regulatory obligations". She said affected individuals were provided information and support as to how they can protect their personal information. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) and the Australian Cyber Security Centre have been notified of the breach. Ms McCabe said the hospital was working with government agencies to "apply additional protective measures, to help detect and prevent suspicious and fraudulent activity". St Andrew's Hospital says it has notified affected individuals ( ABC News ) Under Australia's Privacy Act, entities covered by Notifiable Data Breach scheme are required to report breaches to the OAIC that are likely to result in "serious harm" to affected individuals. According to the OAIC, information breaches that could carry serious harm can include the exposure of information about a person's health, documents commonly used for identity fraud and financial information. South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said the state government expected to be briefed on the matter later today. "We expect to be updated on exactly what's occurred here and whether or not things have occurred of a criminal nature that might be subject of the South Australian criminal code," Mr Malinauskas said. "That will be of interest to us. The cyber security dynamic globally is clearly under challenge and under threat and it will be important that our law enforcement agencies assess the situation.

events.title: Jacob Coxon says this is why pacing the frontier might not work
events.summary: AI researcher Jacob Coxon said pacing the frontier might not be effective. Adam Gray/Getty Images Jacob Coxon, the Anthropic researcher who quit last month, said slowing AI progress may not be effective. He said he was "90%" certain that Chinese spies had infiltrated US AI labs and could steal progress. AI chiefs called last month for a slower pace of AI development to introduce more checks and balances. Jacob Coxon , the poster child for AI doom and gloom, said there's a reason that pacing the frontier may not work. Coxon, who quit Anthropic last month after accusing it and OpenAI of "gambling with lives," said on businessman Patrick Bet-David's podcast that slowing US AI development may be ineffective because Chinese spies might have infiltrated US labs. He said he was "90%" certain about the presence of Chinese spies at OpenAI and Anthropic, who could steal the labs' progress at any time, and "catch up the lead." "So if we continue, they're going to have access to it. If we don't continue, China's going to create it themselves. So either way, China's eventually going to have access to it," he said to Bet-David in the interview released on Tuesday. However, when Bet-David asked him for details about who they might be, Coxon said he was "not trying to, like, start a witch hunt" and didn't name anyone. A source familiar with Anthropic told Business Insider that there is no evidence to support this claim. Anthropic treats foreign intelligence threats as a serious risk and maintains rigorous personnel vetting, strict access controls, and insider risk monitoring. Coxon and representatives from OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider. Coxon added in the interview that another reason China's AI capabilities are progressing is the use of distillation attacks, a problem that labs like Anthropic have mentioned several times. Distillation attacks involve using advanced AI models to train and improve the capabilities of less advanced models, and Anthropic accused Chinese labs such as Alibaba, Moonshot, DeepSeek, and Zhipu of launching millions of these attacks over the summer. In another part of the interview, he also compared Anthropic staff to worker ants who are "willing to sacrifice themselves for the good of the mission," which is achieving superintelligence. Coxon's interview come after executives at major AI labs, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and xAI CEO Elon Musk, have talked about slowing AI development and adding checks and guardrails into the process. Altman said in a September X post that progress at OpenAI "has been rapid and will continue to be," but will be slowed down slightly to make AI safer. However, many have criticized the call to pace the frontier, saying that it could build hype around Anthropic and OpenAI's much-anticipated IPOs and disadvantage smaller AI rivals. events.title: Prudential Japan executives take pay cuts over staff misconduct involving customers’ money
events.summary: President Hiromitsu Tokumaru and two others will take a 30% reduction in compensation for three months to take responsibility for the matter. PHOTO: JAPAN NEWS/ASIA NEWS NETWORK Prudential Life Japan will cut pay for three top executives after a report found widespread staff misconduct that caused more than 3.1 billion yen in customer losses. The committee blamed weak governance and a commission-led sales model. Prudential will revise pay and evaluation systems to support long-term customer relationships and compliance. Japan’s regulator may punish the insurer, while the company keeps its new-sales halt as it overhauls reforms. The scandal adds to wider trust problems in Japan’s insurance industry. Top executives at Prudential Financial’s Japan unit will take pay cuts after a panel of outside experts issued a report on widespread employee misconduct. President Hiromitsu Tokumaru and two others will take a 30% reduction in compensation for three months to take responsibility for the matter, the company said in a statement on Oct 8 . The investigative committee found that issues at the unit of the US insurance group, Prudential Life, stemmed from structural problems in its governance framework and business model. The case is the latest in a series of scandals to hit Japan’s insurance industry in recent years, undermining confidence at a time when households are looking to invest more of their savings. The country’s financial regulator is considering penalising Prudential Life with measures including a temporary business suspension order, according to a source with knowledge of the matter. Prudential Life established the committee after disclosing alleged misconduct by more than 100 current and former sales employees that caused more than 3.1 billion yen (S$25.1 million) in customer losses. Cases ranged from staff pitching fictitious investments to borrowing money from clients. Evaluation and compensation systems reinforced incentives to prioritise short-term results, the company said in the statement. The company will revise these to encourage behavior that emphasises long-term customer relationships, compliance and sound sales practices, it said. Prudential Life has voluntarily halted new life insurance sales since February to focus on overhauling its governance and sales practices. It extended the initial 90-day suspension until early November, saying it needed more time to complete the reforms. Top executives are scheduled to hold a media briefing later on Oct 8 . Prudential Life, which began operations in Japan in 1988, has carved out a niche in a market long dominated by domestic players including Nippon Life Insurance and Daiichi Life Group. It relies on a relatively small sales force known as “life planners”, who target affluent customers including business owners and doctors and offer highly tailored products and financial planning services. Traditional Japanese insurers, by contrast, employ much larger sales forces that have historically sold more standardised products through community-based, face-to-face networks. Prudential’s sales representatives built a reputation for aggressive selling. At a news conference in January, company executives said a compensation structure heavily dependent on commissions had distorted incentives and contributed to breaches of internal rules. In its annual policy priorities released in September, the Financial Services Agency said it would “take rigorous supervisory action” against misconduct by insurance companies. Three years ago, the authorities penalised the country’s largest property-and-casualty insurers for colluding on insurance premiums for corporate clients. More recently, employees of several major life insurers were found to have mishandled data. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Oil prices rise on potential US strikes on Iran before midterm elections
events.summary: Oil prices jumped on Thursday after reports about Pentagon plans for US strikes on Iran that could be launched before the midterm elections amid continued Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent , the benchmark for two-thirds of the world's oil, climbed nearly 3.77 per cent to $104 a barrel at 11.18am UAE time, after falling below the $100 mark earlier this week. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, rose 3.51 per cent to $91.38 a barrel. Crude prices have been hovering above the $100 per barrel mark despite a lull in the US military campaign. US President Donald Trump, who is facing domestic backlash over the war, earlier indicated that the US would resume strikes only after the midterms. However, rising Iranian attacks in recent weeks on oil and gas tankers in the strait may force Mr Trump’s hand. The Atlantic on Tuesday reported that the US Defence Department was identifying targets for attacks in Iran. The size of potential strikes, if the US administration was to proceeds with hostilities ahead of polls, was still being discussed, it said, quoting unnamed US officials. The US may choose to conduct a limited military campaign and follow it with a larger operation after polls conclude next month, The Atlantic report added. Traffic through the strait, the narrow waterway through which a fifth of the worlds oil and gas passed before the conflict broke out, has remained thin. Strikes on tankers climbed to their highest weekly rate since the conflict began on February 28. The number of vessels transiting the strait fell to the lowest in more than two ⁠months, according to shipping data from analytics firm Kpler. Seven commodity ships passed through the strait on Tuesday, the ⁠lowest figure since July 23, data showed. In the latest attack, a tanker north of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, causing casualties, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Wednesday.
