events.title: WA treasurer surprised by High Court outcome and seeking advice
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts What a High Court decision on a NSW coal mine could mean for WA gas projects Industry bodies in WA have raised concerned about a High Court ruling relating to a NSW coal project. ( ABC News: Chris Lewis ) A landmark ruling in the High Court has found planning authorities in New South Wales are required to consider global climate change impacts when approving local fossil fuel projects. Industry bodies and consultants are concerned the ruling could have a broader impact on investment in the resource-rich state of WA. WA Premier Roger Cook said his government would need to look closely at the implications. A High Court ruling in New South Wales has Western Australia's energy industry "deeply concerned" about future investment in the resource-rich state. The ruling stymied the planned expansion of MACH Energy's coal mine after it had already been approved by NSW planning authorities in 2022, after three out of five judges ruled in favour of a community group, Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG). The ruling found the planning authorities were required to take into account the emissions caused by using the coal MACH would export, otherwise known as the project's scope 3 emissions. While the ruling is an interpretation of NSW planning laws, the energy industry is concerned effects could be felt on the other side of the country. In WA, Woodside's $30 billion Browse gas proposal, which would produce more than 11 million tonnes of gas per year, is still being considered by state and federal environmental bodies. WA Treasurer Rita Saffioti said the High Court's assessment came as a surprise, and said the government was seeking urgent legal advice. Rita Saffioti says the High Court decision in New South Wales came as a surprise. ( ABC News: James Carmody ) "Everyone was slightly shocked by the decision, [particularly] a state like WA, which continues to develop significant resources to help our trading partners deal with their emissions," she said. "I'm no legal expert, but it was made in relation to a planning decision in NSW. "The question for us is under what guidelines the High Court made their decision, and whether that impacts every state or just the NSW planning framework." Ms Saffioti said it was likely the decision would require a federal government response. "The whole nation will need to look at work we can continue to support resources development," she said. Independent oil and gas consultant Jeanette Roberts said the decision affirmed industry fears of "lawfare". "One of the issues that concerns the industry in general is this lawfare of an approval being given, and then an opportunity for it to be challenged, and the approval rescinded," she said. "International investors will come because they believe that there's certainty and a rule of law and understanding what the rules and ground rules are. "That certainly swings the pendulum away from that." Aaron Morey says the implications of the decision need to be taken seriously. ( ABC News: Kimberley Putland ) Chamber of Minerals and Energy WA chief executive Aaron Morey said it was "deeply concerning". "If we shoot ourselves in the foot and we don't allow the development of these sorts of projects, then what you'll find is that new projects will spring up in other countries with lower environmental controls and standards," Mr Morey said. Mr Morey said it was important that everyone took the implications of the decision as seriously as possible. "Those are the sorts of issues that we need to more deeply understand," he said. The Conservation Council of WA executive director Matt Roberts said it was common sense for all the environmental and climate impacts of a project to be considered in the approvals process. "Australia can't wash its hands of the emissions caused when coal, oil or gas that is extracted here ends up being burnt overseas," he said. "Gas export projects like Woodside's Browse proposal at Scott Reef risk massive climate damage because of their scope 3 emissions. "We've always said that state and federal governments need to consider these scope 3 emissions when assessing these projects." Johnson Legal director Elaine Johnson said while it was an interpretation of NSW laws, the decision would be relevant to courts in other jurisdictions. "The High Court of Australia has issued its first climate ruling, so obviously the content of that decision is going to be relevant to other courts in different jurisdictions around the country, including, I would assume, Western Australia," Ms Johnson said.

events.title: South Korea pledges legal action over alleged fuel exports to Russia
events.summary: Ukrainian reports of South Korean fuel exports to Russia come amid strained tensions between Seoul and Kyiv. South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said the government will take legal action over illegal fuel shipments to Russia if allegations from an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are confirmed. The Foreign Ministry said on Thursday it had not confirmed whether South Korean fuel, including diesel, had been exported to Russia. list 1 of 3 S Korea demands Ukraine apology over disclosure of N Korea’s POW transfer list 2 of 3 Why South Korea is demanding an apology from Ukraine over North Korean PoWs list 3 of 3 Row between Ukraine, South Korea mounts over North Korean POWs It added that exports of some products, such as diesel and jet fuel for commercial purposes, were not included in a South Korean exports control list to Russia. On Wednesday, the South Korean presidential office dismissed a statement by Vladyslav Vlasiuk, an adviser to the Ukrainian president on sanctions policy, that 176,000 tonnes of fuel were shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers in July and August. Ukraine’s top sanctions official said the alleged findings run counter to South Korea’s sanctions policy towards Russia. “Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, our government has consistently implemented sanctions and export controls against Russia in close cooperation with the international community,” South Korean presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said on Wednesday, according to the Yonhap news agency. “We ask that Ukraine also refrain from distorting the relevant policies of the Republic of Korea without sufficient verification of the facts and making public remarks that can damage international trust,” she added. Relations between South Korea and Ukraine have been strained for the past couple of weeks after Seoul accused Zelenskyy of having “unilaterally disclosed” to the United Nations General Assembly that Kyiv had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. Seoul Korea demanded an official apology from Kyiv, claiming the Ukrainian president had breached a non-disclosure agreement. Kyiv said no such agreement was in place. Pyongyang and Moscow, meanwhile, have deep ties, with the two countries having signed a mutual defence treaty in 2024. According to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, about 14,000 to 15,000 North Korean soldiers were sent to support Russia’s war efforts against Ukraine. North Korea and South Korea remain technically at war because the 1950–1953 Korean War ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

events.title: Hormuz traffic hits lowest level in two months as tanker attacks surge
events.summary: ​The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz fell to the lowest in more than two ⁠months after attacks on tankers in the key waterway reached their highest last week since the start of the ​ Iran war , shipping data showed. Seven commodity ships passed through the strait on Tuesday, for the ⁠lowest figure since July 23, data from analytics firm Kpler showed. “Crude crossing the strait fell ​27 per cent ⁠from a wartime high the week ‌before, to at least 10.1 million barrels a day,” Kpler analysts Emmanuel Belostrino and Yui Torikata ​wrote in a note on October 6. “That is back to its September average, but 74 per cent of its prewar level.” Most of the fall was in ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, where cargoes move between tankers, they added. However, exports from the Gulf of Oman coast and the Red Sea rose to 6.7 million bpd, more than twice prewar levels, analysts said, making up for lost supply from Hormuz. This helped keep overall exports of Middle East crude at the prewar level, they said. The number of vessels transiting the strait edged up to 10 on Wednesday, but was well short of the daily tally of more than 20 on Sunday and Monday, the data showed. More vessels entered the strait than exited in the past two days. The figures exclude vessels crossing with their ​Automatic Identification System transponders turned off to avoid detection. LSEG data of all ‌vessels crossing the strait showed eight ⁠on Tuesday, evenly divided between entries and exits, ​down from the previous day's 14. These included five oil tankers and the liquefied ​natural gas tanker ‌Al Mafyar which loaded at Ras Laffan in Qatar and was set to head for Port Qasim ⁠in Pakistan, LSEG added. Attacks on tankers sailing through Hormuz hit their highest last week of ⁠any week since the Iran war began, maritime security sources tracking incidents said, as Gulf producers made a bigger export push. In the latest incident, projectiles struck a tanker 94km north of Qatar's Madinat ash Shamal, with casualties reported, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said ​on Wednesday. Before the February 28 start of the Iran war, about 125 large commercial vessels went through the strait each per day, comprising tankers, gas carriers, bulkers and container vessels. Their cargoes accounted for a fifth of global supplies of crude oil and liquefied natural gas.

events.title: Exhibits A, B, and C that Ben Affleck knows more about AI than you
events.summary: Ben Affleck talked AI, Python, and convolutional neural networks in a recent interview. Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic/Getty Images Ben Affleck showed off his AI expertise in a GQ interview, discussing Python and neural networks. Affleck has gone viral for AI takes before and sold his AI film-tech startup to Netflix this year. "He was the real Good Will Hunting all along," one X user wrote. Ben Affleck is once again surprising people with his AI chops. The movie star conveyed an impressive understanding of generative AI systems in an interview with GQ's "One More Question" series published Tuesday, in which Affleck said he could write roughly in Python , a popular programming language, and discussed the workings of convolutional neural networks. "I've always been kind of into computers since I was young. Then, when film started to move from analog film to digital, I became more interested in that aspect of it," Affleck said, adding the "visual-effects workflow for many years has included machine learning." He then spent several minutes explaining concepts behind modern AI systems, using words and phrases that are likely unfamiliar to those who don't know AI terminology: transformers, tensors, and edge detection. "I appreciate the way you're talking to me like I understand any of it," interviewer Zach Baron joked in response. "I'm really flattered and honored by that, so thank you." The clip of Affleck talking about AI went viral, sparking surprise, delight, and jokes. "Turns out he was the real Good Will Hunting all along," one X user wrote, referring to the 1997 film Affleck wrote with Matt Damon, who plays the genius Will Hunting in the movie. "TLDR. Ben Afflick admits the movie 'The Accountant' was actually semi-autobiographical," another user said, referencing the 2016 movie where Affleck plays a math savant. For those paying attention, Affleck's proficiency with AI shouldn't come as much of a surprise. The actor has sparked "Ben Affleck knows AI?!" reactions several times over the past few years. He also sold InterPositive , the AI film-tech startup he quietly founded in 2022, to Netflix earlier this year for a reported $587 million, though Affleck said in the GQ interview that figure was "not right." Ben Affleck's AI knowledge has made headlines before Affleck first drew attention for his AI prowess in November 2024 at a CNBC investor summit, where he explained  AI's limitations  in filmmaking. "AI is a a craftsman at best. Craftsmen can learn to, you know, make Stickley furniture by sitting down next to somebody and seeing what their technique is and imitating them. That's how large video models, large language models, basically work: a library of vectors of meaning and transformers that interpret in context," Affleck said. "But they're just cross-pollinating things that exist. Nothing new is created." "Craftsman is knowing how to work, art is knowing when to stop. And I think knowing when to stop is going to be a very difficult thing for AI to learn because it's taste," he said. A clip of Affleck's remarks went viral on X, racking up over 20 million views. The actor again went viral in January this year for comments he made about AI on "The Joe Rogan Experience" podcast. Affleck said much of the fear and existential dread connected to AI comes from "people who are trying to justify valuations around companies." "Where they go, 'We're going to change everything. In two years, there's going to be no more work.' Well, the reason they're saying that is because they need to ascribe a valuation for investment that can warrant the capex spend they're going to make on these data centers," he said. In addition to going viral, a clip of the interview was praised on X by Michael Burry , the "Big Short" investor and AI boom skeptic who had voiced similar doubts about some of the AI hype. "Ben Affleck is clearly a smart guy. So this does not surprise me. It sounds familiar and on point," Burry said at the time. While fans may continually be surprised by Affleck's AI knowledge, the actor may be used to people underestimating him. He told GQ that after he recently won "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire," the underlying tone in the texts he got was "slight bafflement." "Like, 'How the fuck does this guy do that?'" events.title: Trump says he is not keen on a deal with Iran as U.S. reportedly prepares for 'massive bombing'
events.summary: The U.S. president and his national security team have discussed possibly resuming large-scale U.S. military operations in the coming weeks: NBC News. Trump has seen his approval ratings fall to a record low amid concerns over high living costs spurred by soaring gasoline and diesel prices. Crude oil prices have remained elevated even as Middle East exports have been recovering to near pre-war levels, according to Kpler. U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he no longer wants a deal with Iran, following reports that the U.S. military is preparing for possible strikes against the country, likely before the midterm election. "I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop," Trump said at a campaign rally with Republican candidates in San Antonio, Texas, late Wednesday stateside. Steve Witkoff, the U.S. special envoy to the Middle East, has been working on the deal and "doing very well," Trump added. The U.S. president and his national security team have discussed possibly resuming large-scale U.S. military operations in the coming weeks, NBC News reported Wednesday, citing a U.S. official and another person with knowledge of the discussions. Axios reported earlier in the day that a possible resumption in armed conflict could include "massive bombing" of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets, adding that military aggression could influence the outcome of the upcoming midterm elections. Earlier this week, Trump said the biggest problem for Washington was that nobody knew who was running Iran during the talks to end the conflict. Iranian officials rejected those claims, saying "the problem is actually the opposite." Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeli Baghaei pointed to the "contradictory positions and mixed messaging from U.S. officials." Crude oil prices have remained elevated even as Middle East exports have been recovering to near pre-war levels, according to Kpler. Combined crude volumes exiting the Gulf, excluding Iran, plus volumes from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, were around pre-conflict levels of 18.5 million barrels per day (Mbd). "Normalisation no longer needs to wait for a deal," said Matt Wright, lead freight analyst at Kpler, forecasting "slower, uneven normalisation" under continued conflict, with traffic recovering through operational adaptation rather than waiting for a diplomatic trigger.

events.title: Samsung flags $95.7 billion profit on AI boom, highest quarterly for any tech company
events.summary: Samsung’s shares rose 0.3% in early trade, outperforming a 0.1% fall in the benchmark KOSPI. Samsung said quarterly profit could top 100 trillion won, a first for a tech company, as AI chip demand pushed memory sales and prices higher. The boom should keep memory supply tight into 2028, and Samsung faces risks from higher costs, a strong won, Chinese rivals and possible US tariffs. Strong memory earnings may help Samsung’s chip arm, but they also raise costs for phones and electronics, while its foundry unit still struggles and seeks more demand. SEOUL – Samsung Electronics on Oct 8 projected its quarterly profit would top 100 trillion won (S$95.7 billion), a world first for a technology company, estimating a nearly ninefold jump in third-quarter earnings as booming demand for AI chips drove strong memory sales. The world’s largest memory chipmaker estimated an operating profit of 107.4 trillion won for the July-September period, slightly ahead of an LSEG SmartEstimate of 106.1 trillion won, a regulatory filing showed. The forecast marks Samsung’s fourth straight quarter of record operating profit, underscoring a deepening global memory chip shortage as AI infrastructure investment outpaces supply growth, which has driven chip prices up sharply. Samsung and Micron expected the imbalance to persist into 2028, although rising costs, Chinese competition and potential US semiconductor tariffs pose risks to the longer-term earnings outlook. “There were uncertainties surrounding Samsung’s earnings as analysts cut their estimates, but the results turned out to be better than expected,” said Lee Jae-won, an analyst at Yuanta Securities. Lee said investors would also be closely watching for details of Samsung’s shareholder return policy during its earnings call later in October . Prices have soared owing to the tight supply of conventional DRAM and NAND chips as well as growing demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), essential for processing vast amounts of data for AI applications. Third-quarter revenue would likely rise 127% to 195 trillion won from 2025 , Samsung said. The company will release detailed results, including a breakdown of earnings by business division, on Oct 29. Memory chips are expected to account for the bulk of the earnings improvement. Analysts expect supply to continue to lag demand, with the imbalance potentially widening in 2027 as AI-related demand absorbs an increasing share of global memory capacity. Against that backdrop, conventional DRAM bit shipments are expected to remain broadly flat because of limited inventories, while HBM shipments could rise sharply from the previous quarter on strong demand for HBM4, analysts said. Douglas Kim of Douglas Research Advisory estimated that Samsung’s HBM bit shipments expanded by close to 50% quarter-over-quarter in the third quarter. US rival Micron, a key supplier of high-bandwidth memory to Nvidia, said the chip market could be tighter in 2027 and 2028 than in 2026 , after forecasting quarterly revenue well above estimates on Oct 7 . A stronger South Korean won may offset some of the gains by reducing the value of dollar-denominated overseas sales when converted into local currency. The memory chip boom also presents a challenge for Samsung’s other businesses, particularly its smartphone and consumer electronics divisions, which face mounting pressure from higher component costs. Higher memory prices, while benefiting Samsung’s semiconductor arm, are raising costs for its own smartphones and other electronic devices, squeezing margins in those businesses. Meanwhile, Samsung’s contract chipmaking, or foundry, business is expected to remain loss-making because of the burden of fixed costs and still-low utilisation rates, analysts said. However, utilisation is expected to improve over the next several quarters, supported by stronger demand for advanced manufacturing processes. Samsung has been seeking to narrow the gap with industry leader TSMC in advanced contract chip manufacturing. In a potential boost to its foundry ambitions, AMD chief executive officer ​Lisa Su said on Oct 7 that the US chipmaker continues to explore partnership opportunities with Samsung in the memory and foundry businesses. Chinese competition, US tariffs cloud outlook Despite the favourable supply backdrop for Samsung and other memory makers, the longer-term expansion of Chinese memory-chip makers remains a potential challenge. For now, Chinese memory makers are also expected to remain more dependent on domestic customers, including Chinese AI-chip developers and PC and smartphone manufacturers. Analysts said, however, US restrictions on China’s access to advanced chipmaking equipment continue to limit how quickly Chinese producers can expand. Another uncertainty is the prospect of US semiconductor tariffs, as Washington pushes chipmakers to expand manufacturing capacity in the United States.

events.title: Anthropic's secret weapon is its CEO's charm, one of its earliest investors says
events.summary: Business Insider's Ben Bergman speaks with Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy at Tech Insider: Growth Mode. Charles Rollet/Business Insider Anthropic's CEO has charisma where it really matters: with AI researchers, an early investor says. Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy backed Anthropic when it was worth $4.1 billion. Anthropic is now aiming to go public at a $2 trillion valuation. Anthropic has a secret to its success, says one of its earliest investors: the aura of curly-haired CEO Dario Amodei. Speaking at Tech Insider: Growth Mode, sponsored by Fidelity, in San Francisco on Wednesday, Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy said that Amodei can charm AI researchers with his intelligence and mission-driven attitude. Amodei may not have quite the same type of energy as Silicon Valley's master salesman, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Still, Amodei's brainiac vibes chime well with AI researchers, Murphy said. Murphy said that Anthropic has been able to outperform because of Amodei's "commitment to culture" and being able to bring on researchers who want to work for him. "He's like them, and he's one of the best," Murphy told Business Insider's Ben Bergman. Amodei was an early OpenAI researcher who left in 2020 over safety concerns to cofound Anthropic. Since then, Anthropic has become the largest AI startup by valuation — it could soon go public at a $2 trillion valuation . Menlo Ventures first invested in Anthropic in 2023, when it was valued at $4.1 billion, and has invested in every follow-on round. Murphy said that Amodei wins people over by doing spontaneous things, like popping in unannounced on Zoom calls. In one investor call with Anthropic cofounder Tom Brown, that's exactly what happened, Murphy said. "Then all of a sudden, Dario pops in. It was just like, 'Oh' — and the energy went way up," he said. "There's just a charm about him, maybe like a boyish charm, especially back then. He's just a very curious person, incredibly smart." Overall, Murphy remains optimistic about Anthropic, despite its high valuation, financial losses, the threat of Chinese open-source models, and concerns about AI safety. "If I could buy more, I would," he said of Anthropic's stock. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles off north coast of Qatar, UKMTO says
events.summary: British maritime agency has recently reported a rise in attacks on vessels in the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz. A number of casualties have been reported after a tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency has announced. The vessel was hit by several projectiles 94 kilometres (58 miles) north of Madinat ash Shamal, UKMTO said on Wednesday. The incident comes as the British maritime agency reported a recent rise in attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. list 1 of 3 Hormuz ship attacks surge: Are increased oil exports sustainable? list 2 of 3 Has Russia’s fuel crisis given Iranian oil an opening in Central Asia? list 3 of 3 US sets new demands for Iran deal: What are they? UKMTO did not say how many people were killed or injured in this latest attack, adding that authorities were investigating. It did not specify the origin of the ship. An attack on a vessel in the middle of the Gulf is unusual. The Maritime Executive, a publication specialising in commercial shipping, said it was the first reported attack on a tanker in the western half of the Gulf in weeks. Qatar has not commented on the reported attack, which falls within its exclusive economic zone. Vessels have more commonly been targeted in the strategically important Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway linking the Gulf with the Gulf of Oman. Before the United States-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, the strait typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day, and shipments through it accounted for about 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies. In retaliation for US-Israeli attacks, Iran effectively closed the strait, while Washington has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports. UKMTO said on Tuesday that there had been nine attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz this month, representing half of the September total in the waterway and the Gulf combined. Despite the attacks, oil exports from the Middle East have risen to, and according to provisional data even surpassed , pre-war levels in recent weeks. The seven-day moving average of Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on September 30, compared with about 18 million bpd on average in the 12 months before the war, according to Kpler, a data firm.

events.title: Oil rises as Middle East supply concerns persist amid shipping attacks
events.summary: Threats to oil shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz have increased in October as the US-Israeli conflict with Iran enters its eighth month. Oil prices rose as shipping attacks in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz kept supply fears high, with Brent at US$101.53 and WTI at US$89.39. A tanker north of Qatar was hit by multiple projectiles, causing casualties, while Gulf producers kept exporting oil despite higher risk and costs. US stock data supported prices, with crude inventories down 3.2 million barrels and diesel stocks also falling, Reuters said. Oil prices rose on Oct 8 on persistent worries about supply from the key Middle East producing region amid an increase in attacks on shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures rose US$1.33, or 1.33%, at US$101.53 a barrel by 0116 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures gained US$1.11, or 1.26%, to US$89.39. Prices settled lower on Oct 7 after the International Energy Agency agreed to accelerate the release of oil stocks and to prioritise diesel supplies under a plan launched in March, as governments seek to tackle record fuel prices and supply disruptions caused by the Iran war. However, threats to oil shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, which carried shipments equal to about 20% of global oil and fuel before the war, have increased in October as the US-Israeli conflict with Iran enters its eighth month. Attacks on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest last week of any week since the Iran war began as Gulf producers increase exports. The increase in attacks is occurring as more crude is flowing out of the Gulf but at higher costs and risk to cargoes and crew. In the latest attack, a tanker north of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, causing casualties, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Oct 7 . “In the past, such attacks have resulted in a reduction in shipments from the Persian Gulf. This time around, producers appear to be willing to take the risk of their vessels being damaged, as there is no alternative way to get their oil to international markets,” Daniel Hynes, senior commodity strategist at bank ANZ, said in a note on Oct 8 . Hynes also said the IEA’s oil release would likely consist of barrels that were already part of the group’s original 400-million-barrel release plan at the start of the Middle East conflict, meaning it does not appear to represent an additional draw on strategic inventories. “Ultimately, strategic stock releases can augment supply flows temporarily but do not create new production capacity,” he said. Inventory data from the US, the world’s biggest oil consumer and producer, were supportive for prices as crude stockpiles fell by a higher-than-expected amount, while diesel inventories declined slightly. Crude inventories fell by 3.2 million barrels to 424.1 million barrels in the week ended Oct 2, the Energy Information Administration said on Oct 7 , compared with analysts’ expectations in a Reuters poll for a 1.7 million-barrel decline. Distillate fuel inventories, including diesel fuel and jet fuel, dropped by 42,000 barrels to 105.14 million barrels, well below their levels reported for this time of year in the past five years. events.title: Lime's CEO shares how he overcame a stroke to take his company to a $1.7 billion IPO
events.summary: Wayne Ting, Lime's CEO, speaks with Business Insider's Katie Roof. Stephen Council/BI Wayne Ting, Lime's CEO, survived a serious stroke and brought his company public the next year. At Tech Insider: Growth Mode, he talked about the need for humanity in Silicon Valley. Ting talked about outlasting Bird, overhauling Lime's e-scooters hardware, and more. Lime CEO Wayne Ting needed brain surgery to survive a serious stroke. Less than two years later, he's navigated his e-scooter company to a $1.7 billion IPO. When he was in the hospital last year, Ting said he couldn't find examples of other CEOs who had publicly spoken about their stroke recovery. Now, he wants to be someone people can go to for help and guidance, he told Business Insider's Katie Roof at Tech Insider: Growth Mode , sponsored by Fidelity, on Wednesday. "In Silicon Valley, you want to be hardcore," Ting said. "You can't be pumped; you have to be super pumped. Showing weakness and showing that you're a human is frankly the image that not a lot of CEOs want to portray." Ting tied his fight to the tumultuous road that Lime took to its IPO this July. The company fought for years with scooter rivals like Bird in the infamously tough micromobility industry, and weathered a 95% drop in revenue during the pandemic. He said that financial improvement, like stroke recovery, required getting "1% better" every day. Lime used to have to replace its entire fleet every month, he said; now the company's redesigned e-scooters and bikes last more than five years. And adoption takes time, Ting noted: the mature market of San Francisco is now growing 100% year-over-year, he said. Ting, a former chief of staff at Uber, also touted the need for sustainability, something he said he had hammered in under Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi. When Khosrowshahi joined Uber, Ting said he overhauled a culture in which employees thought "there was no line that we're not willing to cross." Now, as Ting sees it, "Win-at-all-costs is an insane idea." "If you're not doing the right things, you can win for a long time, but things will ultimately catch up to you," Ting said. Uber owns about a fourth of Lime and lets users book its scooters on its app, providing a boost that's helped Lime emerge as a victor of the 2010s' so-called "scooter wars." Lime raised around $167 million in its IPO. The company's stock price swelled higher in the late summer and has since dropped back to around its listing valuation of $1.7 billion. Chief rival Bird, which was once worth more than Lime, filed for bankruptcy in late 2023. Ting said that questions about Bird popped up again and again during Lime's IPO road show. events.title: Amazon makes fresh job cuts, mainly in retail division
events.summary: The cuts are the latest in a series of small reductions since a larger round of 30,000 job cuts that began in 2025. Amazon confirmed a small number of job cuts, mainly in its Stores unit, during Prime Big Deal Days, according to Reuters. Fewer than 1,000 white-collar workers were affected, including staff in the US, India and Britain, with customer service and selling partner services also hit. Amazon said the changes will better support its priorities, while Jeff Bezos said cuts were needed because the company overhired during the pandemic. SAN FRANCISCO – Amazon confirmed on Oct 7 it had cut what it said was a small number of jobs, primarily in its Stores unit which oversees the main e-commerce website. The layoffs to its retail unit coincide with one of Amazon’s biggest shopping days, which it calls Prime Big Deal Days. The promotion, which started on Oct 6 and runs through Oct 7, offers varying discounts. The cuts are the latest in a series of small reductions since a larger round of 30,000 job cuts that began in 2025 and continued into January. Some affected employees reached out to Reuters and shared posts from internal Slack channels about the news. Amazon let go fewer than 1,000 white-collar workers, a person familiar with the matter said. Business Insider had earlier reported the layoffs. “We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” a spokesperson said in an e-mailed statement. The internal Slack channel suggested a number of divisions within Stores were involved, including customer service and selling partner services, and possibly other units across Amazon. Employees in the United States, India and Britain were among those getting pink slips. Jeff Bezos, the founder and executive chairman of Amazon, said in a Fox News interview aired on Oct 7, that continued job cuts have been necessary because the company had overhired during the Covid-19 pandemic. “People were staying home and they were ordering, and it was an incredible, stressful period for us, by the way,” he said when asked about the 30,000 jobs lost in the previous round. “The whole team worked extremely hard and did so much, but we really grew our head count.” REUTERS

events.title: Nation's second-largest ASX float in doubt as investors get cold feet
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Data centre company Firmus tries to save its mega share market float as interest underwhelms The Firmus Technologies site in St Leonards, Launceston. Its data centres require a lot of energy and expansion plans have been described as ambitious. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) The $44 billion Australian float of data centre operator Firmus appears to be in trouble. But Firmus is not currently listed on the ASX's "upcoming floats and listings" webpage, and analysts who spoke to the ABC have raised concerns over the firm’s debts and the wild increase in its valuation over a short period of time. The company is scheduled to float on the ASX on October 23. It was touted as the biggest float since Telstra in the 1990s, but the share market debut of data centre operator Firmus is in trouble before it has even hit the share market. Investment banks stopped taking bids for the initial public offering (IPO) today and will now determine at what price the company lists on the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX). But Firmus is not currently listed on the ASX's "upcoming floats and listings" webpage, and analysts who spoke to the ABC have raised concerns over the firm's debts and the wild increase in its valuation over a short period of time. Adding to concerns, Goldman Sachs was reportedly tapped to rescue the float from collapse at midday today. The ABC has contacted several industry players directly connected with Firmus's fundraising, including Wilson Asset Management, Bank of America and Goldman Sachs. The investment bank told the ABC it had no comment. Fund manager Roger Montgomery said there had been inconsistencies in the messages given to market participants about the capital raising. "Investors were previously told that indicative orders were already above the size of the offer at $11 a share," he said. Indicative orders are what investors suggest to brokers they are willing to pay for a stock before orders are formally taking for a public listing. "If that were true, why has the price been cut to get the deal away?" Mr Montgomery said. "Warren Buffett said you want to invest with people who are energetic, intelligent and honest." The ASX told the ABC it does not comment on individual companies. The floats and listings webpage, however, makes it clear that "it only records new listings for which ASX has received a formal listing application". "A formal application would typically only be made late in the listing process when the entity has made all necessary preparations to list in the near term (i.e. within four to six weeks)," it says. This would suggest a formal application has not been made by Firmus to the ASX within 15 days of its expected listing. The caveat to this is that the ASX webpage also states that is "usually updated within three business days of receiving a formal application", meaning the official application may have been lodged. Firmus was set to hit the boards of the ASX at $11 per share, but reports suggest that price may have been set too high. Market participants have been underwhelmed by the float's roadshow, with some criticising it for having an "unprecedented lack of detail" and others concerned about its debt and energy needs. The float, or total number of shares on issue, is reportedly having to be revalued down because of the lacklustre interest, with reports it could drop to about $8 per share. Late on Wednesday, the company's representatives also pulled out of an appearance before a parliamentary inquiry into artificial intelligence today, with reports the troubled IPO was the reason for the no-show. Is Firmus here for a good time or a long time? Data Centre operator about to float on Australian share market. Firmus is a so-called neocloud technology company. It builds, owns and operates upscale data centres or so-called "AI factories", used to run and train artificial intelligence models. The firm is raising cash from investors to build an AI factory in Launceston and plans for two more in Tasmania. But its ambitions extend across Australia and into South-East Asian markets as well. Reports suggest Firmus intends to raise up to $7 billion from institutional and retail investors in its IPO, which could value the company at more than $50 billion. But the conclusion of a $73 billion partnership with data centre firm CDC and community backlash for proposed suburban data centres has caused concern for investors. Firmus co-founder Oliver Curtis was also jailed for 12 months in 2016 for a 2007 insider trading scheme.

The Feds allege that Zohar Pinhasi – aka “Zack Silver” and “Zack Green” – ran a Florida company called “MonsterCloud” that advised ransomware victims not to pay because it had a way to recover encrypted data. “The charges relate to Pinhasi’s claimed ability to decrypt ransomware without paying cybercriminals, purportedly using ‘proprietary tools’ and ‘advanced decryption techniques' on behalf of distressed business owners who came to his company,” according to a DoJ press release . “In fact, Pinhasi allegedly used a portion of his clients’ fees to pay off the ransomware attackers, and then kept the rest, often extracting a substantial markup.” In one case, Pinhasi allegedly charged his client $150,000, paid the $8,200 ransom, and pocketed the rest – but didn’t admit he had paid the ransom. That scheme allegedly worked so well that Pinhasi charged clients more than $19 million and paid more than $8 million in ransom payments. The DOJ’s indictment [PDF] says MonsterCloud’s website mentions its use of “advanced decryption techniques and cutting-edge technology” – the same language found on this monstercloud.com page . The site also contains this claim: “At MonsterCloud, we are not a team of IT Experts. We are the most sophisticated Counter Cyber Terrorism team in the world.” The indictment suggests MonsterCloud was nothing of the sort, and that its claims rang hollow for years. “MonsterCloud's website included ‘testimonials’ and other promotional content, including from at least one compensated spokesperson,” the indictment states. “In May 2019, one such spokesperson – an individual who had provided a paid testimonial for the MonsterCloud website – contacted the defendant Zohar Pinhasi with questions about Pinhasi’s business practices and truthfulness.” “Among other things, the spokesperson asked Pinhasi whether MonsterCloud actually had any proprietary software that would allow MonsterCloud to decrypt encrypted data. Pinhasi responded: ‘MonsterCloud doesn't hold any proprietary technology [to] decrypt the ransomware data.’” Pinhasi faces two counts of wire fraud, and one of wire fraud conspiracy. He could do twenty years on each count, if convicted. events.title: ‘The best address in Singapore’: Why Malaysia’s IOI Properties is betting billions on the CBD
events.summary: IOI Properties chief executive Lee Yeow Seng says high-net-worth individuals’ presence in the Republic will support demand for prime offices, luxury homes and high-end hotels. IOI Properties chief Lee Yeow Seng is betting billions on Singapore’s CBD, calling Marina Bay “the best address in Singapore” because of safety, prestige and limited land supply. The group has bought major assets, including South Beach and Asia Square Tower 2, and may acquire One Raffles Place to grow its Downtown Core portfolio. IOI plans more luxury homes, ultra-high-end hotels and a Singapore REIT to cut debt, while Lee urges land sales reforms to avoid rising property prices. SINGAPORE – IOI Properties chief executive Lee Yeow Seng is betting billions on Singapore’s Central Business District (CBD), which he regards as the best location for property investments in the country. “If you want to invest in properties, location is always the most important overriding consideration,” he told The Straits Times in an interview on the sidelines of the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore on Oct 7. “There’s no better address and location than Marina Bay.” Underlying that bet is Lee’s belief that Singapore has established itself as a safe haven for high-net-worth individuals, whose presence in the Republic will support demand for prime offices, luxury homes and high-end hotels. “Rich people, when they look to park their money, the first thing they look at is safety,” he said. “I think Singapore has managed to brand itself very well as a safe haven for rich people. And probably now, after the Middle East conflict, there isn’t any country safer than Singapore.” The arrival of more rich people to the Republic would also draw multinational companies and create demand for the best property offerings. “When high-net-worth individuals come in, they want nothing but the best,” Lee said. “That is the segment I think is still very much underserved.” This explains IOI’s focus on the CBD, where it has assembled a portfolio spanning offices, hotels and luxury residences. These include IOI Central Boulevard Towers, which it built from scratch after acquiring the site in 2016; South Beach, which it fully owns after buying out City Developments’ 50.1% stake for around $835 million in September 2025; and Asia Square Tower 2, which it bought from CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust for $2.5 billion in April. According to The Business Times, IOI Properties and CapitaLand Investment are conducting exclusive due diligence for the proposed acquisition of One Raffles Place, after jointly submitting a 50-50 bid to owners OUE Reit and UOB. If completed, the deal would broaden IOI’s exposure to the Downtown Core. One Raffles Place, which comprises two office towers of 62 and 38 storeys respectively, as well as a six-storey retail podium, also sits on an exceptionally long 841-year lease. The development has an indicative value of between $2.3 billion and $2.4 billion. Asked about his confidence in Singapore’s CBD, Lee said the limited supply of land, as well as the Government’s control over its release, gives property investors greater certainty. “You feel very secure investing in properties in Singapore because the supply is controlled and very limited.” He added that land for new Grade A office developments in the CBD has not been released for about 10 years. Lee is bullish on CBD offices despite the growth of flexible working and government efforts to decentralise jobs to commercial centres outside the CBD, saying companies and employees continue to value a prestigious downtown address. If he was a worker, he said, he “would still prefer to work in the city centre because it is much more glamorous”. “You want to tell people that you work for a company that has an address in the CBD. You feel more proud and you feel happier working downtown because there are many more amenities and transport links.” IOI Central Boulevard Towers is within reach of several MRT stations and sits close to Marina Bay Sands, for example. The convenience and prestige has also allowed the development to command higher rents of close to $18 per sq ft, compared with about $8 psf a decade ago. The group has also raised rents at Asia Square Tower 2 since taking control of the property. “When we first purchased the property, the average rent was only about $11. Now we are getting renewals at $13 to $14.” IOI’s investments in the CBD extend beyond office towers. Lee said mixed-use developments allowing people to live, work and spend their leisure time in the same district represent both the present and the future of cities. “People go for convenience. They want access to a lot of amenities and to live, work and play near one another.” At Marina View, IOI is developing the 683-unit W Residences Marina View, which comes integrated with a W Hotel of about 360 rooms.

events.title: 'Enough is enough': Alan Jones emails to schoolboy read in court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Complainant denies deceiving Alan Jones for financial assistance, trial hears Veteran broadcaster Alan Jones denies all allegations against him. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Complainant A is giving evidence in the Alan Jones trial in the New South Wales Local Court on Thursday. The complainant, who is now an adult, is accusing Mr Jones of kissing him and touching his buttocks when he was a 17-year-old. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching related to five male complainants. A man accusing Alan Jones of kissing him when he was a 17-year-old schoolboy has denied he and his mother tried to deceive the veteran broadcaster to obtain as much financial assistance as possible before he came forward with his allegation. The now-adult, known as Complainant A, alleges Mr Jones kissed him, put his tongue in his mouth, and touched his buttocks when he visited the radio host at his farm on the Southern Highlands as a 17-year-old. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexually touching relating to five male complainants between 2003 and 2020. Mr Jones is facing 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Complainant A said he first reached out to Mr Jones when he was 13 years old, sending the 2GB host a letter asking for help with his family's serious financial struggles. Emails read to the court showed Mr Jones had extensive correspondences with the young boy over a three-year period and used his influence to help the boy's mother re-negotiate a more favourable home loan, which included $600,000 being wiped off her initial debt. The trial heard Mr Jones also provided more than $100,000 of his own money to help with the completion of the boy's family home and to help with their legal fees. The court is hearing from Complainant A, who is the fifth and final male complainant. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Under cross-examination, defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC raised an email sent by Mr Jones to the boy, three years after they started communicating with each other, and a year before the alleged indecent assault occurred. The court heard Mr Jones informed the boy in the email about how he had provided his family more than $100,000 in support, writing "enough is enough" and "there must come a point where I have to say, no more". Complainant A said he believed Mr Jones's email expressed frustration but told Ms Bashir he did not believe the email meant the end of the broadcaster's financial support to him and his mother. "Isn't it that the case that your intention was on obtaining as much financial assistance from Mr Jones as you possibly could?" Ms Bashir suggested. "That is not true," the complainant replied. "It's the case that your mother had the intention of obtaining as much financial assistance from Mr Jones as she possibly could?" Ms Bashir asked. "That is a lie," the complainant said. The court heard the boy replied to the email, writing that his family was "happy to make arrangements to make repayments", with Mr Jones's reply asking about when a legal matter would end and that "he was not a mobile bank". Ms Bashir questioned the complainant about whether he had drafted specific emails to Mr Jones or whether his mother also had some level of involvement. Complainant A repeatedly told the court he could not remember who may have drafted specific sections of emails but said there was certain information contained in correspondence that he would have only been able to obtain from his mum. "You were you trying to deceive Mr Jones about the author of the email when you sent emails signed off just from [your name] that your mother had input into?" Ms Bashir suggested. "I suggest that you were, what do you say to that?" Ms Bashir said "[I say] that you're wrong," he answered. The trial heard Mr Jones and the boy met in person on several occasions, including at his Circular Quay apartment, at the boy's home and alone at a pub. It is alleged that after many invitations over several years, the boy agreed to spend two nights at Mr Jones's Fitzroy Fall's property when he was 17 years old. Complainant A said the alleged indecent assault occurred on the second day at the property and that it left him feeling "violated". The court heard, the boy later wrote a letter to his mother saying, "something happened at Fitzroy Falls" and took his allegation to police the next year.

events.title: Democrats sue US President Trump over taxpayer-funded ad campaign
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Trump has faced a bipartisan backlash over ads that critics say violate prohibitions on taxpayer-funded propaganda. The Democratic National Committee has filed a lawsuit against United States President Donald Trump over television advertisements that were publicly funded and allegedly used to promote his political policies. Ken Martin, who heads the Democratic Party’s leadership body, suggested in a statement on Wednesday that the ads were designed to bolster Republican odds in the upcoming November 3 midterm elections . list 1 of 3 US FCC head says controversial Trump ads do not raise concerns list 2 of 3 ‘We’ll decide’: Trump hints he may pay for US government-funded ads list 3 of 3 Most Americans oppose Trump’s taxpayer-funded ‘golden age’ ads: Poll “Donald Trump is misusing millions of taxpayer dollars to fund pure propaganda ads in a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November,” Martin said. Later that day, Common Cause, a democracy watchdog group, filed a second lawsuit over the same set of ads. It argued that the ads were “overtly political” and therefore ran afoul of laws that bar public funds from being used for political propaganda. “These ads are not public-service announcements,” Common Cause said in its lawsuit, citing a justification Trump has offered for the television spots. “They are personal publicity and political propaganda through and through.” Both lawsuits argue that, to create the ad campaign, Trump directed the White House to repurpose $20m in funds that Congress allocated for commemorative activities related to border security, including for those killed in the line of duty. That manoeuvre, they argue, violates the separation of powers established in the US Constitution. “The founders made clear more than 200 years ago that the executive can spend money only according to Congress’s direction,” Common Cause’s lawsuit said. The two lawsuits also point to a provision Congress includes in its appropriations bills barring the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda purposes”. Both complaints seek to have the ads declared illegal, and the expenditures stopped. They also call for steps to be taken to recover any money already spent on the ads. The Democrats’ lawsuit was filed in Washington, DC, while the Common Cause complaint will be heard in the Southern District of New York. Trump has faced mounting criticism over the ads, which began airing in September. So far, the advertising campaign has cost more than $12m to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. The $20m Trump tapped for the ads comes from a $175m package Congress assigned to the Department of Homeland Security as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda. Critics have pointed out that one of the ads appears nearly identical to a television spot Trump used in his 2024 re-election campaign. Three ads have aired so far. In one, a choir sings “love me” over a montage of Trump as he declares the US will “never be a communist country”. Another uses images of Mount Rushmore as Trump heralds a new “golden age of America”. The third is darker: Trump walks towards the camera in black and white, warning of a “final battle” against the “deep state” and other perceived enemies. On Wednesday, the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos released a poll showing the ads are highly unpopular . Some 86 percent of the Americans surveyed, including four out of five Republicans, said it was inappropriate for Trump to have used public money for them. Trump has defended the ads as “promotion for the country”, and he has argued they were similar to public outreach campaigns put out by previous administrations. But after a bipartisan backlash, Trump said on Monday that taxpayer funds would no longer be used for future ads . He did not, however, commit to paying back the money already spent on the existing ads. Members of Trump’s Republican Party have been among those speaking out against the ad campaign. Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said the advertisements resembled something former Hungarian leader Viktor Orban would put out. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, meanwhile, indicated he agreed with the message in one of the advertisements, but he emphasised that “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars”.

events.title: Yemeni government forces claim 1,860 Houthis ‘neutralised’
events.summary: Yemeni government forces say in a social media post they carried out 2,103 ‘precise targeting operations’. Yemeni government forces have said they “neutralised” 1,860 Houthi fighters since launching a large-scale counteroffensive to retake territory under the control of the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God. The spokesperson for the internationally recognised government’s military said in a social media post early on Thursday it had carried out 2,103 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi military positions across several fronts as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” campaign. list 1 of 3 Yemen’s Houthis attack Aden airport; Saudi forces down missile near Riyadh list 2 of 3 More than 200,000 displaced as fighting escalates in Yemen, UN says list 3 of 3 Three killed, 36 injured in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, Riyadh says The Yemeni government, backed by Saudi Arabia, also says its forces have captured strategic mountain positions in western Taiz overlooking the coast. Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced on Sunday the Dawn of Yemen operation to retake all Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group has controlled since 2014. Battles in Yemen have focused in recent days on areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the US-Israel war on Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz. Forces aligned with the Yemeni government launched an operation on Tuesday to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the city of Mocha, which the Houthis had taken last month. The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday it destroyed 82 Houthi military targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada, Hodeidah, al-Jawf and Marib. The spokesperson for the coalition said in a statement that the targets included missile sites, including “11 mountain-based ballistic missile storages in Saada, command and control centres, communication systems, missile and weapons storages”. The latest operation followed Houthi attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday targeting King Khalid international airport in Riyadh and Abha international airport, according to the spokesperson. The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said the attacks on the two airports killed three people. One person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid airport, while two people were killed and 28 were wounded in the attack on facilities at Abha airport, the GACA said in a statement. The attacks have drawn condemnation from across the region. Kuwait denounced the attacks as a “flagrant violation” of Saudi sovereignty and international law. Egypt said the attacks threaten the security of the entire region. The Mecca-based nongovernmental organisation Muslim World League also condemned the strikes, describing them as “treacherous terrorist attacks”. As the fighting rages on, Yemen’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Abdullah al-Saadi, met the UN secretary-general’s special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, on Wednesday to discuss the situation in the country. During their talks, al-Saadi accused the Houthis of rejecting peace initiatives and de-escalation efforts proposed by the Yemeni government. He stressed that the government’s goal is to extend its control across the entirety of the country and end the Houthis’ ability to wage war. He said the government is seeking a permanent end to the war and is not interested in a temporary truce, arguing that such a scenario would only lead to fighting later.

events.title: Revolut to open new Singapore office; will invest $350 million and grow staff to 300 here
events.summary: Revolut Singapore CEO Raymond Ng said that the new office signals the company’s commitment to Singapore. Revolut will open a new Singapore office at Collyer Quay Centre in early 2027 and invest nearly $350 million over five years. The fintech plans to grow its Singapore staff from nearly 170 to over 300 in three years, with more hires in engineering, product, data and AI. Revolut wants to move beyond travel services and become a daily app for money, with more digital banking, investing and AI tools for users and businesses. SINGAPORE – Revolut will open a new office at Collyer Quay Centre as a mark of its expansion plans in Singapore and the region , the London-headquartered fintech company said on Oct 8. It will also invest nearly $350 million in Singapore over the next five years, spanning product innovation, business growth and the expansion of its local workforce. Revolut, which opened in Singapore in 2019, now hires nearly 170 people here, but plans to grow its headcount to more than 300 over the next three years . It already nearly doubled its headcount in 2025, and is planning to hire more people for roles across engineering, product, data and artificial intelligence. The new office, which will occupy 8,880 sq ft of office space on the ninth floor of Collyer Quay Centre, is scheduled to open in early 2027. The company will also have its name on the building. Revolut currently operates out of co-working space WeWork at Funan. Revolut Singapore chief executive Raymond Ng told The Straits Times: “I think having our own space is very important not only for our staff, but also for our users, so they get more familiar with us and our logo. “We want to be their daily app, not a travel app, because our ultimate aim is to be all things money to our users.” He added that the new office also signals the company’s commitment to Singapore, and forms a base for expansion into the region. Besides Singapore, Revolut is already in Japan, India, Australia and New Zealand in the Asia-Pacific region, and it is on the lookout for more opportunities. It also has a tech hub in the Philippines. Ng said: “We are always looking at opportunities to go into markets. It’s all about timing, and it’s all about whether there’s a market fit. We need to look at the business case and talk to the regulators.” Within Singapore, Ng also wants to shed the image of Revolut as solely a travel app for Singaporean travellers to hold different currencies. Revolut already has a cryptocurrency licence in Singapore, and users can also make investments and trade on the app. Revolut announced its new office building in Singapore on Oct 8. It also offers tiered subscriptions where users can access wealth and lifestyle products, such as VPN services, AI services and travel insurance, according to their tier. Ng said: “In Singapore, we started off by doing travel-related services, but now we want to be used more for daily services, too.” He added: “We have many very sophisticated users here, and the way we are going now is that by giving them all these services, they will be using us more and more daily, and not only for travel.” The firm’s investment in Singapore is to scale its retail and business user bases, particularly because Singapore is a financial and logistics hub. He noted that many companies set up regional offices in Singapore, and they have immediate needs like remittances and doing financial transactions. That is where Revolut can enter to help small and medium-sized enterprises and cross-border companies that might be scaling up or looking for a more integrated financial operating system. When asked about whether Revolut is applying for a digital bank licence in Singapore, Ng said he is unable to comment at this time. Revolut already holds digital bank licences in markets like Britain, Mexico, France and Australia. Ng said: “We don’t think of the licence first. We think of what is needed in the market, get feedback from the consumer, then at the right time, we will apply for the right licence. It’s all about product fit. And we don’t want to be making any comment till we are ready.” He noted that the main difference is that institutions without a banking licence are unable to hold customer deposits, provide interest on the deposits or offer loans the way a bank can. But Ng also sees Revolut as a tech company first, then a finance one. “It is a very tech-driven company, and then we go into providing many financial services and lifestyle services,” he said, adding that the company has written its own AI model using internal data and in-house data scientists. He added that an AI-enabled interface will soon arrive on the app for users here, too, which includes allowing users to execute commands on the app using voice control or prompts. Ng said: “We can’t escape that everything is going to be very digital. The consumer is actually asking for more now...

events.title: Singapore’s central bank wants all FinTech AI use cases subject to independent review
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Failures of third-party services no excuse for island nation’s financial sector Singapore’s government creates a dating app 7 days ago DeepMind bigbrain calls for America to set AI standards before it's too late July 14, 2026 Singaporean sovereign wealth fund Temasek thinks AI is going to pay off July 9, 2026 OpenAI job listing suggests ChatGPT could someday replace junior analysts at Goldman Sachs July 8, 2026 UN warns of need for global governance to avoid an AI-pocalypse July 2, 2026 Singapore’s Monetary Authority, which acts as both central bank and finance industry regulator, wants all local industry players to seek independent review of AI use cases before deployment. The island nation’s combination of strict regulation and low taxes have made it one of the world’s premier finance hubs. One of the roles of Singapore’s Monetary Authority (MAS) is ensuring the nation retains that status, but in its first Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management for Financial Institutions , published on Wednesday, warns that AI increases risk. “The use of AI can improve performance across business and functional areas but its complexity and probabilistic nature can lead to greater uncertainty, as well as unexpected or more biased behaviour that is harder to identify compared to the use of simpler methods,” the guidelines state. And that’s MAS’s view of old-school AI: it rates generative AI as even riskier. “The greater complexity of Generative AI gives rise to even greater uncertainty and unexpected behaviour compared to AI,” MAS warns, citing “noise that is inherent in training data, training data that may not be representative, or when the model encounters scenarios that are not present in its training data” as sources of risk. The regulator fears agentic AI “could further amplify these risks.” MAS therefore calls for financial institutions (FIs) to expand their risk management frameworks to cover AI and expects board and senior management to make that happen. The regulator also wants all AI use cases to undergo independent review before going into production. “Prior to deployment, an FI should subject the AI use case, including its underlying systems or models, to reviews by parties not involved in its development to ensure that the relevant controls, such as evaluation and testing, have been adhered to,” the guidelines state. MAS also wants regulated entities to run technology and cybersecurity reviews “to ensure that AI can be deployed into the production environment in a controlled and secure manner.” If an AI project survives those reviews, MAS wants ongoing monitoring of both the FI’s own systems and any third-party AI powering an application. “Given the uncertainties associated with AI, their dynamic nature and the potential for model staleness and performance degradation due to data or model drifts over time, ongoing monitoring is critical to ensure that deployed AI operates as intended and remains fit for purpose over time,” the guidelines state. MAS does not see failings by third-party AI suppliers as an acceptable excuse for AI problems at entities it regulates, and it wants FIs to monitor their suppliers’ products and services to ensure they remain stable and secure. “FIs remain accountable for AI used in the services they deliver, including AI developed, operated or provided by third parties,” the regulator explained. “FIs should obtain sufficient assurance from third-party providers, assess whether third-party AI is suitable for their intended use, and apply compensating controls where practical constraints or assurance gaps arise. If the risks cannot be brought within the FI’s risk appetite, it should consider limiting, suspending or replacing the use of the third-party AI service.” The regulator also wants Singaporean FIs to maintain up-to-date inventories of all AI used in their business.

events.title: Samsung forecasts record third-quarter profit of $80 billion as AI boom fuels chip demand
events.summary: Samsung Electronics estimated its third-quarter operating profit topped 100 trillion won for the first time in the company’s history. It reported preliminary operating profit of 107.4 trillion won, with more detailed results due later this month. Samsung Electronics on Thursday reported third-quarter preliminary operating profit of 107.40 trillion won ($80.2 billion), surging past 100 trillion won for the first time in the company's history as booming demand for artificial intelligence continues to fuel its chips business. Projected quarterly operating profit is 782% higher from a year earlier. Revenue forecast of about 195 trillion won is up nearly 127% from the same period last year. Samsung shares, however, dropped 0.7% Thursday morning. "Samsung has delivered a record profit and still fallen short of expectations, which tells you just how demanding the AI trade has become," said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at investment platform eToro. "When expectations are so high for memory makers, the market doesn't hand out points for effort." With AI spending driving demand for memory and supply remaining tight, the larger story of the chip sector remains intact, Gilbert said, highlighting growth of AI agents that can consume far more memory than a chatbot answering a single question. "Memory buyers are also committing to multiyear supply agreements, giving Samsung greater visibility over demand in a business where investors have always worried about the next downturn," he added. In the second quarter, the company posted record revenue of 171.5 trillion won and record operating profit of 89.5 trillion won, driven by its memory business. The company has also stepped up investments and partnerships tied to AI. In September, Samsung announced a strategic partnership with French artificial intelligence startup Mistral AI, with plans to deploy the startup's AI models across its semiconductor operations. Samsung is expected to release its full third-quarter earnings, including a breakdown by business division, later this month.

events.title: How kidnappings are hitting Nigeria’s Borno families hard
events.summary: Across Borno, abductions are leaving families with depleted savings, missing loved ones and disrupted education. Maiduguri, Nigeria – When Musa Abdullahi Wakawa learned that his wife and seven-year-old son had been abducted, disbelief quickly gave way to fear. Then came the question confronting many families caught in Nigeria’s kidnapping crisis: How could he raise the ransom demanded for their release? For days, Musa searched for a way to bring his family home, confronting the financial burden imposed by the kidnappers. Across northeastern Nigeria, families sell livestock, seek loans, dispose of property and exhaust savings in the hope of securing the release of loved ones. In Borno State, kidnapping has become more than a security threat. Families are losing money, living with the trauma of abduction and, in some communities, keeping their children away from school. ‘Please just help me with your prayers’ Laraba Dauda, 45, still remembers the last conversation she had with her younger sister. Her sister was abducted on January 13, 2026, along the Biu–Buratai road, according to Laraba. Shortly after the abduction, the phone rang. Her sister was calling from somewhere in the bush. “Aunty, unknown people have kidnapped us and taken us somewhere in the bush. We don’t know where they are taking us. At this moment, Aunty, please just help me with your prayers,” Laraba recalled her sister saying. Months later, Laraba and her family still do not know where she is being held or whether she is safe. Laraba is calling on the Nigerian government to intensify efforts to rescue those still in captivity. “We need the government to come to our aid and help rescue our relatives who have spent more than six months in captivity,” she said. A journey that never reached Maiduguri For Anjikwi Hena, his son’s disappearance came just as the family was looking towards a better future. His son was abducted on March 30, 2026, according to Hena. He had completed his education and was preparing to travel to Maiduguri in search of work. His father encouraged him and prayed for his success. Instead, the young man disappeared into captivity. Hena said their close relationship has made the uncertainty especially painful. The kidnapping crisis is also threatening education in communities already weakened by years of rebellion. In Askira-Uba Local Government Area of Borno State, only 56 of 113 primary schools are currently functioning, according to Fasuma Askira, the local government education secretary. Before the May attack in Mussa, 76 primary schools were operating. The threat of violence subsequently forced authorities to close another 20, leaving only 56 functioning. On May 15, suspected rebel fighters attacked Mussa and abducted dozens of children. A register later obtained by news services identified 40 missing children, although figures provided by the community and government have varied. The Borno State government has more recently referred to about 44 children still missing from Mussa. Then, on June 29, armed rebels attacked the Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were taking National Examinations Council examinations. Some students were recovered shortly after the attack, but 36 students and a teacher have been reported as remaining in captivity. The attacks have deepened fears among parents and teachers already living with the threat of rebel violence. The education authority moved junior secondary students from Mussa to a government boarding school in Uba and advised the local government to deploy community vigilantes around schools. Soldiers have also been deployed in Mussa and Lassa alongside local vigilantes, according to the Askira. For families in these communities, keeping children in school now means weighing access to education against the risk of further attacks. Borno’s crisis reflects a national problem The situation in Borno is part of a wider kidnapping crisis across Nigeria. Amnesty International Nigeria says at least 1,100 people were abducted across the country between January and April 2026, while warning that the actual figure could be considerably higher because many incidents in remote communities go unreported. “Apart from killing people, gunmen are now on a rampage of abductions, largely for lucrative ransom,” said Isa Sanusi, director of Amnesty International Nigeria. “Some stay months at the mercy of gunmen in punishing situations.” Amnesty says victims can face torture, starvation and sexual violence, while families are often forced to raise money under extreme pressure. The organisation has also warned that fear of abduction is pushing children out of school, particularly in rural communities. Government says security and humanitarian measures are under way Borno State Commissioner for Information and Internal Security Usman Tar said the government was using both military and nonmilitary measures to confront insecurity.
