events.summary: Oil prices rose on fresh concerns about Middle East supplies, before falling over possible release of more reserves. US financial markets have been whipsawed as bond market fears grow, pushing Treasury yields to their highest levels in more than 20 years, and oil prices continue to fluctuate, despite the Nasdaq and S&P 500 hitting record peaks. Wall Street closed lower on Wednesday as oil prices rose then fell due to renewed concerns about disruption to Middle East supplies. list 1 of 4 Southeast Asia’s energy chiefs meet against backdrop of Iran war list 2 of 4 Is Iran charging a toll to allow oil traffic through Hormuz? list 3 of 4 What new measures is Iran taking to counter US economic pressure? list 4 of 4 Has Russia’s fuel crisis given Iranian oil an opening in Central Asia? Stocks fell after closing at record highs in the previous session on Tuesday, with yields on US government bonds climbing to 24-year highs as investors worried about the impact of high oil prices on inflation and interest rates. Oil prices increased on Thursday on persistent worries about supply from the Middle East amid an ⁠increase in attacks on ⁠shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. ‌Brent crude futures rose to $101.53 a barrel as of 01:16 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures climbed ⁠to $89.39 a barrel. IEA member countries said they stand ready to release additional oil from their reserves if necessary and will prioritise diesel due to tight supplies of the fuel, the head of the organisation said on Wednesday. G7 countries, in coordination with the IEA, agreed last Friday to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by fallout from the United States-Iran war. The latest announcement from the IEA calmed oil markets after prices had climbed on Wednesday following a report from UK Maritime Trade Operations. The maritime agency said on Tuesday that there had been nine attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz this month, representing half of the September total in the waterway and the Gulf combined. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, repeated Washington’s claims that it was in control of the strait and that oil flows were at close to normal levels. Oil exports from the Gulf have recovered significantly in recent days, despite a surge in attacks on ships around the Strait of Hormuz, maritime experts and trackers say. Gulf oil flows, excluding Iran, recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, while crude exports from the wider Middle East exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days during the month, maritime intelligence firm Kpler reported. However, the recovery has come as attacks on tankers increase and shipping companies face higher freight, insurance and security costs. On Tuesday, 12 crew members on a Panama-flagged tanker were injured in an attack by an unknown projectile while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement.

events.title: Amazon employees hit by fresh job cuts across several teams
events.summary: The Amazon headquarters in the South Lake Union neighborhood of Seattle David Ryder/Bloomberg via Getty Images Amazon had fresh job cuts across several teams on Tuesday. Fewer than 1,000 people were affected by the layoffs. The cuts follow roughly 30,000 job eliminations late last year and early this year. Amazon employees reported a new round of job cuts across several parts of the company on Tuesday. A group of employees wrote in an internal Slack channel that they had received emails telling them their roles had been eliminated, according to messages viewed by Business Insider. The channel, which had nearly 37,000 members, quickly filled with questions about severance, access to internal job postings, and whether further notifications were still coming. The messages suggest cuts across several business units, including customer service, marketplace support, and engineering roles in Amazon’s retail business, as well as in India and the UK. Fewer than 1,000 employees were affected in total, according to a person familiar with the matter. The new cuts show that Amazon's cost overhaul is still reshaping its corporate workforce even as the company embarks on its biggest spending binge yet. After eliminating roughly 30,000 jobs late last year and early this year to cut costs and flatten its organization, Amazon is now preparing to spend a record $220 billion on data centers, chips, and other infrastructure for AI. An Amazon spokesperson confirmed to Business Insider that the company eliminated “a small number” of roles on Tuesday, primarily in its Stores business. "We're always looking at our team structures to ensure we're best set up to move fast as we innovate for customers," the spokesperson said. "We've adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities. As part of these changes, we've made the difficult decision to eliminate a small number of roles, and we're committed to supporting affected employees through their transition." The layoffs followed months of anxiety among Amazon's corporate workforce over the prospect of another broad round of cuts, according to people familiar with the matter. Employees have been bracing for layoffs after prior reductions, and some leaders have scaled back planning for the next several quarters partly because they expected their teams or priorities could change, according to one of the people. The uncertainty left employees parsing leadership meetings, calendar invitations, and team changes for clues. In the Slack channel, workers asked whether all notices had been sent, how medical leave would be handled, and whether they would retain access to Slack and Outlook during their notice periods. Others wondered whether cuts would reach Mexico and elsewhere in Europe. For many employees, the immediate question was whether they could find another job inside Amazon before their employment ended. One post asked whether workers who received an outside offer during the 90-day notification period would have to forfeit severance if they left early. Amazon is not alone in pairing job cuts with a bigger AI push. Meta eliminated roughly 8,000 roles in May while shifting thousands of other workers into AI initiatives, and Microsoft cut more than 5,000 jobs across July and September. Amazon, meanwhile, has also been reaching out to former employees , including some laid off in earlier rounds, about open roles in AWS and its AI businesses. Have a tip? events.title: Inside India newsletter: Food crisis, economic shock ahead as India braces for El Niño
events.summary: Between June and September, India received its lowest rainfall in more than a decade owing to the El Niño effect. India’s foreign minister has warned El Niño, coupled with fertilizer shortages due to wars, will lead to a major food crisis in the coming months. El Niño is expected to materially slow down India’s rural economy and lead to a sharp rise in inflation. Rural demand in India is key for major multinational companies such as HUL, Colgate-Palmolive, Nestle, and the automaker Maruti Suzuki. Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to the latest edition of " Inside India " — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy. India is one of the largest producers of farm products and ranks among the world's top exporters of rice and sugar. Its farms help to feed almost 1.5 billion people, keep supply-side inflation under check, and sustain 46.1% of India's workforce, driving consumer spending. But this crucial sector now faces the heat from the so-called super El Niño. This week I dig deeper to understand what this global weather event holds for India . Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team. This year is not getting any better for the world's fastest-growing economy. The super El Niño weather phenomenon is emerging as the latest headwind for India's growth, which is already facing global energy shocks, trade uncertainty with the U.S. and record exits of foreign investors from its equity markets. From June to September, a key season for its mostly rain-fed farms and reservoirs, India received its lowest rainfall in more than a decade , as per local media reports. It was the fourth lowest since 2001, and the 13th driest since 1901 , according to the India Meteorological Department. Reservoirs in the country were 28% short of full capacity at the end of September and posed a risk to winter crops, according to a report by Nomura on Monday. Several parts of key farm states such as Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, and Haryana are facing extreme "drought conditions," Nomura stated. India and other countries are contending with " significant fertilizer shortages " as key producers in the Middle East and Russia have been impacted by geopolitical conflicts, Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said at an event organized by the non-profit Asia Society in New York last week. Jaishankar warned that with the super El Niño added to the mix, "there is going to be a major food crisis" in the coming months. Energy shocks and the flow of money to safe harbors have been "very stressful" for economies of the Global South, he said. The Global South is a term used to characterize less-developed or emerging economies. Following Jaishankar's comments, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's political opponents blamed the government for not acting in time to avert the crisis . Inflation in India has been rising for 10 straight months, crossing the central bank's medium-term target of 4% in August, even as economic growth has been resilient so far. While the share of farming in India's economy is around 17%, it provides a livelihood to roughly 46.1% of India's workforce . Its produce is pivotal in curbing supply-side inflation domestically, and the country ranks among the top global exporters of rice and sugar. The rural economy, largely dependent on farming, is also an important pillar of consumer spending. India's " monsoon deficit appears to be larger than originally expected," the World Bank said in a report on Tuesday. "This is expected to reduce agricultural output and rural demand while increasing food inflation, adding to existing pressure from higher energy prices," the report said. Rural areas account for nearly 40% of sales of fast-moving consumer goods, according to data from consultancy Nielsen Consumer. Rural demand is key for major multinational companies in India such as Hindustan Unilever , Colgate-Palmolive India , Nestle India , and the automakers Maruti Suzuki and Hyundai Motors , per market data based on annual reports and earnings calls. According to Hanna Luchnikava-Schorsch, head of Asia-Pacific economics at S&P Global Market Intelligence, India's rural economy is likely to slow "materially" in 2026 and 2027, "as drought conditions, below-normal monsoon rainfall and depleted reservoir levels reduce crop yields and farm incomes." While broader indicators have remained resilient so far, Luchnikava-Schorsch told CNBC that "early signs of stress are already emerging," adding that tractor sales had slowed and "demand for rural employment support programs has begun to rise." Morgan Stanley estimated that the gross value added by India's agricultural sector will grow by 1.6% in the financial year ending in March 2027, much slower than the 3.5% growth seen over the past three years. S&P Global Market Intelligence Analysis forecast growth would cool to 1.9%.

events.title: DNC sues to stop Trump's taxpayer-funded ad blitz
events.summary: The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration on Wednesday over its campaign-style ads . Why it matters: The DNC alleges the ads, which have drawn considerable backlash as they were originally paid for with taxpayer money, violate several federal laws. What they're saying: "These ads are a clear violation of the Congressional ban on the use of appropriated funds for 'publicity or propaganda purposes,'" the DNC's legal counsel wrote in the lawsuit . "The president has nationalized the midterm election, made himself the center of a two-day 'midterm convention,' and repeatedly directed voters to 'pretend that I am on the ballot," it added. "As the 2026 midterm election has approached, Republican poll numbers have plummeted in both traditional battlegrounds and typically favorable states, and Democrats are poised to take control of Congress, governors' mansions, and state legislatures around the country." Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom in: The lawsuit alleges the White House crafted the ads to boost the president's approval ratings and help Republican candidates. The complaint largely focuses on its allegation that the ads were paid for with money originally allocated for Customs and Border Protection that was rerouted for the TV spots. The DNC argues that the ads violate the Administrative Procedure Act, the Antideficiency Act, and the Purpose Act. The DNC asked a federal judge to step in, declare the administration's actions illegal and immediately block them from airing any more ads paid for with taxpayer money. It's not clear how the judge will rule, given President Trump said Monday that a Trump-affiliated super PAC would begin paying for the ads moving forward. A White House spokesperson confirmed Tuesday to Axios that the administration would not repay the government for the ads. Catch up quick: According to the suit, Trump personally hand-picked the ads that aired on television, which were broadcast to millions of Americans, including during NFL and college football games. The lawsuit says the ads aired "nearly 90 times across national television networks, including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now, and CBS" over four days in late September. Those spots likely cost around $337,000. In that same time period, the ads aired on local television stations at least 2,311 times and those placements cost around $1.4 million, the suit says. Advertisement tracking firm AdImpact estimates that over $2.5 million was spent on the ads the first week they were aired. Worth noting: Using public funds for campaign ads hasn't sat well with American voters. Nearly nine in ten voters said in a Reuters-Ipsos poll published Wednesday that using taxpayer money for campaign ads featuring a president or Cabinet member is inappropriate. Go deeper: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

events.title: Trump trade chief Greer reports higher cash holdings as law firm pay topped $650K
events.summary: U.S. trade representative Jamieson Greer reported roughly $1.17 million to $3.75 million in cash, retirement accounts and other investments in his 2025 financial disclosure. Greer reported $652,610 in salary and bonus from King & Spalding in 2025, while one bank account increased to $500,001 to $1 million. Greer received a $10,000 honorarium from Coupang in May 2024 and met with the company at USTR 11 months later, though public records do not establish that the meeting violated federal ethics rules. U.S. trade representative Jamieson Greer reported roughly $1.17 million to $3.75 million in cash, retirement accounts and other investments according to a CNBC analysis of his newly obtained 2025 annual financial disclosure. The 16-page filing from the Office of Government Ethics, offers a new look at the finances of President Donald Trump's top trade official after he left a lucrative partnership at the King & Spalding law firm to join the administration in February 2025. Greer reported receiving $652,610 in salary and bonus from the firm in 2025. In his nominee disclosure , he listed an anticipated performance-based bonus for work performed in 2024, valued at $250,001 to $500,000, that would be paid before he entered government. He had previously reported about $1.5 million in salary and bonus from King & Spalding. One of the clearest changes in the new filing is Greer's cash holdings. An account labeled "U.S. bank #2" jumped from $250,001-$500,000 in his nominee filing to $500,001-$1 million in the new disclosure. It generated another $15,001-$50,000 in interest. Federal disclosures report most assets in broad ranges, making it impossible to determine precisely how Greer's wealth changed. The asset total is also not an estimate of his net worth; his personal residence is not valued in the filing, while he reported a mortgage of between $1 million and $5 million at a 2.375% interest rate. Pete Hegseth reports at least $3.1 million in cash, investments and bitcoin Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reports more than $250 million in income last year NYSE CEO Sprecher, SBA head Loeffler’s husband, has ties to Trump Jr.-backed private club David Sacks sold $200 million in crypto-related holdings before taking White House job Beyond Greer's newest disclosure, CNBC's review of his finances and ethics records show a previously unreported timeline involving Coupang , the e-commerce giant often dubbed the "Amazon of South Korea." Coupang has become a trade flashpoint , with U.S. investors accusing Seoul of unfairly targeting the company after a major data breach — claims the South Korean government disputes. Greer's nominee disclosure shows that Coupang paid him a $10,000 honorarium in May 2024. Eleven months later, on April 24, 2025, he met with the company at USTR during a day of trade talks , shortly after meeting South Korean trade minister Ahn Duk-geun. Before taking office, Greer had pledged to avoid certain matters involving former clients for one year unless ethics officials cleared his participation. Public records reviewed by CNBC do not show whether USTR treated Coupang as a former client under that commitment or whether Greer received authorization to participate in the meeting. His nominee filing describes the Coupang payment as an "honorarium," while separately identifying other companies as legal services clients. USTR and Coupang did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

events.title: Military ordered to be ready for possible Iran strikes as Trump weighs timing
events.summary: The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran , U.S. officials said. Why it matters: The directive didn't include a specific date for launching strikes, and President Trump hasn't made any final decisions. But U.S. and Israeli sources say it could happen before the U.S. midterm elections and possibly the Israeli elections a week earlier. The big picture: If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include massive bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say. Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterm elections, in part because oil prices might rise in response. "The Department's job is to develop and present military options to the President," a Pentagon official told Axios. A White House official said Trump has all options available at any time. "The U.S. is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways: the easy way or the hard way," the official said. "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States." The Atlantic reported earlier Wednesday that Trump is weighing striking Iran before the midterm election. Driving the news: On Friday, Trump's national security team met at Camp David for several hours to discuss the war and other issues. An Israeli official told Axios that part of the meeting focused on a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said after the meeting that it focused on "long-term" foreign policy planning. Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran haven't made any progress. Qatari mediators are still waiting for an Iranian response to a U.S. counterproposal that included demands for nuclear concessions. "The discussion about possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran has increased. The chances of it happening before the elections is not high but we don't rule it out. After the midterms the chances of it happening increase significantly," a second Israeli official said. Behind the scenes: President Trump spoke Wednesday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It was their second call in days , after barely speaking for many weeks. A U.S. official said Trump and Netanyahu spoke about "remembrance and respect for the victims of the October 7 massacre." The call took place after Netanyahu held a meeting with his national security team about Iran, the first Israeli official said. Netanyahu spoke to Rubio on Monday. If major combat operations resume, they will most likely be with the U.S. and Israel working in tandem and with the Israeli military participating. The two Israeli officials said the Iranian regime is desperate and paranoid, which might lead it to strike first. They said the Iranians have suffered two surprise attacks and don't want to experience a third. Between the lines: Resumption of the war could also affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation. A renewed escalation — or even a heightened state of tension or emergency — could benefit Netanyahu politically and prevent his opponents from attacking him in the final stretch of the campaign.

Loan approvals would be assessed on a “case by case” basis, said a banking industry source, adding that lenders would look at whether buyers had a high net worth or were otherwise considered reliable customers. A property agent handling sales at One Stanley, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said their company had suspended viewings at the development unless clients proactively requested a visit.

events.title: Seafood shop owners fear being forced to close due to gillnet ban
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Gillnet ban will lead to seafood shop closures and fishers retiring, businesses warn Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Neil Green says the ban might see him out of the industry. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) A couple running a seafood restaurant say they may be forced to close if commercial fishers leave the industry when gillnets are banned in the Great Barrier Reef Zone. In 2023 the state and federal governments made the commitment to phase out gillnets in the zone. Temporary gillnet licences are set to expire on June 30, 2027, with the state government running trials with fishers to find alternative fishing methods. Business owners in north Queensland are concerned about the economic flow-on effect of the looming Great Barrier Reef gillnet ban. Some commercial fishers fear they will have to leave the industry and seafood shops may be left with no other option than to close. Peter and Heather Bradford are worried about the future of their business. ( ABC News: Brooke Tindall ) In Ayr, Heather and Peter Bradford serve locally caught seafood to about 150 families a week and say their business will not survive without gillnet fishers on the water. "Next year we'll have to probably close the shop," Mr Bradford said. "Cut out the netting, there's 80 per cent of our business, so we've got no other option but to close." Gillnets are used to catch certain species of fish, including barramundi, by their gills. In 2023 the Queensland and federal governments made the decision to phase out the use of gillnets in the Great Barrier Reef fishing zone by June 30 2027. The governments provided financial assistance to licensed fishers at the time of the decision and established the temporary NX licence, which allowed fishers to use gillnets under strict on-board camera monitoring. The state government has been working with fishers to find an alternative fishing method in the last three years, such as trapping and line fishing. Barramundi is largely caught using gillnets. ( ABC News: Brooke Tindall ) But as the expiry of the NX licences approach, no solutions have been rolled out to fishers. South of Townsville, Alva Beach commercial fisher Neil Green said the other options trialled had not been successful so far. "The intent was to have alternative gear running by 2027. That's been a failure," he said. Neil Green is one of 25 NX licensed fishers in Queensland. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) Mr Green said without change he would probably be forced to retire, but he was worried about more than his own future. "It's not about me — it's about the next generation of fishers that are coming on that we're talking about," he said. Mr Green is among several fishermen in the industry pushing for a three-year extension to the ban, which has the support of Shadow Minister for Northern Australia Susan McDonald. "It will allow [the fishers] to demonstrate that gillnet fishing is incredibly targeted on the species that the fishermen are taking," she said. Susan McDonald supports the seafood industry's call for a three-year extension on NX licences. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Senator McDonald said the 2027 deadline would increase reliability on imports. "If we allow more seafood to be imported from offshore, we are handing over seafood production to countries that don't have the same high standards that Australia does," she said. Back in Ayr, Ms Bradford said importing seafood had not worked for her and her husband's business in the past. "We couldn't compete with [the major supermarkets] price-wise, so it's not going to be viable for us at all," she said. Ms Bradford said other small seafood businesses were in the same boat. "Fish and chip shops will be gone, especially all up along the north coast," she said. Not everyone agrees that putting off the eventual gillnet ban is a viable option. Australian Marine Conservation Society (AMCS) Great Barrier Reef fisheries campaign manager Simon Miller said a three-year extension of the NX licences would come at a cost to wildlife. "The current gillnet fishery, the NX fishery, is still catching thousands of threatened species each year," he said. "We do urge the Queensland and Australian governments to fully deliver their commitment to phase out gillnet fishing from the reef by June 30 next year." The AMCS is against extending temporary licences but Mr Miller says there is support for finding alternative fishing gear. "We need to be looking to the future for genuinely sustainable ways to catch these fish and put them on Queenslanders' plates, but without this impact on threatened species," he said.

events.title: Trump awarding medals to Musk, Dell, Nadella and other tech execs at science summit
events.summary: President Trump is awarding a number of top tech executives with medals at a science summit on Thursday. Elon Musk, Michael Dell, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Google co-founder Sergey Brin are among those slated to receive awards. The recipients all contributed financially, in some capacity, to President Trump or Republican campaigns and causes. President Donald Trump is awarding medals to a number of leading tech executives, including Elon Musk and Michael Dell , at a science summit on Thursday, CNBC has confirmed. Musk, who leads SpaceX and Tesla , is receiving the National Medal of Science, as are Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, according to the White House. Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will be given the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. The event is titled Science: A New Golden Age Summit. Fox News was first to report on it. "The Trump Administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology," Liz Huston, White House assistant press secretary said, in an emailed statement. "These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation." The summit comes a little over a week after Trump hosted a lunch at the White House focused on artificial intelligence that included several of those executives and many others in the industry. Trump told reporters after the gathering that he signed a "morally binding" document with the tech leaders, as calls for a slowdown in the development of AI models reached a fever pitch. Each of the awards recipients at Thursday's summit has financially contributed, in some capacity, to President Trump or Republican campaigns and causes. Musk was Trump's biggest financial backer in the 2024 election cycle, contributing over $290 million, and then led an effort to slash the federal workforce as a special government employee of the Trump administration. Brin attended Trump's inauguration and contributed hundreds of thousands of dollars to the Republican National Committee in 2025. Huang donated to a fund to build Trump's White House ballroom, and Nvidia contributed $1 million to Trump's inauguration ceremony. Dell is a longtime Trump donor. Along with his wife Susan, he committed $6.25 billion to seed Trump Accounts designed to jumpstart savings for children in the U.S. AMD is also contributing to Trump funds. According to his most recent disclosure, Trump bought or sold shares in SpaceX, Tesla, Nvidia, Microsoft, AMD and Google parent Alphabet as recently as July . — CNBC's Eamon Javers contributed to this report. events.title: Anthropic will be 'most ridiculous IPO' of year, analyst says
events.summary: Research firm New Constructs wrote in a note on Tuesday that Anthropic's IPO would be "the most ridiculous IPO of 2026," posing a historic risk to financial markets. Anthropic is reportedly seeking a $2 trillion valuation in its upcoming Nasdaq listing. The company's growing operating losses, combined with the rise in popularity of open-source models, leaves Anthropic without a "viable business," according to the report. As Anthropic barrels toward a potential $2 trillion market cap on the Nasdaq, one research firm is valuing the artificial intelligence company at a mere $150 billion and says Wall Street is about to face an "unprecedented test of investor gullibility." In a report on Tuesday, independent financial research provider New Constructs called Anthropic's upcoming offering the "most ridiculous IPO of 2026." To reach its desired valuation, the firm estimates Anthropic would need to record double the trailing year of profit for Nvidia , the world's most valuable tech company. Nvidia's net income over the past four quarters topped $190 billion. Meanwhile, Anthropic's revenue in 2025 was $4.6 billion as the company racked up a net loss of $42 billion, according to Reuters , which cited a leaked copy of the company's prospectus. Anthropic's mounting operating losses coupled with emerging competition from a plethora of open-source models led New Constructs to conclude that, "We don't think Anthropic has a viable business." "Since the arrival of open-source models, it's been clear that the closed models would struggle to generate profits," the firm wrote. David Trainer, founder and CEO of New Constructs, has built a reputation on Wall Street as a notorious bear on IPOs. He's been right in the past. New Constructs called WeWork "the most ridiculous IPO of 2019," ahead of the office-sharing company's planned offering. WeWork had been valued privately at $47 billion, but just six weeks after the New Constructs report, the company pulled its IPO amid weak demand and intense criticism surrounding its financials. WeWork filed for bankruptcy in 2023. "While Anthropic offers more to society than WeWork ever did, at a $2 trillion valuation, its IPO presents far bigger risks and is positioned to be a far bigger rip off of U.S. capital markets," New Constructs wrote, adding that the IPO's purpose isn't to provide wealth for public markets investors, but rather liquidity for the company's Wall Street backers. Anthropic didn't respond to a request for comment. New Constructs was also bearish on Allbirds ' IPO in 2021. The shoe company debuted on the Nasdaq and reached a valuation of $4.1 billion on its opening day. Earlier this year, the company sold its assets to American Exchange Group for an estimated $39 million, pivoting to AI in the process. Trainer's firm has also missed the mark on calls. Its "most ridiculous" 2020 IPO choice was DoorDash , which the firm also compared to WeWork, calling the food delivery company "similarly disadvantaged." However, DoorDash has held up on the public market. The stock shot up on its first day in December 2020, giving the company a market cap of over $60 billion. That number has since swelled to $83 billion. In an interview with CNBC in 2021, Trainer acknowledged that "crazy stuff happens" and New Constructs doesn't always get it right. "I can't let that bother me," he said at the time. "I have to stay true to what I think is right." Anthropic still hasn't made its prospectus public, so New Constructs hasn't seen the actual filing. However, the firm cited figures that have been reported, including from the New York Times, which reported in September that the company was on pace to generate $100 billion in annualized revenue by the end of 2026. Anthropic claimed at the end of July that its annualized revenue run rate was up sevenfold year-over-year to $65 billion. The New Constructs report also notes that Anthropic's assertion that AI could pose "a catastrophic or existential risk to humanity" is another reason why investors should avoid the IPO. "While we were not fortunate enough to be one of the few to whom Anthropic's S-1 was selectively disclosed, the reports of the leaked financials reveal more than enough to assess the gargantuan risks of investing in this IPO," New Constructs wrote. events.title: Cramer says higher rates are splitting the market in two — and AI stocks have a big advantage
events.summary: CNBC's Jim Cramer said higher borrowing costs are splitting the market, putting pressure on credit-sensitive sectors while AI companies remain largely insulated. He said strong demand for AI growth allows companies such as SpaceX to access capital on attractive terms even as higher rates make borrowing tougher elsewhere. CNBC's Jim Cramer said Wednesday that rising borrowing costs are dividing the stock market into two camps: companies constrained by the bond market and artificial intelligence businesses that seem largely insulated from higher rates. The " Mad Money " host said Wednesday's 10-year Treasury note auction reminded him of his hedge fund days, when investors waited for the results of government bond sales before buying stocks because a poorly received sale could send rates higher and equities lower. Wednesday's $39 billion auction drew strong demand, helping bring Treasury yields off their multidecade highs earlier in the day. Still, stocks ended the day lower after investors were spooked by the benchmark 10-year yield briefly climbing to 5.365%, its highest level since April 2002. Cramer said the market's renewed focus on Treasury auctions underscores how much borrowing costs matter for stocks. "Any market where you need to wait to see the results of a Treasury auction is simply not as good as a market where you don't care about them," Cramer said. "Every time you add a new variable into the equation, it makes owning stocks tougher." Higher rates can ripple across much of the economy. Cramer pointed to finance, housing, utilities, entertainment, retail, autos and industrials as sectors where companies or their customers depend heavily on credit. However, he said AI-related companies appear to play by different rules. Data center builders, semiconductor companies, power providers and cybersecurity firms are far less constrained, according to Cramer, because lenders remain eager to finance their growth. And that also explains why the stock market has lately been so narrow, with AI stocks leading the S&P 500 back to record highs this week. "They seem to be able to borrow at their leisure," Cramer said. "They're crowding out other borrowers with their demand for money." SpaceX is one example. According to a Financial Times report , Elon Musk's rocket and AI company is looking to borrow $40 billion to buy Nvidia chips for data centers and sell the resulting computing power, as it already does with Alphabet's Google and Anthropic . Despite SpaceX's BBB credit rating and the size of the potential borrowing, Cramer expects it could secure relatively attractive terms because of enthusiasm around AI. "If it were any non-data center related company, its [borrowing] rate would skyrocket," Cramer said. "Not the data centers, though." He contrasted that with the newly named Skydance , which recently issued a similar amount of debt as part of its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The bonds quickly fell as investors weighed challenges facing the economically sensitive movie and television businesses, including cord cutting and advertising pressure. The contrast underscores Cramer's larger point: traditional companies remain vulnerable to higher borrowing costs, while AI businesses are largely escaping those same credit concerns. The bifurcation has been showing up in the stock market, with Cramer calling AI stocks "sainted" names. "The AI data center stocks, aside from maybe Oracle, have nothing to do with what price the Federal government borrows at," Cramer said. "They only have to do with a future that's considered so bright that it obscures any problems, any bumps, even any pimples. The rest of corporate America should be so lucky." events.title: A top McKinsey exec shares what keeps him up at night and why he says AI is the solution
events.summary: Eric Kutcher, North America chair at McKinsey & Company, said concerns about the US debt levels keep him up at night. Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Fortune Media McKinsey's Eric Kutcher says AI could help lift US productivity and GDP growth. The firm's North America chair called AI a potential "magic bullet" for reducing the nation's debt. Yet Kutcher warned that energy constraints could cut projected data-center capacity by 25% to 30%. A top McKinsey & Company executive said AI offers the best hope for easing the US debt burden. Eric Kutcher, a senior partner and chair of McKinsey North America, said Wednesday that the technology could lift the nation's productivity and help push US GDP growth closer to 4%. Real GDP grew at a 2.2% annualized pace in the second quarter, according to the latest government estimate. "That would be the magic bullet," he told reporters at the firm's media day in New York. Kutcher made the statement in response to a question about what he hopes AI could solve for the firm or its clients. He said the country's debt is the chief issue that keeps him up at night. Without the productivity gains AI could bring, Kutcher said, he sees no other way to tackle the national debt, which has topped $40 trillion. Investors' concerns about the country's rising debt have helped push Treasury yields higher , making the debt more expensive to finance. Kutcher isn't the only prominent voice to recently sound the alarm about the nation's debt. Billionaire investor Ray Dalio warned Tuesday that he expects a debt crisis "within the next three years." Dalio, the founder of Bridgewater Associates, told Bloomberg Television that the size of the national debt and the speed at which it is growing mean the US is "approaching our limits." Data-center constraints Infrastructure could stand in the way of the AI gains that Kutcher hopes could help ease the debt burden. He said energy constraints could curb data-center capacity by 25% to 30% unless the country expands power supplies. "That's not a simple problem to solve," he said. Kutcher also spoke about hiring at the firm . He said that McKinsey expects to keep adding consultants in North America. He said the firm's consulting staff could grow at roughly the same pace as last year — about 12% — with 85% to 90% of hires continuing to come from campuses. "I am actually incredibly bullish about what this opportunity is for our profession, in part because this is the most transformative moment that this generation will get to lead through," he said. "I think this is a once in every 50-year technology, and this is not new news. We're all seeing it, and experiencing it." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Routers never break right? Embedding the human factor into AI agent adoption now Singapore’s central bank wants all FinTech AI use cases subject to independent review 7 hours ago OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties 11 hours ago Argonne scientists create chatty X-ray microscope that zooms in where you tell it to 11 hours ago Microsoft N1Xes Intel in favor of Nvidia's shiny new SoCs in Surface Laptop Ultra 12 hours ago If you thought Windows Recall was creepy, buckle up. Microsoft is about to shoehorn even more AI into its desktop operating system, giving Copilot access to every file on your PC. But don't worry, Redmond insists it's totally secure and safe since the agents powering the functionality will run entirely on your PC — some of the time. Microsoft describes the new functionality, announced alongside a new Nvidia N1X powered Surface Laptop, as "hybrid intelligence." Built atop Microsoft's HydraFusion model router, Windows apps and Copilot features will soon be able to use local models when it makes sense and cloud-based models when it doesn't. For example, Windows might use a local model for simple or privacy-sensitive tasks, or decide complex or performance-sensitive requests need OpenAI's GPT-6 or Anthropic's Claude. Local agents will run in Microsoft's Execution Containers (MXCs), agent sandboxes with fine-grained permissions applied at runtime. According to Microsoft EVP of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri, MXCs mean Windows is now "the most secure platform for agents." (That claim will surely age well because models never escape their sandboxes and routers never misbehave.) To support this hybrid intelligence functionality, Microsoft is extending support for Windows ML, its inference framework built on the ONNX runtime, to Llama.cpp – one of the highest-performing inference engines for local AI inference. By adding support for Windows ML, Llama.cpp should be able to take advantage of a broader range of accelerators. Microsoft is rolling out its hybrid intelligence functionality to GitHub Copilot — its AI code assistant — next week and its Copilot app over the next few months. The new Copilot features look and sound suspiciously like OpenClaw in a business suit. Copilot's agentic functionality will not have access to your entire file system, opening the door to advanced search functionality and productivity tasks through integrations with Microsoft Office. In a demo, Microsoft showed how Copilot could be used to find and organize a user's tax documents, then draft an email with those files attached, addressed to an accountant. Microsoft insists it'll only go snooping through your docs if you ask it to. Windows is also getting AI-enhanced search functionality enabling users to surface settings like dark mode. The OS will also get a conversational interface to perform tasks like sending a text message to a friend. Finally, for those interested in coloring outside Microsoft's agentic lines, the company is rolling out a new onboarding experience to make deploying agent harnesses like OpenClaw a bit easier and more secure. Keeping sensitive tasks on device may help to assuage anxieties over privacy, which have dogged Microsoft since the first Copilot+ PCs arrived in 2024 alongside Qualcomm's Snapdragon X Elite SoCs. It should also help to reduce the load on Microsoft's servers by keeping low-priority, low-complexity requests on devices. That said, the impact of running these models locally on battery life, fan noise, and workload quality could prove a turnoff for many users.

events.title: Lululemon poaches Athleta CEO as new chief product officer
events.summary: Lululemon announced Wednesday that Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger has is joining the company as its chief product officer, a newly created role. The announcement comes just a month after Heidi O'Neill took over the company as CEO. Athleta owner Gap told CNBC in a statement that the leadership transition will allow it to accelerate its work in repositioning the brand for growth. Lululemon announced Wednesday that Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger is joining the company as president and chief product officer, effective later this month. The move marks the latest shake-up among the top executives in the increasingly competitive athleisure space: Gauger joined Athleta from Nike only last year. Lululemon said Gauger's job is a newly created role. It also appointed Joseph Godsey as chief operating officer. Alongside the new announcements, Lululemon also said Nikki Neuburger, the company's chief brand and product activation officer, and Ted Dagnese, its chief supply chain officer, are leaving in November to "pursue other opportunities." "We are establishing a deeply experienced leadership team that will work in a more coordinated manner, aligned around the strategy and execution that delivers the most impact for our guests, our communities, and our business," Lululemon CEO Heidi O'Neill said in a statement. "That starts with putting product, design, and innovation at the center of how we operate, with the focus and accountability to create a stronger pipeline of differentiated product to raise the bar for our guests across every touchpoint, in stores and online." In a statement provided to CNBC, Athleta parent company Gap confirmed Gauger has left the company. It said Erika Everett, the brand's current chief marketing officer, will oversee the brand CEO role in the interim. "We have been actively shaping Athleta's next chapter and the changes needed to position the brand for long-term growth," Gap said in its statement. "This transition enables us to accelerate that work, strengthen our connection with customers, and unlock Athleta's full potential." Separately, Lululemon said it is also searching for a chief brand officer, a chief communications officer and a chief technology officer. O'Neill took the helm of Lululemon last month after the athleisure company saw more than a year of disappointing sales performance in the midst of a proxy battle, drawing criticism from founder Chip Wilson.

events.title: I can't take back the vacations I never took with my kids. At 51, I'm saying yes to solo travel.
events.summary: The author said she regrets not traveling more with her children when they were younger, but she's trying to make up for that now. Courtesy of Tatyana Gann. At 51, I took a solo trip to Washington, DC, and had a wonderful time exploring museums on my own. Seeing others with young kids made me miss my own and regret not traveling with them more. I always had dreams of traveling with my family, but other things got in the way. I regret that. As I walked through the Julia Child kitchen exhibit at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, I felt like I was experiencing the moment I had seen in the movie "Julie and Julia," when the main character, Julie, took a photo in the museum with a stick of butter. Fourteen years later, I stood in the same spot right beside the famous portrait of Julia Child. I could not believe my dream came true, and I asked myself a question that made me sad," Why didn't I do this sooner?" I felt free and proud, yet sad, on my first solo trip. I was eager to share my excitement and the moments I'd only dreamed of with my sons, who were in college at the time. It was bittersweet because I should have been sharing these moments with my sons and seeing their eyes light up as they s aw C-3PO from "Return of the Jedi" or Prince's Yellow Cloud Guitar, also on display. Instead, I was exploring the world of Smithsonian museums alone. While I strolled the halls, I watched parents and kids in the gift shops together buying different trinkets to remind them of their time together. Yet, here I was finally traveling, just me, my phone, and my suitcase. Do you have a parenting regret? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. After my day at the museum, exhausted from the long walks and metro rides, I looked through the dozens of photos I'd taken and realized again that the two most important people weren't there with me. I took my very first vacation to the capital of America without my sons, and that hurt. I dreamed of travel, but never made it happen The idea of taking vacations with kids , seeing new cities, and visiting the East and West coasts was always on my dream board. But vacations always seemed expensive, and I know that taking little kids on trips wasn't always as enjoyable in practice as it was in theory. Instead, we stuck to local fun, like long drives to the beach. In my mind, I always believed there would be another summer when we could go on vacation as a family. I planned for it, too, looking through travel magazines in the bookstore and hoping that one day we would take adventures together. The author said a friend encouraged her to take a solo trip to DC. Since then, she's been on more vacations on her own. Courtesy of Tatyana Gann. Life threw us some curveballs Over the years, the dream board had to evolve. My divorce changed everything in my life and the lives of my kids. Vacations weren't my priority when I had to learn to survive and face life's trials during and after the divorce. I craved stability, not vacation time. That is what I told myself. I believed that when things settled, we could travel. Divorce changed me as a mother. I took on different roles in the household to make sure my kids had what they needed for school and their future careers. Looking back, I now see that I left out one of the most important aspects of their childhood — traveling and seeing new cities, dipping toes into the sand at different beaches, and exploring the world together. I postponed the vacations till they got older, and I postponed the joy. The author said she has traveled quite a bit after taking her first solo trip to DC. Courtesy of Tatyana Gann. My kids eventually grew up, graduated high school, and went to college. They became independent, wanted to spend time with their friends, and no longer needed me in the same ways they once did. The survival mode we lived in consumed me, and the joy of planning and taking a summer vacation with kids never had a chance. Looking back, I know that's not something I can get back. I'm finally doing it As I embraced being an empty nester , a friend in DC called me and said, "Why don't you travel? Come to DC and see all the art you want here." That is when I decided to permit myself to start a new chapter. My life was not over just because my kids grew up and moved out, or because my marriage or other relationships ended. I booked my trip and started planning. And this time, I went. Since then, I've taken more trips to DC and Chicago, I visited beautiful cities on Lake Michigan and Lake Geneva, and created moments just for myself without waiting for the perfect companion or perfect timing. At 51, I pack my own suitcases and enjoy my company at home and in new places. And now, I'm even planning future travel with my sons. I know I can't change the past, but I can commit to changing the future. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Brazilian students in Rio de Janeiro march against the prospect of another Bolsonaro presidency
events.summary: Thousands of Brazilian students have marched in Rio de Janeiro against the possibility of Flávio Bolsonaro winning the presidency RIO DE JANEIRO -- Thousands of Brazilian students marched in downtown Rio de Janeiro on Wednesday to protest against the possibility of Flávio Bolsonaro winning the presidency, after the far-right candidate received more votes than incumbent and left-leaning Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election . A sea of red-clad demonstrators made their way between two historical squares in Rio’s center, chanting and holding signs referencing Brazil’s sovereignty and democracy in the South American country , which they said were under threat. “We’re fighting for Brazil, not for Lula,” said Talita Amaral, a 19-year-old environmental science student at a nearby university. She was wearing Brazil’s yellow and green soccer jersey, often worn by supporters of Bolsonaro, which she said was a gesture aimed at reclaiming the national colors. “We don’t have time to be sad, we need to be doing this, occupying the streets, sending messages in WhatsApp groups, trying to convince people,” Amaral said, as the chant “Olé olé olé ola, Lula Lula” rang out across Cinelandia square. Neither Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup, nor Lula received more than the required 50% of the vote needed to become Brazil’s leader on Sunday. Therefore, they will face each other in an unpredictable runoff on Oct. 25. But Flávio Bolsonaro has at least two advantages: He received 2 million more votes than Lula on Sunday and the candidates who placed third, fourth and fifth are all on the right of the political spectrum. They gathered more than 8 million votes between them. Bolsonaro is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion because of his ties to the failed Banco Master — a case that many protesters in Rio made reference to on Wednesday. Some pointed to Jair Bolsonaro's handling of the coronavirus pandemic , during which 700,000 people were reported to have died from the disease, while others held signs emblazoned with messages such as “Brazil isn't anyone's backyard” and “I don't vote for someone who sells Brazil.” Many on the left fear a Flávio Bolsonaro presidency would fully align the Brazilian government with the United States because of the proximity in ideologies between U.S. President Donald Trump and the Bolsonaro family. Last year, Trump imposed a 50% tariff on Brazilian goods and imposed sanctions on a Brazilian Supreme Court justice, citing Jair Bolsonaro’s trial, which he called a “witch hunt.” Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Army to execute Fort Hood mass shooter by firing squad Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys “If Bolsonaro wins, Brazil will become a colony of the United States,” said João Victor Vieira, 20, who studies literature. He said that Bolsonaro represented a threat to minorities such as people of color, women and the LGBTQ+ community. Bolsonaro's father was notorious for homophobic remarks. Vieira said that while he was initially dispirited following the results on Sunday, he has since regained hope. “This protest shows that social movements are still very much alive,” he said. “We will resist.” This story corrects a previous version that stated the candidates who placed third, fourth and fifth gathered 6 million votes. The correct number of votes is more than 8 million. events.title: Wall Street ends lower, off record highs, as Treasury yields climb
events.summary: Iran war-related supply concerns have led to soaring oil prices, which in turn have revived inflation worries and raised the chances of a prolonged central bank rate hiking cycle. - Wall Street fell as long-dated US Treasury yields rose and oil prices revived inflation and debt fears after record highs. - The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all ended lower; small-cap stocks, housing, homebuilders and chip shares were weak. - Investors now expect the Fed to pause in October, while earnings season will test AI spending and US consumer strength. NEW YORK – Wall Street closed lower on Oct 7, as long-dated US Treasury yields resumed their climb, reviving fears about inflation and mounting debt the day after the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq hit record closing highs. All three major US stock indexes were modestly lower, with the S&P 500 and the Dow snapping four-day winning streaks. The Nasdaq notched its first down day in six. The small-cap Russell 2000 underperformed its larger cap counterparts, dropping 1.3%. In the wake of a stock market rally on Oct 6, Brent crude settled above US$100 per barrel and long-dated Treasury yields touched a 24-year high. Iran war-related supply concerns have led to soaring oil prices, which in turn have revived inflation worries and raised the chances of a prolonged central bank rate hiking cycle. Those concerns, combined with mounting corporate and sovereign debt levels, have caused a global bond sell-off, which rattled global markets in recent weeks. Investors “have been looking for some relief on oil, which would drive some relief on rates and that would therefore help the stock market”, said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at Globalt in Atlanta. “The third quarter was supposed to be the weak quarter of the year. We were supposed to get a correction,” Martin added. “That didn’t happen, so it’s three cheers and let’s take some money off the table.” Stocks pared losses after crude prices turned lower following the International Energy Agency’s agreement to speed up the release of oil stocks, prioritising diesel. Minutes from the US Federal Reserve’s September monetary policy meeting, at which the central bank unanimously approved its first interest rate hike since July 2023, revealed divisions over the rationale of the increase. Some participants saw a hike as necessary to keep the impact of energy price shocks at bay, while others felt the increase was necessary to curb demand-driven inflation. Financial markets are pricing in a 17.2% likelihood that the Fed will implement a second consecutive rate hike at the conclusion of its October meeting, down from 37.6% a week ago, per CME’s FedWatch tool. “The market’s Fed expectations are going to seesaw as it gets new bits of data,” Martin said. “There’s still an expectation for more rate hikes, but it isn’t necessarily going to be a hike every meeting and that’s what the market is telling you. October will be a pause.” The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 341.11 points, or 0.66%, to 51,180.17, the S&P 500 lost 17.18 points, or 0.22%, to 7,801.75 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 61.19 points, or 0.22%, to 27,538.69. Among the 11 sectors in the S&P 500, industrials suffered the steepest percentage drop, while healthcare stocks led the gainers. Following the upward march of benchmark Treasury yields, the 30-year fixed mortgage rate surged last week to a near three-year high, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Housing slipped 2.3%, while home builders were down 2.9%. Chip stocks, which have soared over 80% so far in 2026, dropped 1.2%. SpaceX lost 2.5% following media reports that Elon Musk’s aerospace firm was seeking US$40 billion (S$50 billion) in financing to fund purchases of Nvidia chips. Next week, third-quarter reporting season is expected to begin in earnest with a spate of high-profile financial firms expected to post results. Investors are likely to scrutinise the extent to which massive expenditures on AI technology are beginning to show results, while also watching for clues regarding the health of the US consumer at a time of mounting inflationary pressures. Analysts expect year-on-year S&P 500 earnings growth of 30.6%, on aggregate, for the July-through-September period, according to LSEG. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.34-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 115 new highs and 497 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 1,421 stocks rose and 3,371 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 2.37-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted nine new 52-week highs and 12 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 32 new highs and 250 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 16.21 billion shares, compared with the 17.57 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

events.title: Student protest unrest spreads across Europe
events.summary: Police and protesters clashed in Liège, Belgium, on Wednesday as student anger over education costs and school conditions grew, echoing massive protests in neighboring France. Why it matters: The protests are exposing broader anger across Europe over school funding and classroom conditions. Catch up quick: Protests that began in Paris in mid-September as a localized demonstration by high school students have escalated into a massive nationwide movement, with students, parents and teachers' unions demanding more education funding. There have been clashes between French police and protesters in recent days, culminating in a 15-year-old boy's hand being blown off by a police-fired stun grenade. More than 6,500 people — most of them minors —have been arrested since the protests began in France. In Belgium, police have made at least 139 arrests in Liège since the protests began Oct. 1. The big picture: The current wave erupted in France, but education grievances across Europe predate it, with crowded classrooms, teacher shortages, university cuts and soaring education costs fueling protests over government investment in education. In Greece, students called nationwide school actions for Thursday, according to Euronews , including assemblies, walkouts, demonstrations and potentially occupations. In Italy, high-school occupations began in Turin and Rome on Monday under the slogan "Let's do as in France." Italian students cited underfunding, deteriorating school buildings and rising living costs among grievances they share with French students, and a delegation traveled to Paris in solidarity, ANSA reports . In Ireland, thousands of university students demonstrated in Dublin earlier this month, demanding lower fees, more higher-education funding and affordable accommodation, per RTÉ . In Germany, students, teachers, parents and unions rallied in September to demand greater education investment, more teachers and a more equitable school system, according to Tagesschau . In Austria, student groups are preparing fresh demonstrations in mid-October after the country's university association warned of possible cuts of around €1 billion from the next three-year university budget, ORF reports . Between the lines: The education unrest comes as several European governments face mounting pressure to rein in deficits while higher borrowing costs make their debts more expensive to service. France and Belgium are each running budget deficits of more than 5% of their GDP this year, while Austria's is above 4%, according to European Commission forecasts. That squeeze is forcing governments to make difficult choices over public spending. The bottom line: The protests aren't one coordinated European movement, but students across several countries are mobilizing around their shared concerns. events.title: Levi Strauss hikes profit guidance after tariff refunds, but its sales outlook is less optimistic
events.summary: Levi Strauss on Wednesday posted earnings that beat expectations, though it saw benefits from tariff refunds. The denim retailer raised its earnings per share guidance for the full year but lowered its net revenue growth projection to the bottom end of its previously provided range. Levi said it saw a 4% increase in net revenues in the Americas during the quarter, though revenue in the U.S. decreased by 1%. Levi Strauss on Wednesday increased its profit outlook after it received tariff refunds, but gave less rosy revenue guidance. The denim retailer raised its adjusted earnings per share expectation for the full fiscal year to between $1.54 and $1.56, from a previous range of $1.46 to $1.52. Analysts were expecting a range of between $1.52 and $1.59, according to LSEG. The company also lowered its net revenue growth guidance for the full year to 7%, the bottom of its previously provided range of a 7% to 7.5% increase. For its fiscal third quarter, the denim retailer said it saw a 4% increase in net revenues in the Americas, though revenue in the U.S. decreased 1%. It also reported an operating margin of 13.8% for the quarter, compared to 10.8% in the same quarter last year, boosted by tariff refunds that contributed 4.9% to operating margin and gross margin. Levi also said its tariff refunds contributed a 16-cent benefit to its earnings per share, of which 5 cents were "redeployed to support the business." On a call with analysts, CEO Michelle Gass said that money is going toward marketing and promotions during the holiday season. Here's how Levi performed in its third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 48 cents adjusted, it was unclear how that figure compared to the 36 cents Wall Street expected Revenue: $1.61 billion vs. $1.62 billion expected For the three-month period ending Aug. 30, Levi reported net income of $168.6 million, or 43 cents per share, down from $218.1 million, or 55 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose roughly 4% to $1.61 billion from $1.54 billion last year. Levi said direct-to-consumer net revenues increased 2% in the quarter, but comparable sales were roughly flat. DTC comprised 45% of total net revenue in the third quarter, the company said. On the other hand, wholesale revenues increased 6% for the quarter. "While we delivered strong results across much of the business, our DTC performance fell short of our expectations during the quarter," Gass said on the call with analysts. "We have a clear understanding of what worked and what did not, and we have already taken targeted actions to improve performance." The company previously said it's been seeing broad-based growth across its business segments, including its core Levi's and its premium blue tab. Last month, the company announced John Vandemore will take over as chief financial officer effective Nov. 1, succeeding Harmit Singh, who announced his retirement in April.

events.title: Here's how the largest fraternities earn and spend their millions
events.summary: Students at the University of Michigan gather at the Sigma Chi fraternity house to party on a Saturday afternoon. : Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Greek life is a dominant force on US college campuses, and organizations manage millions annually. Fraternities generate millions through member dues, alumni donations, and real estate investments. Many Greek-letter organizations report tax filings under various entities. Fraternities are a staple of the American college experience, whether it's for their social influence on campus, sprawling alumni networks , or, at times, controversies . But behind the parties and secretive traditions are tax-exempt organizations that bring in millions of dollars each year. Tax filings offer a partial glimpse into how the country's biggest fraternities earn and spend their money. Sigma Phi Epsilon Fraternity Inc., the national organization behind one of the largest fraternities across US college campuses , reported $10.6 million in revenue in fiscal 2025 and ended the year with $29.4 million in net assets, according to public tax filings . In comparison, Chi Phi Fraternity Inc., which has about 48 active chapters nationwide and is affiliated with Cornell's now-shuttered Chi Phi chapter, reported $1.8 million in revenue and $2.1 million in net assets in the same year, per its tax filings . Chi Phi declined a request for comment from Business Insider. Because many fraternities' local chapters, philanthropic foundations , and housing groups operate independently, tax filings often show only part of their broader, more complex financial picture. Take a look into how the US's largest fraternities earn and spend their millions — and what little is known about their internal finances. Every semester, thousands of students rush to join fraternities across the US. GAINESVILLE, FL - SEPTEMBER 12: College freshmen "rush" a fraternity at the University of Florida in Gainesville on September 12, 2016. (Photo by Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis via Getty Images)'Rushing' for a fraternity at the University of Florida, Gainesville Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis via Getty Images Recruitment brings new dues-paying members to Greek life organizations, reaching thousands of students across college campuses. At Miami University in Ohio , for example, 2,208 students registered for Greek-life recruitment in spring 2026. This included 859 men who registered for recruitment with the school's 25 Interfraternity Council fraternities. That same semester, nearly one in three full-time undergraduate men at the school's main Oxford campus belonged to a fraternity. Member dues are a major revenue source. At the University of Arizona, members of the 20 fraternities in the Interfraternity Council pay an average of about $1,573 per semester in active-member fees, excluding housing, as of summer 2026, according to the university's Sorority and Fraternity Programs website. Including housing, the average is about $5,535 per semester. The university adds that the organizations set and collect their own dues independently. Contributions, including alumni gifts, can be another source of income for national Greek organizations. In 2017, the Oklahoma State University chapter of Pi Kappa Alpha dedicated a new 32,500-square-foot, $12.8 million mansion (equivalent to $17.5 million today, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics ' inflation calculator). President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the U.S. does not think the death of a Russian laboratory worker from a suspected case of plague is the result of a bioweapon. events.title: Trump’s diesel order exposes White House limits to counter surging fuel prices
events.summary: President Donald Trump's order allowing highway truckers to use off-road diesel only defers federal excise taxes. Truckers may still have to pay later. Trump's order does not defer state excise taxes, which can be higher. The latest move comes after the president abandoned the idea of banning diesel exports. Analysts say the only real solution to high fuel prices is an end to the war in the Middle East. Truckers likely won't see much in the way of relief from President Donald Trump's executive order that allows them to use off-road diesel fuel on America's highways without federal penalties, analysts say. Off-road diesel is exempt from federal and state excise taxes because it is used for construction and farm equipment, railways and to heat homes. It is dyed red to differentiate it from taxed on-road diesel, but is otherwise the same fuel. The federal government charges an excise tax of 24.4 cents per gallon for on-road diesel. In theory, Trump's order spares truckers the tax by allowing them to use red-dyed fuel on the highway, without worrying that the federal government will impose penalties. But the president's action only defers the actual tax payment itself until the end of the year, while calling on the Treasury secretary to look for ways to eliminate the deferred obligation altogether. "While it might be deferred, it may not disappear entirely," said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. "Maybe you save a little bit of money up front, but you might have to pay it to the government later." Treasury is preparing guidance to provide "clarity on the obligations for users and sellers of dyed diesel," a White House official told CNBC. The official asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly about the the plans. Treasury has enforcement discretion, the official said. The Internal Revenue Service will only enforce the deferred tax liability if it is directed to do so by the Treasury secretary and the president, the official said. The IRS will soon make a determination on "whether dedicating its limited resources to fuel tank inspections and fuel sampling investigations represents the best use" of its resources, the official said. Trump cannot defer state excise taxes, which can be higher than the federal obligation, at a national average of 35.5 cents per gallon. Some states have taken independent action to give relief to diesel users. Although Trump is waiving federal penalties for using off-road diesel on highways, states in principle could enforce their local laws prohibiting the red-dyed fuel on the road. "It's not like every state trooper is going to pull over the truck and look at your diesel fuel, but you're a trucker — do you need that aggravation?" Lipow said. Trump's executive order comes as he faces political pressure to take action on diesel prices ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3, when Republicans face competitive races in farm states such as Iowa. Retail diesel prices hit a record high in September and currently average $6.30 a gallon nationally, according to AAA. The president flirted with a diesel export ban last month but ultimately abandoned the idea, telling reporters Friday that "it was never really on the table." The oil industry and big business groups were staunchly opposed. Trump publicly voiced concerns that a diesel export ban would raise gasoline prices. Diesel futures dropped overnight Monday into Tuesday morning after Trump's executive order, but ultimately turned higher. Futures were up more than 1% Wednesday. "What it shows you is there are no good options for the administration or any administration to bring down the price of fuel, because the bottleneck is refineries," Lipow said. Diesel prices are high around the world because Ukraine is bombarding Russian refineries and strikes by Iran and its allies have taken capacity offline in the Middle East. G7 countries led by France, facing pressure from the Trump administration, agreed Friday to release diesel stocks , though it's unclear in what quantities. "They're pulling every lever they can," Jeff Currie, CEO of Real Macro and a senior advisor at Carlyle, told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Tuesday. But Trump's executive order allowing red-dyed diesel on the road "won't have a profound impact" on fuel prices, Currie said. There is one action the administration could take that would be effective, Lipow said. "End the conflict." "The Strait [of Hormuz] reopens, oil flows, those refineries in the Middle East start kicking up runs, more refined products make it to the market," the analyst said. "The market will react to that."

events.title: SpaceX just scored a key Starlink approval that could shake up the wireless market
events.summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX was handed a win by the FCC. Sebastian Gollnow/picture alliance via Getty Images The FCC approved SpaceX's plan to deploy 15,000 Starlink satellites for direct-to-device service. The federal agency also waived a rule that requires a leasing agreement with a ground-based carrier. The decision could strengthen SpaceX's ability to take on major wireless carriers. Elon Musk's SpaceX just scored a regulatory win that could give Starlink more power to compete with wireless giants Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile. The Federal Communications Commission officially granted SpaceX's request to deploy and operate 15,000 Starlink satellites to provide direct-to-device connectivity. Additionally, the FCC waived a rule that requires a leasing arrangement with one or more terrestrial wireless carriers, allowing SpaceX to use its own spectrum for the service. "With this action, SpaceX's planned deployments will reshape spectrum-based connectivity by improving competition, allowing more consumers more choices in more places to further the Commission's goal to 'connect everyone, everywhere to modern communications services,'" the FCC said in its order released Monday. Still, SpaceX faces skepticism from the carriers it hopes to take on. "We've seen no zero discernible impact on our broadband growth from any LEO, low earth orbit satellite provider, including Starlink," Verizon CEO Dan Schulman said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month. Schulman added that he does not view satellite as a "viable competitor in the medium and even longer term." Read the original article on Business Insider
