events.title: OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Persistent agents appeal to AI companies, but demand isn't obvious AWS launches open-source AI agent sandbox to prevent YOLO mode disasters 14 hours ago Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism 23 hours ago COSMIC shuts the door on AI code as GNOME debates letting bug reports in 23 hours ago South Korean president calls for creation of tools that stop all cyber-attacks 1 day ago Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI's, study says 1 day ago When OpenAI introduced dots last month , it pitched them as "always-on agents" running in their own cloud computer, but that may be overstating the readiness of the technology and of the people trying to use it. Presently, multiple users are reporting task failures and connection issues with their dots. Others have flagged cloud connectivity problems, dots that disappear , and dot refusals that appear to be related to abuse prevention. And the OpenAI Developer Community forum shows several similar concerns . OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment about the usage of dots. ABI Research argues that "AI claws" – always-on agents – will shape enterprise AI adoption. The biz sees "a market evolving from isolated assistants toward modular agent ecosystems built for longer-running, enterprise-grade automation." Despite the hiccups that have afflicted dots, some skepticism on social media forums, speculation that OpenAI rushed dots out in response to Meta Muse and Grok Bot , and security issues , dots have some enthusiastic users in addition to detractors who just don't see the point. They also have competition from companies and developers who believe they can deliver a similar service more affordably, with fewer restrictions. A company called Tawkit that makes an SDK called CopilotKit has released OpenDots . "OpenDots is completely open source and gives you the same thing [as OpenAI Dots] as a template you host yourself," the biz said in a post last week. "Bring any agent through AG-UI, use any OpenAI-compatible model, and make every part of it your own." The company previously released OpenMuse and OpenBot . These projects essentially separate the user interface, the AG-UI agent layer, and the backend to provide an alternative personal agent. This doesn't eliminate the token expense of whatever agent is deployed, but it does mean that OpenAI may not be doing the billing. Then there's a potentially lower cost option, called (confusingly) Open Dot , powered by AI models running on OpenRouter. And as it's open source, the code could be altered to run using a local model – a feature that we understand is planned. "Open Dot is an open source version [of OpenAI Dots] that runs on your own Mac with your own OpenAI key, or with open models like Kimi, DeepSeek and Qwen through OpenRouter," the project repo explains. It allows users to connect to various apps like Gmail, Calendar, Slack, Notion, and GitHub via Composio . Prathit Joshi, the project's creator, told The Register , "I enjoy building and shipping tools for developers, especially tools that can support use cases that closed model companies aren't necessarily incentivized to support, like allowing open source models." Joshi is based in Bangalore, India, and works as a growth engineer at Composio. He said he's been using Open Dot to handle personal tasks like setting "to do" lists for the day based on Slack messages and summarizing posts on social media. Open Dot is based on the Electron framework, Joshi said, because he wanted it to be a desktop app. Distinguishing between OpenAI dots, OpenDots, and Open Dot may be confusing, but don't expect things to get any better in the near future. Everyone is busy wrapping increasingly commoditized models in a gatekeeping layer, in the hope of developing a sustainable business. For example, Elon Musk said on Tuesday that Grok Bot would become a model router rather than a front-end for a specific model.

events.title: What Amazon's customer profiles got right — and hilariously wrong — about us
events.summary: Amazon's "About You" page has been all the rage in our newsroom conversations this week. Getty Images/Business Insider Conversations about Amazon's customer dossiers have taken over the Business Insider newsroom. Some insights were spot-on. Others were weirdly personal. Here's what Amazon thinks it knows about us based on our shopping data. Amazon thinks Thomas Gryta really likes beef jerky. He doesn't really know why. "I've ordered more energy bars and vitamins than jerky," Business Insider's interim corporate editor wrote in Slack. He added that his Amazon "About You" customer profile "feels like a judgy accusation from a nutritionist." Thomas says he doesn't live with another adult, has kids, doesn't wear women's clothes, and only eats jerky from time to time. Amazon disagrees. Thomas Gryta/Business Insider That was just one of the messages that blew up Business Insider's Slack on Wednesday morning after I reported that people online were having a field day looking up their own Amazon "About You" page . People noticed the shopping profiles making bizarre — sometimes unflattering — judgments, like telling one Amazon user they have " flat buttocks " or another that their husband has " skinny legs. " The e-commerce giant launched About You in May. The page acts a bit like a customer dossier, pulling information from customers' marketplace searches, purchase histories, saved lists, product reviews, and conversations with Amazon's Alexa for Shopping assistant. Amazon says the goal is to connect customers with products that better fit their needs, and shoppers can update or remove details from the profile. Naturally, Business Insider's nosy newshounds with semi-voyeuristic relationships with the internet wanted to share what we found out about ourselves, whether brutally accurate or laughably off base. Per our own Slack channels, we found that Amazon typically made 30 to 45-ish observations for each subject. Those inferences frequently got the transactions right, but the human conclusions were sometimes a little off. "My wife and I share an Amazon account, so our 'About You' profile was a bit warped," wrote Paul Squire, our deputy editor of homepage and programming, noting that Amazon correctly gleaned that he has a cat and a MacBook. "But it missed the mark by not realizing our second cat, Sylvie, even exists. 'Has one cat'? Try again, Jeff Bezos." For Taylor Rains, a partnership editor, Amazon got a little personal about her taste in movie actors. "One of mine is: 'used to like Ryan Reynolds , but not so much anymore,'" she wrote on Wednesday. "How does it know?" Sorry, Ryan! Taylor Rains/Business Insider Still, the majority of Amazon's judgments from our very unscientific newsroom poll proved correct. Correspondent Madeline Berg said Amazon properly clocked that she was a stereotypical Brooklynite who prefers glass food storage and organic produce. Deputy executive editor Taylor Berman said his account is optimized for "bathroom safety," a finding likely tied to his need for a shower chair after he tore his Achilles tendon last May (he asked me to make sure readers knew that his other purchases were "very cool"). Amazon is just looking after Taylor's health. Taylor Berman/Business Insider Another editor, who has young kids, said Amazon reported that she frequently buys waterproof sheets. Debbie Strong, deputy executive editor, said the system clocked her as a "boy mom" after it said she prefers Hot Wheels toy cars. Other big themes: Amazon is very good at recognizing where we live (no surprises there), what kinds of groceries we frequently buy at Whole Foods, and if we have pets. Apparently, Business Insider's staff likes to buy a lot of books and Pokémon cards , too (many said the cards were for their kids. Sureeeeee .) Amazon's crystal ball was less good at deciphering family size. Several people said their About You page incorrectly identified how many kids they had. Some relationship specifics were off too. It incorrectly said one editor had a girlfriend named "Barry." As for yours truly, who knows what Amazon knows about me — I haven't had an account for years. Like my colleagues, I will be uncomfortably forthcoming with my results if that changes. Do you have a funny story or screenshot to share from your Amazon "About You" page? Send it to bshimkus@insider.com and we might include it in an upcoming story! Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Michael Stuhlbarg had no idea what 'Digger' was about when he filmed the movie
events.summary: Michael Stuhlbarg stars alongside Tom Cruise in "Digger." Focus Features; Jeff Spicer/Getty; Sony Pictures Classics; BI Michael Stuhlbarg didn't know what to expect when he got to the set of "Digger." He just knew he had to be there. The production of Oscar-winning director Alejandro González Iñárritu's new movie with Tom Cruise was shrouded in mystery, even to its star-studded cast, which was kept on a need-to-know-basis about what kind of movie they were making. Still, Stuhbarg and the rest of the cast, which includes John Goodman , Riz Ahmed, Sandra Hüller, and Jesse Plemons, wanted answers. "Our rehearsals allowed us that kind of time to ask as many questions: 'What have you heard?' 'What can we expect?'" Stuhlbarg told Business Insider over the phone, describing the cast as a "repertory company" that filmed over seven months. "We were all in the same boat of learning about the movie at the same time." Those who haven't seen Iñárritu's provocative, twisty new climate-change satire have been kept similarly in the dark. Here's what I can tell you: Tom Cruise plays an oil tycoon named Digger Rockwell who has a lot of explaining to do when one of his wells explodes. Riz Ahmed plays an environmentalist on Rockwell's team, John Goodman plays the president of the United States, who is leaning on Rockwell to fix the problem, and Stuhlbarg plays his sheepish vice president. Riz Ahmed, Tom Cruise, John Goodman, and Michael Stuhlbarg at the "Digger" premiere. Lia Toby/Getty Images Stuhlbarg's performance matches the movie's satirical tone as he delivers perfectly timed comedic reactions, often without dialogue, as the situation becomes increasingly dire. He attributes that talent to his training as a child under the iconic mime Marcel Marceau. "It was one of those things where silence and thought was captured in a large scale," he said. "Every beat, every moment, every breath, every gesture needed to be registered by Alejandro's orchestration."  Business Insider's " Role Play " series features interviews where acting legends revisit their most memorable roles. See more here . It's just the latest top-notch performance from Stuhlbarg, who broke out playing the lead in the Coen brothers' 2009 drama "A Serious Man" after decades in theater. Since then, he's had memorable roles in everything from "Boardwalk Empire" to " Call Me by Your Name. " For the latest interview in Business Insider's Role Play series , Stuhlbarg spoke about playing Timothée Chalamet's dad in "Call Me by Your Name," getting blindsided by Woody Allen's directing tactics on "Blue Jasmine," and the unique way Daniel Day-Lewis connected with him on the set of Steven Spielberg's "Lincoln." On learning the movie business from the Coen brothers and getting acting tips from Woody Allen Stuhlbarg in "A Serious Man." Focus Features Business Insider: You got your start on the stage, appearing in over 35 productions playing everyone from King Richard II to Hamlet, before you got "A Serious Man." At that time, were you content to be a stage actor the rest of your life? Michael Stuhlbarg: I hadn't really thought about it, to tell you the truth. Theater was where I was initially most comfortable, so to get to work with Joel and Ethan [Coen] for an extended period of time in front of the camera for the very first time, it was absolutely a learning experience. I remember speaking to Joel before we started and he said, "Do you want to look at what we're doing?" And I was like, "Nah, you let me know if you need me to see something, but otherwise I'll do it and you tell me if it's working or not working."  Michael Stuhlbarg playing Hamlet in Shakespeare in the Park in 2008. Bruce Glikas/FilmMagic/Getty What was it like to be the star of a Coen brothers movie? You were the face of that movie, on the poster, all over the trailer, the award campaigns. For someone from the stage, was it daunting? I was ready for it when it happened to me. I had built my sea legs enough; I felt like I was the right guy for that moment. And the rest of it was a delight. It was a remarkable welcome into a craft that, even though I knew very little about it, I felt like I was ready to listen and apply what I needed. And I had the best people in the business to guide me.  That's quite the understatement. By 2013, you had worked with the Coen brothers ("A Serious Man"), Martin Scorsese ("Hugo"), Barry Sonnenfeld ("Men in Black 3"), Steven Spielberg ("Lincoln"), and Woody Allen ("Blue Jasmine"). Would you say working with Woody Allen on "Blue Jasmine" was the project where you had the most restrictions put on your performance? He knew what he wanted, and I think I just went along for the ride. There were some cases where he would basically go through it himself, being the actor that he is.  Michael Stuhlbarg and Cate Blanchett in "Blue Jasmine." Sony Pictures Classics Meaning, you're standing there watching him act out the scene as you? Yes. If I wasn't giving him what he needed, he would jump in, give it a go, and then I would jump in and try to provide the color that he was asking for.  As an actor, do you just think, OK, this is the gig? Or is there a shot to your ego? Hey, look at my resume! Why did you hire me? I don't really mind, to be honest with you. I'm there to help a director achieve a vision. Very rarely am I so imprinted with a role that I know deep in my bones that what I have to offer is the right answer for something, because I never know how it's going to be captured —from what angle? I might be just part of the frame; who knows how things will be captured. So that's a part of cinema. I choose my battles very carefully. I'll say that.  On going down mobster rabbit holes for 'Boardwalk Empire' and working with Timothée Chalamet Stuhlbarg in "Call Me by Your Name." Sony Pictures Classics You said you got obsessed with playing infamous Jewish Mob kingpin Arnold Rothstein on the HBO series "Boardwalk Empire." How obsessed did you get? When you're given a real person to inhabit, like I was, obsession can be helpful in terms of learning as much as you can, which was simply my objective. Gambling, I had a tutor for, and billiards, I also had a tutor for. And there was a biography about him that gave me a lot of things to apply to my performance as well. He was a historical character in a historical fiction story, so his real life provided the background. And that then led to the imaginative leap that we all have to take in storytelling.  Your performance as the father of Timothée Chalamet's character in "Call Me by Your Name" is a career highlight. How do you go about working with younger actors, and did working with Chalamet change at all when you did "Bones and All"? We all meet each other where we are. So I don't think of it as young and old, I think of it as individuals meeting and sharing energy together. With "Call Me by Your Name," I felt naturally draw

events.title: Data shows rental tenants have hit breaking point
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tenants unable to pay higher rental prices, Domain data finds The rental market is slowing despite prices remaining at record highs. ( ABC News ) Despite severe rental shortages, landlords are struggling to increase rents due to tenants hitting their affordability limit. New data shows rent is flatlining in most capital cities and has even fallen in a few in the past three months. Although the market is slowing, with the national vacancy rate rising to 1 per cent, it is still much tighter than it was a year ago. Australia's rental market is beginning to lose steam despite rents remaining at record highs. It is the rapidly emerging disconnect that experts say could suggest tenants are being pushed to the brink as rents flatline and even fall across most of the major capitals. New data from Domain shows capital city house rents were unchanged at $700 a week over the September quarter, while unit rents rose by 1.5 per cent despite very low levels of rental properties available on the market. That slowdown is challenging the long-held relationship between tight rental supply and growth, according to Domain's chief residential economist Nicola Powell. "Tenants' ability to absorb further increases is really the dynamic that is limiting further rental growth," she told The Business. "There's almost a disconnect now between where vacancy rate sits and what is occurring for rental growth." Lack of supply not translating into rent rises Dr Powell said although it was still "a landlords' market" in all major capitals and regional areas, the severe supply shortage was not necessarily transferring into rental increases as tenants hit their ceiling. Rents for houses are at or near record highs, with Sydney, Darwin and Perth the most expensive cities to live in. But most of that growth occurred earlier in the year. Nicola Powell says the data indicates cannot pay more rent. ( ABC News: Thorsten Joses ) The new data from Domain found rents in Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide flatlined over the past three months. events.title: Microsoft to sell $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra containing Nvidia AI chip
events.summary: Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra contains an Nvidia chip that can run large AI models without generating cloud bills. The device contains a magnetic USB-C port similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector. Microsoft also said that Meta will introduce its Muse AI agent for Windows. Microsoft said its new laptop containing an Nvidia AI chip will start at $2,599, as the software maker tries to bring more artificial intelligence capabilities to its consumer devices. The Surface Laptop Ultra is now available on preorder and will begin shipping on Oct. 16, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's executive vice president of Windows and devices, said at a company event in San Francisco on Wednesday. The computer has the world's first magnetic USB-C port, similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector, along with two other standard USB-C ports, Microsoft said in a blog post . While Microsoft Windows is the most popular operating system for PCs, the company isn't among the top six PC vendors in terms of unit shipments, according to an estimate from researcher Gartner. As the AI boom matures and chip technology advances, tech giants including Microsoft, Apple and Google are aiming to allow users to run more AI workloads from their devices rather than relying on the cloud. Users can install and run a variety of models on the new laptop without having to worry about racking up high monthly bills. Microsoft first talked about the Surface Laptop Ultra in May, but is just now providing specifics. "Microsoft might get me back to Windows," Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies, wrote on X after the announcement. Davuluri also said that Meta will introduce a version of its popular Muse AI agent for Windows, capitalizing on the surging popularity of the personal agent, which has jumped to the top of Apple's App store, surpassing ChatGPT. Microsoft is still trying to solidify its role as a key player in AI. The company offers its own AI models, but they're less popular than leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic and aren't at the forefront in terms of performance, according to one benchmark . Developers are more likely to have used alternatives, according to a recent survey . This isn't the first time Microsoft has sought to use the AI boom as a way to boost sales of its devices. In 2024, the company introduced the Copilot+ PC standard, requiring the inclusion of neural processing units that ensure a minimum level of AI performance, along with compliant Surface computers. But Microsoft has since "simplified product naming to lead with the Surface brand, while continuing to deliver premium hardware and hybrid AI experiences," a spokesperson said. The new device sports a 15-inch display and weighs 4.4 pounds. It can contain up to 128 gigabytes of unified memory and supply up to one petaflop of computing power. The Blackwell RTX Spark GPU inside the computer has as much processing power as Nvidia's DGX-1 data center server from 2016, which cost $250 million, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at Wednesday's event. A presenter showed how apps on the Surface Laptop Ultra can route some AI coding requests run on the computer's local GPU, displaying a green leaf icon, and others to the cloud. Through Windows 11, developers can confine coding agents to Microsoft Execution Containers that will prevent unwanted system access. Microsoft is updating its Windows 11 device setup experience to help people get started quickly with open-source OpenClaw AI agent software. Microsoft has been releasing its own computers since 2012, and CEO Satya Nadella indicated on Tuesday that the company's position in the market is evolving. "I think today is the day we'll start talking and thinking about the frontier ecosystem taking maybe slightly different contours two years from now, five years from now, 10 years from now," Nadella said at the event. "That classic edge that distributed computing will always remain distributed will be more true." WATCH: Microsoft unveils Muse for Windows

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Talking to an X-ray nanoprobe beamline is far better than talking to a toaster, we assume Singapore’s central bank wants all FinTech AI use cases subject to independent review 7 hours ago Microsoft is about to let Copilot loose on your file system 10 hours ago OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties 11 hours ago AWS launches open-source AI agent sandbox to prevent YOLO mode disasters 14 hours ago When one datacenter is no longer enough 17 hours ago Researchers at Argonne National Laboratory have plugged an agentic AI platform into an X-ray nanoprobe beamline, creating a system that can get a closer look at areas researchers ask it to focus on. Argonne reported the success of an experimental run of the agentic microscope this week, with the device initially tested on its ability to locate the interface between two regions on an integrated circuit device, and all by just telling the microscope what they wanted it to determine using natural language. “Microelectronics was simply the example used to showcase the technology,” Argonne computational scientist Mathew Cherukara said of the project. “The real achievement is developing a next‑generation, AI‑enhanced microscope that can benefit many scientific fields.” The microscope itself is part of Argonne’s 26-ID hard X-ray nanoprobe beamline, which uses a tightly focused X-ray beam to perform nanoscale imaging and measurements of target samples. Such devices are considered a prime use case for scientific applications of AI because they produce a massive amount of data that can take human researchers considerable time to comb through thanks to their use of a technique known as ptychography. The method collects multiple diffraction patterns as X-rays interact with a sample, with modern X-ray experiments capable of generating millions of images in just a few hours of beam time. Conventional ptychographic reconstruction and analysis can take hours or days, whereas Argonne says its AI system can reconstruct images in real time as the data arrives. Argonne’s X-ray nanoprobe beamline is the sort of scientific facility the Trump administration is looking to boost with AI through its Genesis Mission . Launched by President Trump in November 2025 and led by the Department of Energy, Genesis aims to find ways to use AI in scientific research, including the Synergistic Neutron and Photon Science - Intelligence ( SYNAPS-I ) project that Argonne is undertaking in partnership with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, which is leading the effort. Brookhaven National Laboratory, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory are also participating in the project. The inclusion of agentic AI in the Argonne X-ray microscope is actually the second phase of the project; the first was simply to see if, as mentioned above, AI could be used to reduce ptychographic image processing time. That was a success, as the lab reported in April, and phase two’s addition of natural language agentic AI appears to have been a win as well. “Combined, these SYNAPS-I advances lay the groundwork for self-driving microscopes, closed-loop experimentation and automated defect-detection tools that promise to accelerate discovery across fields ranging from semiconductor manufacturing to advanced materials and national user facilities,” Cherukara said of the project’s work thus far. In addition to the speed at which the new machine can process data, the conversational AI added in phase two gives researchers the ability to just ask the microscope to examine an area of interest rather than having to figure out how to aim the beam themselves. The AI can not only handle data collection and processing, but also analyze the results itself and flag additional areas of interest, which it can then further investigate on its own.

events.title: David Robinson says a sense of 'cognitive dissonance' led him to leave OpenAI
events.summary: David Robinson said he experienced 'cognitive dissonance' at OpenAI, which led him to leave the company. World Economic Forum David Robinson said that despite advocating for slowdowns, OpenAI was racing ahead with development. The disconnect produced in Robinson a sense of "cognitive dissonance," he said. Robinson quit the company last week, saying that the AI giant isn't being careful enough. David Robinson says OpenAI was saying one thing while doing another. Robinson, formerly a leader on OpenAI's Safety Systems team, sat down with Ezra Klein for The New York Times' "The Ezra Klein Show" for his first interview since quitting the AI company last week. Robinson told Klein that, despite repeated warnings about the capabilities of new models and expressing interest in slowing down AI development , OpenAI was moving as fast as ever behind the scenes. "Part of what was the fundamental cognitive dissonance for me was we keep publishing these warnings, but ultimately, we're still training and deploying these dangerous models that we're warning about," Robinson said. In July, hundreds of OpenAI employees signed an open letter titled " Pacing the Frontier ," which urged the government to impose regulations that would slow down AI development. Then, in September, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he agreed with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who had earlier published an essay advocating that AI companies coordinate a slowdown among themselves. "We need to pace the frontier," Altman said at the time on X. "This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks." Within OpenAI's office, though, Robinson told Klein that there was continued "frenetic" activity and that people were "running on fumes." "It feels almost like a ballet or a kind of dance because all these different functions are kind of all streaming together," he said of OpenAI. "There's a lot of adrenaline." Researchers at OpenAI have been rather frank about the dangers of letting AI build itself, a process called recursive self-improvement, or RSI. "This is a time that calls for extreme caution," Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, said in a blog post about RSI in September. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this article. An OpenAI spokesperson previously said, in response to an essay Robinson wrote in The Atlantic, that the company is taking steps to improve security for its AI models. "As our models become more capable, we continue to strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today while building safety cases to anticipate the risks of future advances," the spokesperson said. "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down." events.title: Trump's executive order on dyed diesel will offer little relief, farmers and truckers say
events.summary: Farmers, truckers, and economists say cutting taxes on diesel may not ease record-high fuel prices SIOUX FALLS, S.D. -- Farmers, truckers and economists say a move to cut taxes on diesel will provide little relief from record-high fuel prices that have soared since the U.S. attacked Iran months ago. Industry groups said they appreciate President Donald Trump’s executive order expanding the use of a diesel now reserved for off-road work, but farmers already have access to the fuel and many have already wrapped up harvest. Truckers will struggle to navigate differing state rules. “In the context of diesel prices that are over two dollars more than they were last year, it just doesn’t come close to closing that wound,” said Matt Perdue, president of the North Dakota Farmers Union. With less than a month to go before the November election , diesel prices continue to hit record highs as some farmers transport their crops for processing and others rush to complete their fall harvest. Many have been feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared thanks to refinery constraints and supply disruptions amid the Iran war. Diesel averaged $6.30 per gallon across the country on Wednesday, more than 70% higher than one year ago, according to motor club AAA. The executive order defers the $0.24 federal tax per gallon of regular diesel, used for road projects, until the end of the year. Most states also levy their own tax on diesel. “Dyed” diesel is the same as regular diesel, except for its red dye to help law enforcement enforce penalties for on-road use. It's already allowed for off-road purposes like farming equipment, such as tractors and combines, as well as construction and heating uses. Savings can compound if states take similar actions ; many have eased restrictions or waived taxes on dyed diesel, including South Dakota and Iowa. Perdue said North Dakota has waived the tax on regular diesel. But where the state decision is focused on farmers, he believes the federal decision would largely benefit those on other levels of the supply chain. Farmers who will see the most benefit are those who haul their own product, like livestock or fresh produce, on public roads. Those who have already wrapped up harvesting won't see savings. “Most of our diesel use is behind us,” said Perdue, who grows spring wheat, durum and canola on his family farm. Both trucking companies and independent truckers may not see much relief either. The effect is likely to be negligible for big trucking companies because the order is on a federal level and states make their own rules, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote in a social media post. “The largest diesel users are the least likely to use dyed diesel,” he wrote. “A national carrier crossing five or six states in a day faces enormous risk with a patchwork of rules, legal in one state, and subject to fines in the next.” Many states exempt road diesel from sales tax but apply sales tax to dyed diesel instead, he said. Easing limits on red-dyed diesel will likely have a minimal effect for small truckers, who pay for fuel up front, said Todd Spencer, president and CEO of trade group the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association. He estimates every $1 increase per gallon in fuel costs independent truckers about $400 more per week. Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Army to execute Fort Hood mass shooter by firing squad Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys The savings will be small, but it could still increase competition for dyed diesel, said David Ortega, food economics and policy professor at Michigan State University. “I think there's a real chance this could backfire and make the situation worse for farmers," he said. “Basically anybody that’s running a truck on the highway on regular diesel can now be using this off-highway diesel. Even someone that owns a diesel pickup truck potentially has access to this other type of diesel.” Perdue in North Dakota said he expects a “rush for dyed diesel, and we’ll see how the supply responds.” But not all dyed diesel pump stations are set up for larger trucks like semis, said Paul Mitchell, a professor of agricultural and applied economics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. “It’s going to come down to infrastructure ability to get your vehicles to a place that you can use and fill them up with,” he said. Henry Hanscom, American Trucking Associations chief advocacy and public affairs officer, pointed out that the executive order directs temporary penalty relief and potential tax deferral for using red-dyed diesel, not outright tax forgiveness. He said the ATA would review the Internal Revenue Service’s implementing guidance of the policy when it is available. Last month, Trump had threatened a diesel export ban, though he later said it is off the table.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Poverty-spec model starts at $2,599 with 24 GB of RAM and 512GB of storage with 128 GB models topping $5,899 Microsoft is about to let Copilot loose on your file system 10 hours ago Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism 23 hours ago Google teams with nuclear power giant to give reactors a tune-up 1 day ago Schneider Electric drops $22.6B on PTC as datacenter boom rains money on infra companies 2 days ago Cohere offers to put agents in lockdown mode with strict ACLs 2 days ago Look out, Intel! Microsoft released its first Surface notebook powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark system-on-chip (SoC) during an event in San Francisco on Wednesday. The Surface Laptop Ultra is one of several new Copilot+ PCs powered by the N1X chip that Microsoft says is aimed at "builders," which are available for preorder starting today and expected to begin shipping next week. The machine is arguably the vehicle for a slew of new AI features including hybrid compute functionality that dynamically routes workloads to on-device or cloud models depending on factors like connectivity, privacy, cost, and complexity. The aluminum clad system largely keeps with Microsoft's existing design ethos. It features a high-res, 15-inch mini-LED display capable of reaching a peak brightness of 2,000 nits in Microsoft's signature 3:2 aspect ratio, a standard ten-keyless keyboard layout, haptic trackpad, and a slew of ports including one you won't find on a MacBook Pro. Connectivity includes three USB-C ports, including one equipped with magnets for MagSafe-like connectivity, full-size HDMI, an SD card reader, and a solitary USB-A port because after more than a decade still can't shake the aging connector. But arguably the notebook's most interesting feature is the inclusion of Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X SoC. As we reported earlier this year, these aren't exactly new chips. The N1X is based heavily on Nvidia's now year-old GB10 platform, with a few CPU and GPU cores fused off on lower end models to meet pricing. This tells us that the Surface Laptop Ultra should ship with either an 18- or 20-core CPU designed by MediaTek and Arm and an Nvidia Blackwell-based RTX GPU with between 5,120 and 6,144 cores. In terms of memory, Microsoft says the notebook can be equipped with up to 128 GB of memory, enough to serve large language models up to 284 billion parameters in size, if you can live with just 1.6 bits of precision. As we've previously covered , the GPU is a pretty potent one with a peak theoretical throughput of 1 petaFLOPS at 4-bit precision, not that you're likely ever to see that in many real world workloads. Nvidia's marketing team is leaning on support for 2:4 sparsity to hit that target, so it can theoretically achieve that figure. Unfortunately, almost none of the AI inference workloads anyone cares about these days actually take advantage of the functionality. As a result, the chip's peak performance is actually closer to 500 teraFLOPS, which still gives it an edge over competing chips like AMD's Strix and Gorgon Halo processors. Local AI inference, as we mentioned earlier, is a major selling point for this class of hardware, though Microsoft was also keen to highlight the GPU's capabilities for more traditional creative and gaming workloads, claiming 60 FPS in the latest Gears of War release. We suspect that Nvidia's DLSS AI upscaling tech is probably doing the heavy lifting here. In order to keep the system from overheating, Microsoft says that the Surface Laptop Ultra features a beefed up cooling system with 2.5x more capacity than past Surface notebooks. From the renders we've seen, the extra cooling comes courtesy of a big fat vapor chamber. The Surface is expected to begin shipping next week at a starting price of $2,599 for the poverty-spec gray variant with the lower-end 18-core N1X, 24 GB of unified memory, and 512 GB user serviceable SSD. Jumping up to the 20-core chip, 128 GB of memory, and 1 TB of storage will set you back $5,899, and assuming memory prices haven't gone up even more by then.

events.title: Trump's midterm strategists draw scrutiny over Russia-aligned work
events.summary: President Trump threatened Wednesday to fire two of his top political consultants if he finds a conflict, after reports that they advised a Russia-aligned government ahead of local elections there. Why it matters: Chris LaCivita and James Blair are leading Republicans' midterm election strategy, putting their foreign consulting work in tension with their prominent roles in Trump's political operation. What they're saying: Trump called the pair "outside consultants" in a Truth Social post Wednesday. "They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them. They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C." "I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there's a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!" The other side: A source familiar with both consultants and the trip tells Axios that it was "a normal weekend full of calls and texts on the various races and our strategy/tactics in each." Context: The nationalist party warned that new voting machines could threaten its hold on power, echoing Trump's repeated attacks on voting machines in the U.S. A national election commission required the territory to use the new equipment. The source said Blair and LaCivita were there for about 48 hours to give "strategic advice on Election Integrity and what to look for to spot and avoid potential election fraud, because it was the first election where Republic of Srbska was forced to use new ballots and Smartmatic voting equipment…which obviously made them nervous." Between the lines: Caroline Wren, a registered lobbyist for Srpska, said the republic's abiding interest is in gaining stronger relations with Trump's administration. "It's not about Russia. It's not about Putin. It's about Christians who want their freedom and autonomy," Wren said. "The Trump Administration has made a huge priority of protecting and promoting Christians around the world and there is no better place to do that than the Pro-Trump Christians in the Republic of Sprska who have been demonized by the Europeans and Brussels for their Western values," she said. Blair and LaCivita were "maybe on the ground for 36 hours," she said, observing that she saw Blair constantly on the phone discussing elections back in the U.S. "Chris and James work around the clock to deliver wins for President Trump and Republicans here at home," she said. Zoom in: Blair , who previously served as White House deputy chief of staff, left the administration earlier this year to work for MAGA Inc., a super PAC affiliated with the president. He was also a senior adviser on Trump's 2024 campaign. LaCivita , the former co-manager of Trump's 2024 presidential campaign , is a senior adviser at MAGA Inc. Catch up quick: LaCivita and Blair visited Republika Srpska, a semi-autonomous entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, ahead of local elections, according to the New York Times. The two were reportedly recruited to advise the government on voting-related issues. They were hired to work for the government, not the nationalist party that controls it, though the party dominates the territory's government. Yes, but: American political consultants have a long history of taking on foreign clients. Zoom out: Trump's family businesses have expanded their foreign dealings since he returned to office. The Trump Organization and its partners have more than 20 Trump-branded projects planned, under construction or opening abroad — more than triple the number of overseas properties operating before his return. His administration accepted a luxury Boeing 747 from Qatar slated to eventually go to Trump's presidential library, while a UAE royal-linked firm bought a 49% stake in the Trump family's cryptocurrency business. Donald Trump Jr. had his wedding bankrolled by a Putin-linked Russian oligarch and later repaid him after public outrage. Go deeper: Trump's presidential profit machine bursts into the open

events.title: Every public appearance Melania Trump has made during Donald Trump's second White House term — and what she wore
events.summary: First lady Melania Trump broke with tradition by wearing pants to a state dinner held in honor of Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Yuri Gripas/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images Melania Trump is an enigmatic first lady who has, at times, been an infrequent White House presence. There was a 32-day stretch this summer where she did not make any public appearances. Recently, she spoke at an event at the Rose Garden and joined the president at a state dinner. Melania Trump has been known as an enigmatic first lady since President Donald Trump's first term, but her public appearances and outfit choices can provide a window into her approach to the role. Ahead of the 2025 inauguration, Melania Trump told Fox News that she planned to divide her time between the White House, Trump Tower in New York City, and Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida. This schedule has at times made her an infrequent presence at the White House. Over the summer, there was a 32-day stretch from mid-July to mid-August where she did not make any public appearances. However, she has attended numerous events during Donald Trump's second, non-consecutive term, such as the premiere of her "Melania" documentary, King Charles and Queen Camilla's state visit, and appearances promoting her Fostering the Future and Presidential AI Challenge initiatives. Melania Trump's muted fashion choices could also indicate a more guarded approach to the role of first lady. At White House events, she has largely appeared wearing suits and neutral basics in black, beige, cream, and gray. It's a departure from the bold outfits she often chose during Donald Trump's first term. A spokesperson for the Office of the first lady declined to comment. Take a look at the first lady's White House activities and appearances thus far. January 20, 2025: Melania Trump attended the inauguration. US President Donald Trump (L) and First Lady Melania Trump arrive for the Liberty inaugural ball in Washington, DC, on January 20, 2025. JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images Melania Trump held the Bible as Donald Trump was sworn in for his second non-consecutive term, and the couple danced together at several inaugural balls later that evening. For the swearing-in ceremony, Melania Trump wore a navy coat and skirt by Adam Lippes, an American designer. She accessorized with a matching wide-brimmed hat by Eric Javits. Her black-and-white inaugural gown was designed by Hervé Pierre. January 21, 2025: The president and first lady joined Vice President JD Vance and Usha Vance at the National Prayer Service. U.S. President Donald Trump, first lady Melania and U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance with second lady Usha attend the National Day of Prayer Service at the Washington National Cathedral in Washington, U.S., January 21, 2025. Kevin Lamarque/REUTERS The service, the last of Donald Trump's inaugural events, was held at the Washington National Cathedral in Washington, DC. January 24, 2025: Melania Trump and Donald Trump visited California and North Carolina to survey damage caused by natural disasters. U.S. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump attend a briefing on wildfire damage as they visit the Pacific Palisades neighborhood that was damaged by the Palisades Fire, in Los Angeles, California, U.S., January 24, 2025. Leah Millis/REUTERS Melania Trump joined Donald Trump to visit Los Angeles in the aftermath of multiple wildfires and neighborhoods in North Carolina damaged by Hurricane Helene . Together, they met with first responders and residents who had lost their homes and businesses. Melania Trump was photographed hugging and shaking hands with those affected by the natural disasters. February 22, 2025: Donald Trump and Melania Trump hosted the National Governors Association dinner at the White House. US President Donald Trump and US First Lady Melania Trump arrive for the National Governors Association Evening Dinner and Reception in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on February 22, 2025. ROBERTO SCHMIDT/AFP via Getty Images Melania Trump wore a black Dolce & Gabbana tuxedo, similar to the outfit she chose for her official White House portrait , while posing for photos with governors from across the US. Donald Trump thanked Melania Trump in his speech, saying that she "made the evening beautiful." March 3, 2025: She participated in a roundtable discussion on the "TAKE IT DOWN" Act targeting revenge porn. U.S. first lady Melania Trump, U.S. Senator Ted Cruz (R-TX) and Elliston Berry attend a roundtable discussion on the "Take it Down Act," a legislation against revenge porn, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., March 3, 2025. Kent Nishimura/REUTERS "TAKE IT DOWN" is an acronym for "Tools to Address Known Exploitation by Immobilizing Technological Deepfakes on Websites and Networks." The act criminalizes the publication of non-consensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated deepfakes, and requires websites to remove them. "Every young person deserves a safe online space to express themself freely, without the looming threat of exploitation or harm," Melania Trump said in her opening remarks. She wore a tan three-piece suit by Ralph Lauren with a black tie. March 4, 2025: Melania Trump attended Donald Trump's speech to a joint session of Congress. First Lady of the U.S. Melania Trump waves on the day of U.S. President Donald Trump's speech to a joint session of Congress, in the House Chamber of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., U.S., March 4, 2025. Kevin Lamarque/REUTERS The first lady's guests included the families of Corey Comperatore , the firefighter who was fatally shot during an assassination attempt against Donald Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania, and Laken Riley , who was killed by a man who had entered the US illegally. Melania Trump wore a gray skirt suit by Dior. April 1, 2025: She attended the International Women of Courage Awards. U.S. first lady Melania Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio pose with Philippine marine activist Angelique Songco, known as Mama Ranger, an International Women of Courage Award recipient, during a ceremony at the Department of State in Washington, D.C., U.S., April 1, 2025. Nathan Howard/REUTERS Melania Trump, joined by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, presented awards to several notable women in a ceremony held at the State Department. She wore a leopard-print coat designed by Milly Park. "These extraordinary women illuminate the transformative power of love in shaping our world," she said in her remarks at the event. "Their journeys remind us that true courage is born from a deep commitment to others, showing that love fuels the call for justice." April 2, 2025: She spoke at the annual Congressional Club's First Lady's Luncheon. First Lady Melania Trump delivers remarks at the annual Congressional Club's First Lady's Luncheon, Wednesday, April 2, 2025, at the Washington Hilton in Washington, D.C. Official White House Photo by Andre

Attackers hijacked top-level domains, allowing them to alter DNS records and mint fraudulent HTTPS certificates for several Google domains, and those belonging to other organizations. Google said it became aware of the series of attacks last week in the .gh (Ghana), .sl (Sierra Leone), and .as (American Samoa) country-code top-level namespaces (ccTLDs). “During these hijacks, attackers modified authoritative DNS records and obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates covering several Google domains, as well as domains belonging to other organizations,” Google security warned on Tuesday. Google did not say which specific domains or organizations were affected. The attacks did not compromise Google’s systems, and Chrome quickly blocked suspected counterfeit certificates across the affected ccTLDs - meaning Chrome browser users are already protected - according to the Chocolate Factory. “Due to the nature of the attacks, we have no reason to believe the Certification Authorities (CAs) that issued the impacted certificates did anything wrong,” the alert said. These types of attacks allow criminals to impersonate legitimate organizations and websites without triggering any browser security alerts. The attacker controls the traffic routing (via DNS) and the private key associated with the unauthorized certificate, which means they can potentially intercept or modify data sent by users to the impersonated site - and abuse the trusted organization's brand to distribute malware or conduct phishing attacks. “While Chrome took steps during these incidents to identify and block suspected unauthorized certificates across the affected ccTLDs, browser-side intervention should not be relied on to protect your users,” Google warned domain owners. “Due to the complexity of DNS hijacks, we cannot guarantee that our analysis identified every affected domain, nor do Chrome interventions reliably protect non-Chrome users.” To ensure that their domains and users are protected, Google recommends ongoing monitoring of Certificate Transparency (CT) logs across all of an organization’s domains, including parked or regional ccTLD properties. This provides near real-time alerts whenever someone obtains a certificate for one of your domains. And if you operate a domain in .gh, .sl, or .as, definitely review recent CT log entries for unexpected certificates. Organizations can also publish restrictive Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS records, which allow domain owners to specify which CAs are permitted to issue certificates for their domains. While this won’t stop certificates from being issued during a DNS hijacking attack, it helps safeguard domains after DNS control is restored.

events.title: Syria considering sending troops to Yemen to fight Houthis
events.summary: Saudi Arabia and Syria are discussing sending Syrian troops to Yemen to join the counteroffensive against the Houthi rebels, three U.S. officials told Axios. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa is seriously considering it, but hasn't decided. Why it matters: While the discussion is mostly between Saudi Arabia and Syria, the Trump administration has been consulted by both countries and is not opposed in principle to such a move, the U.S. officials said. But sending Syrian troops could inject a religious dimension into the Yemen war and exacerbate the conflict. The troops could include Islamist Sunni foreign fighters who participated in the rebellion against the Assad regime. They would be fighting against the Houthis, who follow Zaydi Shiite Islam. Driving the news: The Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a massive ground operation over the weekend against the Houthis. The offensive was designed to retake territories the Houthis control, including the capital Sanaa and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait. A U.S. official said the issue of sending Syrian troops to Yemen came up during the meeting between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and al-Sharaa in Riyadh earlier this week. The Saudis want al-Sharaa to send troops in order to boost the Yemeni forces that are less trained than the Houthis. While al-Sharaa hasn't signed off on the decision yet, the U.S. official said it is highly likely the Syrian president will accept the Saudi request. Behind the scenes: The U.S. doesn't oppose sending Syrian troops to Yemen. It would provide more support for the Saudi-backed operation against the Houthis without the U.S. having to get deeply involved, a U.S. official said. Trump administration officials also believe that deploying Syrian troops to Yemen would strengthen the relationship between two U.S. allies, Saudi Arabia and Syria. Two U.S. officials said U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) has been consulted on how Syrian troops could be deployed. The White House and CENTCOM declined to comment. Spokespeople for the Saudi Embassy and the Syrian Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment. Zoom in: A source with knowledge of the discussions said the Syrian military could send 10,000 to 20,000 troops to Yemen. The units under consideration are the 90th division near Damascus and the 84th division based in southern Syria near Sweida. The 84th division includes thousands of Islamist foreign fighters who came to Syria during the civil war to fight against the Assad regime under the umbrella of the HTS rebel group.

events.title: Browser-in-browser attacks use fake Meta Muse Ad lure to steal credentials
events.summary: A phishing campaign targeting advertising managers by impersonating Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Manus to steal credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes has added a fake Muse Ads product to its lure lineup – just eight days after Meta launched its personal AI agent. Meta announced Muse on September 8, and by September 17, a very convincing website – museads.ai – for a product called Muse Ads that promised to help advertisers reach buyers and run sponsored placements popped up online. “The operators already had the platform, so adapting it to a new brand can take minutes,” Oleg Zaytsev, lead security researcher at Island, told The Register. “The striking part is how quickly they turned a timely announcement into a credible reason for someone to act. The same platform could then be repackaged around other familiar tasks, from connecting a business tool to claiming a refund or applying for a job.” The security startup spotted the Muse Ads webpage, and upon digging into the scam uncovered that just the page was new. “Its code, from the sign-in forms to the fake browser window, came from a wider operation that had already run fake ad products for Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Manus,” Zaytsev and fellow Island researcher Ofek Ronen wrote in a blog post published Tuesday. All of these products served as lures for browser-in-the-browner (BitB) attacks designed to trick agency staff, media buyers, and manager-account administrators into handing over their advertising account credentials – along with stored payment methods and client accounts – to digital thieves. “For victims, the potential cost is loss of access to an advertising account, unauthorized ad spend, and exposure of linked client accounts,” Zaytsev told The Register. How the scam works BitB is a clever phishing technique originally detailed by a researcher called mr.d0x in 2022. It involves building a fake login window directly inside a legitimate one. The fake window looks like the real thing, featuring an address bar, title, and URL, but it's just an overlay to steal users’ credentials. According to Zaytsev, this one has likely proved very lucrative for its criminal operators, with hundreds of victim submissions to the platform, and activity still ongoing. “From one frontend alone, we observed submissions involving roughly 200 distinct email addresses over about a month,” he told us. “The operators used the same platform across many similar sites, so we estimate the campaign-wide volume is substantially higher.” Each phony ad product has its own page, with ChatGPT promising users a Monday Google Ads brief, Gemini offering manager account and linked-client support, Claude an advertising portal, Perplexity pitching campaign planning and spend audits, and Manus providing a private Meta integration. Each fake product page also has a “connect” button. When the victim clicks “connect,” it opens the browser-in-browser overlay, with a fake address bar showing accounts.google.com, or an Okta tenant to gain the victim’s trust. The real browser, however, stays on the phishing domain and steals credentials when the victim types them in. A human operator running the campaign sees each submission and chooses what the victim sees and is prompted to do. This includes asking for another password, requesting an SMS or Okta authenticator code to bypass MFA, showing a Google approval code or Okta push request, or displaying a QR code. The platform supports Google, Meta, TikTok, and Okta workflows, and the browser overlay adapts to whatever the victim runs: Window, macOS, iOS, ot Android, and even mimics Safari’s URL pill, Chrome’s custom tabs, and a dark mode. And while the researchers told us they haven’t identified the people operating the kit or found a name under which it’s sold, the operators did expose older source code through misconfigured public GitHub repositories that connected this to a campaign to a larger operation. In addition to the AI ad pages, this operation also used fake refund claims and job recruitment sites as lures with separate builds for Adidas, Google Careers, Robert Half, Tesla, and Louis Vuitton. All of these pages run on one Next.js and Socket.IO stack. Many of the pages also used Vercel frontends with Railway or Render services behind them for state and commands. “A new brand or polished page doesn’t necessarily mean a new attack. Operators can change the lure quickly, but the workflow still has to move someone onto a site they control, collect credentials, and steer them through authentication,” Zaytsev said. “Security teams should maintain a continuous baseline of trusted domains, check the real browser address, and connect similar behavior across different sites,” he added. “Attackers can generate a convincing website quickly; building the domain history and reputation of a legitimate service is much harder. AI can help defenders keep pace with AI-generated websites, especially as they become more convincing and appear more quickly.”. ®

events.title: Town questions $15b data centre set to use enough power for 1m homes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts CDC Data Centres told not to take Wagga Wagga for granted over mega plan Eden Summers has started a petition looking to halt a proposed data centre near Wagga Wagga. ( ABC News: Melinda Hayter ) Residents in Wagga Wagga have started a petition to halt development of a $15 billion data centre campus outside the town. CDC Data Centres plans to acquire 100 hectares to build the proposed 1.4-gigawatt facility. The proponent has submitted a scoping report and has two years to develop an environmental impact statement once the state government sets the guidelines. When residents of the NSW city of Wagga Wagga learnt one of the country's largest data centres was proposed for down the road, they had questions. For resident Liz Warrell, the biggest was: how does it benefit her community? "It's a big box; it sits there," she said. "I don't know if it generates employment, I know it's using resources and I know it's creating emissions. "So what effect is that having on us as a community as our climate dries?" Liz Warrell wants information about how much water and power the proposed data centre would use. ( ABC News: Melinda Hayter ) CDC Data Centres is proposing to build a $15 billion campus on a 100-hectare council-owned site next to the city's landfill. If approved, the 1.4-gigawatt facility is expected to consume more electricity each year than a million typical NSW homes. Just 4 kilometres from the proposed site, Eden Summers is also worried her peaceful rural lifestyle is at risk. Eden Summers is not supportive of a proposed data centre near Wagga Wagga. ( ABC News: Melinda Hayter ) "Government likes to take action on big business projects without actually thinking of the locals," Ms Summers said. The land CDC is eyeing for the project is currently zoned for primary production use, but the company proposes to change the zoning. "We have restrictions on what we can do on our land, but then when it comes to big business, everything changes; there's just no consistency," Ms Summers said. A petition to halt the development, started by Ms Summers, has attracted more than 1,000 signatures and states locals "should not have to sacrifice our rural community for a data centre". "If it was on land designated for this sort of project, opposition wouldn't be as strong," she said. Other residents cautiously open to plan However, some Wagga residents, like Katrina Walker, think the site, 15 kilometres from the city's centre, made sense. "If it's out at Gregadoo, that's a fair way out, so I think it'd be OK," she said. Katrina Walker says the proposed site is appropriate. ( ABC News: Melinda Hayter ) So far, only a scoping report that provides an overview of the proposed state significant development has been made publicly available. Advocacy group Committee 4 Wagga has cautiously welcomed the proposal, having campaigned previously for more industry in the city. But co-chair Richard Pottie said support for the centre would depend on the details. "We can't take on the 'not in our backyard' philosophy," he said. The proposed layout of CDC Data Centre's proposed Gregadoo facility. ( Supplied: NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure ) Calls for information on water and power usage The first community consultation sessions will be held in Wagga on Wednesday and Thursday next week. Once the state government releases its State Environmental Assessment Requirements (SEARs) for the project, CDC will have two years to submit an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS). The full outline of the data centre's electricity infrastructure needs, as well as a noise and vibration assessment and a water management plan, will be included in that EIS. An artist's impression of CDC's proposed data centre at Gregadoo. ( Supplied: CDC Data Centres ) A CDC spokesperson said that in the proposed centre's first stage of operation, it was estimated that 1.28 million litres of water, or the equivalent water use of seven households, would be needed for an "initial fill". "CDC typically undertakes this from rainwater collected onsite, with a backup from water trucks or, depending on local conditions, town water," the spokesperson said. The company said on an ongoing basis, the first stage of the project was expected to consume as much water as a typical office building. "We estimate our annual water consumption to be approximately 1,512,000 litres per year. "The town water usage is estimated to be equivalent of a little less than nine Australian households." events.title: Victorians say 'lazy planning' leading to poor social housing outcomes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bendigo residents say 'lazy planning' leading to poor social housing outcomes Michael Jurca and Ben Pengelly say neighbouring residents will suffer from poor traffic and environmental outcomes. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) Central Victorian traditional owner group Djaara wants to build 34 social houses for 75 residents in the regional city of Bendigo. Neighbouring residents say state planning laws mean "lazy planning" cannot be contested by local councils or residents. If approved, Djaara says construction is scheduled to begin in mid-2027 and be completed by the end of 2028. Residents living near a proposed social housing project by central Victorian traditional owner group Djaara, in the regional Victorian city of Bendigo, say the state government's fast-tracked planning process is allowing "lazy planning" to go ahead without sufficient scrutiny. Djaara, the trading name for the Dja Dja Wurrung Clans Aboriginal Corporation, is proposing 34 one and two-storey houses for about 75 people at the site of the old North Bendigo Primary School on Nolan Street. But neighbouring residents said Victorians should be able to question planning applications and oppose conditions when there are other alternatives. "We recognise that social housing is needed in Victoria. We know we're under-housed," resident Ben Pengelly said. "But there's a number of issues that we don't agree with. Concept drawings show 34 houses would be built on the site of the old North Bendigo Primary School. ( Supplied: Djaara ) In December last year the Victorian government awarded Djaara $21.6 million for the project. Among the residents' concerns was that the land owned by the Department of Education and Training had been repurposed for social housing without consultation, going against a Victorian government-backed 2019 public space plan that slated the site as parkland. "I feel for some of the people in the area who I know have bought their house according to that Victorian government document," Mr Pengelly said. "That's not transparent. That's changing the rules. "And in the words of a lot of these politicians nowadays, they all say they want to be transparent." Mr Pengelly's neighbour Michael Jurca said Barney Street was already full of Bendigo Health workers needing all-day parking and did not have the space for more vehicles without negatively affecting residents. "If you have visitors or services we already have to move the car three or four streets away," Mr Jurca said. Neighbouring residents say current traffic plans don't properly address the increased traffic conditions. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) Fast-track planning an election sore point The proposal is expected to go before Planning Minister Sonja Kilkenny as part of the Victorian government's Development Facilitation Program, which fast-tracks priority projects such as housing and renewable energy developments. The program has taken planning powers away from local councils and strips residents of the right to object at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal. Djaara's Transport Impact Assessment (TIA) submitted to the Victorian government shows its consultants, Impact Traffic Engineering, used a New South Wales report to illustrate its assumptions of vehicle movements by each house, each day. Mr Pengelly said the TIA was another example of lazy planning. "That is just ticking a box, making sure they meet some sort of requirement. But let's be realistic, why isn't it a Victorian planning traffic management plan?" Mr Pengelly said. Residents say they bought next to the old primary school site when it was designated for parkland, not social housing. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) The City of Greater Bendigo said it supported the application in principle, but environmental constraints and remediation of the site needed "further consideration". In a letter to residents, the city's senior transport engineer Muaid Ahmed said a review by the city's engineering unit "identified that while the TIA estimates the additional traffic generated by the development, it does not provide a detailed assessment of existing traffic conditions or future traffic conditions following development". Sonya Kilkenny will decide whether the social housing project gets the green light. ( AAP: Joel Carrett ) In a statement, Djaara's acting chief executive officer Harley Douglas said its housing provider subsidiary, Mayam Mayam, would review any submissions received and consider how best to respond, in consultation with the Department of Transport and Planning.

events.title: Former RBA member explains what happens inside interest rate meetings
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Former RBA board member says November interest rate hike 'plausible' The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised the cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent. ( ABC News: Kylie Silvester ) A former RBA member says the board has typically had split votes on monetary policy about 30 per cent of the time over the past decade. Ian Harper says none of the treasurers in power during his 10-year tenure ever tried to influence him on interest rate decisions. The market is pricing in a one-in-three possibility of a rate hike on the first Tuesday in November. Another interest rate hike this year is "plausible", but not necessarily likely, according to former Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) board member Ian Harper. A distinguished economist, Professor Harper was on the RBA board for a decade, from 2016 until after the Monetary Policy Board's (MPB) August meeting, when interest rates were left on hold. The cash rate was subsequently increased at the bank's September meeting to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent. Speaking at a Centre for Independent Studies lunchtime event in Sydney on Wednesday, Professor Harper declined to offer his view on where interest rates might settle over a five or 10-year horizon, but did make this comment on the short-term prospects for the cash rate. "The bank moving again before the end of the year is plausible, from what I can see of the circumstances," he told the audience. "But, again, I don't have the [board meeting] papers in front of me." In a subsequent one-on-one interview with David Taylor for The Business, Professor Harper declined to characterise the chances of a back-to-back rate hike in November as "likely", repeating his assessment that it was "plausible". This matches market pricing, which has the chances of a hike on Melbourne Cup Day at about a third. Harper offers rare insight into RBA board processes Much has changed since Professor Harper joined the RBA board in 2016, with a major governance overhaul sparked by a federal government-commissioned review of the bank resulting in a split between the MPB and a governance board, taking effect in March 2025. Ian Harper joined the RBA board in 2016 and left in August this year. ( ABC ) However, Professor Harper indicated the biggest change to the interest rate decision-making process was that the meetings now ran over two days. He explained that the board convened at 1pm on the Monday and mets until about 5:30pm, hearing briefings from RBA staff and having the opportunity to put questions to them. He said the governor often took an informal straw poll at the end of that first day about what people thought should be done with rates. Sometimes the board members will go out to dinner together before "people go off and think about it overnight and come back the next day," Professor Harper explained. "The meeting starts at 9[am] and you run through to 11:30. "And in that process, of course, there's further discussion, the decision gets made, the statement gets drafted, the draft gets considered, discussed and agreed." Since the board began publishing the vote tallies from its July 2025 meeting onwards, there have been eight unanimous decisions and three split votes. Professor Harper told The Business that such dissent was fairly typical before the board began publishing vote tallies. The RBA isn't trying to stop inflation.
