events.title: These Researchers Made AI Drive a Toyota Corolla to Get In-N-Out
events.summary: Aditya Ramabadran, Simon Mahns, and Tobias Gessler, three AI engineers at a startup called Axiom , recently fancied In-N-Out Burger for lunch. They weren’t about to drive themselves, though. Sitting in a 2024 Toyota Corolla near the Bay Area restaurant’s drive-thru lane, they opened a laptop and asked OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra to take the wheel. They linked a chat interface to a server, which was connected to several windscreen-mounted cameras and the car’s power steering system. A safety driver kept one foot above the brake, just in case. The AI model, which is normally tasked with generating text, code, and the odd image, slowly but surely navigated the vehicle up to the take-out window so they could collect their food. “Maybe AGI is here after all,” one of the engineers remarked, referring to artificial general intelligence , the much-ballyhooed idea of machines that can match human intelligence. Self-driving cars are nothing new, of course, but they’re normally operated by algorithms specifically trained and engineered for the task. In this case, the operation came from a model designed to output text, and it happened on the fly, with no prior coaching by the trio. The fast-food stunt, as well as a number of other experiments , suggest that language-based AI models are starting to gain a rudimentary but useful understanding of the physical world. Though nothing overtly alarming happened during the trio’s lunchtime jaunt, they admit that putting a general-purpose model in charge of a fast-moving, two-ton hunk of steel is a high-stakes undertaking. As physical understanding improves, we could see AI models reach into the real world in impressive—and perhaps dangerous—new ways. Today’s smartest models are incredibly good at answering complex questions and even performing some virtual tasks autonomously , but their skills tend to be limited to the world of computers and the internet. Take these models into the real world and they quickly become befuddled. Despite claims that AGI has arrived , AI companies evidently see physical reasoning as a yet-to-be-conquered frontier for AI. Some researchers have left big companies to found startups focused on solving physical reasoning. Andrew Dai, the CEO of one such outfit, called Elorian AI, previously worked as a researcher at Google DeepMind. He says better visual reasoning will open up a lot of new applications for AI, like systems that understand whether diners are enjoying their meal in a restaurant or robots capable of functioning in a home. Dai says robotics is a crucial test case for physical reasoning skills. “It’s pretty essential for robotics,” he says. “You can’t really imagine home robotics without this.” Elorian and Scale AI, a company that provides training data to big AI labs, recently developed a new benchmark , Humanity’s Sixth Sense, which measures models’ ability to understand physical scenes. “Most visual AI research is about perception,” says Xingang Guo, a research scientist at Scale AI who was involved with developing the benchmark. “We wanted to ask what it would actually take for a model to understand a scene intuitively, the way a person does without thinking about it.” For Ramabadran, Mahns, and Gessler, the goal with their In-N-Out project, done outside of their work at Axiom, was to measure how well models can operate in the messy real world. They got the idea to test models’ driving skills while hanging out one weekend. They noticed that models like Astra were capable of building complex 3D simulations, and wondered if it might translate to an ability to navigate the real world. “We all live in the Bay Area, and we’re exposed to Teslas and Waymos, so maybe that played a role,” Ramabadran tells me. The engineers tried testing SpaceXAI’s Grok before experimenting with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic. At first, the models refused to take control of the vehicles—they spat back things like, “I can help interpret road images, but I can’t issue motion commands to a physical car.” But with a little careful prompting, they could be coaxed into going further. The three were stunned when models began driving. The engineers say big AI companies seem to be focusing on improving the spatial reasoning capabilities of their latest models, but they doubt this means they’re actually training them to drive cars. The models’ vehicular talents likely materialized as part of training focused on 3D reasoning, they say. “This could be like an emergent capability of just scaling up the multimodality of the model,” Mahns tells me, referencing inputs like images, video, and 3D models that are now used to train models. Still, a new vehicular benchmark from the trio, called DrivingBench , suggests that these models still have a long way to go before they could pass a driving test. The benchmark measures a model’s ability to drive around a simple course, set up in a parking lot. Only Astra is able to complete the course—and very slowly at that.

events.title: Elon Musk took heat at chaotic Memphis data center moratorium vote
events.summary: A Memphis City Council meeting that took focus on data centers turned chaotic. USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect A Memphis City Council meeting turned chaotic after a vote to delay a vote on a data center moratorium. Roughly 200 attendees packed the meeting, most of them opposing AI data centers. Council members repeatedly took aim at Elon Musk before voting 7-5 to postpone the decision. Elon Musk and his company's data center footprint in Memphis, Tennessee, repeatedly came under fire Tuesday during a packed city council meeting that descended into chaos. The heated Memphis City Council meeting, attended by roughly 200 residents — many of whom held signs opposing data centers — was ultimately shut down after council members voted 7-5 to postpone a vote on a proposed data center moratorium in the city. Police were called to the scene as shouting from attendees consumed the room. Livestream footage of the meeting showed a person with a bullhorn prompting a crowd to chant, "ain't no power like the power of the people." In online cellphone video footage, some activists were seen screaming at council members, with one repeatedly yelling, "You're a sellout." A physical fight also broke out between two people in the City Hall lobby, though it was unclear what prompted the brawl. The tumultuous end to the city council meeting offered a snapshot into the fury fueling a growing nationwide backlash to AI data center development . Absolute chaos at Memphis City Council right now. This is the scene after they voted to push the data center moratorium down the line. Council members being ushered out, heavy police presence and advocates are not happy. https://t.co/BQZBsMbpP3 — Annie Goldman (@AnnieSGoldman) October 6, 2026 Ahead of the vote, city councilman JB Smiley Jr. asked community members to stand if they supported the proposed 12-month data center moratorium in Memphis. Nearly all attendants got out of their seats. Some held signs reading, "people over billionaires," "pause data centers," and "data center moratorium now." Councilwoman Jerri Green, who voted against delaying the vote on a proposed data center moratorium, urged her colleagues to greenlight the pause while criticizing tech titan Musk. Green, the Democratic nominee for Tennessee governor, pointed to the many locales that have already imposed data center moratoriums "because they see the harm that is happening around the country." "That is the whole point of the moratorium — is for us to take a pause to get the community input, which was overlooked completely by Elon Musk and xAI when they came in," Green said to cheers from the audience. Musk's rocket and AI company, SpaceX , operates two massive data center facilities in the Memphis area and is developing a third. SpaceX, which acquired xAI earlier this year, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story. About 200 attendees packed the Memphis City Council meeting. Neil Strebig/The Commercial Appeal / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images/Reuters Green was not the only councilmember to take aim at Musk during the meeting. Councilwoman Rhonda Logan, who voted in favor of postponing the vote, said Memphis' zoning laws opened the door to Musk's projects and other data center development in Memphis. "We do not have safeguards to protect our people," Logan said. She added, "If you don't address your zoning and determine where you want things in your city, you're always going to be vulnerable to those that have money and power and can come in and do what they want to." Another councilwoman, Yolanda Cooper-Sutton, also referenced Musk when she warned: "You better be careful because you're dealing with a trillionaire in this city that's here right now." "There's some stuff that went on," Cooper-Sutton, who voted to postpone, said. "There was more money going out than was coming in when xAI was here." The Memphis City Council is expected to vote on the proposed data center moratorium on October 20. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Microsoft looks to reboot the AI PC with Nvidia
events.summary: Microsoft on Wednesday unveiled a new class of Nvidia-powered Windows laptops, its latest effort to tie the operating system more closely to the AI boom. Why it matters: Microsoft is trying to carve out a high-end laptop category for people who want to run demanding AI workloads locally, rather than rely entirely on the cloud. Driving the news: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former White House AI official Sriram Krishnan were on hand in San Francisco as the company officially launched Microsoft Surface Ultra, a high-end laptop powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark chip that starts at $2,599. "We have reinvented the computer as we know it," Huang said. Microsoft previewed the laptop back in June but left out key details around price and exact availability. It said at the time that Nvidia-powered devices would also be coming from the likes of Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, among others. Those devices, and the Surface Ultra, will be available starting Oct. 16. On the software side, Microsoft unveiled a version of Copilot that can work using local models alongside those in the cloud, and the company also announced that Meta is bringing its Muse personal agent to Windows. The big picture: Microsoft's first push into AI-powered Windows machines, known as Copilot+ PCs, got off to a rocky start after the delay of Recall, its signature feature. Between the lines: Microsoft's pitch for on-device AI is that developers' appetite exceeds what their companies' AI budgets can afford, with the ideal being an approach that uses both frontier models in the cloud and local models when they can be effective. "Hybrid intelligence exists because people's appetite for intelligence is effectively unlimited," Microsoft executive VP Pavan Davuluri said. And before it even got to the hardware, Microsoft spent a fair bit of time outlining how it is making Windows more secure, ensuring that agents' actions are separated from those taken by humans and remain within preset limits.

events.title: Federal Reserve officials expect another rate hike will be needed this year, according to minutes
events.summary: Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, minutes released Wednesday from the central bank’s most recent meeting showed WASHINGTON -- Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, according to minutes released Wednesday from the central bank's most recent meeting. The officials unanimously agreed that inflation was still elevated and had not made much progress toward their 2% target in recent months, the minutes said. The Fed increased its key interest rate at the Sept. 15-16 meeting by a quarter-point to about 3.9%, its first increase in three years. The increase defied President Donald Trump's repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates and prompted the president to criticize the Fed's rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The rate increase comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries , gas and housing , and as affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away. Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Army to execute Fort Hood mass shooter by firing squad Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Longer-term interest rates for mortgages and other borrowing have also jumped in the past few months for a range of reasons, including rising government debt, heavy borrowing by tech firms to finance data center construction, climbing oil and gas prices, and signs that growth and inflation remain elevated. The Fed's rate hike has likely played only a limited role in the increase. Still, key policymakers have said since the meeting that the Fed can take some time to monitor the economy and the impact of last month's rate hike before making another move. Wall Street investors now forecast the Fed will keep its rate unchanged at its next meeting Oct. 28-29, according to futures pricing, and raise it when they meet in December. events.title: The most famous diner in every state
events.summary: The Palace Diner in Biddeford, Maine, has been open for nearly 100 years. Erin McDowell/Business Insider We rounded up the most iconic diners in every state, from classic railcars to cozy breakfast spots. Many on this list are historic establishments that have been serving up diner classics for decades. Others have been ranked among the best restaurants in their respective states. Chrome stools, bottomless coffee, and a menu filled with page upon page of classic comfort foods — there's no argument: Diners are quintessentially American. Diners nationwide have been recognized for their historic pasts , award-winning menu items, and high volume of positive reviews, making them must-stop destinations on any cross-country road trip. While diners are disappearing across America — due to rising rents and labor costs, declining profit margins, and changing customer habits — some have remained fixtures thanks to loyal locals, beloved menu items, and distinctive atmospheres. From decades-old landmarks like Tops Diner in New Jersey to no-frills lunch counters that have quietly become cultural icons in their respective towns, these are the most iconic diners in every state. ALABAMA: Duck's Diner in Orange Beach Duck's Diner. Sandra P./Yelp Duck's Diner is a laid-back Alabama restaurant that's become a go-to stop for locals and vacationers. The casual spot is best known for its hearty breakfast plates, Southern comfort food, and classic diner favorites like grits and French toast, served just minutes from the beach. ALASKA: Kriner's Diner in Anchorage Kriner's Diner. Yun-Wen L./Yelp Kriner's Diner offers a classic diner experience in the heart of Anchorage. The longtime favorite draws crowds for generous portions, classic breakfast plates, and traditional American comfort food, all served in a retro setting. ARIZONA: Welcome Diner in Phoenix Welcome Diner. Glen L./Yelp Welcome Diner puts a modern spin on the classic diner while staying true to its roots. Set inside a restored 1945 diner car, the Phoenix favorite is known for its creative comfort food, craft cocktails, and a nostalgic atmosphere with a contemporary edge. ARKANSAS: White House Cafe in Camden White House Cafe. Chantelle S./Yelp White House Cafe is a longtime Camden institution, serving diners since 1907. The historic restaurant is known for its classic Southern comfort food, friendly service, and old-school diner atmosphere. CALIFORNIA: Mel's Drive-In in West Hollywood Mel's Drive-In. Richard L./Yelp Mel's Drive-In is one of the most recognizable diners in California, thanks to its retro decor and Hollywood history. The West Hollywood outpost draws crowds for its milkshakes, burgers, and all-day breakfast served in a classic 50s-inspired setting that nods to the golden age of drive-ins and diners. COLORADO: Sam's No. 3 in Denver Sam's No 3. Casey D./Yelp Sam's No. 3 is a Denver staple that has been feeding locals since the 1920s. The bustling diner is famous for its gigantic portions, green chile-smothered dishes, and extensive menu that spans classic breakfast plates to comfort-food favorites. CONNECTICUT: Laurel Diner in Southbury Laurel Diner. Alejandra S./Yelp Laurel Diner delivers typical roadside diner fare in a classic setting, located conveniently just off I-84 for all roadtrippers passing through the state. The popular stop is known for its expansive menu, including its corned beef hash and breakfast plates. DELAWARE: Smyrna Diner in Smyrna Smyrna Diner. Ha O./Yelp Smyrna Diner has been slinging up breakfast favorites in Delaware since 1956, and is still famous for its all-day breakfast, made-to-order comfort food, and casual setting that may not be the height of luxury, but is certainly worth a stop along the way on a road trip. FLORIDA: Peter Pan Diner in Fort Lauderdale Peter Pan Diner. Michael G./Yelp Peter Pan Diner is a retro roadside staple that has been serving Fort Lauderdale since 1979. The classic diner is known for its breakfast plates, old-school counter service, and burgers. GEORGIA: The Dwarf House in Hapeville The Dwarf House. Chris W./Yelp The Dwarf House holds a special place in fast-food history as the original Chick-fil-A restaurant. The quirky, low-ceilinged spot draws visitors for its familiar Chick-fil-A menu items, exclusive Dwarf House items, table service, and its role as the birthplace of the nationwide chain. HAWAII: Liliha Bakery in Honolulu Liliha Bakery. Bailey I./Yelp Liliha Bakery is a beloved Honolulu institution that blends diner classics with local flavors. Open since the 1950s, the bakery-restaurant is especially famous for its signature Coco Puffs, hearty breakfast plates, and Hawaiian comfort food, served around the clock and well worth the wait in line. IDAHO: Dixie's Diner in Idaho Falls Dixie's Diner. Dixie's Diner/Yelp Dixie's Diner brings Southern-inspired comfort food to eastern Idaho in a cozy, 1950s-inspired setting. The popular spot is best known for its burgers, homemade pies, and classic diner dishes served with a side of small-town charm. ILLINOIS: Lou Mitchell's in Chicago Lou Mitchell's. Leang E./Yelp Lou Mitchell's is a Chicago breakfast institution located near the start of Route 66. Open since 1923, the historic diner is known for its big, fluffy omelets, house-baked pastries, and old-school hospitality, including complimentary Milk Duds for guests. Located in Plainfield, the retro spot attracts diners with its classic American fare and preserved slice of midcentury history. IOWA: Drake Diner in Des Moines Drake Diner. events.title: IEEE Report Predicts Tech That Will Transform Lives
events.summary: By 2028, genetic engineering and gene therapy will be used frequently to treat a variety of diseases, thanks to advances in artificial intelligence, according to the recently released 2030 Technology Megatrends Report from IEEE. “We are seeing a fundamental shift in how technology evolves,” says IEEE Fellow Dejan Milojicic , chair of the IEEE Future Directions Committee ’s Industry Advisory Board, the group responsible for the report. “ Artificial intelligence is no longer operating in a vacuum; it is now deeply connected to our energy, infrastructure, and physical systems.” Milojicic, a Hewlett Packard Enterprise Fellow, is a vice president at HPE Labs in Milpitas, Calif. AI underpins many of the report’s 30 technologies and five “megatrends,” which are technology shifts with the potential to reshape industries and everyday life for decades. A megatrend isn’t a single breakthrough but a collection of related technologies. For the 2030 report, 166 experts—from 38 countries across six continents—drawn from industry, academia, and government identified 30 breakthrough technologies across the five megatrends: AI, energy, health, space, and physical AI. The experts graded the trends against five criteria: likelihood of success, impact to humanity, maturity, market adoption, and horizon to adoption. AI as a common thread Interconnected systems drive the megatrends, and the connection among them is AI. The report notes that AI technology is advancing faster than any previous revolution, including industrial, electrical, and digital. The pace has turned the technology into general-purpose infrastructure, Milojicic says. That evolution carries risks, though, the experts say. The report cites the lack of computing infrastructure and energy sources as constraints on the ability to scale up AI, and it says the technology’s growth will require reshaping the workforce. Workers have always needed to adapt to stay competitive, Milojicic says, adding that AI adoption isn’t an all-or-nothing approach. Businesses should decide when and how to apply it, he says. The experts say long-term success will require both technical capabilities and attention to the human-AI relationship. Conditions including trust, security, explainability, and policymaking will determine which AI-supported technologies are most likely to scale, they say. “This report shifts the conversation to something far more important: how these advances will intersect with one another to shape human lives,” Mary Ellen Randall , 2026 IEEE president and CEO, said in a news release about the report. “The data makes clear that trust, safety, and human connection must guide every major breakthrough in the decade ahead.” Health care is a high-impact bet The experts scored personalized medicine as the study’s highest-impact technology, at 4.93 out of 5, for its potential to improve human life. The report credits AI-driven breakthroughs in personalized diagnostics and therapeutic treatments, driven by innovative biotech startups. Within two years, the experts predict, genetic engineering and gene therapy will be used in therapeutic areas. Within five years, earlier disease diagnoses will move out of the lab and into day-to-day medical practice, the report predicts. Meanwhile, it says, researchers likely will be able to manufacture simple synthetic proteins—molecules engineered from scratch, rather than found in nature—to perform a specific job in the body, such as targeting a tumor or supplying a missing enzyme. Energy wakes up for AI Increased power demand by AI is outpacing the energy sector’s ability to keep up. Tech infrastructure—data centers, networks, and computing hardware—already uses an estimated 10 percent of electricity globally, according to the news release. The experts predict that within two to three years, energy storage will double in developed countries. The energy industry has been relatively dormant for years, Milojicic says, with little breakthrough innovation since the times of Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla. “Data centers can ramp up within milliseconds, yet it takes months for the power and energy sector to ramp up,” he says. “The governments of various countries will have to rethink their approach to power generation to stay ahead of demand.” The experts cite the Jevons paradox —the idea that efficiency gains tend to increase overall consumption. As AI chip efficiency improves, organizations will run more hardware to build ever-larger frontier models—those advanced AI systems currently in development—the experts say. Data centers will draw as much power as grids can supply, leaving no surplus, the experts predict. Physical AI moves the fastest Physical AI refers to systems embedded within machines that sense and act in the world, including robots and autonomous vehicles. In the report, the category originally was called “hyper-automation and robotics,” a broad, software-driven process automation paired with physical machines. The Industry Advisory Board later folded it into the single physical AI megatrend. The experts found that human-AI interaction has the shortest adoption horizon of any of the 30 scored technologies, at two to three years. They also say physical AI has the biggest chance of technical advancement of any megatrend during the next four years. “The data makes clear that trust, safety, and human connection must guide every major breakthrough in the decade ahead.” —Mary Ellen Randall, 2026 IEEE president and CEO Smarter, more efficient robots will substantially cut energy consumption in the next two years, the experts say. Communications between humans and AI—whether in an android or another device—will shift from text-based commands to predominantly audio and video instructions within two to three years, the experts predict. Androids used in factories will use tactile and haptic feedback within two to five years, letting them sense what they’re touching and adjust their grip or force in response, the experts say. Bio-inspired skin, tissues, and sensors will advance in the same timeframe, the experts predict, giving robots perception that better mirrors human touch. Space is just getting started Space technology , as the report defines it, covers more than exploration. It spans satellite communications, in-space manufacturing, launch technology, and other infrastructure. It is one of the lower-profile megatrends in the report, not for lack of promise but because of where the sector presently sits. “It’s not lagging,” Milojicic says. “It’s the current state of maturity. People are talking about satellite communication right now because it’s very cool and practical. events.title: Australia wants to sell Singapore solar power. But does anyone want it?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts What Singapore really thinks of Sun Cable, the Australian solar power export plan Tiny, rich Singapore has big power needs and wants to go green. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) Australia and Singapore are neighbours, but not exactly close. As the crow flies, the distance from Darwin, the capital of Australia's Northern Territory, to the South-East Asian island nation is 3,400 kilometres — by most standards, a very long way. And yet it is this distance over which an Australian energy company is vying to lay the world's longest subsea electrical cable in the hope of tapping into a green dream. That company is Sun Cable, a renewable energy developer backed by Australian tech billionaire Mike Cannon-Brookes. Sun Cable aims to generate colossal amounts of solar power in the endless, sun-drenched expanses of Australia's Top End, supplying Singapore's 6 million consumers via a 4,300km transmission cable through the Indonesian archipelago. "I'm not aware of too many other projects on this scale," James Bowen, an energy and geopolitical analyst, said. Indeed, the exact scope of Sun Cable's $35 billion ambition is hard to comprehend. It would involve building solar panels to produce up to 10 gigawatts across as much as 12,000 hectares — an area twice the size of Manhattan. Battery storage on a similarly massive scale would back up the solar farm when the sun was not shining. A computer-generated image of Sun Cable's proposed solar farm in the NT. ( Supplied: Sun Cable ) Electricity would be transported 800km from the desert to Darwin, where some of it would support the local grid. The vast majority, however, would be sent onwards to Singapore. There, Sun Cable would supply up to 1.75 gigawatts of power, or about a quarter of the country's typical demand. Amid persistent questions about the feasibility of Sun Cable's grandiose plans, the ABC travelled to Singapore to speak to potential customers. Puah Kok Keong, chief executive of the Singapore Energy Market Authority, is the regulator of the nation's power and gas industries and one of its most senior energy officials. Puah said his country's energy needs were intense. Puah Kok Keong runs Singapore's Energy Market Authority, a regulator. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) He said air-conditioning in the famously steamy climate ran around the clock while industry chewed up as much as 80 per cent of power demand. Added to the challenge of meeting that demand, he said Singapore wanted to become carbon-neutral. Plus, Singapore is tiny — at fewer than 750 square kilometres, it is 13 times smaller than greater Melbourne. "We have set for ourselves a goal of reaching net zero by the year 2050," Puah told the ABC. Singapore, Puah said, was doing what it could within its own borders. Solar panels are being installed everywhere — on roofs, on car parks and even on the city's reservoirs as floating installations. With land at a premium, Singapore has resorted to floating solar farms. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) But he acknowledged it was a strategy with severe limits. Even with the feverish activity, Puah said solar only supplies about 3 per cent of Singapore's power, a figure unlikely to increase by much more than double. To reach net zero by the middle of the century, he said Singapore had started to look further afield. "We are also looking at importing electricity from around the region," he said. "We have set for ourselves a target of importing up to around 6 gigawatts of clean energy from the region by the year 2035." It is into this equation that Sun Cable hopes to insert itself. Currently, Singapore gets about 95 per cent of its electricity from natural gas, more than half shipped into the country as liquefied natural gas (LNG). Singapore is heavily reliant on gas supplied by the likes of Shell. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) The rest is sourced via pipelines from neighbouring Malaysia and Indonesia. Christophe Inglin from the Sustainable Energy Association of Singapore said the island state would have to do with renewable electricity what it had long done with fossil fuels. "We've imported the oil and gas," Inglin said. According to Inglin, Singapore already imports some electricity from Malaysia through a high-voltage transmission line, but these imports do not amount to much. There are plans to dramatically increase the amount through a regional "super grid" that would much more closely weave together the electricity systems of South-East Asia. From the highest levels, Singapore is seeking a more integrated Asian grid.

events.title: The release of Sarah J. Maas' 6th 'ACOTAR' book is just weeks away. Here's everything we know.
events.summary: Sarah J. Maas is publishing the sixth "A Court of Thorns and Roses" book. Alexandra Genova / SAINT LUCY Represents Sarah J. Maas is returning to the "ACOTAR" world with two new books. The sixth book will be released on October 27, 2026, and the seventh on January 12, 2027. Teasers shared ahead of its release confirmed two characters who will return in book six. Sarah J. Maas fans, gather round. We finally know what's coming in the "A Court of Thorns and Roses" series (sort of). On August 17, 2026, Maas announced the titles of the sixth and seventh "ACOTAR" books, along with initial descriptions of the novels. Book six is called "A Court of Splintered Harmony" and will be released on October 27, 2026, and book seven is "A Court of Forgotten Melody," hitting shelves on January 12, 2027. Maas first announced she would publish the sixth and seventh installments of her series in March 2026, remaining tight-lipped about them until the title announcement in August. The books are eagerly awaited not only by fans but also by Maas' publisher, Bloomsbury. The company's sales fell 10% for the 2025-2026 fiscal year because Maas didn't release a new book, Publishers Weekly reported . And in recent weeks, Bloomsbury has been sharing quotes from "A Court of Splintered Harmony" on social media, building hype for the novel and teasing what's to come. Here's everything we know about "ACOTAR" six so far. Warning: Some spoilers for Maas' work — including "ACOTAR" and "Crescent City" — ahead. Maas is releasing the sixth 'A Court of Thorns and Roses' story in multiple volumes In March 2023, Bloomsbury announced that Maas had signed a deal for three more books with the publisher. At the time, she was already under contract for four titles, including "House of Flame and Shadow," the third installment in her "Crescent City" series , published in January 2024. Readers didn't find out what the next book she would write would be until her March 2026 appearance on the "Call Her Daddy" podcast with Alex Cooper. She told Cooper she finished the sixth "ACOTAR" book while writing in Montana over the summer of 2025, but she didn't share details about it because of its nontraditional release structure. "This book's coming out October 27, and then on January 12, like two months later, I can't do math, whatever that is, the next ACOTAR book will be coming out," Maas said. "So there will be two books within, like, a very short span." Sarah J. Maas for "Call Her Daddy." Call Her Daddy As her fans will know, Maas' books are typically split into parts, separating different sections of the story she is telling. However, when it comes to the sixth "ACOTAR" story, Maas said the individual parts became longer than she anticipated as she started writing, with part one coming in at 400 pages at one point. As she continued writing, Maas decided the parts didn't have to be in a single physical book. "What if this book was really long?" she said. "What if it took me more than a thousand pages to tell the story that needed to be told, the arc that I wanted to create from start to finish?" Maas said the story for "ACOTAR" six was ultimately divided into four parts, though it is still one cohesive story. Part one is the novel Bloomsbury will publish  on October 27, 2026, and parts two and three will be published together on January 12, 2027. Maas has yet to write or give a publication date for part four, but she told Cooper all three volumes would be published "in a very short time." "It's meant to be read, ideally, as one massive, massive story as opposed to in a trilogy," she said. "It's not a trilogy. Like, arcs aren't wrapped up." Maas finally shared some details about the books in August 2026 On August 16, Maas cleared her Instagram of all its posts, changing her profile photo to a black-and-white illustration of a monster and a spider. Then, on August 17, she shared the covers and titles of books six, "A Court of Splintered Harmony," and seven, "A Court of Forgotten Melody," on her wiped Instagram. The "Splintered Harmony" cover features a pink-and-orange backdrop with a sketched drawing of a monster with teeth and bones, and the subtitle is "The Valkyrie Cycle: Movement I." The Valkyrie were introduced to "ACOTAR" in "A Court of Silver Flames," when Nesta Archeron brought the legendary all-female fighting squad back to life alongside her friends Gwyn and Emerie. "A Court of Splintered Harmony." Bloomsbury Maas posted the book alongside the tagline, "What was broken will be remade." The blurb shared on booksellers' websites reveals that the Night Court is facing new threats when book six opens: Koschei the Deathless, one of three legendary monster siblings introduced throughout "ACOTAR," and those willing to ally with him to claim the newly freed human lands. The description also notes that there is tension among the members of the Night Court because of "recent betrayals and revealed truths," which they must work through if they want to defeat Koschei. "A Court of Splintered Harmony" will be 352 pages and will include three bonus chapters from the "ACOTAR" series. Those bonus chapters were previously published in specific editions of Maas' novels, but they will be in all copies of "ACOSH," as the publisher shared on its social media on September 24. One chapter focuses on Feyre and Rhysand, one on Cassian and Nesta, and one on Azriel's experience on the Winter Solstice that takes place in "A Court of Silver Flames." Teasers from the new book In mid-September, Bloomsbury began sharing quotes from "A Court of Splintered Harmony," offering more insight into the novel than the vague blurbs. The first quote Bloomsbury released on September 17 revealed that at least some of the novel will be told from Lucien Vanserra's perspective. "Lucien's heart thundered, throat drying out," the quote read . "Maybe this had been a terrible idea." Lucien has only played a supporting role in the "ACOTAR" books so far, but Maas has been teeing up his expanded role in her books through his unaccepted mating bond with Elain Archeron, Feyre's middle sister, and his connection to Koschei. He serves as an emissary to the human lands for the Night Court in "ACOSF," alongside Jurian and Vassa, a human queen who was sold to Koschei and cursed to turn into a firebird each day. It would be surprising if Vassa — and by extension Lucien — weren't involved in fighting against Koschei in book six. No other quote shared by Bloomsbury so far has made clear which character is telling the story. The passage shared on October 6 mentions Rhysand, whom the narrator calls Rhys — indicating it could be the POV of one of his close companions — giving a "savage smile" before saying, "With pleasure." A quote shared on September 22 referenced "sisters lost to us — ones we pray each day will find a way home to our sides." events.title: AWS launches open-source AI agent sandbox to prevent YOLO mode disasters
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Strands Box is the latest open source AI control tool from the cloud giant; like its predecessors, it promises tighter reins on autonomous agents Ransomware fixer claimed he could decrypt files, allegedly defrauded clients instead 5 hours ago OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties 11 hours ago Attackers hijacked top-level domains, minted fake security certs for Google and other orgs 12 hours ago US states sue popular kitmaker TP-Link over China risks 14 hours ago Poetry is the new AI security threat as PoeLLM malware infects 3K+ servers 15 hours ago AWS has offered multiple open-source strategies for holding AI agents accountable, and now it’s adding a full-on sandbox to this stack. Dubbed Strands Box , the new solution uses OS-level isolation and some of AWS’ other recent open-source AI control tools to, ostensibly, retain greater control over autonomous AI agents’ behavior. “Agents increasingly run in ‘ YOLO mode ,’ approving every action without human review,” the AWS team explained in its announcement. “The usual solution to this problem is a sandbox … but access is only part of what we want to control.” The problem with containers and microVMs typically used to isolate AI agents, as AWS explains it, is that their strong isolation doesn’t come with contextual rule enforcement. In other words, when a containerized or virtualized agent gets hold of a tool, there may be no stopping it from doing whatever it wants - like deleting a production database, or gaining access to the internet and doing dog knows what . That’s where the other open-source tools inside Strands Box come in: It uses the Dogwood Local Engine to give the policy engine in Box temporal awareness, so tool calls can be checked against not only what the agent wants to do, but what it’s already done. As one example, AWS noted that an agent could be allowed to post status updates to Slack, but no more than three times every ten minutes to prevent it from spamming its human operators. An AWS spokesperson further explained that Box could be used to control when an agent can perform a Git push, or it could be used to put a cap on API calls that could end up costing a small fortune. Additionally, Strands Box includes Strands Shell and Monty for Python, which expose shell and Python operations to the same Dogwood policy engine and event history, making agentic actions clearer to developers and allowing policies to account for what an agent is trying to do. AWS VP and distinguished engineer Marc Brooker , one of the folks behind Dogwood and Strands Box, explained to The Register that the interpreters are a key part of making agentic behavior more intelligible, which allows for devs to write more precise policies to prevent agents from taking bad actions. “Box’s Shell and Python interpreters expose operations such as file deletions, while its gateways expose API requests and tool calls,” Brooker told us in an email. “Policies can then account for the action being attempted and earlier activity.” Box, Brooker added, enforces those rules without trusting or relying on agents to actually follow instructions, which should ideally prevent them from running roughshod over their operators’ wishes. As for the reason behind AWS’ push to develop open-source tools like Dogwood, the Dogwood Local Engine, and Strands Box, Brooker said that AWS wants to find the right balance between boundaries and policies that prevent agentic AI disasters of the kind we regularly report. “Box enforces the policies developers configure, deterministically, and the agent can't talk its way around these rules,” Brooker explained, though he added that, even with properly configured permissions, an agentic action can still produce an unwanted result. “Developers remain responsible for deciding what access to grant and where human review is needed,” Brooker added - in other words, don’t let your YOLO mode go too YOLO. A bit of human oversight is still necessary.

events.title: Americans don't want taxpayer dollars funding campaign ads: poll
events.summary: Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Nearly nine in 10 voters say using taxpayer money to pay for election-related ads featuring the president or Cabinet members is inappropriate, including 80% of Republicans, according to a recent Reuters-Ipsos poll . Why it matters: The administration's decision to spend millions of taxpayer dollars on Trump-fronted ads weeks before the midterms is facing an uproar and overwhelming public opposition. While the administration insisted the ads were actually PSAs, Trump later announced that a super PAC affiliated with him would foot the bill for future ads (but not reimburse the taxpayer dollars already spent). Friction point: New polling suggests the TV spots, which the White House said "are a reminder for Americans to love their country," might not get much love from voters. The poll of 4,506 adults found that just 9% of Americans find it appropriate to tap taxpayer funds for election-related television ads featuring the president or cabinet members. Zoom out: A majority of Americans also panned other actions Trump has taken: 68% say it's inappropriate to block media outlets from entering the White House, and 72% say the same about naming federal institutions and buildings after a sitting president. Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Zoom in: A White House official contended in a statement to Axios that the "PSAs are clearly not political," saying Trump "is not on the ballot and the ads don't have a call to action." But one is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad, using the same footage and narration, with the campaign sponsorship tagline replaced with a disclaimer: "Paid for by the U.S. Government." Earlier this month, Democrats called on the Government Accountability Office and the U.S. Office of Special Counsel to investigate the use of taxpayer money to produce and air the ads. Between the lines: Axios' Alex Isenstadt scooped late last month that the ads released so far were "just the beginning" and that Trump himself — pleased with the war-room-style social media posts his digital team regularly pumps out — was hand-picking the ads himself. And it's not just the White House that's gotten in on promotional hype that blurs the lines with campaign content: The FBI's rapid response account released a video Tuesday applauding director Kash Patel — and criticizing Democrats, including Senate candidate Abdul-El Sayed. The bottom line: As an election approaches where cost-of-living concerns are paramount, Americans have strong feelings about how their taxpayer dollars are spent. events.title: US states sue popular kitmaker TP-Link over China risks
events.summary: The attorneys general of Florida, Iowa, Montana, and Nebraska have sued ubiquitous networking and smart home tech maker TP-Link, alleging its security claims were misleading and it hadn't properly disclosed ties to China. The company has a large presence in US retail and the tech channel, especially in consumer routers, with stats from Circana asserting it had around 36.6 percent US market share by units and 31 percent by dollars in 2024. The complaint [PDF] accuses California-based TP-Link Systems, whose brand originated in Shenzhen, of deceptive and unfair marketing practices concerning its routers' security and its connections to China. It cites exploitation of TP-Link devices by Chinese and Russian state-backed hackers. The suit also claims TP-Link allegedly concealed facts about its "past and ongoing ties to the People's Republic of China," accuses it of having a supply chain that's reliant on PRC players, repeated firmware vulnerabilities, and being subject to Chinese laws that force companies to cooperate with state intelligence. According to the states' attorneys general, the hardware vendor still relies on Chinese companies for research and development and manufacturing operations, despite previously claiming to have moved into Vietnam after severing ties with China. The complaint alleges that only 0.5 percent of components used at TP-Link's Vietnamese plant, measured by value, are bought in Vietnam, with "all other inputs" imported "from or through China." The complaint also claims that a US-designated Chinese military company carried out construction work at the Vietnamese factory, challenging TP-Link's assurances about its supply chain's security. The complaint cites 2025 testimony [PDF] from former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce that TP-Link's share of the US retail market for Wi-Fi systems and small-office/home-office (SoHo) routers at at least 60 percent. Lawyers pointed to various snippets from TP-Link's marketing materials. These included claims that its HomeShield product "covers all security scenarios" and, on a version of its website available in November 2025, provides a "100 percent safeguard" for network security. The complaint argues that TP-Link's security assurances were misleading because its routers contained critical vulnerabilities. It further cites Joyce's that TP-Link routers were among the brands exploited in the China-linked Volt Typhoon and Flax Typhoon campaigns. The complaint also alleges that TP-Link's privacy policies permit it to collect customer data and share it with affiliates without disclosing how its Chinese connections and China's intelligence laws could expose that information to Chinese intelligence agencies. "Iowans' sensitive data and our national security is at risk because of TP-Link and their connection to the communist Chinese government," said Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird. "TP-Link tells Iowans its routers are safe, our personal data is secure, and that they have no ties to China. They are not telling the truth. It's time to hold China and China-backed companies accountable." "TP-Link's false statements and deceptive advertising are a violation of Montana law," said Attorney General Austin Knudsen. "As a result of their nefarious practices, millions of Americans have unknowingly invited a foreign adversary into their living rooms and put their personal information at risk. "I will do everything I can as Attorney General to hold TP-Link accountable and protect our privacy and security." Steve Kovsky, corporate affairs officer for TP-Link Systems Inc., said the lawsuits were based on false premises, did nothing to advance national security, and unfairly penalized a US company. Kovsky added that the company has spent months providing officials with clear documentation showing that it is not owned or controlled by any foreign government and that its devices sold in the US are manufactured in Vietnam. "Any claims that our products present a threat to user security or grant unauthorized network access to foreign governments are baseless," he said. "TP-Link Systems is a US company that complies with US privacy and data protection laws. We perform comprehensive security testing and rely on trusted third-party security labs for additional scrutiny to ensure our products meet the highest security standards and are recognized as among the most secure on the market. "We meet or exceed all industry best practices for monitoring and preventing vulnerabilities and actively support our customers to mitigate any issues that occur as they are identified. We do not, and will not, share customer network data with foreign governments or unauthorized third parties. "We stand fully behind the security of our products, the integrity of our company and our people, and our commitment to serving the best interests of our customers in the United States and globally. We look forward to refuting these baseless allegations in court." The allegations echo those made by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose office sued TP-Link earlier this year over its Chinese connections and router security. US officials began weighing restrictions on TP-Link router sales in 2024. In March 2026, the FCC imposed broader restrictions [PDF] on new foreign-produced router models, barring new equipment authorizations unless an exemption is granted. Previously authorized models were not automatically banned. ®

events.title: 10 things we want to see in season one of HBO's 'Harry Potter' show
events.summary: The new "Harry Potter" trio: Arabella Stanton, Dominic McLaughlin, and Alastair Stout. Warner Bros. Pictures The "Harry Potter" TV adaptation will premiere on HBO this Christmas. It will cover the first book, " Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone " — or the Philosopher's Stone. There were a few cuts from the book in the film adaptation that we want to see in the TV series. It seems that every other week, we're getting a new cast announcement for the "Harry Potter" TV series that's hitting HBO — most recently, Kit Harington was announced as Gilderoy Lockhart in season two. But we're getting ahead of ourselves. Season one of the show, which is set to drop on December 25, will cover the events of JK Rowling's first wizarding book, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone," which was first published in 1997. If you live outside the US, you'll know it as "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone," which HBO is going with this time around. Since HBO's CEO Casey Bloys promised that each season will "dive deep into each of the iconic books," Potterheads expect the TV series to include details that had to be cut from the films for time constraints. Here are the 10 biggest things we want to see included in season one of "Harry Potter." The first chapter from Vernon's POV Vernon Dursley. Warner Bros. Pictures The first chapter of " Harry Potter " begins not from Harry's perspective, but from his obnoxious Uncle Vernon's. The first chapter follows a typical day in the life of Vernon — except this day isn't typical at all, as it's the day that Lord Voldemort was defeated by his baby nephew, Harry Potter, though he doesn't know it yet. This first chapter sets the tone for the book series, as it explains how the wizarding world (sort of) blends in with the Muggle world, establishes how bigoted the Dursleys are toward their magical relatives, and shows just how famous Harry is in the wizarding world. In comparison, the movie begins with Professor Dumbledore and Professor McGonagall rolling up to the Dursleys' house and dropping Harry off. Speaking of that scene … More of Harry's life pre-Hogwarts Harry Potter and his letters. Warner Bros. Pictures A not-insignificant chunk of the " Sorcerer's Stone " book is spent explaining what Harry's day-to-day life in the Muggle world is like, including the unexplainable things that happen to Harry, like his hair growing out after a particularly bad haircut or how he somehow jumps up onto the ceiling of his school to avoid bullies. Also, hilariously, when Harry starts receiving letters addressed to the Cupboard Under the Stairs, the Dursleys, fearing that someone is aware of their abuse, let Harry move into the second bedroom, which had once been occupied by Dudley's toys. There's also supposed to be a very awkward month between Hagrid's first meeting with Harry and taking him to Diagon Alley, and then the Dursleys dropping him off at King's Cross , which would add some comedy to the proceedings. A little Sirius Black foreshadowing Gary Oldman played Sirius Black in the films. Warner Bros. Pictures In the film (and the book), Harry gets dropped off by Hagrid, the kind half-giant groundskeeper at Hogwarts, who scoops him up from his parents' house and brings him to the Dursleys via a giant, flying motorcycle. In the movie, Dumbledore asks if there's been any trouble, and Hagrid just replies that Harry fell asleep over Bristol. However, in the book, Hagrid mentions that he borrowed the bike from "young Sirius Black." This is a small detail, but one that will pay off in two seasons from now, since, of course, Sirius is Harry's godfather, which we don't learn until " Prisoner of Azkaban ." Seeding Sirius' name early on in the TV show is a fun Easter egg for devotees and a little thing to chew on for newbies. Harry and Draco's first meeting Draco, played by Tom Felton, and Harry, played by Radcliffe. Lox Pratt will play Draco in the show. Warner Bros. Pictures In the movie, Harry meets Draco for the first time at Hogwarts, right before the sorting ceremony, and he coolly tells Draco he can tell who the "wrong sort" of people are for himself, after Draco tries to befriend the famous Harry Potter. In the book, this takes place in Diagon Alley, when the two are shopping for robes. They have a brief conversation, during which neither introduces themselves, but Draco insults Hagrid. They meet once more on the Hogwarts Express, which is when Draco learns who the boy he spoke to at Madam Malkin's was — and they have the same "wrong sort of people" conversation. Harry's first meeting with Draco is important for a few reasons. One: It makes the reader and Harry nervous that everyone at Hogwarts is a major snob, so it's a huge relief when Harry meets Ron. Two: It's effective exposition, showing us that there are hierarchies within the wizarding world based on blood status. Three: It helps Harry and the reader understand just how much Harry doesn't know about this world he's entering — crucially, this is when he learns about Quidditch. More of the friendships between Harry and his classmates Harry (Radcliffe) and Seamus Finnegan, played by Devon Murray. In the show, Leo Earley will play him. Warner Bros. Pictures Since the movies are pressed for time with all the plot they have to get through, the friendships Harry forms outside Ron and Hermione take a back seat. But in the books, Harry is relatively popular — at least, in the first book. He's good friends with the other Gryffindor boys, Seamus Finnegan and Dean Thomas, and is protective of Neville Longbottom. He also has strong bonds with the Gryffindor Quidditch team. We hope that the TV show is able to expand upon the other students at Hogwarts outside the core trio. Peeves Peter Serafinowicz is set to play Peeves. Danny North/Comic Relief/Getty Images This might be a little bit of a cheat, since Peeves has already been cast (Peter Serafinowicz will play him in the series), but the omission of Peeves from the entire film series, not just the first movie, is probably one of "Potter" fans' most disliked choices. This devious poltergeist takes pride in messing with students, professors, and ghosts alike, but when it comes time to protect the residents of Hogwarts from truly evil forces, Peeves is up to the task. Also, as the series gets darker, it's always nice to have some comic relief from Peeves. All the Norbert drama Hagrid, as played by Robbie Coltrane, and Norbert. Nick Frost will play Hagrid in the show. Warner Bros. events.title: Changing Your Career Isn’t Easy
events.summary: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum ’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written i n partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free! When I changed careers at 30 to become a software engineer, I expected it to be hard. I expected to struggle to fit in, and I expected to bomb a lot of interviews (I did). What I didn’t expect was how few people would support me. As a parent, I get it now. A career change is a risk, and the people who care about you tend to project their fears onto you. They don’t want to watch you struggle or fail, so they discourage you or just don’t offer much enthusiasm. Right now is a strange time to be in engineering, or knowledge work in general. Plenty of us are excited about what AI means for our jobs. More of us are nervous, and I think that fear is justified. Employment for entry-level software developers has fallen nearly 20 percent since late 2022, according to Stanford’s 2026 AI Index , and it can feel like the knowledge we spent our careers building is being commoditized. Lately I’ve seen a flood of social media content telling software developers to go into the trades. YouTubers are telling you to become a plumber or a goat herder. But before you do that, I want to warn you, there is no EASY path. Even if you want to become a goat herder. I’ve changed careers once so far, but my business has forced me through several pivots that felt a lot like career changes—new audiences, new skills, new identity. Here’s what I’d tell anyone considering a change, whether you’re moving into engineering, leaving it, or finding a new speciality. Find someone who’s done it and ask how This is exactly what I told my oldest son, who’s getting ready to enter the job market full-time. Outside of the primary social media feeds, the internet is full of free and paid communities on Facebook, LinkedIn, and other sites. Reddit works, too, if you can stomach the trolls, because there’s valuable information buried in there. Many of these spaces are flooded with people trying to break in, so look for the ones full of people who already do the work and talk openly about what is and isn’t going well. Then find one or two people in your own circle who’ve done it and ask what the job takes. You’ll often find the degree matters less than you assumed. Indeed Hiring Lab found the share of U.S. postings requiring a bachelor’s degree fell from 20.4 percent in 2019 to 17.8 percent in early 2024, and more than half listed no education requirement at all. Build proof of work, even if it’s unpaid Yes, you’ll probably need to do some work for free, or at least far cheaper than you’re used to. I’ve had to do this in my business over and over. Nobody cares that I’ve been a software engineer for 12 years. They want to know whether I can do the thing they need. When I started pitching businesses, I offered to build something for free as a case study, then used it to land clients who paid well. You can copy this in most fields. Say you want to get into marketing: Learn how Facebook ads work, find a friend or small business that needs help, and run the campaigns at a low price. Now you’ve picked up the jargon, and you have something concrete to show a hiring manager. Stability is a myth It may be corny, but change is the only constant. If you’re a software engineer, you could argue you’re in the middle of a career change already, whether you opted in or not. Programmers in the 1990s had the same experience when the web showed up and they had to quickly learn new tools just to stay relevant. If you’re looking for stability, you’re in the wrong place, and I think it will get scarcer as AI and other forces reshape work. The best move is to build a strong foundation so you can adapt when the ground shifts. I wrote about the foundational skills to focus on if you’re interested. —Brian Barbara Mazzolai Wants to Build a New Field of Robotics Roboticist Barbara Mazzolai is a prime example of someone who advanced her career by switching fields—and now, she’s helping to create a new one. Learn how her background in biology led her to co-author a manifesto on “sustainability robotics.” Read more here . Turning Tech Talent Into Leadership Legacy The transition from a technical role to a leadership position can be challenging. To help seasoned professionals navigate the shift, IEEE is hosting its first International Leadership Conference in Budapest. Read more here . IEEE Celebrates Innovators Shaping the Future Every year, IEEE recognizes engineers whose technical achievements and leadership have made a lasting impact with its Technical Field Awards. See who’s on the 2027 list of awardees, which was announced in late September. Read more here .

events.title: UAE seeks to boost Gulf industrial integration and supply chain resilience
events.summary: The UAE is seeking to boost industrial integration with Gulf states, as the region explores ways to strengthen supply chain resilience at high-level meetings in Bahrain. A UAE delegation led by Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology, is participating at the GCC Industrial Co-operation Committee and the Ministerial Committee for Standardisation Affairs meeting being held in Bahrain. The UAE’s participation focuses on “strengthening industrial integration among GCC countries, building more resilient and competitive Gulf supply chains, accelerating the deployment of advanced technology and artificial intelligence in the industrial sector, and enhancing the role of the private sector in building partnerships and joint industrial opportunities”, the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology said in a statement on Wednesday. The meetings, which began Tuesday and will continue until Thursday, highlighted the need for co-ordination in standards. Dr Al Jaber emphasised the importance of advancing joint efforts to develop a more advanced industrial sector that supports the diversification of national economies and strengthens the GCC's position as a global hub for industry and innovation. “Industrial integration is a cornerstone of Gulf competitiveness,” he added. The meetings took place on the sidelines of the inaugural Made in GCC Forum and Exhibition 2026 being held in Manama. The event is aimed at boosting collaboration and partnerships across investment, manufacturing, supply chains and technology. Key outcomes of the meetings include the launch of the Gulf Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution and its digital platform aimed at enhancing the digital maturity of factories and supporting industrial transformation, the GCC Council said in a statement. The evaluation period for the amended rules on exempting industrial inputs from customs duties was extended until the end of 2027. UAE manufacturing push The UAE’s participation comes amid a strong push towards domestic manufacturing in the country. The industrial sector plays a key role in the national economy, with its contribution having reached Dh200 billion ($54.45 billion) – an increase of 70 per cent. Its industrial exports reached Dh260 billion last year, including Dh92 billion in medium-and high-technology industrial exports. The Emirates also launched its industrial strategy, Operation 300bn , in 2021, to position itself as a global industrial hub by 2031. The UAE’s overarching agenda is focused on priority industries including chemicals, electrical, construction, machinery and equipment, food, transport, metals, pharmaceuticals, rubber, plastic and fibreglass, and wood and paper. The Emirates has in recent years also invested heavily in advance technology and AI, with multibillion-dollar projects being built. In May, the UAE launched the Dh1 billion National Industrial Resilience Fund to support the industrial sector and announced a national strategy to secure supply chains and boost local food, medicine and industrial production. Meanwhile, the country's National In-Country Value (ICV) programme has redirected more than Dh473 billion into the national economy. The UAE is pushing for deeper industrial co-operation across the Gulf as countries seek to localise supply chains and reduce their reliance on imports following disruption exposed by the Covid-19 pandemic and other global shocks, Dr Farah Al Zarouni, assistant undersecretary for the Standardisation Affairs sector at the ministry, told The National . “We need to benefit from all the resources available across the GCC countries,” she said. The Made in GCC event is expected to involve the signing of a number of initial pacts between UAE entities and Gulf companies, the ministry said. The UAE is participating with 23 Emirati companies spanning sectors including basic industries, pharmaceuticals, defence and spare parts. “We no longer look at industry as simply traditional manufacturing. We are moving our national industry towards more advanced manufacturing,” Ms Al Zarouni said. “Technology is a very important and fundamental component of our national industrial sector.” The experience of the six years since the pandemic has highlighted the vulnerability created when countries depend heavily on overseas suppliers for relatively small components for manufacturing. “If I had been able to source that small component locally, the component that enabled me to produce the final product, I would not have been affected to the same extent,” she said. The priority now should be to identify which raw materials and components can be produced within the UAE or elsewhere in the GCC, she said. “Supply chains are long, so you need to benefit from all the resources available across the GCC countries.”

events.title: IEA members support faster release of reserve oil stocks
events.summary: Members of the International Energy Agency (IEA) expressed support on Wednesday for accelerating the release of roughly 100 million barrels of reserve oil stocks previously agreed to in March. About 325 million barrels of oil have been released under the March agreement to ease oil markets after the onset of the Iran war led to a surge in energy prices. The IEA also said members had agreed to prioritise the release of diesel stocks. Member countries still hold roughly 1.1 billion barrels of emergency oil stocks, including more than 200 million barrels of diesel. “The IEA stands ready to release more of these stocks to the market if and when required,” executive director Fatih Birol said in a statement. “Participants in the meeting expressed strong appreciation for the IEA’s response to the energy impacts of the Strait of Hormuz crisis." Mr Birol said members also welcomed last week's statement by G7 leaders on global energy and security, and agreed to assess and review the situation at the IEA governing board meeting next week. G7 member countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves through the IEA, following pressure from US President Donald Trump's administration. Conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have triggered a global surge in fuel prices, adding to pressure on Mr Trump ahead of November's midterm elections. On Monday, he signed an executive order waiving restrictions on cheaper red-dyed diesel, which could ease price pressures for lorry drivers, who are facing higher costs at the pump that could be passed down to consumers. Diesel prices have risen to more than $6 per gallon in recent weeks, compared to the average price of $3.60 per gallon this time last year. The White House said the federal diesel tax is 24.4 cents per gallon, or about $60 on a 250-gallon fuel. Europe is also facing higher diesel prices, which hit a record of €2.24 per litre, compared to €1.59 before the Iran war began on February 28. The US is currently in the process of a 172-million-barrel drawdown from its strategic petroleum reserve. Once completed, the SPR is projected to fall to its lowest levels since 1982.

events.title: Starlink's plan to avoid orbital near-misses: Ephemeris sharing
events.summary: SpaceX has acknowledged the need for satellite operators to collaborate to avoid collisions and has taken the unusual step of sharing imagery showing how close spacecraft are coming to each other. The company has called on other operators to share their satellites' ephemeris (a set of parameters describing the position and velocity of a spacecraft over time) to facilitate timely avoidance maneuvers. "In 2026," the company wrote, "Starlink encountered conjunctions with about 650 unique maneuvering third-party satellites, with only about half of them actually sharing ephemeris. "Some operators don't share ephemeris out of a concern that sharing upcoming maneuvers gives away proprietary information. In other circumstances, operators are willing to share data, but are unable to receive permission from the government to do so. "Such policies are counterproductive, and largely only serve to create preventable collision risk between satellites." "Over six months," the company went on, "Starlink observed ~164,000 conjunctions where time of closest approach (TCA) was within four hours after an unannounced manoeuvre. "While not all of these conjunctions were high-risk, they represent cases where Starlink would not have sufficient information to reliably avoid the other vehicle if the other operator’s action created a high-risk conjunction. "In many cases, the lack of high-accuracy post-manoeuvre trajectory information can cause such conjunctions to go unnoticed, giving operators a false sense of confidence and not realising how much risk their actions are creating." How many sats is that again? It's all worthy stuff, until you consider that SpaceX has applied for permission to operate 100,000 Starlink satellites and up to 1 million Starmind AI satellites. Arguably that is a substantial contribution to orbital overcrowding. Not to worry though – space isn't really getting crowded, according to SpaceX. "A good analogy is air travel," the company wrote. "Airspace around the world has grown more congested since aviation began. Yet air travel is the safest form of transport on Earth in part because every aircraft publishes a flight plan and then continuously broadcasts its position during flight." Er, kind of. Although if aircraft collide, the debris falls rapidly to Earth, rather than lingering in the sky and potentially striking more aircraft weeks or months later. Plus, SpaceX is helpfully not counting other debris, from spent rocket casings to flakes of paint, that also pose a hazard in orbit. The company noted its successes, where Starlink satellites successfully dodged other vehicles. One in October 2025 occurred when the other satellite made an unexpected maneuver, reducing the predicted miss distance from 9 km to a bottom-clenching 57 meters. Another example happened in August 2026, when the risk was identified too late for the Starlink satellite to move out of the way, and the satellite had to "duck" instead, slewing to present a narrower profile. "The vehicles ultimately passed within 134 metres of each other," the company said. "This approach could have been prevented if the other object shared its manoeuvre ahead of time." SpaceX was keen for operators to connect to sites such as space-safety.com and talked up its Stargaze service, which uses star trackers on the Starlink fleet to observe nearby objects in orbit. A far cry from 2019, when a Starlink satellite failed to move out of the way of the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Aeolus Earth-observation satellite due to a bug in SpaceX's on-call paging system. There is no shortage of companies with capabilities to monitor and advise on traffic in orbit. Neuraspace, for example, springs to mind. As the company's CEO Chiara Manfletti observed, humanity has not done a particularly good job of looking after the space above the planet. While the technology used to prevent satellite collisions is impressive, and data sharing should be encouraged, we can't help but wonder whether another solution might be to not launch tens of thousands more satellites into orbit in the first place. Manfletti told The Register that the problem was very real. She said, "As the number of satellites increases, knowing where an object is today is no longer sufficient. Manoeuvrability is becoming essential, and operators increasingly need timely, accurate information about where other spacecraft intend to be, including planned manoeuvres." "Initiatives such as SpaceX's space-safety platform are certainly welcome. But the long-term solution cannot depend on every operator joining a single company's system. What we ultimately need is a federated and interoperable space-traffic ecosystem in which operators can securely exchange trusted trajectory and intent information across different platforms, organisations and national systems. "Neuraspace has reached out to SpaceX to enable such coordination on behalf of our customers. We have extended an open hand, and it would be a strong sign of leadership for SpaceX to take it — demonstrating that improving safety in orbit ultimately requires cooperation not only within individual platforms, but across them." ®

events.title: Authorities investigate Japan's four biggest beer brewers over price rises
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Asahi, Kirin, Sapporo and Suntory in Japan raided over price-collusion accusations Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Sapporo Breweries and Suntory have confirmed the raids. ( Reuters. ) Asahi, Kirin, Sapporo and Suntory breweries have been raided in Japan. The four beer giants make up around 90 per cent of Japan's beer market share — and are popular brands in Australia too. Japan's Fair Trade Commission is investigating whether the beer brewers colluded to raise their prices over several years. Japanese authorities have raided four global beer manufacturers over suspicions they colluded to raise their prices. Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Sapporo Breweries and Suntory have confirmed the raids on Wednesday. Sales of Asahi's Super Dry variety in Australia have increased 40 per cent in Australia since 2020, according to the company. A spokesperson for Asahi in Australia said: "The investigation cited in media reports concerns Asahi Breweries in Japan and is entirely unrelated to Australian operations." The ABC has also contacted Kirin and Sapporo for a response about whether Australian production of the beer has been impacted. Japanese beer is suddenly everywhere Due to a combination of business and travel Japanese brewers have come to dominate our domestic beer market. Japan's public broadcaster NHK said the Fair Trade Commission was investigating whether the companies had formed a cartel and colluded to raise their prices at the same time over several years, together citing factors including rising raw material costs. The anti-trust watchdog is expected to continue its investigation and could file a criminal complaint if they were found to have breached the country's anti-monopoly laws.
