events.title: DBS, OCBC and UOB shares have fallen. Is it a good time to buy?
events.summary: Citi expects OCBC’s Q3 earnings to be flat year on year, and growth optimism for the lender to be derailed. OCBC fell 5.9% after Citi downgraded it to “sell” on softer third-quarter 2026 earnings hopes. DBS and UOB also dropped after recent record highs. Analysts said the fall may be profit-taking, not weaker bank basics. They expect lending and wealth income to stay firm, but trading and fee income may normalise. Broker views differ: Citi is cautious on OCBC, while RHB and others still like Singapore banks. DBS is favoured for dividend safety, and UOB for valuation and higher upside. SINGAPORE – Shares of OCBC fell more than 5% on Oct 7, after Citi cited softer-than-expected third-quarter 2026 earnings expectations and downgraded the stock to “sell”. The stock slipped 5.9% to close at $30.30 from the previous day’s close of $32.20. Its peers DBS and UOB also took a hit. DBS shares slid 1.36% to $77.49 on Oct 7 while UOB dropped 2.93% to end the day at $42.44. On Oct 7’s sudden pullback, Macquarie Capital head of Asean equity research Jayden Vantarakis said investors may have sold their shares to take profits after recent gains. “The banks’ share prices have done well this year, especially OCBC, so we are likely seeing profit taking before investors make clear assessments of their views of third-quarter 2026,” he said. Jefferies Asean research analyst Joanna Cheah said that it is increasingly about expectations and valuation rather than a deterioration in fundamentals, as the sector has had a very strong run. “OCBC has fallen more because expectations were particularly high after a very strong second quarter and investors are now questioning how much of that trading, insurance and fee-income strength is repeatable,” she said. Citi downgraded OCBC from “neutral” to “sell” on Oct 6, with a target price of $27.50. It expects flat year-on-year third-quarter earnings for OCBC and growth optimism for the lender to be derailed. On the outlook for the banks’ third quarter earnings, Cheah said Jefferies does not expect a repeat of the exceptional momentum seen in the second quarter, though performance should stay broadly resilient. “Loan growth and wealth should stay supportive, while net interest margin (NIM) pressure is becoming less severe. The main normalisation is likely to come from trading and other non-interest income.” Jefferies has a “buy” rating on DBS with a target price of $91, while rating OCBC “hold” at $35 and UOB “buy” at $48. NIM is the core profitability metric for banks and measures how much money a bank makes on its loans and investments compared to the interest it pays out on deposits and borrowings. While Citi turned bearish on the short-term upside for OCBC, other brokerages like RHB remained positive on the lender. In its Oct 7 note, RHB named OCBC its top pick, citing the bank’s all-round balance sheet strength and strong earnings momentum. UOB ranked second, supported by its attractive valuations, while DBS remained a core pick for investors seeking dividend safety and attractive yields. RHB rated both UOB and DBS as “buy”, with target prices of $47.60 for UOB and $81.20 for DBS. Just days earlier, the bank reiterated its buy call on OCBC and raised its target price to $33.70 from $32.85. “We continue to like OCBC Bank for its solid balance sheet, positive earnings growth momentum (backed by a strong wealth business), relatively decent valuation and dividend yield,” RHB said on Oct 2. The bank said it turned more optimistic in its NIM outlook on Singapore banks, as the US Fed hikes interest rates by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75% to 4% on Sept 16 – the first time in three years. “The trend of rising benchmark rates could support the operating income of Singapore banks with another leg for growth, which has predominantly been carried by non-interest income in recent quarters,” said RHB. Meanwhile, Citi on Oct 6 maintained a “buy” on DBS and reiterated its sell call on UOB, while citing a preference for UOB over OCBC, “due to relative valuations or positioning”. CGS International on Oct 1 maintained “neutral” on Singapore banks due to stretched valuations. It expects limited factors to drive earnings in the near term, as growth in wealth management fees is slowing alongside slower deposit growth in Singapore. It also expects net interest income (NII) to see an uplift from improved NIMs only from fourth-quarter 2026. CGIS prefers DBS, with a target price of $77.10, because of its attractive dividend yield of 4.3% expected in 2026 and 5.7% expected in 2027. This is supported by its excess capital, which can be returned to shareholders through its capital return initiatives. It holds a target price of $29.80 for OCBC and $42.60 for UOB.

events.title: Conflict in the Red Sea is forcing cloud giants to find a new route for the internet
events.summary: Google, Meta, and Microsoft are said to be securing expensive land routes as fighting around Yemen threatens the submarine cables connecting Europe and Asia. U.S. cloud giants are facing steep prices to secure backup internet routes around the Red Sea as fighting rages over the Red Sea strait that carries most data cables between Europe and Asia. More than 90% of data capacity between Europe and Asia runs through cables under the Red Sea. The cables enter the sea at Bab al-Mandab, a strait less than 32 kilometers (20 miles) wide between Yemen and the African nations of Djibouti and Eritrea . The Houthis, a U.S.-designated terrorist organization, seized Yemen’s side of the strait in September, including the island of Mayyun. On October 5, Saudi-backed government forces said they had retaken key positions around the strait and the port of Mocha, claims the Houthis denied . In September, Google bought a pair of fiber strands running along Turkish state pipelines, paying two to three times the roughly 6 million euros ($7 million) that newer lines crossing Turkey are expected to cost, said a person familiar with the deal, requesting anonymity because the details are not public. Long-distance fiber is usually sold with a single upfront payment covering 15 years or more of use. Buyers also pay a separate annual fee for maintenance. Microsoft said on September 23 that it plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and land links across the Middle East by 2030. Iraq also signed a contract with Qatari telecom company Ooredoo on September 10 to carry data toward Europe through an underground route from the southern port of Al-Faw. Almost all major cloud companies are looking for backup routes around the Red Sea, the person told Rest of World . Google and Meta have started sending some live traffic through a land route across Iraq that they had previously held in reserve, the person said. Google and Meta did not respond to Rest of World ’s requests for comment by the time of publication. With Yemen’s side of the strait now contested, a single cable cut there could take months to fix, because repair crews need permission and safety guarantees to work in the water, industry experts told Rest of World . Switching to another sea cable does not help because almost all of them pass through the same narrow gap, they said. “You can have capacity on multiple cables, but if they’re all routed through the same tight expanse of water, suddenly your route resilience isn’t looking so resilient,” said Paul Brodsky, senior research manager at TeleGeography, a U.S. research firm that tracks telecommunications infrastructure worldwide. “The repair ship issue is very real.” Three Red Sea cables were damaged in 2024, most likely by the anchor of a drifting cargo ship that a missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthis had disabled. Those repairs took months because crews had to wait a long time for permits, Brodsky said. “Depending on the availability of a repair ship, a cable repair might take one to two weeks,” Doug Madory, head of internet analysis at Santa Clara-based Infoblox, which runs core network services and tracks how internet traffic moves, told Rest of World . “But the last time there were cable cuts in this body of water, repairs took months because the repair ships needed assurances they would not be fired upon.” The last time there were cable cuts in this body of water, repairs took months.” Doug Madory, head of internet analysis firm Infoblox Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon use about three-quarters of the world’s international internet bandwidth , according to TeleGeography. When Iranian drones struck Amazon’s data centers in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain in March, bank and payment apps in the region stopped working, and U.S. software company Snowflake reported service disruptions . Since the start of September, cloud companies have been telling operators the minimum number of fiber strands they will start using, and by when, Martin Frank, a strategic adviser at IQ Networks, an Iraqi company that sells capacity on a fiber line it built from southern Iraq to the Turkish border, told Rest of World . Cloud companies will likely test their land backups so they are ready if a sea cable breaks, Madory said. Until then, most of their data will keep flowing under the sea. “Submarine cable routes are much cheaper, which is why they are so preferred,” he said. “I would expect land route alternatives to remain dormant until pressed into service due to a cable cut.” Cloud companies have been hoping Yemen would settle down under a normal administration, Frank said. What would end that hope is what he called an Afghanistan scenario, in which the international community accepts the reality on the ground as the new normal. “From what I see and hear, I would say that this scenario is getting more and more priced in by the day,” Frank said. Who gets to decide if AI is safe?

events.title: Dubai home sale transactions fall in third quarter amid regional uncertainty
events.summary: The volume and value of residential property transactions in Dubai fell sharply in the third quarter of this year as buyers became “more cautious” amid regional uncertainty over the Iran war, according to a new report. Dubai recorded home sales worth a total of Dh72.6 billion ($19.7 billion) in the three months to the end of September, down 47 per cent compared to the same period last year. The number of transactions dropped 38 per cent to 34,000, which reflected “the impact of reduced activity as the lag in property sales registrations begins to clear”, the report by property consultants Cavendish Maxwell said. “The Q3 2026 data captures a mix of recent and earlier buying activity, reflecting the time between a purchase being agreed and formally registered as a sale,” Ronan Arthur, director and head of residential valuation at Cavendish Maxwell , said. “Purchasing activity became more measured, with buyers being more cautious in the weeks and months following the start of the conflict.” The off-plan sector continued to dominate residential sales during the quarter, accounting for 65 per cent of total sales values and 72 per cent of property purchases. Dubai's property market has boomed in recent years, benefiting from government initiatives such as residency permits for retired and remote workers, expansion of the 10-year golden visa programme and overall growth in the UAE’s economy on diversification efforts. However, the market started to cool during regional tensions triggered by the Iran war that began in late February. The war also affected hospitality, tourism and aviation as the US and Israel attacked Iran, and Tehran retaliated by striking energy sites and civilian infrastructure across the Gulf region and Iraq. “While the fundamentals driving Dubai real estate demand remain, near-term activity will continue to be shaped by a number of factors, including the frequency and number of launches, regional uncertainty and a broader normalisation in buyer activity,” Mr Arthur added. Residential sales transactions fell for the first nine months of the year, Cavendish Maxwell data showed, with total volumes down 23 per cent on annual basis to 112,580 and values declining 27 per cent to Dh292 billion. A report by S&P Global Ratings also found a significant drop in Dubai's residential property transactions as a result of the war. Citing Dubai Land department data, the ratings agency said total real estate sale transactions averaged 12,644 per month between March and September 2026, a drop of 26 per cent from 17,198 in January and February 2026. It also said prices declined by 5 per cent to 15 per cent between the end of 2025 and September 2026, quoting industry reports. Price correction S&P Global Ratings expects a “gradual” price correction in Dubai’s property market. “Over the medium term, we anticipate that the UAE and Dubai governments will remain focused on developing the emirate's attractiveness through reforms and large-scale infrastructure projects. That is why, for the residential real estate market, we expect a gradual price correction rather than a rapid price decline,” it said. The ratings agency expects secondary-market transactions to become more prevalent as price declines prompt investors to offload their properties. The greatest impact could be on investor sentiment and demand within the luxury and ultra-luxury segments, it added. Emaar Properties founder Mohamed Alabbar also indicated an “adjustment of 5 per cent to 10 per cent” in Dubai’s broader real estate sector because of the war. “But then again, you know, if the situation settles, God knows what could happen in this market. It could become pretty fast [paced],” he said last month at AIM Congress in Dubai.

events.title: Iraq devalues currency as war and Hormuz closure squeeze cash
events.summary: Iraq has officially devalued its currency again, setting a new official exchange rate of 1,500 Iraqi dinars per US dollar, according to a document seen by The National . The Council of Ministers approved the move late on Tuesday, based on a recommendation from the Central Bank of Iraq, the banking regulator said in a directive sent to all licensed banks, electronic payment companies and exchange houses on Monday. According to the directive, the new structure is that the central bank will purchase from the Ministry of Finance at the price of 1,500 dinars. The sale price to banks will be at 1,510 dinars, and then to the public at 1,520 dinars. All institutions were ordered to update their systems, notify branches, stop using the previous rate, and adopt the new price from the start of business on Tuesday, the document says. It is Iraq’s second major devaluation in six years. In December 2020, during the Covid-19 oil crash, the central bank cut the dinar rate from 1,182 to 1,450 per dollar to cover a crippling deficit. That rate was later adjusted to 1,320 as the official rate under the previous government, though the market rate often hovered higher. This time, the decision is driven by a deepening cash crunch since the outbreak of the Iran-Israel war in June 2025 and the intermittent closure and threat to the Strait of Hormuz. Iraq earns more than 90 per cent of its budget in dollars from oil exports, almost all of which must pass through Hormuz – the narrow waterway carrying a third of the world’s seaborne oil. Since the Iran war broke out on February 28, shipping insurance costs have soared , tanker traffic has been disrupted, and Iraq’s oil loadings from its southern terminals at Basra have faced delays and discounts. The result: Iraq gets fewer dollars, and when it converts those dollars into dinars to pay nearly eight million public employees, contractors, farmers and pensioners, it needs more dinars than it has. In recent months, Baghdad has delayed salary payments in several provinces, deferred payments to wheat farmers and construction firms, and relied on short-term borrowing from state banks. The country's finance ministry warned parliament that without adjustment, it could not fund the 2026 budget, which includes 100,000 new public jobs demanded by political blocs as part of government formation talks. Devaluation is the fastest fix. By lowering the dinar’s value from 1,320 to 1,500, the government gets about 13 per cent more dinars for every dollar of oil it sells – enough to print salaries without printing dollars it does not have. But the cost is passed to Iraqis. A weaker dinar makes imported food, medicine, cars and construction materials – almost everything Iraq imports – more expensive. After the 2020 devaluation, inflation jumped and triggered protests in southern provinces.

events.title: America's changing disaster risk hits energy
events.summary: Hurricanes have long dominated efforts to make the power system more resilient to extreme weather . But America's energy buildout is running into growing risks from severe thunderstorms. Why it matters: New energy infrastructure and data centers are being built in harm's way as severe weather risks shift , leaving more for developers and insurers to lose when storms hit. Driving the news: Severe thunderstorms account for 40% of modeled global insured catastrophe risk, compared with 27% for hurricanes , according to analysis from risk analytics firm Verisk. The U.S. accounts for $117 billion, or 68%, of Verisk's modeled global insured catastrophe losses . Threat level: A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, potentially creating more favorable conditions for powerful thunderstorms. But the effects of climate change on severe storms are complicated. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration research scientist Harold Brooks told Axios that other atmospheric conditions needed for severe storms may become less favorable as the planet warms. Reality check: Verisk's Jay Guin said growing exposure, more than climate change, is the dominant driver of rising insured losses, as more and increasingly valuable property is built in harm's way. Guin says climate change contributes, but expanding development and higher reconstruction costs are much larger drivers. Zoom in: America's changing energy system is creating new kinds of exposure. Verisk is assessing risks to renewable projects in tornado- and hail-prone areas, where Guin said large hail can cause major damage to solar farms. "While they are renewable, you have a new asset class that is quite vulnerable," he said. Data-center developers must balance natural-hazard exposure against access to land, power and water. Some sites have billions in property and hardware, raising the stakes for siting and engineering. State of play: Tornado activity has increased about 10% in the Mid-South while declining by roughly the same amount from the Texas Panhandle through western Kansas, Brooks said. Population densities in rural areas of the Southeast are roughly 100 times those in the High Plains. "It's 10 people per square kilometer in rural areas of northern Mississippi and Alabama, and so a tornado in that area can't miss buildings and can't miss people," Brooks says. Zoom out: For infrastructure, Brooks said the biggest thunderstorm-related concern is flooding. Heavy rain and flooding are "a huge threat to virtually all of our infrastructure," he said. The bottom line: "There is no ... safe climate zone," Guin said.

events.title: Exclusive: Paxton privately blames campaign woes on Iran war, gas prices
events.summary: Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately lamented the impact of the Iran war and gas prices on his campaign in a meeting last month, telling a group of donors and lobbyists, "I don't make the decisions," according to audio obtained by Axios. Why it matters: It's a candid admission from a close Trump ally about the challenging environment Republicans face this cycle. Paxton, the Texas attorney general, was speaking to donors and lobbyists at a closed-door fundraiser in Washington, D.C. The audio was provided to Axios by a person, granted anonymity because it was a private event, who was in the meeting and is opposed to Paxton. President Trump is set to rally with Paxton in San Antonio on Wednesday. Driving the news: Asked by one attendee what issues are "dragging" on his campaign, Paxton responded, "It's not tariffs. ... It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," according to an audio file obtained by Axios. "When it's over $6 per gallon for diesel ... people are feeling the pinch," he continued, adding that the rising cost of fuel "drives up food prices and everything else." The Republican candidate said affordability is "by far our biggest problem" and "why we're having a hard time with numbers." Paxton pointed to his tax cut plan — which includes new housing and health care write-offs and an expansion of the child tax credit — as his proposed remedy on affordability. "I'm just trying to figure out ways I can help people. That's the only way: I can propose legislation," he said. When an attendee posited that Paxton "can't stop the war," the candidate responded "right" and said he has "no control over gas prices." "So many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable. I don't make the decisions, and I don't ... know what's behind some of the decisions," he added. What they're saying: "This is a non-story. The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store," a Paxton campaign person told Axios. "President Trump is doing everything he can to bring prices down, and Ken Paxton is going to Washington to help him by putting money back in families' pockets." Between the lines: Paxton said in the same meeting that Trump's midterm convention in Dallas "dropped our numbers," and that control of the campaign is "all coming ... from D.C.," according to separate audio obtained by The New York Times and Politico . State of play: Paxton is facing off with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico after unseating Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in a May primary runoff . Polls of the race have largely shown Talarico narrowly leading. He would be the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas since the 1980s. Paxton has for years been one of Trump's most loyal allies. Trump returned the favor in the primary by endorsing Paxton despite Senate Republicans' pleas for him to back Cornyn. events.title: 3 years later, Netanyahu faces reckoning over Oct. 7 in Israeli election
events.summary: Israel is marking the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 terror attacks three weeks before an election where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's personal culpability for the country's worst-ever security failure will be a central issue. Why it matters: Netanyahu has never looked more politically vulnerable than in the weeks after Oct. 7, but he has defied expectations by keeping his government afloat — presiding over simultaneous wars and an atmosphere of perpetual emergency. Though the polls are tight, they leave a clear path for the ultimate political survivor to hang on yet again. But Oct. 7 still looms over the country and his candidacy. The opposition lambasts him for refusing to take responsibility or allow an independent inquiry into the Hamas attacks that killed around 1,200 people. Every other senior national security official who was in office at the time of the attacks has resigned, except Netanyahu. Netanyahu's chief opponent, former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, lost his son and two nephews during the war in Gaza. Sources close to Eisenkot say he sees his main mission as replacing the man he holds responsible for allowing the Oct. 7 attacks. Netanyahu blames the deep state. His political and media allies — as well as his wife, Sara — have even spread conspiracy theories implying Israel was betrayed by its own security chiefs. Netanyahu himself has claimed those security chiefs deliberately kept him in the dark and suggested he could have prevented the massacre if only they'd woken him up when early warning signs came in. Driving the news: Recent reporting suggests Netanyahu had at least some warning. Haaretz reported that United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed warned Netanyahu days before the attacks that Hamas was planning a major operation. Three sources with knowledge confirmed to Axios that UAE intelligence gave a general warning to its Israeli counterparts and that MBZ spoke to Netanyahu to make sure he received it. A former U.S. official said then-CIA Director Bill Burns was told several months later by MBZ that he had warned Netanyahu. Other outlets including the New York Times also confirmed the story. The Atlantic and the Wall Street Journal reported that Netanyahu received a similar warning ahead of Oct. 7 from Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel. Netanyahu denied ever receiving warnings from the UAE or Egypt and sued several media outlets and journalists that reported he had. Between the lines: While those stories have been widely discussed in Israel, the three violent years that have passed since Oct. 7 — the leveling of Gaza, the release of the hostages, the attacks on Hezbollah and two wars with Iran — have given Netanyahu ample opportunity to restore his reputation among many Israelis as a strong and decisive leader. By the numbers: Most polls show Netanyahu's Likud party with 20-22 seats in the Knesset, down from 32, and his right-wing coalition with 50-54 — short of the 61 needed for a majority. But the opposition is also unlikely to secure a majority without the support of Arab-Israeli parties, which are projected to win a combined 12-14 seats. Polls reported by Netanyahu mouthpiece Channel 14 show the opposite, projecting the prime minister and his coalition winning a decisive 63-seat majority. Seizing on the right-wing turn in Israeli society, Netanyahu has pressured his main opposition to rule out forming a coalition with the Arab-Israeli parties. That taboo could keep Eisenkot from taking power, though he could try to cobble together a minority government. One possible scenario, if the polls prove accurate, is a hung parliament with Netanyahu staying on as a caretaker prime minister until another election is held. The vote could determine not just Netanyahu's political survival, but his legal future as well. Losing power would also mean losing any levers to delay or influence his ongoing corruption trial. But if he wins, Netanyahu could argue he was acquitted by the people of Israel — and take stronger action to thwart the proceedings. The intrigue: President Trump could give Netanyahu a boost by endorsing him, but so far he's declined. Asked several times recently by Time magazine whether he supported Netanyahu, Trump dodged the question. He added, however, that he didn't believe the press reports that MBZ had warned Netanyahu. Trump has privately blamed Netanyahu for the Oct. 7 failures, according to two people who have discussed the matter directly with the president. He's also mused about Netanyahu damaging Israel's international reputation. However, Trump has stuck close to Netanyahu during the war in Iran and may still endorse him. What to watch: Israel's election takes place a week before the U.S. midterms. If Democrats take back one or both houses of Congress, that will set up a battle over arms sales to Israel and even over the fate of $3.8 billion in annual military assistance. The tenor of that debate may hinge in part on whether Netanyahu remains in power.

events.title: "Not safe for kids": Advocacy group urges OpenAI to keep teens off ChatGPT
events.summary: Common Sense Media is urging OpenAI to keep teens off ChatGPT, saying its new teen experience poses an "Unacceptable Risk" after extensive testing found shortcomings in safeguards meant to protect younger users. Why it matters: OpenAI has made protecting younger users a central part of its effort to make ChatGPT safer, but the findings suggest some of those protections may give parents more confidence than they warrant. "We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice," an OpenAI spokesperson said. Driving the news: Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute said it tested more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds. The group found ChatGPT generally did not provide instructions facilitating suicide or self-harm, eating disorders or sexual or romantic roleplay, but said it was less reliable at recognizing when a teen needed outside help. Common Sense Media said ChatGPT missed more than one in four instances in which its testers determined a crisis referral was warranted. The group also said that on more than a dozen newly created, parent-linked accounts, testers could spend up to an hour discussing suicide, self-harm or disordered eating without triggering a parental alert. Common Sense also found that Study Mode could be circumvented: Teens could choose "Show me the answer" and, during parent-set Study Hours, could easily bypass the rules. OpenAI confirmed to Axios that the ability to exit Study Mode during Study Hours is intentional, not a loophole. The company said it designed Study Hours as a more flexible experience after consulting education experts and teens, rather than as a hard parental lock. What they're saying: "ChatGPT is not safe for kids to use," Common Sense Media Youth Safety Institute head Tom Siegel told Axios. Siegel said that what the company announced in August still has the potential to be industry-leading, but gaps remain between what was promised and the current reality. "It feels much more of a marketing announcement that really was not backed up with the engineering work." The other side: OpenAI says it has issues with Common Sense Media's methodology and findings. OpenAI says much of Common Sense's testing of parental alerts occurred before the parent and teen accounts had finished linking, a process the company says can take several hours. As for its age prediction system, OpenAI says it deliberately relies on multiple signals rather than simply accepting a user's stated age and can take up to two weeks to make a prediction. During that time, the company says users are given added content protection, though not as strong as the ones used in ChatGPT for Teens. On crisis referrals, OpenAI says its larger-scale data shows an increase in hotline resources being displayed to under-18 users during the period studied. Between the lines: Some of the disagreement reflects different ideas of what the safeguards are supposed to accomplish. Common Sense treats the ability to exit Study Hours as evidence that the parental control is ineffective; OpenAI says that flexibility is deliberate. Similarly, Common Sense's age test treats a user repeatedly identifying themselves as 13 without being moved into ChatGPT for Teens as a failure, while OpenAI says it intentionally requires multiple signals before making an age determination, while offering some strengthened protections during the time it is making its assessment. Bottom line: Siegel says parents need to have strong conversations about AI and its risks with their teenage children and find other ways to make sure they are getting support, whether it be for homework or the challenges of life. "We just can't outsource taking care of our kids to a tech product that is very early on and still quite buggy," he said.

events.title: Homeless Shelters Around Phoenix Are Full. His Phone Is the Unofficial Hotline for Struggling Families.
events.summary: Austin Davis, center, a 26-year-old poet and advocate for homeless people, has become a point of last resort for families who are experiencing homelessness in the Phoenix area. For about a year, Austin Davis’ phone has been flooded with hundreds of pleas for help from across the Phoenix metropolitan area. A school employee wanted to help a homeless family but couldn’t find space at a shelter. Could Davis pay for a hotel room? A mother of five living in a storage unit contacted a homeless services organization for help. They told her to call Davis. A mother panhandling with her six children said passersby gave her Davis’ phone number, telling her he might be able to provide shelter. “I feel like the worst mother in the world,” she texted him. Nearly every person who’s reached out to Davis, a 26-year-old poet and advocate for homeless people, says they’d first called 211, seeking help through the official channel, only to learn it could be months before they’d get shelter or a housing placement. His phone has become the unofficial hotline for emergency shelter. Caseworkers, teachers, social workers, police and hospital workers have called and texted to see if Davis can help people without a place to go. Even workers from the official channel — 211 and the Family Housing Hub — have sent people to him. Davis’ path to becoming the de facto advocate of last resort illustrates how the system set up to care for families who are homeless in Maricopa County is failing them. ProPublica found that calling and visiting the official channel to address family homelessness rarely leads to offers of help, leaving families feeling hopeless. Davis’ nonprofit, AZ Hugs, holds daily food distributions at “The Hill” for homeless people in Phoenix. In January, I started coming to Tempe’s Moeur Park, known as “The Hill,” to meet the families Davis was assisting. I was struck by the scene of desperate parents, some of whom had recently been evicted, lost a job or fled domestic violence, surrounding Davis to tell him about their situation. As he listened, he played with their children, always with an energy drink in hand. The scene was both heartening and disconcerting. Davis was helping families stay off the street, which was good. But why, I wondered, in a county of nearly 5 million people, was a man in a park their best chance at getting help? And why were government agencies and multimillion-dollar nonprofits, some tasked with helping the very same homeless families, sending people to him? Davis, who runs a small nonprofit called AZ Hugs, is known for working outside the system. With the help of volunteers, he hosts a nightly meal for homeless people at a suburban Phoenix park. This has drawn the ire of Tempe officials and led to 35 citations against him for trespassing and holding picnics without permits. (In 2024, he reached a deal to plead guilty to one permit violation, and the city dismissed the other citations, according to court documents. He’s spent three nights in jail.) In 2025, Davis and two other advocates for homeless people filed a lawsuit against Tempe, alleging it had violated their free speech protections by citing them for feeding people in parks. The city revised its permit ordinance, and Davis withdrew the lawsuit. In recent months, he has tried to draw attention to what he calls the “family homelessness crisis,” raising money on social media to pay for hotel rooms for families, many with young children, who would otherwise sleep on the street or in their cars. Davis said he cannot assist everyone who asks for help. A much bigger effort is needed, he added, involving nonprofits and local and state officials, but he sees little evidence that it’s happening. The number of people in homeless families in Maricopa County reached 2,103 this year, its highest level since 2015, according to the latest figures that are compiled locally and reported to the federal government. And those numbers are considered an undercount because the tally is taken on a single night by volunteers who can miss people who are trying to stay out of sight. In late September, nearly 200 families were on the waitlist for shelter in the county. It doesn’t include those who couldn’t get on; were kicked off because they weren’t considered homeless; or those who called 211, found it unhelpful and never called back. (Solari, a nonprofit that runs the statewide 211 line, said that the Family Housing Hub, which is run by UMOM, a nonprofit, sets the eligibility criteria for placement on the shelter waitlist.) I spoke to more than 30 families searching for shelter. Parents told me they worried how their situation was affecting their children. Research shows homelessness harms children, disrupting brain development and growth and leading to permanent changes in the brain and body. Davis’ phone is flooded daily with pleas for help from people who are homeless across Maricopa County. Blurred for privacy by ProPublica Candice Ortiz had tried since spring to find stable shelter and housing. As the months dragged on, she noticed the toll on her 8-year-old son. He was hospitalized for heat exhaustion after spending the day outside, and she worried about the school he missed. Davis helped Ortiz as she hit dead ends in her search for a place to stay, according to text messages reviewed by ProPublica. She said she had called 211 over and over, answering the same questions about her living situation, only to receive information she could have found through a simple internet search. She said a worker with the Family Housing Hub told her that since she and her children were sleeping in her car, she wasn’t actually homeless. Another told her the waitlist was full. In June, she spent the day at a Phoenix cooling center to escape the heat. A representative told her to go to UMOM, which runs an emergency shelter for families. She said she used her last $20 on a rideshare to the shelter. They took her information again and told her she wasn’t “in the system.” Nothing was available. UMOM said to protect the privacy of clients, it does not comment on individual families. At the end of August, she connected with the Phoenix Rescue Mission, a nonprofit that offers programs for homeless people. The group sent Ortiz to a local apartment complex where she viewed an apartment. Later, a worker with the Phoenix Rescue Mission told her that it ran out of funding to pay for it, text messages reviewed by ProPublica show. Phoenix Rescue Mission did not respond to requests for comment. UMOM, which during the last fiscal year received more than $7 million in government grants, set aside 23 units of shelter and about a dozen tents for families this summer, as temperatures reached 117 degrees. The program, which is part of the city of Phoenix’s heat relief effort, has helped nearly 300 households so far but is winding down this month. In early April, Davis had tried to force a broader effort to address the crisis by launching an online petition .

events.title: Guyana: The tiny country with big ambitions fast emerging as a global oil producer
events.summary: A tiny South American country is emerging as a reliable oil supplier globally as flows from the Middle East face disruptions and European nations seek alternatives to Russia. Guyana's rapid increase in crude production, from zero in 2019 to about 900,000 barrels per day in the first half of the year, is catapulting the country to one of the world's fastest-growing economies, lifting thousands of people out of poverty with newfound wealth. The non-Opec country's oil output is expected to reach 1 million barrels per day (bpd) imminently, with the country targeting 1.7 million bpd by 2030. “With disruptions in the Middle East, Guyana’s oil is becoming strategically more important to global markets,” Stephanie Rivera, research analyst at S&P Global Energy told The National. “Guyana’s light-to-medium, low-sulfur crude is not exposed to Middle Eastern shipping chokepoints, providing refiners with an attractive option for diversifying away from Middle Eastern supply. As the conflict in the Middle East continues, Guyanese crude can help enhance energy security in an increasingly tight market.” The Middle East conflict, which broke out on February 28 after the US and Israel attacked Iran, has roiled global markets, with prices jumping to an intraday high of about $120 per barrel in April. Tehran carried out retaliatory strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure leading to curtailment of production, with 10 million bpd of Gulf output remaining shut as of August amid heightened security risks, according to the International Energy Agency report last month. The Strait of Hormuz, through which more than 20 per cent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies used to pass before the war, has been a restricted route since the war began, raising supply concerns. Europe focus Countries in Europe, North and South America have been the main importers of Guyana’s oil, but the Middle East crisis has also prompted some Asian countries to look towards Guyana for oil. Europe imported up to 57 per cent of Guyanese crude between March and August this year, Kpler data shows, with the Netherlands, Sweden, Germany, the UK, Italy, Poland and Spain being the main buyers. The Americas took about a third, while Asian nations, including China, Thailand, Singapore and Indonesia, imported about 6 per cent of Guyanese crude during the period. Turkey bought roughly 5 per cent. Another factor that is contributing to a rise in demand for Guyana's crude is the Ukraine war. European nations are looking for alternative sources of supply as they seek to reduce dependence on Russian crude and squeeze off Moscow’s oil revenue as it continues to wage war against Ukraine. Guyanese crude is also highly valued for its low sulfur content, high yields of middle distillates such as diesel and jet fuel, and competitive break-even costs of $30–$40 per barrel that "make it particularly attractive to refiners, especially in Europe", Ms Rivera said. Investment of $60 billion An oil boom is a recent phenomenon in Guyana, with production starting only seven years ago following the discovery of oil in 2015. An ExxonMobil-led consortium – including Chevron, and China’s CNOOC have been dominating production, with total investment estimated at between $55 billion and $60 billion at the Stabroek Block. The group hit a milestone last month by producing its billionth barrel of oil at Stabroek less than seven years after production began in 2019. “With an estimated resource base of just under 11 billion oil-equivalent barrels and plans for up to eight offshore developments by 2030, the Stabroek block is helping meet demand across the Americas, Europe and Asia, contributing to global energy security and market stability,” ExxonMobil said in a statement last month. More projects are expected to come online, with Uaru expected to start up by the end of 2026, Whiptail expected to start up in 2027, and Hammerhead expected to begin production in 2029, it added. Last year, France’s TotalEnergies, QatarEnergy and Malaysia’s Petronas also signed an agreement with the Guyanese government to explore a shallow block off the coast of Guyana for oil production. Economic boost Oil revenue, spurred by a rise in production and higher prices, has transformed Guyana from a small, agriculture and services based economy into one of the world’s fastest-growing economies. From an annual growth rate of 5.4 per cent in 2019, when it first started producing oil, the country’s economy expanded by 43.5 per cent in the following year, 20.1 per cent in 2021, 63.3 per cent in 2022, 33.8 per cent in 2023, 43.8 per cent in 2024 and 19.3 per cent in 2025, International Monetary Fund data shows. The country's GDP is projected to grow by 16.2 per cent this year, the highest rate globally, as oil revenue continues to increase due to higher production and rising crude prices. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, is currently trading at about $100 per barrel. "The economic outlook [for Guyana] remains highly favourable," the IMF said in July. "Oil production is expected to continue expanding, and the non-oil economy is projected to grow by about 7 per cent on average over the next five years as the government continues its ambitious plans to address infrastructure and developmental needs."

events.title: Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism
events.summary: Last month at Rails World 2026, Ruby on Rails creator David Heinemeier Hansson gave a relentlessly optimistic keynote in which he suggested AI has all but eliminated the need for developers to manually write code. But perhaps DHH, as he is known online, shouldn’t delete his code editor quite yet. On Sunday, DHH posted about a test in which he had frontier agents implement and optimize his company’s Campfire group chat app in three languages: Elixir, Go, and Rust. He then compared the runtime performance of those versions with the original Ruby on Rails implementation. DHH’s post includes data that seemingly demonstrates the efficiency of the Rust programming language, and AI agent coding itself. But many observers came to another conclusion: Don't trust DHH’s benchmarks. As of press time, the post and accompanying chart garnered over 900,000 views. It showed the Rust rewrite of the chat app outperformed others by a wide margin on five tasks, including searching or posting a message. DHH did not say which AI services he used for these rewrites, but noted that each rewrite took only a few hours, as the original code itself, largely written in Ruby, is relatively compact. Many observers, notably advocates of other languages, quickly surmised from the source material that DHH had optimized the Rust results but didn't do the same for the other languages he tested. Whither high-level languages? Rewriting applications in Rust, often with the help of AI agents, seems to be a popular undertaking these days, with Microsoft's Copilot runtime, the pnpm JavaScript installer, and the Bun JavaScript toolchain all getting the Rust treatment. In DHH’s test, the Rust implementation handily bested the others across all five workloads, sometimes by a wide margin. To serve a “room page,” for instance, Rust knocked out 36,260 requests per second. In contrast, Ruby on Rails was only able to fulfill a paltry 241 requests, while Elixir delivered 722 requests, and even runner-up Golang only knocked out 3,860 requests a second. Rust executed the other tasks with similar alacrity, easily besting the other languages DHH used. The takeaway was obvious to DHH: Rewriting an application in Rust, or better yet having AI agents do the job, may very well result in major performance improvements for an app. DHH suggested that many factors go into choosing a programming language for a particular job, and execution speed is not the sole criterion. Rust can be agonizingly slow to compile, and for many, writing or even reading Rust code is an arduous job. DHH himself began developing Rails in 2003 while building Basecamp in the then relatively obscure Ruby programming language to ease the developer experience. He doesn’t seem to mind that Ruby ranked the slowest in his own tests. “I didn't care about [performance] when the pay-off was huge in terms of productivity and developer joy.” But AI agents don’t give a hoot about joy. “You really have to bury your head in the sand not to see that when agents write the code and validate the output, we need to adjust to a new reality,” he wrote. Chips on the table DHH’s ad-hoc test was quickly met with skepticism, criticism and outright mockery, especially on X. (It’s as if DHH’s conservative views on immigration and his work to bring yet another Linux desktop into the world didn’t give him enough headaches). “What worries me about the future of programming is you see this and don’t immediately know there must be something wrong with the results or what you actually measured,” wrote prominent Google engineer Jaana Dogan in an X response to DHH’s tests. Dogan did not elaborate on the test’s shortcomings, but many others, especially advocates of other languages, were more than happy to provide details. One Elixir advocate called DHH’s implementation “moronic,” while a couple of others actually rewrote the Elixir code to make its performance comparable to Rust’s. After that rewrite, the Elixir version of the app bested Rust’s performance on some tasks, despite further third-party Rust optimizations. DHH expressed surprise that others would assume a high-level language like Elixir or Ruby could even compete with a language like Rust, which runs closer to the metal. But he also noted on X that “It's not exactly extra points for Elixir if frontier agents can't find the magic ‘go fast’ switches.” Elsewhere, observers noted that the Rust rewrite got a lot more post-coding attention than the other implementations of Go and Elixir, both of which seemed to be quickly wrapped up after the initial agent requests. “You're not benchmarking languages, you're benchmarking how much attention each port got,” one observer wrote on X. Golang advocates were likewise unamused. “The benchmark was unfair. More time was put into the Rust code while the rest were one-shotted,” one wrote on X. Someone else even made their own chart showing how much more the Rust code was tuned compared to the quick passes on the other languages. None of these rebuttals actually negates DHH’s advocacy of using agents to code. But clearly, skipping a manual review of the resulting work will still leave a lot of potential gains on the table. ®

events.title: Your Next Great Read Might Be Certified ‘Organic’
events.summary: As scandals involving the use of artificial intelligence by professional authors pile up , a British startup has established a way for publishers to certify their books as “organic”—written by real people, no machines in sight. On Wednesday, Books by People confirmed it had received approval from the UK’s Intellectual Property Office to begin distributing a mark that indicates a published book has been authored by a human. The stamp, which looks like a thumbprint, will be displayed on the cover. “If people are going to be writing AI books or seeking it out for their own enjoyment, that’s their prerogative,” Esme Dennys, cofounder of Books by People, tells WIRED. “But if you want to read something that’s written by a person, you should be able to find that. We’re just trying to create that choice.” Previous book-labeling schemes, like Human Authored , have operated under an honesty system, where an author promises they haven’t used AI in the development process. To try to add more weight to its certification, Books by People asks for an authorship declaration, runs each manuscript through proprietary software, and manually examines early drafts and research materials supplied by the writer and editor for “indicators of humanity.” The organization is "looking at all the things that give us the best sense of whether a person wrote the work—whether the work was made during a natural process of drafting and redrafting,” says Dennys. Books by People will charge publishers a flat membership fee, plus an additional sum for every book they put forward for certification. Five publishers have signed up so far. The startup expects the new mark to feature on its first book by the end of the year. This year, the publishing industry has been caught up in a flurry of scandals involving the suspected use of AI by authors. A literary agent canceled a book deal reportedly worth $2 million; a publisher withdrew a novel from the shelves; readers alleged that a prize-winning short story had been generated with AI. Writers and publishers are not necessarily worried about being replaced by AI , industry insiders tell WIRED. They believe that few people will ultimately want to read machine-generated books. “You are essentially standing at the end of a conveyor belt, watching stuff fall off the edge. Once you know that, it prevents you from getting really emotionally invested in whatever falls into your hands from the belt,” says sci-fi author Ted Chiang, whose 1998 novella Story of Your Life was adapted into the Academy Award–winning film Arrival. “The knowledge of how something was created cannot be separated from your experience.” However, repeated scandals could shake public confidence in the unspoken rule of publishing: That every book that reaches the shelf has been authored by a real person who has not indulged in plagiarism. “Publishing has always relied on trust between the publisher, writer, and reading public. Cases where that trust is betrayed have been rare,” says Sam Jordison, codirector at independent publisher Galley Beggar Press, which intends to adopt the Books by People mark. “There’s almost a feeling of revulsion about the idea of reading an AI text that purports to be human. It feels like a con job.” Against that backdrop, the idea of a certification for human-authored books has received backing from various writers and editors. In a statement praising Books by People, Markus Dohle, former CEO of Penguin Random House, described human storytelling as “the lifeblood of our industry.” But while publishers might relish the chance to signal their commitment to “organic literature,” the routinization of AI detection is a double-edged sword for authors, who risk a false positive result spoiling their reputation . “We need to be quite careful that this doesn’t end up becoming a witch hunt,” says Tom West, CEO of the Publishers’ Licensing Services, which helps publishers to collectively license works to third parties. “Obviously, the devil is going to be in the detail.” New York–based startup Pangram , which has emerged as the leader in the field of AI detection, claims to be able to sniff out generated text with a 99.7 percent accuracy. But authors have questioned the reliability of its approach, which itself involves AI. In September, Jerry Falade, the debut author whose agent reportedly pulled the $2 million book deal, alleged that detection software had misconstrued his Nigerian dialect as evidence he had used AI. Pangram’s software scored the book as 97 percent AI-generated. “It takes months, even years to write a book,” Falade wrote in a recent essay . “It takes AI-detection software two minutes to ruin your life’s work.” (Pangram did not respond to a request for comment.) Others have warned against normalizing extreme scrutiny of authors.

events.title: COSMIC shuts the door on AI code as GNOME debates letting bug reports in
events.summary: System76 is banning AI-generated content from contributions to the COSMIC desktop. Some GNOME sub-projects also restrict AI-generated contributions, but one developer is urging them to make an exception for vulnerability reports. The COSMIC desktop project has changed its contributors' guidelines. The latest version now has a clear no-AI rule, insisting that contributors declare: "I have not included any LLM (also known as AI) generated content in this PR, including code, comments, and descriptions." In other words, you can teach yourself using AI, you can find bugs with AI, but if you want to submit your code for inclusion in COSMIC, you can't use AI to write the code, its docs or notes, or even the submission requests. This position is in keeping with some other desktop projects. For instance, the GNOME Calendar guide to contributing says: "This project does not allow contributions generated by large languages [sic] models (LLMs) and chatbots." GNOME Extensions also restricts AI-generated submissions, although it permits AI learning aids and code completion. Its review guidelines spell it out: "Extensions must not be AI-generated." COSMIC is one of the newest complete Linux desktop environments, but even so, it's been under development for years. The Register first reported on the effort nearly five years ago, meaning that it's older than ChatGPT, which debuted in late 2022 (it only feels so very much longer). COSMIC does use some GNOME components, and its default config looks not unlike GNOME, with a top panel and a dock-like launcher at the bottom. There are good reasons for that: the original System76 desktop called "COSMIC" was based on GNOME, quite heavily customized with GNOME extensions. Saying that, though, this new COSMIC is a very different beast. Its first stable release shipped with Pop!_OS 24.04 in late 2025. Although it looks similar, it's an entirely new, ground-up effort, written in Rust using the Iced toolkit. COSMIC itself is Wayland-only. GNOME is much older, larger, and more complicated. The project was announced in 1997, the year after the KDE project announcement. KDE 1.0 came out in 1998, and GNOME 1.0 in 1999. In part, GNOME was a response to KDE. KDE is built on the Qt toolkit, which was not fully open source. As such, in KDE's early days, Red Hat refused to include it in Red Hat Linux. Qt is aimed at C++ developers, so KDE was built in C++. Linux, like Unix, is built in plain old C and many Unix traditionalists scorned the much more complex C++. So GNOME was built in plain old C, using GTK, the toolkit built for the GIMP. In 1998, Red Hat Linux 5.1 included a preview of GNOME, and by Red Hat Linux 6.0 in 1999, GNOME 1.0 was the default desktop. GNOME is still the default desktop in RHEL to this day, and many GNOME developers' day jobs are at Red Hat. As we noted back in March, Red Hat management is noticeably enthusiastic about AI – although six months later, it was capping developers' AI spend. GNOME is largely written in C, which lacks automatic memory safety guarantees, although other languages feature too: GNOME Shell combines JavaScript and C, and some components are written in the GNOME-centric Vala programming language. Michael Catanzaro, GNOME developer, just published a blog post titled "The Era of Software Quality, or the Era of Ostriches?" which argues that the GNOME project must accept AI-generated bug reports. This is not a new subject for him. His post links to an earlier one from June, "Please Do Not Ban AI-Assisted Issue Reports." The following month, he announced a reduction in the disclosure deadline for issues reported to GNOME Security, from 90 days to 30, effective August 1. We recently reported on the 1,313 CVE identifiers listed in Debian's latest Linux kernel security advisory. AI is resulting in the discovery of vast numbers of bugs in the equally vast codebases of modern FOSS. GNOME is one of the biggest desktops in the Linux and BSD world, with much of its code written in memory-unsafe languages. As Catanzaro says: "No matter how much we try, GNOME developers will fail [to] write secure code when using unsafe languages like C, C++, or Vala: it's just too hard for even experienced developers to do properly." We are not arguing that Catanzaro is wrong. Given the stance toward AI of GNOME's biggest sponsor, it is entirely in keeping, and he makes a strong case. All we are noting is that this could in time prove to be the thin edge of a wedge with the weight of Red Hat behind it. First the project allows AI-generated bug reports. From there, it would not be a huge step to allowing AI-assisted triage. From there, to AI-assisted fixes. Once you're letting AI-assisted code in, then AI-assisted extensions may not seem so extreme, then core components, and in time, to the desktop itself. It would be wildly controversial, just as it already is in the KDE project. That doesn't mean it won't happen – in either project. Debian decided to allow it, and of course, the kernel itself does too. ®

events.title: Family offices branch out into private equity, infrastructure and alternative investments
events.summary: EQT, one of world’s largest private markets firms, sees more emphasis on diversification and flexibility Some financial analysts and wealth managers in recent years have suggested that the second- and third-generation leaders of family offices in Asia are moving away from the basic principles that helped to create and accumulate their existing assets, but that is not strictly accurate. Rather, just as the founding generation did, these investors look to assess available opportunities and adapt to circumstances as they build or adjust their portfolios to find the preferred balance between risk and reward. What has changed, though, particularly in the last couple of decades, is the range of options open to them. Previously, the focus would typically have been on making money in property, listed equities and direct business holdings, and then passing on those assets. Now, in tune with the times, there is much greater emphasis on international diversification, flexible structures and time horizons, and active ownership, while still maintaining a prudent, long-term approach. “In our interactions with family offices, we see that the second and third generations think slightly differently about managing wealth,” says Sueann Yeo, managing director and head of Asia-Pacific global wealth solutions for EQT, one of the world’s largest private markets firms. “When in your 20s to 40s, the mindset and expectations about capital preservation, growth and returns will not be the same as someone in their 60s or 70s. In particular, many of the younger generation are now thinking about private equity, infrastructure, alternative investments and different asset-allocation strategies.” Yeo says that a number of the more institutionalised family offices have been doing this for a long time. The change, though, is that many others are now setting up programmes to scale their allocations to these newer areas materially over a five- to 10-year period. Secondaries have evolved from a niche strategy into a core portfolio management tool for family offices, rather than simply an alternative route to private equity exposure. Global secondaries transaction volumes reached a record US$226 billion in 2025, up 41 per cent year-on-year, with momentum continuing into this year as first-half volumes exceeded US$120 billion, up 20 per cent year-on-year. Rather than framing secondaries as a faster-return alternative to primary commitments, Yeo describes the two as complementary: secondaries provide an additional way to access private markets, with differentiated portfolio characteristics, broader diversification and distinct cash-flow profiles. “There are a few elements to this: an increasing level of sophistication in the understanding of private assets; more attention to DPI [distributed to paid-in capital, a metric for measuring the cash returned to investors compared with the money they put into a fund]; and a more hands-on approach to strategic asset allocation and setting limits for each category.” Yeo points to the Wallenberg model as a reference point EQT draws on for its own investment approach – a model built around patient, multi-generational capital, active support for portfolio companies and reinvestment of returns to sustain long-term growth. She believes this style of long-term, engaged ownership offers a useful frame of reference for Asia’s family offices as they weigh how to balance risk and opportunity across generations. This kind of evergreen approach enables eligible individual investors and family offices to invest into the same strategies that previously only institutions could access. It allows investment in private equity without the operational complexity of managing capital calls, distributions and reinvestment decisions typical of close-end structures, while offering more flexible, though not unlimited, access to liquidity. “Family offices are warming up to the idea of having evergreen structures, which mirrors the content of classic closed-end private equity structures for institutional investors, but with more flexibility,” Yeo says. “EQT’s private wealth strategies comprise a mix of primary funds, co-investment deals and a cash portion with a soft lock period to manage the liquidity.” Eligible investors benefit from the immediate deployment with exposure to a diversified portfolio from day one, without the need for continual involvement or decision-making. Yeo emphasises that this is just one of many options available through the EQT Private Wealth platform, which embodies the principle of active ownership to create value for the private companies taken into its portfolio. This entails a focus on governance and careful use of the right levers to improve operating performance and revenue – but without the slash-and-cut type of management overhauls often seen elsewhere.

events.title: From reactive to proactive: How endpoint monitoring is fixing broken meeting rooms
events.summary: The role of meeting rooms is changing. Traditionally, they were formal spaces built around a large central table and inflexible physical setup, reserved primarily for board meetings, client presentations, or official status updates. The rise of hybrid work and advances in collaboration technology have made that approach increasingly obsolete. Employees now come into the office to connect, collaborate, and brainstorm with colleagues rather than to undertake the solo, focused work they can do better at home. The upshot is that many meeting rooms have transformed into fluid, digitized, data-enabled hubs. With modular partitions, movable furniture, and casual seating, they are designed to adapt to whatever task is at hand. As digital nodes, they also bridge the gap between remote and office workers, so remote and in-person participants get a consistent experience regardless of location. That shift is only possible because of the convergence between IT and audio-visual (AV) equipment, explains Yannic Laleeuwe, marketing director for Barco's ClickShare visualization, collaboration, and networking platform. Cameras, microphones, and wireless conferencing, collaboration and presentation tools, such as ClickShare can now connect to enterprise networks. That allows management through centralized cloud-based systems, so IT teams can monitor, update, secure and tune these systems in ways they could not before. "Historically, meeting rooms have sat in a gray zone between facilities management, AV and IT," Laleeuwe points out. "They were physical spaces first with technology added into them over time, so they were rarely managed by IT departments with the same level of telemetry as laptops, servers or network infrastructure." The impact of reactive tech support IT professionals could often tell whether a device was connected to the network, but struggled to see how the room was being used or whether it delivered a reliable user experience. That lack of visibility explains why meeting room tech support has often been reactive, with staff only intervening once something breaks. "A room was assumed to be working until someone complained that a call wouldn't start, the audio was poor, a display failed, or remote participants couldn't follow the conversation," Laleeuwe says. "Without reliable data on usage, performance and failure patterns, IT had limited ability to predict issues, prioritize investments or optimize rooms before users were affected." The situation had knock-on effects at various levels. For employees, faulty technology creates immediate friction: meetings start late, participation becomes difficult, and unsecured personal devices get pressed into service as a fallback. An additional challenge in a hybrid world is that meeting room technology acts as a bridge between remote and in-office colleagues, so when it fails, the meeting fails with it. For IT teams, poorly maintained technology produces operational inefficiency. Rather than working to make collaboration environments more effective, they end up firefighting individual incidents. For the business itself, a lack of activity data makes facilities planning considerably harder. "Some spaces may be over-engineered with technology that's barely used, while others are under-equipped for the way people actually collaborate," Laleeuwe points out. "This leads to wasted investment, inconsistent user experiences, and missed opportunities to design rooms around real behavior rather than just assumptions." The value of telemetry Endpoint monitoring technology, such as ClickShare's XMS Cloud Management Platform, changes that picture. Organizations can measure occupancy patterns and how their meeting rooms are used in practice, track equipment uptime, connection quality, and software and firmware status, and follow adoption levels alongside the volume and type of support incidents raised. The data helps IT professionals judge not only whether a room is operating effectively in a technical sense, but whether it is delivering the experience employees expect. As Laleeuwe explains: "Telemetry changes meeting room management from a reactive discipline into a proactive one. Instead of waiting for users to report problems, IT can identify patterns, spot underperforming rooms, detect device issues, plan maintenance and make investment decisions based on evidence." In other words, meeting rooms can be treated as managed endpoints, with IT monitoring, patching, securing, supporting, and assessing them against clear performance indicators. That matters because meeting rooms are now hubs where business-critical work happens, not just spaces where calls take place. "They influence productivity, employee experience, meeting equity, collaboration culture, and return on workplace investments," Laleeuwe adds. "When IT has better visibility and control, employees get more reliable rooms, IT teams reduce support overhead, and the business can make smarter decisions about workplace design, technology standardization, and future upgrades." IT shapes organization-wide collaboration While the benefits of such technology are clear, the approach requires IT teams to develop a broader range of skills than traditional device support. Endpoint management, networking, security, and lifecycle management all remain essential, but that expertise must now be combined with AV knowledge, an understanding of acoustics, data analysis, workplace experience design, and change management. This mix of skills "changes IT's role", Laleeuwe indicates, because teams are no longer just fixing what has broken. "They're helping shape how collaboration happens across the organization," she explains. "That means interpreting room data, understanding user behavior, working more closely with workplace, HR, facilities and sustainability teams, and influencing standards for how meeting spaces are designed and used." These skills are best developed through cross-functional collaboration and closer partnerships with AV specialists and vendors, Laleeuwe advises. Rather than regarding room analytics as isolated device data, she recommends treating them as part of a broader palette of workplace intelligence. That makes it easier to improve business performance by understanding how physical spaces, digital tools, people, and their daily tasks interact. AI takes meeting rooms to a new level The introduction of AI-driven meeting environments is expected to reshape meeting room experiences further still. Laleeuwe explains: "AI is moving beyond novelty features, such as basic transcription, and becoming part of the operational layer of collaboration. "We are seriously concerned that rising costs and a compressed tourism season will leave small and medium operators without the cash reserves to survive the coming Wet," Tourism Top End chair Chris Chaffe said. Mr Chaffe said while immediate financial support was needed, policy changes were also necessary to tackle ongoing hurdles including the rising cost of flights and better management of Kakadu National Park, which is operated by the Commonwealth in partnership with traditional owners. "We need action before businesses close their doors," Mr Chaffe said. Closures of popular Kakadu attractions such as Twin Falls have been a concern for the NT tourism sector for years. The changes announced last week mean that backpackers will have to enter a ballot if they want to remain in Australia for more than 12 months. The number of second-year visas will be capped at 45,000, while just 5,000 third-year visas will be issued, and in total Australia will welcome about 38,000 fewer second and third-year backpackers than it did in 2026. Tourism Top End executive Samantha Bennett said the changes would have "severe impacts" on the NT's tourism, agriculture and hospitality sectors. events.title: IMF chief urges countries to do more to curb debt and regulate AI
events.summary: The head of the International Monetary Fund says countries both rich and poor must take faster action to cut debt and counter growing inequality as their economies weather a triple whammy from the AI boom and shocks from wars in the Middle East and Ukr... Countries both rich and poor must take faster action to cut debt and counter growing inequality as their economies weather a triple whammy from the artificial intelligence boom, heavy borrowing and shocks from wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, the head of the IMF said Wednesday. “Some very tough political choices stare us in the face,” IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said in a speech in Singapore ahead of autumn IMF-World Bank meetings to be held in Bangkok next week. “My message to the world's economic policymakers next week will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action — you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said. At the meetings in Bangkok, finance ministers and central bank governors of 191 IMF-World Bank member countries will assess the state of the world economy and discuss strategies to support financial stability and sustained growth. So far, the hardest recent hits to global well-being have come from conflicts in the Middle East, Ukraine and elsewhere, Georgieva noted. But excessive debt is a growing burden for wealthy countries such as the U.S., Japan and Germany, as well as low-income countries that must choose between spending on public welfare or repaying onerous loans at a time of high interest rates, she noted. Georgieva pointed to risks associated with the rapid buildup of data center capacity to deliver artificial intelligence, which has helped push stock prices in many places to record highs, supporting strong economic growth despite high energy costs due to the Iran war. Investments in AI are likely to exceed the relative scale of spending on building railroads, electricity grids and telecommunications networks. “Love it, hate it or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy,” she said. A Kelvin wave is impacting the West Coast, but it's less scary than it sounds Iraq devalues its currency as the US war with Iran disrupts oil shipping routes Medical company announces program for 'AI-powered prescriptions' in Utah The AI building boom is underpinning robust corporate earnings as well as higher inflation. But there is a lag between the heavy investments involved and the arrival of AI's benefits, Georgieva said. “Should earnings fall short,” she said, “hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock.” Seven of the top 10 countries for AI-related trade are in the Asia-Pacific region, where the share of global economic activity has risen to 43% from 25% in 1991, the last time the meetings were held in Bangkok. While China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and other countries with strong tech sectors are benefiting from the AI boom, it is bypassing most others, Georgieva said, adding to economic inequality. AI also is raising energy demand, pushing prices for fuel, fertilizer, food and other key commodities still higher. She urged countries to rein in public spending and to raise the cost of borrowing as needed to control inflation, while protecting the most vulnerable members of their societies. Policies are needed to ensure AI is well regulated and to train workers, make labor markets more flexible, facilitate entrepreneurship and improve energy security, Georgieva said.
