events.title: Eurodrama in currency markets raises U.S. dollar's standing
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios The euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar on Monday as political and fiscal worries rattled European markets. Why it matters: Rising borrowing costs and political instability are reviving concerns about strains within the eurozone — and whether the European Central Bank may eventually have to step in. France is grappling with high deficits, rising long-term rates and political stalemate over how to address them, as our colleague Emily Peck noted . Spain's prime minister called a snap election for Nov. 29, which could strengthen Pedro Sánchez's position or open the door to a populist right government. By the numbers: The euro fell below $1.12, its lowest since May 2025 and down about 4% since Sept. 8. Between the lines: France's rising borrowing costs echo the eurozone crisis of the early 2010s, though the ECB now has more tools to contain market stress. What they're saying: In an opinion article Monday in the Financial Times, former ECB board member Lorenzo Bini Smaghi called for the central bank to suspend its quantitative tightening program in light of stress on long-term rates. Compared with the early 2010s, the ECB "is much better equipped to address tensions in financial markets that could endanger the integrity of the single currency," he wrote. "It has bond-buying tools and programmes that address spikes in yields." "However, one aspect that is more difficult to understand for observers and market participants is why, in the current stress, the ECB continues to implement its policy of quantitative tightening," he continues, or shrinking its balance sheet by not replacing government bonds as they mature. "This policy means that a larger share of the net supply of government bonds has to be absorbed by private investors, at a time when long-term rates are already under upward pressure," Bini Smaghi wrote.

events.title: Dennis Hastert, disgraced ex-House speaker, dies at 84
events.summary: Dennis Hastert, the longest-serving Republican House speaker in U.S. history who later admitted to sexually abusing several teenage boys, died Saturday at 84. The big picture: Hastert was the highest-ranking elected official in U.S. history to serve time in federal prison, and Congress still conducts business under an unwritten rule named after him. Driving the news: Hastert died at his home in Plano, Illinois, while under hospice care, the Kendall County Coroner's Office told Axios in an emailed statement. He is survived by his wife, Jean Kahl, and their two sons. Catch up quick: Hastert pleaded guilty to evading banking laws in 2015 after prosecutors investigated him for concealing large cash withdrawals. Court proceedings revealed he paid hush money to cover up his past sexual abuse of boys while working as a teacher and high school wrestling coach. Prosecutors alleged that Hastert molested at least four boys, some as young as 14. He faced no sexual abuse charges due to the statute of limitations. He was sentenced to 15 months in prison and released in 2017 after serving 13 months. Zoom out: While in Congress, Hastert became known for the unwritten Hastert Rule, under which the speaker will only bring a bill to the floor for a vote if a majority of the majority party supports it. Critics say the rule encouraged partisanship by keeping bipartisan bills off the floor if they lack support from most members of the majority party. Early life Hastert was born in Aurora, Kane County, Illinois, on Jan. 2, 1942. He attended Wheaton College and earned a master's degree from Northern Illinois University. He later worked as a high school teacher and athletic coach at Yorkville High School, where the abuse of at least four athletes took place. He left education for politics, winning a seat in the Illinois House of Representatives, where he served from 1980 to 1986. Hastert then won election to the U.S. House, serving from 1987 to 2007. Professional career Hastert has been dubbed the "accidental speaker" after he won the gavel in 1999 as a compromise candidate after Newt Gingrich resigned and the expected replacement, Bob Livingston , withdrew. Hastert led the House during the aftermath of the 9/11 terror attacks and for most of President George W. Bush's administration. After his resignation , he became a highly paid lobbyist until his indictment. The indictment Hastert pleaded guilty in 2015 to one count of illegally structuring cash withdrawals to evade federal reporting requirements. His plea agreement says Hastert paid an unnamed individual $1.7 million between 2010 and 2014 after the person confronted him about "past misconduct" Hastert committed against them decades earlier. Hastert had agreed to pay the individual $3.5 million to resolve the matter. From 2010 to 2012, he regularly withdrew roughly $50,000 in cash every six weeks to make the payments. After bank representatives questioned him about the large withdrawals, Hastert began taking out less than $10,000 at a time to evade federal reporting requirements. He ultimately withdrew $952,000 in those smaller increments. Hastert later stopped making payments before reaching the agreed-upon $3.5 million, prompting the individual to sue him for the remaining money. That lawsuit was ultimately settled out of court. After the indictment Hastert's state pensions from working as a teacher and in the state legislature were forfeited and revoked in the years after his indictment. His federal pension, worth more than $70,000 a year, was still in place. His name was also removed from Wheaton University's Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy in 2015, and his official House Speaker portrait was removed from the Speaker's Lobby. events.title: Trump's economic tightrope messaging of strong economy, high prices
events.summary: President Trump's economic officials acknowledge that a strong economy alone will not persuade Americans that they are better off under this president. Why it matters: The administration is trying to avoid what it sees as a Biden-era mistake: touting strong economic data while Americans are still reeling from a historic run-up in prices to which Trump's policies have contributed. It is a high-wire messaging act just weeks before the midterms: The administration wants to promote strong growth without appearing to dismiss Americans' frustration over the cost of living. "If I say, 'Oh, people are wrong, the economy is great,' then it looks like I'm insensitive. And if I then go into why the economy is great, then it looks like I'm insensitive," top White House economist Kevin Hassett said on CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday. What they're saying: "What we're not going to do is do what the Biden people did and tell the American people how good they had it," Bessent told Axios' Mike Allen on Friday in a wide-ranging interview on "The Axios Show." Bessent said that the economy remains strong despite the recent inflation surge. "Any of the numbers are quite strong, other than headline inflation," which includes energy prices driven up by the Middle East conflict. He predicted the energy shock would "fade away." He acknowledged that Americans are still dealing with the cumulative hit from higher prices: "Sometimes I feel like an emergency room doctor. ... The American people were backed over by the inflation Mack Truck." The Treasury secretary said that wages keeping pace with inflation now isn't enough to make up for the earlier erosion in purchasing power. "Breaking even after what happened during the Biden years is not our goal." Yes, but: The administration still wants credit for the strong economy on paper, even as the headline economic indicators obscure the financial strain Americans still feel. "There is the stated preference and revealed preference," Bessent said, referring to Americans' spending behavior versus their weak sentiment. The other side: "What we did was to say, 'hey, we know you're struggling and we're trying to help with prices, but look at this good GDP or jobs report!' That talked past people," Jared Bernstein, former White House top economist under Biden, told Axios in an email. "What they mostly say is 'You're not struggling! And the economy's booming.' That too talks past people." Bernstein argued that the administration has not only dismissed affordability concerns — Trump called the affordability crisis a "hoax" last year — but worsened them through tariffs, budget cuts and the war. The big picture: The bond market is complicating the administration's affordability push as long-term interest rates rise sharply and mortgage rates top 7%. Bessent has made lower Treasury yields a pillar of the administration's affordability push. A speech he gave last year had one section titled "Treasury Markets as a Barometer for Affordability." Speaking to Axios, Bessent played down the signal from the recent yield surge, pointing out that borrowing costs have climbed around the world. "I would be concerned if we were having some kind of idiosyncratic rise," he said. "It's been a global rise." What to watch: The Treasury secretary recognized the limits of his influence on the bond market after this summer's intervention . "I can't control the bond market," he said. "What I can do is try to get people to slow down and think." Bessent said he does not regret declaring last month that "I am the house now," a reference to his informational advantage over Wall Street. "The house doesn't win every hand. The house plays percentages." Go deeper: Watch the extended Scott Bessent interview on "The Axios Show"

events.title: The Iran war is hitting America's school buses — and kids are paying the price
events.summary: For millions of children, the school day starts on a diesel-powered bus with a driver behind the wheel. Now, school districts are struggling to afford both. Why it matters: The Iran War is sending diesel costs higher just as districts are grappling with a yearslong bus driver shortage — a double whammy that can ripple into missed breakfasts, late classes and fewer school activities. What they're saying: "We're a non-instructional expense for a district," Peter Mannella of the National Association for Pupil Transportation tells Axios. "The inclination is always going to be let's see what we can cut out of transportation costs because we don't want to affect the school library," he says, adding that districts would rather protect spending on teachers, aides, and special education. The big picture: Districts are consolidating routes, cutting trips and squeezing more efficiency out of their fleets. A May survey of 188 school officials found 40% had adjusted routes, 27% enforced anti-idling rules, 25% cut routes, 20% limited optional trips, 14% changed fuel purchasing and 8% made students walk farther to stops. Mannella said those changes result in more parents driving students to school activities or districts moving pickup points farther from students' homes. "It starts to affect kids and families, which you know you'd rather not do," he said. Case in point: Cherry Creek Public Schools outside Denver is short about 40 drivers, transportation director Mark Ingram tells Axios. "It's an all hands on deck thing," he said. "Every morning and afternoon, we're looking at running some routes 10 to 15 minutes late … we just don't have the people to cover the routes." For some students, that can mean missing the school-provided breakfast or arriving late to first period, he said. Ingram's district has about 611 vehicles, including 320 yellow buses, plus vehicles for students with special needs and other district operations. The district budgeted $1.5 million for fuel this year, up $300,000. It now expects to spend roughly $2 million to $2.3 million. Ingram said the district hasn't cut services but is being frugal. Zoom in: The driver shortage isn't just about wages. Nick Martini, a former school bus driver who is now an executive at a Minneapolis-area school bus contractor, said drivers must simultaneously manage children and traffic while meeting extensive training, licensing and safety requirements. Split shifts can keep drivers tied up for 10 to 12 hours while paying for only a fraction of that time, and districts compete with delivery and logistics companies for the same workers with commercial-driver's licenses . Between the lines: Rural districts have even fewer escape routes. Whereas kids in urban and suburban areas can sometimes walk to school, rural children may live miles from school, requiring longer bus routes, while districts struggle to match private-sector driver pay or hire third-party operators. Special-needs transportation can be similarly expensive because curb-to-curb routes may have long gaps between stops. Flashback: The Biden administration offered federal funding to electrify school bus fleets, but some of those programs have since slowed or ended, Association of School Business Officials International's Elleka Yost tells Axios. Electric buses aren't an immediate fix everywhere. Yost pointed to narrow or winding roads, small bridges, extreme temperatures and a lack of trained technicians. The bottom line: Districts will keep adapting, Mannella said. "We are inherently problem solvers," he said. "Transportation is too important to just let us say, 'Well, we're not going to be able to do that anymore.' We'll find a way." Go deeper: School bus tech drives classroom gains

events.title: Euro plummets against US dollar: Has the next financial crisis begun?
events.summary: Euro falls against US dollar: Is a financial crisis looming? The euro has fallen to a 17-month low against the dollar. That will make inflation worse in the EU, where political worries and concern over French debt are already troubling investors. Is a fiscal crisis at hand? The euro hit a 17-month low against the dollar in early trading on Monday, as concerns about eurozone debt, particularly in France, compounded existing investor concerns over global government bond yields and rising oil prices. The euro has been sliding against the dollar for much of 2026, down about 5% since the start of the year. It reached $1.12 (€0.99) on Monday, the lowest level since early 2025. Ricardo Amaro, lead eurozone economist at Oxford Economics, told DW that the general slide can be attributed to a repricing of investor expectations regarding US Federal Reserve policy in terms of higher interest rates in the face of rising global bond yields. However, he said the latest sell-off was prompted in particular by concerns over France, where "investors positioned for higher fiscal risk." The sell-off in French debt gathered pace last week as doubts grow over its long-term viability. French 10-year government bonds — the cost France must pay to borrow money within 10 years of the debt being issued — rose to a 5% yield before easing slightly. France has long had underlying fiscal problems. Since President Emmanuel Macron came to office in May 2017, public spending has climbed while he has brought in deep tax cuts. As a result, the country's national debt has increased by well over €1 trillion ($1.12 trillion). France's debt-to-GDP ratio now stands at almost 118%. It consistently posts unbalanced budgets. Its annual budget deficit is now regularly more than 5%, above the 3.4% rate when Macron came to office. For many investors, wider concerns over low eurozone growth levels and surging energy prices have contributed to a renewed focus on France, with many retreating to perceived safer options, such as German government debt. The difference between French and German government 10-year debt yields reached its highest level since the eurozone debt crisis last week, a closely watched measure of EU financial stability. The resulting pressure on the euro and on other government bond markets, including Italy's, means there are calls for the European Central Bank (ECB) to take action to prevent concern over France turning into panic. Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid said in a note on Monday that at one point last week, the spread between German and French bonds had become so wide that a "mini-panic" was at hand. "The big question is whether this is the start of a new euro sovereign crisis or whether markets have already overshot," he said. Ricardo Amaro said the situation presents a challenge for the ECB because it needs to act without making things worse. "Sounding too hawkish would also add to pressure on France's bond yields, which became an important driver of euro weakness," he added. He expects policymakers to continue monitoring currency developments between the US dollar and the euro, but to stop short of trying to influence the market for now. Uncertainty abounds due to both political and economic pressures. France has been beset by political crises in recent years, where passing annual budgets has become a major test of government stability. Although the 2027 budget has been agreed, with reforms aimed at reducing the deficit, the right-wing National Rally remains well-placed ahead of the 2027 presidential election, in which Marine Le Pen is likely to be the leading candidate. Concerns over French economic policy in the event of Le Pen winning the presidency are spooking investors, similar to how the rise of the far-right AfD in Germany has raised questions over the future direction of the bloc's key economy. Much of the political instability has been driven by voter anger over the high cost of living. In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has just called a snap election after measures to deal with the country's housing crisis were voted down in parliament. Amaro says a weakening euro could compound the underlying problem of inflation . "Sharper euro weakness would reinforce the inflationary shock at a time when inflation is already expected to stay high into 2027," he said. A weaker euro would increase the cost of imported goods , particularly those that are priced in US dollars. Global commodities such as oil and gas are priced in dollars, meaning soaring energy prices would likely rise further, as would US imports. With memories of the sovereign debt crisis that afflicted the EU in the early 2010s still fresh, many observers are beginning to wonder if the moves on French debt could be indicative of a new crisis in the eurozone . Some, such as Geoffrey Yu, a senior strategist with BNY, believe such concerns are misplaced. "Comparisons to 2012 are well off the mark," he said.

events.title: Scoop: Trump's top national security aides meet secretly at Camp David on Iran, Yemen
events.summary: President Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Friday to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, three U.S. officials told Axios. Why it matters: The highly unusual meeting was not announced by the Trump administration. The last time a similar meeting took place was in June 2025, just days before Israel went to war against Iran. The latest: Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed the Camp David meeting in a gaggle with reporters on Monday before heading to Europe. "We constantly are meeting on long-term strategic planning and things of this nature. It is not unusual for us as a team to get together. That was just an opportunity to do it in a setting where there were less distractions," he said. "That is part of the role the National Security Council plays — to bring together different stakeholders to do long-term planning. Six months, nine months, but in many cases five or 10 years down the road. I wouldn't call it routine ... but we had such meetings before," he added. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance chaired the meeting, the officials said. Among the other participants were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. "Things were decided or at least deeply discussed," one of the officials said, referring to the crisis in the Middle East. The White House declined to comment. Driving the news: With negotiations stalled, President Trump is considering resuming major combat operations in Iran. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said on Thursday. At the same time, Trump is being asked to join Saudi Arabia's planned offensive against the Houthis in Yemen. The Saudis are urging the president to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. Trump has been leaning against it, but U.S. officials say he could change his mind. What he's saying: On Friday afternoon, while his advisers were at Camp David, Trump was asked by reporters what his next move on Iran will be. "If I told you, you would have a major story," he said. "But you will see. It is working out very well. Iran is not doing well."

events.title: Budding food scrap pickup services across the US want your coffee grounds and eggshells
events.summary: Composting leftover coffee grounds, eggshells and carrot tops is a way to reduce the amount of food waste that goes into landfills, where it produces the potent greenhouse gas methane DETROIT -- Every Monday, Ricky Blanding drives his Ford Ranger pickup truck around Detroit along a carefully planned route. Blanding hops in and out of the truck, grabbing buckets of food scraps from porches and restaurants, piling those scraps into bins in the truck bed and driving them to a composting site. Blanding is the CEO of Scrap Soils, one of the many budding food waste collection services across the country helping to divert food from landfills and make composting more accessible. It's especially important for those who can't compost at home, who live in cities without municipal curbside pickup or who can't get to a drop-off location. Composting leftover coffee grounds, eggshells, carrot tops and more reduces the amount of food that goes into dumps where it produces the potent greenhouse gas methane. It also ultimately helps create healthy soil for gardeners and urban farmers. Experts say companies like Scrap Soils are an important part of cleaning up the broader food ecosystem. Emily Cassidy, research associate at climate solutions nonprofit Project Drawdown, said composting offers the dual benefits of reducing landfill methane emissions and, once the composting process is complete, returning nutrients to soil. “Because methane has such a big impact on the climate in a short amount of time, the more we can reduce methane, it is like pulling the emergency brake on climate change,” Cassidy said. Beyond mitigating climate change, composting can also improve local food production, she said. “That’s a way that we can see that we’re benefiting the environment, because we’re taking food and then replenishing the ground with those nutrients,” she said. Blanding, a 34-year-old native Detroiter, co-launched Scrap Soils in 2020 to play a local part in solving a statewide food waste problem that mirrors what's happening around the globe . Food waste is a huge source of methane in Michigan landfills, estimates say, and accounts for millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions in the state. In Detroit, more than 70 homes and businesses are signed up for Scrap Soils’ weekly pickups. It's an easier way to compost than making space in one's backyard or driving to a city drop-off site. Home pickups start at $15 per month, while businesses pay $60 per month or more, depending on volume. One of those commercial customers is The Grand Porter restaurant in the Southwest neighborhood of Detroit. “We go through a lot of eggs, so mostly egg scraps, eggshells and the cardboard. We put all of our bread scraps, stale bread scraps, in here,” said Lou Hammer, the restaurant's executive chef, pointing to a large bin with bags of food waste inside. “Some tomato tops, some avocado skins. Probably a few other things in there, too.” “It doesn’t take any extra effort,” she said of the pickup service. “This was going to go in a bag anyway. It’s just going to go in a green bag instead.” After completing his nine-hour, more than 100-mile (160-kilometer) weekly route, Blanding drops off the waste at Scrap Soils' partner, Sanctuary Farms in Detroit. There, everything from apple cores to rotted pumpkins to corn husks is composted into a rich soil additive that's available for purchase. “Food waste has not only become the problem,” Blanding said, “but it’s also the solution to so many issues in climate change.” The company ultimately plans to purchase a larger truck, as well as its own property and equipment for composting. It's fundraising to meet a matching grant through the state. Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Army to execute Fort Hood mass shooter by firing squad Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys That hasn't been without challenges. As Blanding seeks to grow, he's come up against skepticism that a small team with limited resources can make a big impact. Companies like Scrap Soils also face challenges ranging from gaining visibility to getting people to actually sign up and commit. At the same time, emphasizing what can and cannot be composted, and how to do it correctly — such as removing produce stickers before putting a peel in the bucket — is key to its success, too. “The role of a hauler is very important, and education around composting is also very important,” Blanding said. “Being able to continue to get more engagement and more partnership, those things go far in helping us to expand this tiny effort into something that actually can scale,” he added. Despite hurdles, other independent composting programs and companies are expanding. Examples include the Denver Compost Collective , Nashville’s Compost Co. and Compost Now , which operates in Atlanta and the North Carolina cities of Raleigh, Durham and Asheville.

events.title: Fewer Americans are getting help buying groceries from SNAP benefits as states grapple with the program’s cascade of changes
events.summary: As of Oct. 1, 2026, states must pay more to run SNAP. AP Photo/Allison Dinner The number of people enrolled in the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program is falling fast. The program formerly known as food stamps helped roughly 42 million Americans put food on the table in 2025. As of June 2026, the most recent data available, the number of people enrolled in the program in the whole country had declined by almost 13% to 36.4 million . Among those no longer getting benefits are an estimated 1.5 million children . What explains this decline? President Donald Trump says a strong economy has driven down demand for the program. It’s possible that some people have left the program because their incomes rose. But the enrollment decline has a lot to do with the big tax-and-spending package the president signed into law in July 2025 . States are struggling to keep up For example, the law caused some immigrants residing legally in the country, such as refugees and those seeking asylum, to no longer be eligible for SNAP benefits. In addition, more people enrolled in SNAP now may only get up to three months of benefits if they don’t work, engage in training programs or volunteer at least 80 hours a month. These work requirements previously applied only to adults up to the age of 54; that cutoff is rising to 64. Another change is that parents of older children ages 14-17 are now expected to meet these work requirements . All states are phasing in these restrictions, but the number of people getting SNAP benefits is falling much faster in some states than others. That includes Arizona, where enrollment has fallen by almost half , along with Louisiana and Illinois , where it’s down by about one-fifth. And now, states must pay more to run SNAP , which is federally funded but state-administered. In my research on the history of SNAP, I’ve found that changes in the way states run their programs have a big impact on who can get help. States are struggling to adapt to new federal policies. As additional changes roll out, more families may lose access to SNAP. Covering more of the administrative costs As of Oct. 1, 2026, states have to pay 75% of all administrative costs, which include paying staff who manage the enrollment process and maintaining the program’s computer systems. Previously, states paid 50% of those costs. The federal government estimates that states and local governments will pay roughly US$17 billion more in administrative costs over the next five years. In the 2027 fiscal year, which began on Oct. 1, California – with the largest population of any state – will be responsible for paying roughly $670 million more to run the program. Wyoming, with the smallest number of residents, will pay about $3 million more . Costs will be shifted to local governments in nine of the 10 states where SNAP is administered by counties. Looming changes tied to ‘payment error rates’ State agencies and some state legislatures are imposing stricter rules and requiring applicants to provide more paperwork documenting their income, expenses and the number of people in their household. Caseworkers in states such as Arizona have reportedly been overwhelmed with the paperwork. Those seeking help have spent hours trying to get through on phone lines and have faced monthslong delays. States are taking these steps to get ready for another change that will roll out in October 2027. At that point, many states will also have to cover up to 15% of the costs of benefits for the first time since the program began in the 1960s. This cost is much larger than the administrative costs and could be staggering for many states . How much a state pays will be based on its “payment error rate.” These error rates measure how much in benefits are paid above or below what families are actually entitled to based on their household size, income and expenses. It is calculated based on an in-depth review of a small sample of a state’s benefits payments each year. These inaccurate payments are generally a result of mistakes on the part of the applicant or their caseworker – they rarely are the result of fraud. The payment error rate includes benefits paid to ineligible participants. It does not include payments never made to applicants who were eligible for benefits but wrongly denied them or incorrectly dropped from the program. Supporters of SNAP argue that this makes states err on the side of denying benefits. Range of rates States with an error rate less than 6% won’t face new costs for benefits. But only nine states had rates that low in 2025. States with an error rate between 6% and 8% will be responsible for 5% of the costs of their residents’ SNAP benefits. States with an error rate between 8% and 10% will have to cover 10%. States with error rates over 10% will have to cover 15%. There’s a weird twist: If a state has an error rate over 13.32% , it won’t have to pay part of the cost of residents’ SNAP benefits for up to two years as they would have had it been in the 6% to 13.32% range. Farm bill politics could play a role To reduce their error rates, states need to invest in more staff, training, technology and better application and verification procedures. But states had little time to do all that. The states’ share of costs slated to kick in as of October 2027 is based on the error rates in the fiscal year that ended in September 2026. Organizations representing state and local governments and social workers are pushing for an across-the board two-year delay. What’s more, legislation known as the “ farm bill ,” which sets policies for agriculture, conservation and food-related assistance like SNAP, is now ensnared in the dispute. Democrats, whose support is needed to pass the legislation in the Senate, would like to see most of the new SNAP changes repealed. Congress aims to pass a farm bill roughly every five years, but the most recent one, which was finalized in 2018, has expired . Short of rolling back all the SNAP policy changes, many Democrats have refused to vote for the farm bill unless it includes a two-year delay for all states in shouldering part of the cost of SNAP benefits. If the Democratic Party holds a majority in one or both chambers of Congress after the 2026 midterm elections, their leverage could increase in these negotiations. The Republican Party’s version of the farm bill now pending in the Senate includes a one-year delay in the benefits-funding changes. But it would increase the states’ burden even more than the policy planned for October 2027. That’s a nonstarter for Democrats. What states can do about all this Meanwhile, there are many signs that a large share of the people who have lost their SNAP benefits are struggling to feed their families. More people, for example, are seeking help from food pantries and banks , which fear they will not be able to keep up with growing demand. It’s hard to predict what might happen next. events.title: Why it’s more important than ever to jump-start entrepreneurial careers from the college classroom
events.summary: By teaching entrepreneurship, colleges can better prepare students for a fast-changing job market and technological disruption. Igor Golovniov/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Recent college graduates are facing a job market that’s only getting tougher. Their unemployment rate hit 5.7% , compared to 4.1% for all workers, in June 2026. That may not sound like much, but it’s one of the worst rates in the past 20 years. Meanwhile, roughly 4 in 10 graduates are underemployed, which means they work in jobs that typically don’t require a college degree. That’s the highest rate since the COVID-19 pandemic. As an educator for more than 25 years, I see the growing anxiety every day. In a change from years past, parents are now peppering me with questions: How can their kids leverage their college education in such a fast-changing world? Will they learn skills in school that will soon be antiquated once they graduate? What’s essential to understand is that technology adoption cycles have accelerated at a breathtaking rate over the past few years. While the telephone and television took decades to reach 100 million users, ChatGPT and TikTok attained that threshold in a matter of months. Colleges need to adapt their curricula accordingly. Georgia Tech, where I teach engineering, has focused on pushing entrepreneurship across our campus since 2014. We’re seeing encouraging signs from our follow-ups with graduating students that it’s helping their early careers. I believe one of the best ways to adjust to these changes is to embed entrepreneurial experiences throughout college. Such hands-on learning, in turn, develops versatile, adaptable talent, producing graduates who can pivot across jobs as industries, technologies and opportunities evolve. And this needn’t be confined to business students – young people in all majors can benefit. 3 core lessons The educational value of entrepreneurship isn’t principally that every student will be able to start a company. It’s that entrepreneurial experiences develop the capabilities students need in a rapidly changing economy – and ultimately build more resilient careers. Here are some ways educators can future-proof the college experience, based on what I’ve learned and applied at Georgia Tech. Making adaptability a core skill: Students need to learn how to be nimble . This means recognizing important changes in the landscape, identifying new problems and the opportunities they create, articulating a response and mobilizing the necessary resources. Ultimately, this approach will help students be prepared for the real world. To impart these lessons, I believe colleges should provide hands-on opportunities to help students learn through experience before they enter the workforce. For example, they could encourage students to develop a business venture idea that addresses a newly created opportunity in the marketplace through accelerators, or short-term “boot camps” for young companies to help them grown quickly. One example is Greptile, a startup that came out of the Georgia Tech CREATE-X accelerator . The goal isn’t that a startup will be launched – that depends on several factors coming together – but that the student gains the experience to understand a changing landscape. Understanding customer value: Colleges can also teach students how to think about customer value – namely, why the solution they’re working on matters to the consumers buying it. This isn’t just for business students. All students can gain from learning to think about the customers or clients they will deal with in their careers. In fact, students from 38 majors have participated in the entrepreneurship programs at Georgia Tech . Through on-the-ground experience that requires them to find customers, students can learn about the real-world impact of the products and services they create. When students spend hundreds of hours selling their young startup to the outside world, they learn to understand value at a deep level. Emphasizing fundamentals: Fundamental skills are key because they outlast the technology underpinning the business. In fact, the more quickly specific technologies change, the more important a strong grounding in fundamentals becomes. This means it’s a smarter investment to offer, say, a fundamental course on wireless networking or deep learning concepts over a course that teaches specific wireless technologies or emphasizes the use of a specific model. A strong foundation gives students the tools to adapt to technologies that may not yet exist when they graduate. Students in startup training have to deal with uncertainty, resource constraints and customer interaction, all of which will make them more nimble in their careers. David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images The many paths toward entrepreneurship Another great advantage of entrepreneurial experiences is that they force students to deal with uncertainty, recognize opportunities, work around resource constraints and learn how to create value. But other strategies work as well. A few examples are project-based learning, internships and interdisciplinary capstone classes that let students pursue independent research projects as their final course. That said, entrepreneurial experiences provide an unusually concentrated and effective environment that requires students to solve problems, engage with customers and mobilize resources they don’t directly control – all while getting real-world feedback. More and more universities and colleges understand this point and have ramped up support for entrepreneurial activity for their students, such as Cornell and the University of Washington . At Georgia Tech, we have a playbook that we have developed through our experiences that follows the following principles: Embed entrepreneurship into the curriculum: One simple way for colleges to incorporate entrepreneurial experiences into their coursework is to offer an entrepreneurship minor to all students, regardless of major. This would offer the opportunity to a broader range of students who otherwise might miss out. Build a pathway to business creation: Entrepreneurial education is most effective when it leads to something bigger. To that end, many colleges are now offering a startup accelerator, including MIT , Rice University and the University of Texas . But more is needed: A startup pathway that caters to students at all stages can substantially broaden participation and impact, regardless of whether a business results. At Georgia Tech, we have a learn/make/launch/scale pathway that offers programs and resources for learning about entrepreneurship, building solutions, launching new ventures and eventually scaling them. Offer real venture experience: A successful model combines theoretical learning with hands-on experience. The confidence that students gain through that experience may be at least as important an educational outcome as the viability of the startups they launch.

events.title: The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear
events.summary: AI data centers are driving demand for memory chips, pushing phone makers to raise prices and abandon some of their most affordable models. The world’s cheapest smartphones are disappearing because AI infrastructure is absorbing the components. Prices of existing smartphone models have risen by about 15% globally this year , while newly launched models are roughly 25% more expensive than last year. A global memory chip shortage, driven by demand from AI data centers, is pushing up the cost of making smartphones. Chinese smartphone makers — which have championed affordable, feature-rich devices and account for approximately 60% of all smartphones shipped globally — have “drastically reduced” their entry-level projects this year as memory-chip costs have risen, Ivan Lam, senior analyst at research firm Counterpoint, told Rest of World . They are instead prioritizing more profitable premium devices. The smartphone price increases vary sharply by region: They have risen by 21% in India, 19% across Asia-Pacific, and 18% in the Middle East and Africa. In the U.S., they have gone up by just 5%. The shift could affect more than consumers looking for cheaper phones. For people who have yet to buy their first smartphone, higher prices could make it harder to get online at all — potentially widening the digital divide. The consequences will also reach the U.S. as more essential services move online and the global supply chain for smartphones becomes more expensive. GSMA, the global mobile industry association, had earlier said nearly 800 million more people will use mobile internet by 2030. But it is concerned that rising smartphone costs would affect this projection and widen the gap of digital inequality, Claire Sibthorpe, head of digital inclusion at the group’s nonprofit foundation, told Rest of World . “We live in an increasingly digital world, and the proliferation of technologies such as AI is creating greater digital divides and inequities,” Sibthorpe said. “Stakeholders are increasingly using AI to provide access to important services, but people won’t be able to benefit without access to an internet-enabled phone and the internet.” In 2025, more than one in four smartphones shipped globally cost less than $150 . That market is now shrinking. Chinese phonemakers including Xiaomi i Xiaomi Xiaomi is a Chinese consumer electronics company that leads the country in smartphone manufacturing and sales. READ MORE , Oppo, Vivo, and Huawei i Huawei Huawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions. READ MORE have built their businesses around offering affordable phones with increasingly sophisticated features. But the economics of that strategy are changing. What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300.” Ivan Lam, senior analyst, Counterpoint Chinese companies “would rather reduce investment in products below $150 or $200 and put more resources into higher-margin phones, branding, user experience, and AI,” said Lam. In India, Xiaomi raised the price of a 128GB Redmi 15C from 12,499 rupees ($140) at launch last December to 16,999 rupees ($190) in June, a 36% increase. In Southeast Asia, Oppo’s sub-$100 phone shipments plunged 96%, and Vivo moved its main entry-level model above $100 in most markets, according to research firm Omdia . In Africa, where 81% of smartphones shipped last year cost less than $200, shipments of sub-$100 phones fell 34% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. “What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300,” Lam said, adding that he does not expect costs to return to their pre-2025 levels. The memory-chip shortage is unlikely to ease soon, Ramon Llamas, research director in mobile devices at market research and advisory firm IDC, told Rest of World. “ There are three primary manufacturers of memory, and in late 2025, all of them pivoted the vast majority of their supply towards AI centers instead of consumer electronics,” Llamas said. “That left many companies scrambling for inventory. … Scarcity of memory has driven up prices for memory, and those price increases have been passed on to the consumer.” Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology make up more than 90% of the global memory chip market. These companies have entered several partnerships with U.S. AI giants in recent years. S&P Global has estimated that the capital expenditure of U.S. hyperscalers — Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, and SpaceX — will exceed $1.3 trillion in 2027 , up from a projected $870 billion in 2026 and $470 billion in 2025. Shipments of sub-$100 smartphones are already falling sharply. The 173 million sub-$100 smartphones shipped globally last year are disappearing, with shipments falling almost 60% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to IDC.

events.title: How ProPublica Reporters Became Private School Owners in 24 Hours
events.summary: The only requirement to open a private school in Arkansas is displaying a flag and flagpole, so the reporting team visited the local flag shop in Little Rock. Brian Chilson/Arkansas Times It began as a casual question — and a flicker of curiosity — uttered during a meeting of ProPublica journalists who this year are reporting on publicly funded private schools. We were discussing how, in many states, basically anyone can open a private school wherever they want. No experience, no training, no curriculum required. One of our editors jumped in and asked: What if ProPublica tried to establish a private school? We were intrigued. We are longtime education reporters, not educators. Would that matter? Where, if anywhere, do states draw the line on who is fit to run a school — and in some cases, collect public money to fund their ventures?  We decided that testing the thesis that anyone can open a school would be valuable to our ongoing reporting, particularly at a time when we have found that private schools are growing rapidly across the country — in barns, farms, co-working spaces, people’s homes and parks. These new schools are fueled by taxpayer-funded vouchers and other programs, and our reporting has revealed states have little interest in monitoring them .  We had some inspiration to draw from: In 2015, comedian John Oliver founded a tax-exempt church to show how easy it was for televangelists to avoid paying taxes while soliciting millions of dollars.  Some of us live in Chicago and are well aware of the lore of the Mirage Tavern , a real bar that undercover reporters operated in the 1970s to expose corruption in the city. While that investigation had a substantial impact, and led to a new city oversight agency, it also drew criticism for its deceptive practices.   We drew lessons from that reporting and set some ground rules at the start of our experiment. To be clear, we had no intention of operating schools. We won’t enroll any students.  Most importantly, it would be critical for us to be transparent about who we were in our applications, using our newsroom phone numbers and email addresses. In one state, we even disclosed that we were “journalists exploring opening a microschool.” We also decided we would stop the experiment if it would require doing something illegal or using public resources for our own benefit. Help ProPublica Report on Education Have you had trouble finding a school or using a voucher-style program? Do you have concerns about schools — public or private — in your area? Help us understand how families across the country are navigating their school options. Get in Touch Here’s how we went about the experiment in Arkansas, West Virginia and North Carolina:  First, we partnered with newsrooms in the three states — the Arkansas Times , Mountain State Spotlight in West Virginia and The Assembly in North Carolina — and pursued creating the schools together. No one knows their states better than reporters who live there, so we wanted to work with the experts. Plus, the school applications required local addresses and we reasoned that newsroom addresses, which state officials could easily look up, would be extra transparent.  Then, we came up with names for the schools. We aimed to call them Curiosity Academies to reflect our curiosity as journalists. We succeeded with the ProPublica-Arkansas Times Curiosity Academy and ProPublica-Mountain State Spotlight Curiosity Academy. A word-count limit required us to scrap curiosity for our school in North Carolina. We simply called it the ProPublica-Assembly Academy.   Next, we filed paperwork with each state. That turned out to be easier than working through the legal and ethical questions with our editors, our legal team and our standards editor to design our experiment in the first place.  In Arkansas, we didn’t need permission from the state Education Department, which does not regulate private schools. All it took was filling out a form on the Arkansas secretary of state website, $45 and an American flag to be recognized as a private school business (yes, Arkansas requires all schools to have an American flag — but only public schools also are required to have the Arkansas flag). The secretary of state’s office even emailed us a certificate. The official certificate acknowledging our school Secretary of State/State of Arkansas But when it came to applying for our private school to become eligible for public funds, a process that does add some guardrails, we didn’t think we could do it. In Arkansas, private schools participating in the voucher-like program have to be accredited or working toward it, which often requires creating curriculum and school handbooks. That seemed like a step too far since we weren’t actually opening schools.  However, we discovered that Arkansas allows a subset of schools called microschools to use public money with fewer requirements. So, we decided to apply for public funds as a microschool. That process also took only about 10 minutes. We didn’t need to provide our credentials or a background check, prove our fiscal stability or assure that the newsroom was a safe place for students. (If approved, we would not take the next step and register to receive public money.) Want Your Own ProPublica Academy Merch? Visit Our Store A state employee who reviewed our application, which we submitted in early September, said we missed the deadline for this school year but could apply for next school year. He also suggested another way we could tap into public money. Kaelin Clay, the Arkansas Department of Education spokesperson, said the agency reviews applications to the voucher-like program to determine if the schools meet state requirements. She said microschool families have the “freedom to choose” where and how their children learn. In West Virginia, we spent little time handwriting the required information on notebook paper and submitting it to the state Education Department. We eventually established our school as a microschool after a state employee shared that, unlike the regulations for private schools, we would not need an inspection.  We did need proof of at least a high school diploma, and we shared one of our real college transcripts from the late 1990s with the local school district, which then notified the state of our new school. (We couldn’t find the high school transcript; does anyone keep them?)  In an official statement, a spokesperson for West Virginia’s Department of Education said it “does not approve or deny the operation of microschools for any reason, including the qualifications of the owner/operator.” State law includes no mechanism for oversight of microschools. events.title: A Trump-sized shadow looms over the Supreme Court's new term
events.summary: The Supreme Court 's next chapter begins Monday, with the justices set to decide key questions involving President Trump's immigration agenda, climate -change litigation and gun control in their new term. The big picture: But one of the most closely watched fights may be on Truth Social, rather than the docket, as an increasingly agitated Trump chastises the high court he helped shape. The executive and judicial branches are set for another round in the white-columned ring with a president who moves at breakneck speed . State of play: The court recently agreed to hear two major immigration cases, one over mandatory detention for certain immigrants and another over deporting immigrants to third countries where they lack ties. On the latter, the high court allowed the administration to restart its fast-tracked third-country deportations late last month while it considers the underlying legal questions in December. The court agreed Thursday to take up the detention case, setting the stage to test the Trump administration's legal interpretation that noncitizens who entered the country illegally, but have been living in the U.S., are to be held without bond. While federal appeals courts have been divided on the issue, a vast majority — nine of the 11 — have rejected the Trump administration's interpretation. Flashback: While the Supreme Court shot down Trump's attempt to undermine birthright citizenship last term, it handed him a number of immigration wins and green-lit policies on its shadow docket. Those victories for Trump allowed the administration to end temporary protected status , enforce stricter asylum rules and use a revamped tool to check voters' citizenship . Zoom out: Before those cases come to the bench, the court will hear arguments Monday in a key climate case that could determine the fate of state-court lawsuits nationwide seeking climate damages from oil giants, Axios' Ben Geman reports. The court also added two other cases to its lineup Thursday, on top of the mandatory detention debate: One is about a federal law protecting land use by religious groups brought by a missionary organization, and the other is about military benefits in divorce settlement agreements. Later this year, the court will weigh the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style weapons and consider whether Arizona can mandate proof of citizenship for people registering to vote. More disputes over other Trump policies are sure to reach the court this term. Friction point: Though the high court has inflated executive power and gave the president a number of summer shadow docket wins, it also checked some of his most audacious actions last term. He didn't like that. After the justices blocked the administration's pre-midterm attempt to rewrite mail-in voting rules, the president raged against his own Supreme Court picks. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves," he wrote on Truth Social. In a recent interview with Time, the president said he regretted nominating them, saying, "I gave them the chance of a lifetime, and it's unfortunate what they did." events.title: A Prediction Market About the Past? Sure, Why Not!
events.summary: Would you put money on whether Covid-19 originated from a lab ? How about whether some of the footage from the Apollo 11 moon landing was actually filmed on Earth? Verifact Markets, a new startup that bills itself as a “prediction market for disputed facts,” is betting that people will be eager to weigh in on questions like these. The company’s premise is so quirky it sounds like something a couple of philosophy and economics majors dreamed after too many bong rips in their dorm room: Instead of wagering on the future, why not trade on stuff that already happened? When Verifact Markets launched on Friday, some of the initial topics traders could take a position on included whether Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide and whether insurance behemoth State Farm “intentionally delayed” claims related to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires . The featured market during beta testing was, indeed, about the origins of Covid-19. (As of writing, the market is still open, with “true” priced at 76 cents and “false” at 32; the majority of participants had put money on the pandemic beginning at Wuhan Institute of Virology.) Verifact Markets is being funded and incubated by Positron Capital Management, the family office of tech investor Peter Wokwicz. He envisions the startup as a way to settle debates over hot-button issues like the amount of energy consumed by AI data centers. “I’m excited, because nobody’s done this before,” Wokwicz says. “We’re not going to shy away from controversial markets.” In a regular prediction market , participants buy financial instruments known as event contracts, which are pegged to whether a specific event will take place in the future. Topics range from which team will win the Super Bowl to what the price of bitcoin will be in 15 minutes to whether the US and Iran will reach a nuclear deal. Someone who buys a “yes” contract on Polymarket that the Bears will start Case Keenum next week will make money if that happens. Similarly, someone who bets “no” on Kalshi that it will rain in Miami tomorrow will lose money if there’s a downpour. Each prediction market has its own rules about how it resolves events, and sometimes things can get messy, like when Polymarket bettors tussled over whether Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky actually wore a suit , or when Kalshi traders revolted over how the platform settled a market on whether Iran’s supreme leader would leave power. Verifact Markets’ setup is even messier. That’s by design, since the platform focuses specifically on scenarios where people disagree on what took place. It lists markets for past events that it considers “disputed” and lets its customers wager “true” or “false” on whether they really happened. People can also submit “evidence” for or against their position, and the company plans to offer rewards for credible documentation that helps resolve markets. If Verifact Markets determines that there’s enough evidence to make a call, it does so. If it still can’t tell, the company will “expire” a market and pay out users based on its calculation of the odds at the time. According to Verifact Markets chief executive and cofounder Rodrigo Aquino, the markets themselves won’t determine whether something is true or false. That means even if all of the customers in a given market voted “true,” that won’t necessarily make it so. Trading prices will be factored in alongside other evidence and documentation that is submitted to the company by users. It is also planning to launch its own research system, which Aquino describes as “patent pending.” When I ask Aquino how the system works, he keeps the answer impressively vague: “We are analyzing, multi-dimensionally, a multitude of data points,” he says, noting that the process is “very mathematical, very quantitative” and also “very secretive.” When I point out that credibly determining how the Covid pandemic started would be a massive news story, resolving a mystery that has eluded scientists for years, Aquino remains upbeat. “It’s doable,” he says. Verifact says that it is currently in talks with market makers about providing liquidity. Right now, the project is so small that it is being bootstrapped by Positron Capital Management. There are a number of ongoing lawsuits in the US over whether prediction markets should be considered financial instruments or gambling, but it’s hard to discern how Verifact would factor into that debate because of its rather odd business model. For the time being, the company is only offering its markets to people outside of the United States as it looks for the most viable legal path forward domestically, as it is not a licensed exchange in the US. But Wokwicz claims he purchased a regulated financial exchange in the last year and intends to roll Verifact into it when he can.

events.title: Strong data. Bad vibes. Voters are judging Trump's economy by prices.
events.summary: President Trump's economic data keeps getting stronger. His economic polling keeps getting worse by the day. Why it matters: The midterms are less than a month away, and the administration is circling the drain on voters' No. 1 issue. It may be too late to change that, but it's also not clear anyone has much of a plan to try. What they're saying: "If I say 'oh, people are wrong, the economy is great,' then it looks like I'm insensitive. And if I then go into why the economy is great, then it looks like I'm insensitive," National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett said Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union." "It's true that the polls, which have gotten the president's success wrong every time, have been saying that people are looking a little bit depressed about the economy. But if you look at their actions, the actions speak way louder than words," Hassett added, citing spending and default data. The big picture: There is ample evidence the economy is, statistically speaking, relatively strong. 💰 Economic growth is solid and accelerating. 💪 The labor market is relatively stable . 💵 The K-shaped economy is ending as lower-end wages rise. 🛍️ Public and private data say consumers are spending more than ever. Yes, but: People feel lousy. ☹️ The Conference Board's consumer confidence index is at a 12-year low. 🐘 Republican sentiment in particular is eroding at its fastest rate since the Great Financial Crisis, per University of Michigan data. 🪫 38% of voters told the latest CBS News poll their personal finances are fairly or very bad — a reflection, perhaps, of the fact that inflation has outpaced wage growth for months now. (When respondents were asked what they think about when they rate the economy, 91% said "prices.") 👎 73% disapprove of President Trump's handling of the economy, per the latest AP-NORC survey, the lowest rating he — or President Biden — ever had. (69% say Trump's handling of cost-of-living issues has been worse than they expected in his second term.) Friction point: When voters go to the polls, they don't bring the latest release from the Bureau of Economic Analysis with them. They bring their feelings, and those are very bad. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told " The Axios Show " the administration wasn't going to repeat the Biden-era mistake of telling people how to feel. But Trump himself said last week that Republicans weren't doing a good enough job of messaging . The intrigue: So far, Trump's strategy seems to be the rich-uncle theory, which doesn't appear to be paying off with voters. He continues to promise $5,000 checks for every adult citizen if Republicans win the midterms — a $1.3 trillion bombshell that most people don't believe he'll ever pay. On Saturday, he promised seniors $2 billion in Medicare rebates , a big number that works out to about two weeks' worth of premium payments. Between the lines: Some of the tension comes from the nature of the economic boom, an AI-fueled bonanza that nonetheless appears to be leaving many ordinary Americans behind. It's not a K-shaped economy, says Krishna Guha, head of economics at Evercore ISI, but a "gator economy" — as in an alligator's mouth, where the bottom stays flat and the top is pointing to the sky poised to chomp. The bottom line: There's good reason to think the economy's not that bad. There's even better reason to think voters don't care. Emily Peck contributed reporting.

events.title: Latino men swung hard to Trump in 2024. Now they're swinging back
events.summary: Latino voters, whose dramatic shift toward President Trump helped power his 2024 victory, are moving sharply back toward Democrats ahead of the midterms, two new national polls show. Why it matters: Republicans built pieces of their 2026 strategy, including newly drawn House districts in Texas and Florida, around the assumption that Trump's historic Latino gains would endure. A reversal is complicating that bet in key races. Trump's breakthrough with Latino men was among the clearest signs of a changing GOP coalition in 2024. Two years later, those gains look far less durable, though Democrats haven't recovered all the ground they lost in the last decade. The latest: A new NBC News/Telemundo poll found Latino voters preferred Democratic control of Congress 59%–35% — a 24-point advantage, double the margin the same poll found in 2024. A new CBS News/YouGov poll tells the same story: Hispanic likely voters favor Democratic House candidates 60%–39%. Zoom in: Latino men have undergone a particularly strong political whiplash. Hillary Clinton won Latino men by 31 points in 2016, according to the Edison National Election Pool exit poll , and Biden won them by 23 points in 2020. But in 2024, Trump won them by 10 points. NBC now finds Latino men preferring Democratic congressional control 53%–39%. Stunning stat: About one in seven Latino voters who say they backed Trump in 2024 now want Democrats to take control of Congress. A majority of Latino voters say their congressional vote will be a signal against Trump. Driving the shift: The economic squeeze felt by Latino voters hasn't changed much, but who they're blaming has. Nearly two-thirds of Latino voters say their income is falling behind the cost of living in the NBC poll, almost exactly where that number stood in 2024. But 78% disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living. Democrats now hold a 21-point advantage on handling the economy, after Trump held a 4-point edge over Harris in NBC's 2024 poll. Trump's mass-deportation agenda has also sparked backlash: 67% say Trump's enforcement has gone too far. The enforcement campaign has also become personal: 31% say they or someone close now carries ID because of ICE concerns, and 27% know someone detained or deported. Yes, but: Polling voters a month before a midterm isn't the same as measuring who actually turns out. Pew found that Trump's 2024 Hispanic gains were driven largely by changes in who voted that year, not by Biden voters switching to Trump. In the NBC poll, 17% of voters said they or someone close to them was considering not voting in person because of fear of immigration enforcement. Between the lines: Despite all this, Democrats haven't repaired their brand with Latino voters. Their net favorability has actually fallen by one point from 2024, but the GOP's has fallen by 18 points. In 2016, 55% of Latino voters viewed the Democratic Party positively and 24% negatively — a 31-point net positive rating. Today, it's 41% positive and 42% negative. Republicans have still made lasting inroads: Just 16% of Latino voters viewed the GOP positively in 2016, compared with 27% today. But negative views have also risen, from 57% then to 62% now. What we're watching: Both parties are fighting over a large and growing Latino electorate in key races across Arizona, California, Florida and Texas.

events.title: App-makers are having a blast with the iPhone Duo, turning it into a retro Walkman
events.summary: The iPhone Duo isn't even out yet, but developers are already having fun with the new design, creating apps that turn Apple's first foldable smartphone into everything from an accordion to a retro Walkman. Why it matters: Clever apps that couldn't exist on a traditional iPhone could help persuade early adopters to fork over nearly $2,000 for Apple's first foldable. Flashback: It's reminiscent of the early days of the iPhone, when developers turned its giant touchscreen and sensors into virtual versions of familiar objects, such as the lighter apps with flames that flickered and swayed as the phone moved. Zoom in: Among the apps is Duo-Man , a music player that turns the latest iPhone into a portable cassette player modeled on Sony's Walkman. Users open the Duo to choose an album and "insert" a cassette, then close it to start listening. Even the clicks and static are actual recordings from a real Walkman. It's the brainchild of indie app developer Vidit Bhargava, who created it during a four-hour hackathon late last month. "I love the Walkman," he said. "I was just staring at it. I was like, this thing opens exactly like the iPhone Duo. What if your iPhone Duo was your Walkman, and you had to open up the door to change the album, and once you closed it, it would start playing the music?" Bhargava has a particular affinity for the Walkman, having previously altered one of the vintage players to only work when a person is moving. Zoom out: Developers are finding ways to make the fold itself part of the software. The San Francisco hackathon where Duo-Man was born produced 73 submitted Duo projects, ranging from games to music tools and a virtual pop-up book. Accorduon turns the hinge into the bellows of a virtual accordion: The faster you fold and unfold the phone, the louder the instrument plays. Crate , which took first place at the same hackathon where Duo-Man finished second, turns the Duo into a beat machine, where folding controls effects and snapping the phone open triggers a musical drop. Foldtales uses the hinge to create a virtual pop-up book, with castles, trees and other objects rising as the phone opens. Twofold uses the partially folded screen to hide each player's pieces in virtual versions of classic tabletop games. And Delta developer Riley Testut is working on Duo support that could make the foldable iPhone resemble another familiar hinged gadget: Nintendo's dual-screen DS. My thought bubble: Apple is years behind Samsung and Google in releasing a foldable phone. But its large developer ecosystem could help it catch up quick. And the timing could turn out to be fortuitous. Developers are getting a new piece of hardware just as AI coding tools are making it faster and easier to turn a quirky idea into working software. What we're watching: Whether the initial burst of experimentation produces enduring apps — and whether Apple sells enough Duos to reward developers for building custom apps.

events.title: Oklahoma Oil Company Plugs Disposal Well That Posed Threat to City’s Drinking Water
events.summary: The Flying Monkey disposal well in Enid, Oklahoma. Last year, the city asked the state to revoke the Flying Monkey’s permit to operate. September Dawn Bottoms for ProPublica An Oklahoma oil and gas company plugged a well that disposes of oil production’s toxic byproduct after an investigation by The Frontier and ProPublica revealed that regulators had approved the well in violation of state rules meant to protect public groundwater supplies. The disposal well, named the Flying Monkey, injected oil field wastewater underground and sat roughly a quarter-mile from two municipal groundwater supply sites that served the small city of Enid in northwest Oklahoma. Wastewater injection operations are banned within a half-mile of public water wells unless regulators hold a hearing to ensure that this activity will not pollute groundwater. Regulators at the Oklahoma Corporation Commission did not hold a hearing before approving the well in 2018. The city of Enid filed a complaint last year asking the state to revoke the Flying Monkey’s permit to operate. On Sept. 14, with the complaint still active in the agency’s administrative law court, employees of the Flying Monkey’s current owner — BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings LLC — dropped a cast iron plug into the bottom of the well, followed by more than 200 sacks of cement, to permanently seal it off, according to a report the company filed to the corporation commission. A representative of the state was on site to witness the plugging. Eric Huddleston, an attorney representing BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings, which acquired the Flying Monkey in 2020, said the company decided to permanently shut the well after determining it was “underutilized and operationally unnecessary.” A spokesperson for the corporation commission did not respond to requests for comment, including about the agency’s role in the well’s closure. Enid city officials said they did not know the well had been plugged until our reporter informed them. “This decision is, for lack of a better word, thrilling because this is such a vital issue,” said Frank Baker, an Enid city commissioner. “Our water sources have been put in danger, and for this one well to have been plugged, this is the best possible outcome.” In Enid’s 2025 complaint to the state, its lawyers noted that the Flying Monkey’s original operator, Hinkle Oil & Gas, had incorrectly checked a box on its permit application stating that the injection well was not within a half-mile of a public water supply well. “This was demonstrably false,” Enid’s lawyers wrote. Hinkle previously declined to answer questions about the Flying Monkey. Earlier this year, BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings refiled a permit application for the Flying Monkey, where it acknowledged the proximity of the city’s water supply wells. A building containing one of Enid’s groundwater supply wells sits about a quarter-mile from the now-plugged Flying Monkey disposal well. September Dawn Bottoms for ProPublica The Flying Monkey had a checkered operational history. In the last five years, the state has shut down the wastewater disposal well repeatedly after it failed tests of its structural integrity. These failures can indicate a problem that might allow wastewater to escape, potentially threatening drinking water sources. The well had failed five of these tests since 2021. In early July, nine days after the newsrooms’ investigation published, the Flying Monkey’s owner reported another leak in the well’s tubing. The state gave BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings 90 days to fix the leak or to permanently plug the well. Our investigation identified two other wells in Enid that violated the state distance rule between wastewater injection wells and the city’s groundwater supply sites. Both of those wells, which are owned by other companies, remain active. Read More To Protect Its Drinking Water, This City Has to Appeal to the Oil Regulators That Put It at Risk The proximity of wells to drinking water isn’t only an issue in Enid. Across Oklahoma, the news outlets identified at least 114 injection wells that were located within a half-mile of a public water supply well. More than 300,000 Oklahomans live in communities that rely on these water wells, according to our analysis. Baker, the Enid official, told The Frontier and ProPublica that he hopes the corporation commission will begin to plug other injection wells that threaten public water supplies. “I hope and pray this is an example that we’ll start to see replicated across the state in the near future,” he said. In addition to its request to plug the well, the city of Enid has asked the corporation commission to impose stronger regulations on oilfield wastewater disposal near its water supply, including a wider distance buffer between the injection sites and the city’s water wells. This request comes amid a recent uptick in wastewater injection in the Enid area, according to a legal filing made by the city. The commission previously declined to comment on Enid’s complaint because it is an active case. The case will continue to be heard in the agency’s administrative law court later this year.
